pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Preserve inherited validation status and original receipts. Copied bytes and relocation mappings are recorded in merge provenance.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

provenance.receipt_policy: Original project-relative receipt paths and content remain unchanged.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a general auxiliary-information framework, two bias-correction algorithms and improved target-gradient complexity under suitable similarity and noise conditions. V4's concluding applicability caveat was already discussed in v3 Section 5. The added experiments and revised guarantees do not redefine the stated main contributions.

C2.justification: V3 explains acceleration through improvement and saturation regimes in K; v4 emphasizes the residual helper-noise term and the helper work required as the accuracy target tightens, adding an explanation for the 1/K term. V4 also discusses SARAH's additional bias, the absence of a proved similarity benefit for AuxMOM-V0, and the dependence of its advantage over fine-tuning on similarity.

D1.justification: V4 newly discloses MNIST target/helper batch sizes of 256/64, describes the CIFAR CNN and constant-step strategy, and identifies the Mushrooms data source. Appendix A changes the reported code location from an anonymous repository to a named GitHub repository. These are documentation and access-information changes; repository contents were not inspected.

E1.justification: V4 adds actual coreset-training evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 in Section 6.3. Coresets were only a potential application in v3. The earlier quadratic, corrupted-MNIST and Mushrooms coverage remains.

E2.justification: The new coreset study evaluates coreset-only SGDm, labeled Coreset, against AuxMOM. It also includes target-only SGDm controls labeled W/O and AuxMOM - Coreset, distinguished by work budgets. The original naive, fine-tuning and SGDm comparisons remain; SARAH is discussed but not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Figure 2 changes the toy experiment's step size from min(1/2, 1/(delta K)) to 0.5/(1+delta), with fine-tuning switching to 0.5 during target training. The coreset experiments introduce random 20% subsets, matched-total-work and matched-target-work controls, and constant-step CNN training. Newly disclosed MNIST batch sizes do not establish a change to its retained experiments.

E4.justification: V4 adds CIFAR10 sensitivity tests using 5%, 10% and 25% coresets in Figure 9, examining accuracy and convergence speed. Section 6.2 also newly reports similar MNIST results with helper batch sizes 64, 256 and 512. Existing bias, similarity, helper-step, rotation and mislabeling analyses remain, with revised toy curves.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies experimental run counts, seeds, confidence levels or significance tests. Shaded bands already appear in v3's MNIST plots; the additional v4 plots do not introduce a documented change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Figures 7–9 report coreset accuracy comparisons and size-dependent convergence: AuxMOM largely recovers full-data control accuracy, while coreset-only training loses accuracy. Figures 1–2 contain revised curves; under Figure 2's changed step sizes, fine-tuning can outperform AuxMOM at delta=10. Figures 3–6 and the Mushrooms plot, renumbered from Figure 7 to Figure 10, retain their results.

M1.justification: AuxMVR changes from using a previous-snapshot correction during helper steps and refreshing momentum afterward (v3 Algorithm 4) to refreshing momentum first and using it directly during helper steps (v4 Algorithm 5). V4 also introduces AuxMOM-V0, which applies momentum only to the target gradient and separately subtracts a snapshot helper gradient.

P1.justification: The overall section hierarchy is retained. V4 copyedits prose, standardizes AuxMOM terminology, adds experiment subheadings and acknowledgements, and locally reorganizes the rate discussion and AuxMVR proof exposition.

P2.justification: V4 adds the coreset displays in Figures 7–9, redraws the toy plots with changed scales and captions, and redistributes retained figures, including moving the Mushrooms display to Figure 10. It also adds an algorithm box and revises the AuxMVR pseudocode display. These substantially extend the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V4 adds citations to SARAH, pseudo-labeling, LIBSVM and Kiefer–Wolfowitz, together with discussion connecting assumptions and alternative estimators to prior work. The overall positioning remains unchanged. The additional Robbins–Monro bibliography entry duplicates an already cited work.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C substantially revise the convergence analysis. Lemma C.8 now retains a helper-noise contribution, leading to sigma_h squared/K terms absent from v3's bounds. AuxMVR's proof and decentralized bounds are revised, and Corollaries 4.4 and 4.7 give explicit stationarity complexities. Noisy-helper analysis itself already existed in v3 Appendix C.3.

improvement.justification: V4 addresses an important deficiency by carrying the helper-noise contribution omitted in v3 Lemma C.8 into the convergence bounds and complexity discussion. The revised AuxMVR procedure and proof improve consistency, while controlled coreset experiments test a previously only proposed application. These substantial gains outweigh limited caption problems, notably Figure 1 discussing delta=10 despite specifying delta=1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete 30-page versions of the same work, with matching title and authors. Their text, equations, figures, algorithms and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison despite revisions and renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains those empirical studies and adds coreset experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, including coreset-size sensitivity.

before.justification: V3 reports original quadratic optimization experiments, MNIST rotation and label-corruption experiments, and semi-supervised logistic regression on Mushrooms in Section 6.

results.title: Optimization with Access to Auxiliary Information

C1.justification: The headline deformation framework, three classifier families, and resolution-dependent classification message remain. The CNN contribution expands to a proved cross-entropy guarantee, reflected in the introduction's inclusion of Theorem 4.4; v2 explicitly restricted its analysis to 0-1 loss and conjectured this extension.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive discussion of non-invertible CNN deformations, multiclass extensions, and the gap between ideal empirical-risk minimization and practical optimization. It newly discusses independent versus structured background noise, occlusion, and sharp-edge limitations. Experimental interpretations now explain discretization and capacity effects through deformation coverage, while v2's multiple-template interpretation disappears. These are largely explanations and applicability arguments, not new noise or occlusion experiments.

D1.justification: Section 5 and Table 1 document revised CNN specifications, explicitly identify the experimental cross-entropy loss, and describe CIFAR-100 grayscale/black-background preprocessing and ImageNet resizing from 224-by-224 to 64-by-64. Keras/TensorFlow, Adam, and learning rate 0.001 were already documented. The newly specified loss does not establish that v2's experiments used a different loss.

E1.justification: The simulations expand from MNIST templates to FashionMNIST clothing, CIFAR-100 fox/flatfish, and ImageNet cat/dog templates. CNN evaluations newly include random rotations. MNIST 0/4 remains, while the 1/7 task and the scenario representing each digit through multiple handwriting templates disappear. These are changes in simulated domains and deformation scenarios, not full-dataset benchmark evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 8 directly compares image alignment against CNN1-3. V3 Figure 11 compares only CNN1-3, while Figure 9 introduces comparisons between alignment and inverse-mapping variants. The inverse-mapping classifier was already proposed in v2 but was not empirically evaluated there. Thus the evaluated comparator membership and direct comparisons are substantially reorganized.

E3.justification: The CNN experiments change from 2-64 total training images to 64-2048 images per class, and from 100 to 200 test images. Architectures change from small filters and varying depth to one convolutional layer with 10-by-10 filters and varying filter counts and fully connected widths. The new inverse-mapping comparison uses 2-32 total training images, 50 test images, and several discretization grids. Balanced sampling and the misclassification metric remain.

E4.justification: V3 adds an inverse-mapping grid-size sensitivity study in Figure 9. Its architecture analysis jointly varies filter count and fully connected width, replacing v2's depth comparison. V2's multiple-template generalization analysis is removed. These substantially change the questions examined about discretization, capacity, and within-class variation.

E5.justification: V2 reports medians over 30 repetitions; both redesigned studies in v3 report medians over 10 repetitions. Neither version reports empirical confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed specifications. This is a limited change in repeated-run practice, not an introduction of uncertainty quantification.

E6.justification: V2's three direct alignment/CNN result panels are replaced by new inverse-mapping and CNN results. For example, v3 Figure 9(b) reports zero median error for alignment and inverse mapping with grid size 0.4, while Figure 11 shows CNN errors reaching zero at larger training sizes across four tasks. V2's multiple-template results disappear. Changed architectures, deformations, and sample sizes prevent interpreting the new CNN errors as same-setting improvements.

M1.justification: Section 4 introduces alpha-dependent block weight sharing in convolutional filters and restricts network parameters to [-1,1]. It also adds a cross-entropy empirical-risk minimizer with clipped probability outputs, beyond v2's analyzed 0-1 procedure. The stated 0-1 objective is corrected from v2 Equation (27) to v3 Equation (31). These change the model and training definitions.

P1.justification: The numerical narrative is extensively rewritten and divided into Sections 5.1 and 5.2. A standalone literature overview becomes Section 6, with the conclusion moved to Section 7. Expanded explanations and substantial paragraph revisions in Sections 3-4 and the appendices, alongside widespread copyediting, significantly reorganize the exposition.

P2.justification: The compact three-panel experimental figure in v2 is replaced by larger two-panel and four-panel displays with different axes, legends, and captions. V3 adds an architecture table, support-separation and filter-block diagrams, new deformation examples, and Appendix C's image gallery. Existing cat, CNN, and lower-bound illustrations are largely retained under new numbering and placement.

R1.justification: The new Section 6 substantially develops positioning relative to functional registration, shape analysis, Fisher-Rao representations, and scattering methods. Section 4.2 adds comparisons with generalization-bound and optimization literature. New citations include Kneip and Ramsay, Tang and Müller, Long and Sedghi, and NTK/mean-field work; some earlier citations, including Deng and Shi et al., disappear.

T1.justification: V3 revises inverse-mapping separation to cover compositions with inverse transformations, adds a Jacobian lower bound and enlarged covering domain, and rebuilds Appendix A.1 around these conditions. It adds a support-based separation lemma and revises the nonidentifiability construction and normalized lower bound in Theorem 3.8. CNN approximation and VC bounds become alpha-dependent. Theorem 4.4 and new Appendix B arguments establish a cross-entropy guarantee that v2 only conjectured.

improvement.justification: V3 corrects the stated 0-1 risk definition and addresses important gaps in the inverse-mapping argument through revised separation conditions, assumptions, and Appendix A proofs. Theorem 4.4 and Appendix B replace a conjectured cross-entropy extension with a developed guarantee, substantially strengthening the paper's theoretical contribution. New discretization experiments and broader controlled simulations add useful support. These gains outweigh the loss of v2's direct alignment/CNN and multiple-template comparisons, although the redesigned experiments do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same deformation-based image-classification work. The text, equations, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including Appendices A-B in v2 and A-C in v3.

after.justification: Sections 5.1-5.2 and Figures 9 and 11 report original inverse-mapping, alignment, and CNN experiments using deformed templates from four image datasets.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figure 8 report original simulation results comparing image alignment and three CNNs on randomly deformed MNIST templates.

results.title: A novel statistical approach to analyze image classification

C1.justification: V3 extends the multi-agent speedup contribution from i.i.d. sampling to Markovian sampling and newly claims optimal linear mixing-time dependence. Its introduction also promotes the claim that slowly mixing Markov chains tolerate more aggressive compression, beyond v2's general robustness message.

C2.justification: V2 leaves projection-free stability and the Markov compression/error tradeoff unresolved. V3 attributes the older multiplicative dependence to cruder projection-based bounds and interprets its additive bound as permitting stronger compression for slowly mixing chains. It also explains when convergence without feedback is guaranteed and qualifies the new multi-agent result as applying to a corrected output requiring a final memory exchange.

D1.justification: V3 Remark 2 supplies concrete instructions for obtaining the guaranteed multi-agent output through a single terminal query of agents' memory vectors. Experimental implementation documentation otherwise remains largely unchanged, without new code access, hardware information or concrete simulation step sizes.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic 100-state MDP policy evaluation with linear features, sign/top-k compression and single-agent/multi-agent configurations. The broader Markovian theory does not establish additional empirical dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 2 retains uncompressed TD, SignTD without error feedback and EF-SignTD. The other comparisons retain k = 50, 25, 10 and M = 1, 10, 20, 40. Newly cited methods are not added as empirical comparators.

E3.justification: Figure 2 extends the reported evaluation horizon from 5,000 to 20,000 iterations. Its stated MDP size, feature count, discount factors and mean-squared-error metric remain unchanged; no further setting changes are documented.

E4.justification: Figure 2 extends the existing error-feedback ablation with later-iteration evidence about convergence and residual error, while retaining the same feedback-versus-no-feedback question. The compression-level and agent-count sensitivity analyses are unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging 30 independent trials for Figure 2. Neither adds seed details, confidence intervals, significance tests or other empirical uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: Figure 2 contains revised numerical trajectories and additional iterations: for example, the gamma = 0.9 initial MSE is approximately 17,000 in v2 versus 9,000 in v3. TD and EF-SignTD still substantially outperform SignTD. Other simulation curves are retained. Undisclosed initialization details prevent interpreting the changed values as a performance gain.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain their update and error-feedback recursions. V3 adds an output adaptation in Remark 2: the server collects agents' memory vectors once to form the corrected iterate covered by its multi-agent Markov guarantee.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the contributions and reorganizes the narrative around Markovian results. Related-work discussions are consolidated in Section 1.2, simpler analyses move to appendices, and a dedicated proof-techniques Section 7 and contents page are added.

P2.justification: Figure 2 switches to logarithmic axes and relocates its legends. V2 Figures 4 and 5 are resized and combined as two panels of v3 Figure 4. Figures 1 and 3 retain their visual content.

R1.justification: V3 substantially revises its positioning around Markovian MARL, contrasting its proof and mixing-time dependence with Khodadadian et al. (2022). It introduces IAG/delayed-gradient antecedents and acknowledges subsequent federated-RL speedup papers, while removing several quantized-optimization references and the DIANA-specific discussion.

T1.justification: V3 adds unprojected Markov EF-TD/nonlinear-SA proofs and a multi-agent Markov speedup proof, with new drift and variance lemmas. The new residual bound has additive mixing-time/compression dependence, under different step-size and transient bounds. Appendix B.1 adds a convergence derivation without error feedback. Earlier mean-path, projected-Markov and multi-agent i.i.d. results survive in Appendices B, C and F; the standalone single-agent i.i.d. proof is dropped.

improvement.justification: Appendices D–E address two central limitations explicitly acknowledged in v2 Sections 7–8: the missing projection-free Markov proof and the restriction of multi-agent speedup theory to i.i.d. sampling. These additions substantially strengthen the theoretical support for the proposed algorithms. The new guarantees have stricter step-size/slower transient bounds, and the multi-agent Markov output requires a final memory exchange, but these qualifications do not outweigh the resolution of those important gaps.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EF-TD research work. Their main texts, figures, equations and appendices are readable, allowing reliable comparison despite substantial theoretical and structural revisions.

after.justification: Section 8 and Figures 2–4 report original 100-state MDP simulations, retaining the compression and multi-agent experiments and revising the SignTD comparison.

before.justification: Section 8 and Figures 2–5 report original simulations on a 100-state MDP, including method comparisons, compression sensitivity and multi-agent results.

results.title: Temporal Difference Learning with Compressed Updates: Error-Feedback meets Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: V1 primarily claims continuous-time Wasserstein convergence and leaves full discretized guarantees for future work. V2's introduction explicitly adds discrete-time total-variation convergence as a contribution, broadening the claimed scope while retaining the fixed finite perturbation-time result.

C2.justification: V2 adds the manifold-related limitations of KL/TV guarantees and explains stability, score-learning horizon and complexity implications of its discrete bound. This replaces v1's speculative discussion of ODE discretization advantages while preserving the central explanation for finite T1.

D1.justification: Section 5 supplies an explicit reverse-time grid, discrete update and step-size prescriptions, including h_k = 1/[24L1L2 + (k+1)/16] and a reverse step T1/N1. These make the added variant more precisely specified. Figure 1's training details and code availability remain undocumented.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Gaussian-mixture, two-moons and rescaled Swiss-roll sampling tasks in Figure 1. No additional datasets or test scenarios are reported.

E2.justification: The empirical comparison content is unchanged, with no added or removed evaluated baselines. Section 5.1 introduces comparisons between theoretical bounds rather than new baseline experiments.

E3.justification: Figure 1 retains the fixed-T1, varying-T2 setup and Wasserstein metrics. The new step-size schedules and total-variation analysis concern the added theoretical sampler; no changes to the reported simulations' settings are documented.

E4.justification: The Figure 1 analysis of sensitivity to Langevin duration is retained unchanged. Neither the main text nor the appendices add ablations, robustness experiments or empirical case studies.

E5.justification: Figure 1 retains identical error bars. Neither version supplies their statistical definition, repeated-run counts or seeds, and v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 1 uses the identical embedded image in both PDFs, preserving all curves and error bars. Its accompanying findings are also unchanged; the new convergence rates are theoretical bounds.

M1.justification: The two-stage sampling idea, continuous-time ODE sampler and score truncation remain. Section 5 adds a discrete variant with decaying Langevin step sizes and an exponential-integrator reverse SDE; v1 specified fixed-step correction and discussed possible ODE solvers.

P1.justification: The standalone proof-ideas section becomes Section 4.1, and the revised discretization treatment gains comparison and proof subsections. The introduction, section titles and bibliography presentation are edited, but most retained exposition and appendix text remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with additional labels and a clipping illustration, enlarged and moved from a text-wrapped inset to a centered display. Figure 1 is unchanged apart from placement. No figures or tables are added or removed.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive positioning against concurrent probability-flow ODE, stochastic-localization and finite-Fisher-information research. Section 5.1 adds a detailed theoretical comparison with Chen, Lee and Lu. Seven works are newly cited, while the Kloeden–Platen numerical-SDE reference is removed.

T1.justification: V1 Proposition 6.1 bounded only fixed-step correction. V2 adds the full discrete-sampler TV bound in Theorem 5.1, the decaying-step KL bound in Proposition 5.5, complexity guarantees and proofs in Section 5.2 and Appendix D. Theorems 4.1–4.2 and their core proofs remain. Equations 3.3 and 3.5 also correct the reverse-process coefficients.

improvement.justification: V1 left full discretized convergence largely prospective after bounding the corrector alone. V2 supplies a concrete stochastic sampler, an end-to-end TV guarantee and a supporting complexity analysis and proof, substantially strengthening theoretical completeness. The gain applies under stronger smoothness assumptions and does not settle the earlier Wasserstein/ODE discretization question. Lemma D.1 appears to omit an exponential in its score-error term, but Equation 5.3 identifies the intended loss; this local defect does not outweigh the substantive addition.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same paper. The main theorems, figures and Appendices A–C can be matched reliably; v2 adds Appendix D.

after.justification: Figure 1 retains those original simulations, reporting Wasserstein errors as the Langevin running time varies.

before.justification: Figure 1 reports original sampling simulations on an asymmetric Gaussian mixture, two moons and a rescaled Swiss roll.

results.title: Improved Convergence of Score-Based Diffusion Models via Prediction-Correction

C1.justification: Early directional convergence remains a central claim, but convergence near saddle points disappears from the abstract, introduction and conclusion. V2 instead claims rank-one KKT characterizations, with sufficient conditions and matching necessity under additional assumptions, together with a construction using a smaller optimization problem.

C2.justification: V1 explicitly leaves low-rank structures uncharacterized. V2 interprets them through interlayer alignment and polynomial-activation restrictions, while distinguishing characterization from the still-unresolved question of why gradient methods select these points. It adds nonzero-KKT and non-negativity qualifications and discusses automatic differentiation versus Clarke subdifferentials. The ReLU directional-convergence limitation is retained in Appendix D.

D1.justification: New Appendix C.4 documents PyTorch, data generation, initialization screening, projection, stopping rules and minibatch handling for nonsmooth activations. It states that code was submitted with the paper, without providing a code link. Exact learning rates, stopping tolerances and batch sizes for the new studies remain unspecified, and the input-distribution descriptions conflict.

E1.justification: Synthetic teacher-network regression on 100 unit-sphere inputs in R10 remains. V2 adds NCF maximization with independent Gaussian targets, extending coverage to unstructured random-label data. Figure 3 specifies Gaussian inputs while Appendix C.4 specifies unit-sphere inputs, leaving that aspect of the added coverage ambiguous.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing baseline methods against a proposed learner. V2's activation and depth comparisons probe network configurations rather than introduce baseline methods.

E3.justification: The squared-ReLU example changes from a four-homogeneous to a three-homogeneous network, with step size 0.005 to 0.02, initialization scale 0.1 to 0.05, and 99,100 to 50,360 iterations. New KKT experiments introduce projected ascent, positive-NCF initialization screening, alignment-based stopping, rank/non-negativity metrics and an activation/depth grid; nonsmooth cases use stochastic minibatch ascent.

E4.justification: V1 illustrates low-rank behavior through weight-row and singular-value plots and separately examines ReLU training. V2 adds systematic tests of rank-one and non-negativity assumptions across depths and activations (Section 5.3, Tables 1–2), plus a ReLU versus squared-ReLU sparsity comparison. The original singular-value analysis and separate ReLU training trajectory are removed.

E5.justification: V1 presents illustrative trajectories without repeated-run counts. V2 reports maximum rank and non-negativity deviations across 30 random instances for each configuration in Tables 1–2. These are new repeated-instance summaries, without confidence intervals or significance tests; they do not establish increased runs of the original experiments.

E6.justification: V2 replaces the illustrative trajectories and weight results under changed settings and adds quantitative KKT results. For example, three-layer ReLU has maximum kappa 5.93e-9 in Table 1 and maximum rho 4.44e-16 in Table 2. New sparsity findings accompany Figure 3, while v1's separate ReLU-training and singular-value results disappear. These are replaced or added results, not comparable-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Theorems 3–4 add a constructive reduction for obtaining rank-one network KKT points from a smaller optimization problem's KKT point and prescribed layer norms and alignment. This is a limited procedural addition; the original loss-gradient-flow training procedure is retained.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the narrative into separate early-convergence and KKT-characterization sections, combines preliminary material with problem formulation, and moves the nondifferentiability discussion to Appendix D. The introduction and conclusion are substantially recast, accompanying prose is edited, and numbered citations become author-year citations.

P2.justification: V2 redraws Figure 1 for the changed experiment, replaces weight-row and singular-value displays with heatmaps, removes the original Figures 4–5, and adds Tables 1–2. It also adopts different title, heading and page-template formatting. These changes substantially revise the visual presentation beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 adds supporting references on Clarke calculus, nonsmooth stochastic optimization, numerical rank, PyTorch and matrix sensing. It removes several references, including the saddle-dynamics works by Jacot et al. (2021) and Pesme and Flammarion (2023). The principal positioning relative to earlier two-homogeneous convergence work remains; the Kumar–Haupt preprint-to-publication update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: V2 removes the saddle-point assumptions, Theorem 5.3, Lemma 5.4 and their proofs, replacing them with rank-one KKT characterization theorems and supporting derivations. The retained convergence theorem expands from square/logistic losses to losses with locally Lipschitz prediction derivatives. Appendix B corrects inequalities and adds a growth-rate bound repairing the finite-time KKT-limit argument; Appendix E adds projected/adaptive ascent equivalence.

improvement.justification: Appendix B repairs an important gap in the retained theorem's finite-time KKT-limit argument. The new conditional rank-one characterizations and repeated-instance checks also address part of v1's explicitly unresolved structural question, while leaving the selection mechanism open. These gains substantially strengthen rigor and explanatory support, outweighing the loss of the restricted saddle-point extension. Conflicting input descriptions and incomplete experimental settings remain limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same title, authors and central directional-convergence result. The text, equations, figures and complete appendices support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports an original training example and numerical KKT-point studies, including rank-one and non-negativity measurements across 30 random instances in Tables 1–2.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic neural-network training experiments, including loss trajectories, directional alignment, weight structure and singular values in Figures 1–5.

results.title: Early Directional Convergence in Deep Homogeneous Neural Networks for Small Initializations

C1.justification: The unification thesis remains, but the abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the claimed contribution from principally layer-wise linear-UFM theory to ReLU theory, full-network Hessian structure and validation on actual image datasets. V2 additionally claims the first analytic account simultaneously reproducing all the cited low-dimensional spectral phenomena.

C2.justification: V1 leaves the missing mini-bulk and incomplete ReLU correspondence unresolved. V2 attributes the mini-bulk difference to MSE versus CE loss and explains ReLU behavior through nonnegative features and a slowly decaying rank-one perturbation. It adds substantive qualifications concerning ReLU DNC's nonglobal optimality, differentiability at zero, depth/regularization assumptions and the UFM's applicability to converged overparameterized networks.

D1.justification: V2 supplies explicit UFM regularization and numerical-threshold details and a substantial real-network recipe: ResNet-20 with four linear layers, feature/head regularization, MNIST subsampling, input standardization, batch size 10,000, and dataset-specific learning-rate schedules and training durations. V1 provides much sparser simulation settings, although its Gaussian-initialization disclosure is no longer stated in v2.

E1.justification: V1's original experiments are confined to UFM simulations. V2 retains that coverage and adds actual handwritten-digit and natural-image classification experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10, substantially broadening empirical coverage beyond unconstrained synthetic features.

E2.justification: Neither version reports a competing-algorithm baseline comparison. Linear/ReLU UFMs and Papyan's decomposition remain subjects of theoretical validation; v2's added real-network experiments do not introduce competing comparison methods.

E3.justification: V1 uses K=3 and L=5, with linear d=60, l=3 and ReLU d=65, l=4. V2 uses K=4, L=4, d=65, l=3 for both. It adds ReLU parameter thresholding at 10^-6, changes the derivative convention, introduces orthogonality and effective-rank measurements, and adds real-network evaluation protocols in Appendix G.2.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of ReLU feature nonnegativity, orthogonal-frame convergence and a decaying rank-one perturbation, plus real-network singular-vector alignment and effective-rank analyses. Papyan knockout analyses are retained and extended. V1's gradient-covariance/backpropagation-error spectral experiments and ReLU row-orthogonality tables are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: V2 Figures 6, 16 and 18 introduce averages with one-standard-deviation error bars across class-indexed quantities or outlier values. Appendix G.2 identifies the displayed experiments as individual runs. V1 lacks comparable statistical summaries; the new bars do not establish repeated-run uncertainty or an increase in runs.

E6.justification: V1 Table 1 reports ReLU eigenvector alignments of 0.673 to 0.997 after one million epochs, while Table 2 reports unequal nonzero gradient components. V2 replaces these with trajectories approaching linear-model predictions under revised settings and derivative conventions. It also adds MNIST/CIFAR-10 spectral findings and MNIST effective ranks approaching 10 for weights and 100 for the Hessian. These are revised or new results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The unconstrained-feature framework and linear/ReLU architectures remain. V2 specializes the MSE objective to uniform regularization, adds an analyzed CE-loss formulation in Appendix B, and changes the ReLU derivative convention from strict-positive gates to sigma'(0)=1. These are limited revisions of the analyzed models and derivative procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction, background and conclusion are extensively rewritten. V1's separate model exposition is consolidated into the background, its extended numerical narrative is condensed, and proofs are reorganized into model-specific appendices. Appendix A adds a substantial modeling rationale. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the scientific additions.

P2.justification: V2 removes the two UFM schematics and all four v1 tables, combines alignment measurements into multi-panel figures, and redesigns spectral displays. Weight spectra and knockout figures move into Appendix G, while new real-network plots include shaded variability bands. Figures are integrated throughout the shortened main exposition instead of largely clustering after the experimental text.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands research positioning through Appendix A's justification of UFMs and discussion of newer work on low-rank bias, DNC's nonglobal optimality and correspondence with real architectures. Added Sukenik and Garrod–Keating works directly shape the ReLU and CE analyses, while the introduction broadens connections to flatness, generalization and robustness.

T1.justification: Beyond retaining the layer-wise linear-UFM results, v2 adds full-Hessian results in Theorems 5–6, conditional ReLU extensions and an optimality characterization in Theorems 7–8, and CE spectral analysis in Theorem 9, with proofs in Appendices C, D and F. It also derives explicit spectral scales and weight singular vectors previously unspecified.

improvement.justification: V1's connection from linear UFMs to realistic networks relied heavily on analogy and inconclusive ReLU numerics. V2 substantially strengthens that argument through conditional ReLU/full-Hessian derivations, CE analysis addressing the missing mini-bulk, and documented MNIST/CIFAR-10 validation. Some earlier diagnostics disappear, and the broad claims remain limited by the special ReLU convention, UFM-style regularization and the backpropagation-spectrum mismatch acknowledged in Appendix E.2. Nevertheless, the new theoretical and empirical support materially improves the paper overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UFM-based investigation of low-dimensional neural-network structure. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison; rendered figures and tables resolve information missing from text extraction.

after.justification: V2 reports original UFM simulations and ResNet-20-based classification experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 in Section 5 and Appendix G.

before.justification: V1 reports original gradient-descent simulations of linear and ReLU UFMs, including spectral and gradient-alignment measurements in Section 5 and Appendix G.

results.title: Unifying Low Dimensional Spectra in Deep Learning

C1.justification: The central claims of tall-posterior sampling from individual scores, improved stability, and reduced computation remain. The conclusion narrows the simulation-efficiency contrast from augmented NPE, NLE, and NRE to augmented NPE, refining the scope of that claimed advantage.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly discusses failures on harder benchmark tasks and questions the scalability of the Gaussian approximation. It also distinguishes JRNMM posterior accuracy from concentration when interpreting the new diagnostics. Error accumulation, partial factorization as a remedy, and uniform-prior difficulties were already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: Appendices E, F, and J add evaluation sample counts, diagnostic implementation details, classifier settings, and the selected JRNMM learning rate. V2 also states that the existing repository provides environment guidance and pre-generated data/results. Conversely, the explicit (-3,3) clipping bound is omitted; most network and training details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same Gaussian/GMM toys, SLCP, SIR, Lotka–Volterra, additional Appendix I benchmark tasks, and simplified/full JRNMM. V2 adds measurements and diagnostics within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: V1 Figures 4–5 compare JAC-clip and Langevin variants against GAUSS using JRNMM MMD-to-Dirac. V2 retains only GAUSS in those concentration comparisons, while comparing the samplers through new local accuracy tests. The benchmark, tamed-Langevin, and extension comparator sets otherwise remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds C2ST evaluation across benchmarks and extensions, and introduces a JRNMM local-testing protocol using 10,000 calibration samples and 10,000 posterior samples. Benchmark MMD-to-Dirac evaluation is removed. These substantially expand the evaluation design; the established network training and sampler step budgets remain.

E4.justification: New Appendix J assesses posterior fidelity separately from concentration for both JRNMM variants. V2 also adds C2ST evidence to the existing classifier-free-guidance and partial-factorization analyses, while removing v1 Appendix H.3's benchmark concentration analysis. The toy sensitivity and tamed-Langevin analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V2 introduces explicit hypothesis-testing evidence: JRNMM p-values, a 0.05 significance threshold, null distributions estimated over 100 trials, and mean/std over five classifier-initialization seeds. This is a substantial addition beyond the retained toy-seed and benchmark-parameter summaries, rather than evidence of increased runs for existing experiments.

E6.justification: New C2ST results reveal pronounced failures for multiple-observation Two Moons and raw B-GLM inference. New JRNMM diagnostics report non-rejection for GAUSS and rejection for Langevin in the 4D case when n exceeds 14. Existing MMD curves are also revised, including the partial-factorization panels, and some concentration results are removed. Tables 1–3 retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, covariance estimation, score-network architecture, training objective, and sampling procedures are retained. Classifier-free guidance and partial factorization already appear in v1 Appendix K. The corrected covariance relation and expanded explanations do not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, background, method explanation, experimental narrative, and conclusion receive extensive rewriting. Background subsections are consolidated, the neuroscience discussion is substantially reorganized, and its detailed results move into a dedicated appendix. These changes materially reshape the exposition beyond accommodating new results.

P2.justification: V2 adds C2ST and local-test panels, restructures the JRNMM figures, and relocates the full-model display to Appendix J. Numerous appendix plots are enlarged and separated, training plots are rearranged, and Figure 1 loses its n=64 panel. This is substantial visual reorganization, alongside retained displays such as the toy-result tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds Gloeckler et al. (2024) to position NPSE and Linhart et al. (2023) for local diagnostics, while removing several contextual references, including Aerts, Batzolis, Tarantola, and Vasist. It clarifies factorized NLE/NRE positioning. Bibliographic updates and consolidation of duplicate benchmark references do not constitute additional research changes.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 corrects the covariance–Jacobian relation by including the missing alpha-dependent scaling. V2 removes v1 Appendix D.1's additional Gaussian correction-term derivation and eigenvalue-based positive-definiteness discussion. The central lemmas, their proofs, and Appendix B's general condition remain.

improvement.justification: V1's neuroscience evaluation principally demonstrated concentration around generating parameters without directly assessing posterior fidelity. V2 substantially strengthens this application through local accuracy tests with reported variability and null-based p-values, while C2ST results expose important benchmark failures and motivate clearer applicability limits. Non-rejection does not prove correctness, but the added diagnostic evidence addresses an important validation gap. These gains outweigh the removal of supplementary concentration comparisons and some explanatory detail.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GAUSS/JAC research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds C2ST benchmark evaluations and local posterior-accuracy diagnostics for the neuroscience application.

before.justification: V1 reports original sampling experiments on Gaussian toy models, SBI benchmarks, and the Jansen–Rit neural mass model, with additional robustness and extension experiments in the appendices.

results.title: Diffusion posterior sampling for simulation-based inference in tall data settings

C1.justification: The core claims concerning PAC learnability, capacity bounds and GROD's OOD performance remain. v4 adds explicit architecture-agnostic applicability in its conclusion and incorporates soft synthetic outliers into its abstract-level algorithm claim. The stronger emphasis on theory mainly reorganizes existing contributions.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive qualifications about unavoidable real-world ID/OOD overlap, OOD categories encountered during pretraining, and the limits of guarantees for modern or non-transformer architectures (Section 5; Appendices F.3 and H). It also discusses fairness when comparators receive external outliers and revises the explanation of multiclass performance to include intermittent LDA assistance.

D1.justification: v4 supplies the smoothing coefficient 0.3, GPT-2/Llama learning rates and weight decay, LoRA usage, pretrained-model information and auxiliary-dataset construction details. These extend the documentation; the common training budget, hardware, checkpoint-selection rule and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: The downstream image, semantic-shift, background-shift and Gaussian-mixture coverage remains. v4 adds an auxiliary-outlier training scenario for OE and MIXOE using Tiny ImageNet-597 and ImageNet-800 (Appendix F.3). The additional language-model backbones evaluate retained tasks.

E2.justification: v4 retains the earlier CV comparators and adds OE and MIXOE across all three ID datasets (Tables 1 and 4–6), introducing an evaluated outlier-exposure comparison family. Their computational costs are also compared in Figure 4.

E3.justification: v4 adds GPT-2 small and Llama-3.1-8B evaluation protocols, including CLS/no-CLS controls and LoRA for Llama. CIFAR-100 evaluation changes from PCA-only to an LDA-assisted mode. Appendix F.1 also reports an extension parameter of 0.001 throughout, replacing v2's stated 0.1 for PCA-only experiments.

E4.justification: v4 Figure 6 adds a CIFAR-100 analysis that progressively introduces LDA, initialization, autoregressive smoothing and soft labels, including sensitivity to the smoothing coefficient. Table 8 adds Gaussian and uniform outlier-generation controls. Earlier module ablations, parameter sweeps and Gaussian-mixture analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 6 introduces boxplots showing variability in generation-strategy results, although underlying sample counts and whisker definitions are unspecified. The five-seed Gaussian experiment was already reported in v2 Appendix H and is retained in v4 Figure 1; it does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Reported GROD CIFAR-100 average FPR@95/AUROC changes from 35.20%/91.34% to 22.30%/94.45% (v2 Table 3; v4 Table 5). BERT IMDB-to-Yelp FPR@95 changes from 52.89% to 13.03%. These accompany method and setting revisions. v4 also adds OE/MIXOE, GPT-2, Llama and ablation results; the CIFAR-10 headline results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 assigns synthetic outliers to class K+1 and computes statistics within each batch. v4 introduces Mahalanobis-based soft labels and initialized, autoregressively smoothed centers, covariances and distances. It also revises LDA class selection and filters against all ID classes. These change synthesis, filtering and training targets (Section 6; Appendix E).

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the title, abstract, introduction and conclusion and changes the narrative from algorithm-first to theory-first. Definitions and theoretical results move into Sections 3–4, Gaussian motivation becomes Section 5, and much algorithmic detail and experimental discussion moves to appendices. Author and header information also changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes to a two-column layout. v4 adds a consolidated CV summary table, decoder-model result displays and the generation-strategy boxplots, and expands the timing chart and ablation table. Detailed comparisons move to appendices, while the earlier Gaussian optimization figure moves into the main text.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A substantially expand positioning around auxiliary outliers, covering OE, MIXOE, VOS, OpenGAN, diffusion-based synthesis and soft-label methods. This situates GROD against a broader set of closely related approaches. References supporting GPT-2, Llama, LoRA and architectural applicability are also added.

T1.justification: v4 Section 3 adds an explicit mixture-closure definition for a-priori-unknown distribution families. The principal results and proofs are retained: v2 Theorem 4 becomes Theorem 4.3, while the two cases of v2 Theorem 5 become Theorems 4.5 and 4.6 and are reproduced together in Theorem C.1.

improvement.justification: v2 leaves stable multiclass outlier generation as future work; v4 supplies and ablates stabilization and soft-label components on CIFAR-100. Added simple-generation controls, OE/MIXOE comparisons and decoder-only evaluations substantially strengthen validation. Explicit discussion of pretraining overlap and theoretical applicability improves interpretation. Broad SOTA wording remains insufficiently qualified: GEN-L outperforms GROD on GPT-2 background-shift detection in Table 7(b), but this does not outweigh the substantial evidentiary gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GROD and its transformer OOD learnability framework. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, decoder-only model experiments and generation-strategy ablations in Tables 1–8 and Appendix G.

before.justification: v2 reports original image and text experiments, component ablations, computational measurements and Gaussian-mixture simulations in Tables 2–6 and Appendices G–K.

results.title: How Out-of-Distribution Detection Learning Theory Enhances Transformer: Learnability and Reliability

C1.justification: The principal contribution remains selective momentum updates for forgetting mitigation. v3's introduction adds an explicit no-additional-memory-overhead advantage, while its conclusion narrows the performance claim from surpassing traditional fine-tuning to achieving comparable default fine-tuning performance with less forgetting.

C2.justification: The original proximity and attractor interpretation remains. v3 adds substantive hypotheses about temporal update stability and avoiding second-moment normalization, interprets proxy-subset tuning, and explains the use of IFEval to avoid medical overlap with MMLU. Section 5 newly identifies fixed update fractions and the supervised fine-tuning scope as limitations.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands v1's brief implementation appendix with evaluator metric identifiers, MMLU inference precision, warm-up settings, LoRA configurations, hyperparameter grids, partition and distance calculations, proxy-tuning instructions and training times. These include newly disclosed details, not necessarily changed implementations. Hardware and the stated TRACE training schedule remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 removes dedicated Code-Alpaca fine-tuning and adds PMC-LLaMA medical fine-tuning with PubMedQA, MedMCQA and MedQA evaluation. It also adds IFEval instruction-following tests, RedPajama loss evaluation and an UltraFeedback timing workload. MetaMathQA, TRACE, FLAN/Pile and HumanEval retention evaluations remain.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates LoRA, HMA, CoFiTune with and without soft masking, vanilla soft masking, EWC, Lion and additional MV/GV filtering comparators. TRACE gains EWC and EWC+MoFO but loses the MTL upper bound. Full FT is renamed Default FT; L1/L2 comparisons remain in the Pareto analyses.

E3.justification: The reported MetaMathQA subset changes from 33,000 to 39,500 examples, both described as 10%; retained scores do not establish reruns. Added experiments introduce chat/Gemma configurations, Llama-3-family timing configurations, medical preprocessing, baseline hyperparameter sweeps and proxy-subset tuning protocols (Appendices D–G).

E4.justification: v1 already studies update fractions, random/gradient selection and model proximity. v3 expands these with Pareto tradeoff studies, distance–forgetting correlations, proxy-based fraction selection, MV/GV filtering and update-stability analyses, alternative partitions and efficiency measurements. The original Pythia proximity experiment is retained in Appendix G.1.

E5.justification: v3 adds numerical correlation estimates for distance versus RedPajama loss and MMLU accuracy, reported as 0.97 and -0.79 in Figure 2; v1 provides qualitative proximity comparisons. Neither version reports repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Many original entries remain, including MoFO's 47.7 GSM8K and TRACE OP/BWT of 41.3/-5.4. New results include medical MedQ/general-average scores of 54.3/43.1 and EWC+MoFO OP/BWT of 43.2/-4.4. The retention-sweep peak shifts from 10% in v1 Figure 3 to 15% in v3 Figure 9. Code-Alpaca results and MTL's 50.8 OP are removed.

M1.justification: The central momentum-filtered Adam procedure remains. v3 adds adaptations within LoRA's trainable space, a Lion variant and attention-head partitioning (Appendices F.2, G.4–G.5). Algorithm 1 also omits v1's epsilon denominator term, without establishing a corresponding experimental implementation change.

P1.justification: The introduction, motivation and theoretical narrative are extensively rewritten. Theory becomes a standalone section; related work moves to Appendix A; dataset, implementation and exploratory material are reorganized into specialized appendices. The conclusion gains explicit limitations, alongside terminology and author-list edits.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v3 adds Pareto and distance plots, expands the fraction-sweep display, and pairs several new tables with scatterplots. Retained tables lose accuracy-change subrows, toy landscapes are reorganized, and the original Pythia landscapes move from Figure 2 to Figure 11.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens research positioning through optimization-based and model-averaging approaches, including soft masking, CoFiTune, HMA, FetchSGD and concurrent masking work. It more explicitly positions MoFO as greedy BCD adapted to Adam and adds relevant optimizer, theoretical and dataset references (Appendix A and associated discussions).

T1.justification: v1 proves convergence only for a gradient-descent surrogate. v3 replaces this with full-batch momentum MoFO analysis at O(log(T)/sqrt(T)), specifying momentum constraints and diminishing learning rates. It also introduces an L1-based filtered norm, additional lemmas and a higher-dimensional forgetting-mitigation theorem with proof (Section 3; Appendix B).

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited theoretical coverage and baseline evidence through full-batch momentum analysis, tuned Pareto comparisons, broader evaluations and clearer implementation documentation. These gains outweigh losing Code-Alpaca and MTL comparisons. Reporting weaknesses remain: Appendix F.1 claims a 0.3-point IFEval decline although Table 4 shows 41.4 to 38.6, and Figure 9 has unexplained discrepancies with retained tables.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MoFO. Their complete main texts and appendices, including algorithms, proofs, figures and tables, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds medical evaluations, model and optimizer comparisons, supplementary analyses and measured training times.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction fine-tuning, continual-learning, loss-landscape and ablation results, including Tables 1–5.

results.title: MoFO: Momentum-Filtered Optimizer for Mitigating Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The central claim of a simple RE defense with favorable privacy–utility trade-offs remains. However, v2 makes feature-space mismatch and the distinct roles of Partial Erasure and Random Location central claimed contributions in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The claim of preserving or improving utility in some high-resolution settings already appeared in v1.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes reduced information exposure and localized features producing false-positive reconstructions. v2 develops a different, more detailed account involving mismatch between reconstructed and private-image features, preserved class separation, partial erasure reducing joint-feature exposure, and random locations restoring utility through diversity. It also attributes adaptive-attack failure to optimization fluctuations and discusses inpainting's computational cost. The classification-only and image-domain limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit project/code access address, identifies evaluation architectures and their accuracies in Table A.1, and documents PCA and parameters for new analyses. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments. The existing hardware description and much of the dataset-processing and attack-configuration guidance remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds VGGFace2 evaluation through MIRROR and attacker-aware erasure scenarios in Appendix D.5. CelebA, FaceScrub, Stanford Dogs, FFHQ, and AFHQ Dogs remain represented. The occluded-private-test evaluation from v1 Appendix B.1 disappears. Coverage changes are bounded extensions and removals within the existing image-classification and inversion domains.

E2.justification: The comparison set expands substantially beyond NoDef, MID, and BiDO. v2 evaluates NLS, TL-DMI, and MI-RAD variants RoLSS, SSF, and TTS in corresponding comparisons, and adds actual DP result rows for PPA. CutMix, random cropping, and Gaussian blur are also evaluated against MIDRE. MIRROR and IF-GMI receive reported attack evaluations.

E3.justification: v2 adds high-resolution experiments with maximum erasure 0.8 alongside 0.4, additional model configurations and 160×160 inputs, and distance/FID metrics. The low-resolution user study changes from 150 pairs across 20 identities with two raters and forced choice to 150 identities with three raters and four response options. A 530-identity high-resolution study and controlled erasure/adaptive-attack protocols are also introduced.

E4.justification: v2 adds feature-space analyses, partial-versus-entire and random-versus-fixed erasure controls, alternative augmentations, pixel/multiple-patch masking, aspect-ratio tests, defense combinations, adaptive attacks with loss curves, and inpainting experiments. The original masking-value and area-ratio ablations remain in Appendix D. Conversely, v1's occlusion-likelihood histograms and Grad-CAM false-positive analysis are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report selected low-resolution attack results with ± values and high-resolution results mainly as point estimates. Neither introduces explicit run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Changed uncertainty values belong to results; the additional human ratings change study sampling rather than uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial MIRROR, IF-GMI, baseline-comparison, combination, adaptive-attack, and user-study results. Retained results also change: MID's KedMI attack accuracy is 41.73±4.59 in v1 Table 2 versus 53.33±4.97 in v2 Table B.2. The original user-study counts of 153 versus 147 are replaced by 221 versus 108 under a redesigned protocol, so these are not directly comparable improvements. v1's standalone Stanford Dogs Table 5(a) entries disappear, although Dogs remains in Figure 2.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains random square erasure of every training image, ImageNet-mean filling, and ordinary classification training. v2 additionally implements combinations with BiDO and NLS in Section 4.4 and an inpainting-based replacement for masked pixels in Appendix D.6. These are limited procedural extensions to the retained defense.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten. Analysis becomes a standalone section, high-resolution comparisons take priority, and original low-resolution results, algorithm, metric descriptions, and masking ablations move into reorganized appendices. The author list and publication header also change. This is substantial restructuring beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from three to six panels; feature-space, privacy–utility, masking-strategy, and adaptive-loss plots are added. Figure 2 is redrawn and its setup composition changes. Original accuracy and KNN tables are consolidated, while IF-GMI reconstructions replace the earlier PPA illustration. The user-study interface gains four choices, and the document adopts a different journal layout.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning from a comparison centered on regularization-based MID/BiDO to a broader account of loss-based, transfer-learning, and architectural defenses. NLS, TL-DMI, and MI-RAD receive substantive discussion in the introduction and Appendix G.2. New citations also cover IF-GMI, PPDG-MI, VGGFace2, and inpainting; the author–year citation conversion itself is only presentational.

T1.justification: The underlying MI objective, RE masking construction, and trade-off calculation retain their mathematical meaning. v2's feature notation and named properties support empirical explanations through visualizations and experiments; they do not introduce substantive formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's evidence through broader defense comparisons, controlled tests of the proposed mechanism, adaptive attacks, and experiments validating complementarity that v1 mainly asserted. These address important gaps in the original support for MIDRE. Reporting weaknesses remain: Tables B.11–B.12 reverse the prose's both/none vote labels, and the entire-erasure protocol is described inconsistently. These limit particular findings but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental scrutiny and support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIDRE research despite the changed title. All 19 pages of v1 and 33 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds feature-space analyses, defense combinations, adaptive-attack evaluations, and revised user studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-inversion experiments, masking ablations, qualitative analyses, and an Amazon Mechanical Turk study in Appendix A.2.

results.title: Random Erasing vs. Model Inversion: A Promising Defense or a False Hope?

C1.justification: The exploratory demonstration on three Navier–Stokes models becomes a broadly positioned attribution framework claiming diagnostics beyond residual inspection. New headline contributions include systematic loss-component analysis and recurring differences in initial-condition dependence across five time-dependent PDEs, substantially expanding the abstract, introduction, and conclusion claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's warning that passing an indicator does not establish correctness, v3 interprets temporal symmetry and persistent initial-condition dependence, distinguishes sensitivity from physical causality, and discusses Hessian conditioning and sign cancellation. Appendices C.3–C.4 explicitly qualify monotonicity and show that accurate SOAP solutions can have low indicators, limiting their interpretation as universal accuracy measures.

D1.justification: V3 provides per-PDE configuration tables, Arnoldi settings of 200 iterations and 50 retained eigenvectors with damping 0.001, and CPU, timing, and memory measurement details. However, v2's explicit Hammersley sampling statement and Navier–Stokes test-set counts are omitted. The code-availability statements identify the same repository.

E1.justification: V2 evaluates only steady Navier–Stokes flow around a cylinder. V3 retains that problem and adds five time-dependent problems—Heat, Allen–Cahn, Burgers’, Drift-Diffusion, and Wave—and a steady Poisson problem with a localized source, substantially broadening the represented physics and task requirements.

E2.justification: V3 adds one attribution comparator, Grad-Dot (Charpiat et al., 2019), to the leave-one-out and local fine-tuning validation experiments in Tables 5–6. V2 evaluates no competing attribution method. The PINNACLE, gradient-alignment, and causal-training comparisons in v3 Table 10 are conceptual rather than additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The retained Navier–Stokes setup reports tanh instead of GELU activations, and its stated inflow formula gains a factor of four. New evaluation protocols include relative L2 errors, Spearman correlations, 30 individual point-removal trials, 1000-step L-BFGS fine-tuning, and controlled data-quantity and optimizer sweeps. The inflow revision alone does not establish whether implementation or documentation changed.

E4.justification: V3 adds Hessian-recovery and attribution-fidelity checks, computational scaling studies, continuous data-quantity sweeps, and NNCG/SOAP optimizer analyses. Additional diagnostics test downstream regional influence, Wave symmetry, and Burgers’ shock locality. Conversely, v2's deliberately incorrect-physics Navier–Stokes model is no longer evaluated.

E5.justification: V2 reports averages over test locations without repeated-run uncertainty. V3 specifies ten random seeds and systematically reports means, standard deviations, and shaded uncertainty bands. Appendix B.2 also discloses excluding failed well-trained Allen–Cahn runs, leaving the effective retained count unclear despite ten-seed table captions.

E6.justification: V3 adds PDE-error, temporal-attribution, fidelity, and computational-cost results absent from v2. Tables 5–6 distinguish near-zero retraining correlations from local fine-tuning correlations of 0.08–0.77. Navier–Stokes directionality and regional scores are also revised, but changed model settings, run aggregation, and regional targets prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: V3 adds normalized loss-component contributions, a cancellation score, and temporal diagnostics to the existing point/region influence framework. Influence computation also changes from the NaiveInfluenceFunction specified in v2 to a modified low-rank Arnoldi implementation in v3 Appendix A.2.1. These extend the diagnostic procedure beyond additional explanation.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract, motivation, contribution statements, and conclusion; separates related work and methodology; and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A–C. The Navier–Stokes study moves to the appendix, while a practitioner’s guide and dedicated limitations discussion reshape the narrative. Title and authorship information also change.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text to two columns, introduces a framework schematic and diagnostic overview table, and adds structured validation, configuration, and cost tables. Influence visualizations are redesigned and supplemented with loss-fraction curves and uncertainty bands; Navier–Stokes displays are rearranged and expanded within the appendix.

R1.justification: V3 adds a substantial related-work section and methodological comparisons with training-time diagnostics and alternative attribution approaches. New discussions of influence-function fragility, PBRF validation, efficient influence estimation, and interpretable architectures establish a much more developed research position than v2's brief contextual citations.

T1.justification: The stationary-point lemma and generalized first-order influence derivation already appear in v2 Appendix A.1. V3 refines the Taylor-remainder and finite-addition/removal formulation, adds formal definitions for loss shares, cancellation, and temporal indicators, and supplies computational complexity bounds. These extend the retained mathematical foundation without replacing its central argument.

improvement.justification: V2 offers a narrow demonstration without directly checking influence-estimate fidelity. V3 substantially addresses this deficiency through perturbation validation, uncertainty reporting, and tests across PDEs, data quantities, and optimizers. Reporting failed leave-one-out prediction and accurate-but-low-indicator SOAP cases makes the applicability limits more informative. Although the original incorrect-physics control is lost and Allen–Cahn seed selection remains incompletely quantified, the stronger validation and more qualified interpretation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present PINNfluence and share its influence-function framework and Navier–Stokes study. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained material despite v3's substantial expansion.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A–C report original experiments across seven PDE problems, including attribution validation, data-quantity sweeps, optimizer analyses, and computational measurements.

before.justification: Section 3, Table 1, and Appendix A.3 report original diagnostic scores, predictions, errors, and influence maps for three trained Navier–Stokes PINNs.

results.title: PINNfluence: Interpreting PINNs through Influence Functions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the claimed demonstrated applicability from small-scale SimCLR image classification to ImageNet-pretrained SimCLR and BYOL models and object detection. This broadens the empirical contribution, while the central claim of aligning pre-training and fine-tuning through bilevel optimization remains.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies the duration finding as holding after sufficient pre-training and adds an interpretation of greater stability across runs. It removes v2's Future Work discussion, including uncertainty about larger setups and the requirement for full pre-training-data and pretext-task access. The central information-sharing and feature-alignment explanations remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents BYOL's target decay and prediction-head architecture, replaces and expands the dataset-specific hyperparameter tables for both pretext methods, and adds detection implementation details in Appendix B.6. It also changes the code/model-weight repository pointer. These substantially revise the reproducibility information, without establishing external repository accessibility.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1K replaces STL10U in the main pre-training experiments, although STL10U remains in the duration study. v3 adds VOC07+12 object detection and BYOL pretext training. Downstream classification retains twelve datasets but removes STL10L and FashionMNIST.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates only the SimCLR-pretrained Only FT baseline. v3 adds an evaluated BYOL-pretrained Only FT baseline alongside SimCLR in Tables 1 and 6. BYOL was already cited in v2, but was not an evaluated comparator there.

E3.justification: The main backbone changes from ResNet-18 to ResNet-50, baseline pre-training decreases from 600 to 500 epochs, and the fine-tuning search decreases from 200 to 100 configurations. v2 approximately matches total pretext epochs; v3 instead shares the baseline's 500-epoch checkpoint and adds about eight BiSSL pretext epochs. Detection introduces AP50 evaluation, 50-epoch fine-tuning, batch size 16, and a separate 50-configuration search.

E4.justification: The existing pre-training-duration and latent-feature analyses are revised rather than replaced by new analytical questions. v3 changes the Flowers duration curves and presents updated feature visualizations under its revised main setup. The STL10L and DTD visualization cases from v2's appendix are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten fine-tuning models with different random seeds and report means and standard deviations. Both mark significant results in bold without specifying a significance-testing procedure. v3's discussion of lower variability does not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: The main classification results are replaced under different conditions: CUB200 top-1 scores change from 47.1 versus 45.7 in v2 to 59.2 versus 49.6 for SimCLR in v3, so these are not same-setting gains. v3 adds BYOL results and detection AP50 scores of 60.6 versus 59.6 for SimCLR and 56.7 versus 54.6 for BYOL. The Flowers duration curves also change.

M1.justification: v3 replaces the gamma-weighted downstream loss term with unit weight and removes Algorithm 1's periodic upper-backbone mixing update. Algorithm 2 replaces Hessian-vector averaging over five stored batches with a single-batch calculation. Appendix B.6 additionally adapts the parameter partition for detection by assigning ResNet-50 layers beyond C4 to the pretext head. These change the procedure despite retaining the core bilevel framework.

P1.justification: The title and selected abstract, introduction, experimental, and conclusion passages are rewritten, while the overall section sequence and much explanatory prose remain. Future Work is removed, a generic Impact Statement is added, and the experimental and appendix subsections are adjusted for detection and separate top-5 reporting.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to a two-column layout. The main results table is transposed and grouped by pretext method, with top-5 results moved to Appendix Table 6. The two-panel duration figure becomes separate main-text and appendix figures, detection gains a table, and feature plots and captions are extensively revised.

R1.justification: v3 removes the related-work discussions of Chen et al. (2023) and Somayajula et al. (2023), adds references including Lorraine et al. (2020) and Ren et al. (2015), and prunes future-work citations. Its principal distinction from prior SSL and meta-learning approaches remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The upper-level objective definition and its derivatives in equations (2), (4), and (7) change through removal of gamma weighting. Appendix A.1 otherwise retains the same implicit-gradient derivation and assumptions concerning fixed pretext-head parameters, convexity, and Hessian invertibility; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2 Section 5.1's explicit uncertainty about larger setups and tasks beyond small-scale classification. ImageNet/ResNet-50 experiments with two pretext methods and the detection results materially strengthen support for BiSSL's applicability, with accompanying implementation details. The main comparison now shares starting checkpoints but gives BiSSL additional pretext updates, and the full-data-access limitation is omitted. These qualifications temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gain in empirical support.
