E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. On D100×50, v1 Table 2 reports a 1.33% gap for the proposed solver; v3 Table 1 reports 0.55%, 0.38%, and 0.34% for β = 1, 0.6, and 0.3. M_CNN feasibility changes from 100% to 0% across those later settings. These accompany method and protocol changes, so they are not same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: v3 substantially replaces both phases' rewards with violation-based and objective-dependent terms controlled by β. Transformer/Critic inputs change from objt to objr and objb, training gains a phase1 warm-up, and phase2 search accepts only feasible, nonworsening moves. These change training and inference procedures, beyond the added pseudocode.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, methodology, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces nested background/method subsections and explicit research questions, shortens the conclusion, and redistributes reward explanations, search pseudocode, and generation details into appendices. This is substantial narrative reorganization beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v3 restructures the main results into a wide table with dataset columns and β groups, redesigns the ablation table, and adds a neighborhood-results table. The architecture figure changes its inputs, the reward diagram is revised and moved to Appendix B, and a new two-panel reward plot is added. Headers, typography, and appendix layouts also change.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations supporting rounding, LP theory, local search, and neural optimization, including Cont and Heidari, Shaw, and Son et al., while removing the Zhang et al. 2023 survey. The related-work taxonomy remains, while the novelty statement becomes more specifically framed around full end-to-end RL for integer MILP.

T1.justification: v3 adds Proposition 1 and Appendix A's formal feasible-set proof of objr ≤ objopt ≤ obj′ < objb, extending the interval argument used informally in v1. It also corrects the equilibration-scaling justification from a nonnegative to a positive multiplier. The theoretical addition does not establish convergence or optimality of the solver.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1's validation: local search supplies a direct search control, while bias, neighborhood, and MPNN/Transformer studies test specific design choices. Appendices C and E substantially improve training transparency and reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier ablation discussion, although evaluation remains confined to synthetic integer MILPs and lacks run-level uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-MILP solver. Their complete text, equations, figures, and tables support comparison, including v3 Appendices A–E. v1 has no appendices, and material moved into v3's appendices can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 Section 4 and Tables 1–3 report original solver comparisons, reward-bias and neighborhood experiments, and architectural ablations.

before.justification: v1 Section 4 and Tables 2–3 report original experiments comparing solvers and ablating architectural components on generated MILP instances.

results.title: RL-SPH: Learning to Achieve Feasible Solutions for Integer Linear Programs

C1.justification: V5's conclusion claims theoretically guaranteed feasibility. V7 instead emphasizes theoretical reward–feasibility alignment and empirically observed 100% feasibility. Its introduction also expands the stated contributions to comparisons against seven baselines, cross-problem generalization, distribution shifts, and MIPLIB evaluation, substantially revising the scope and qualification of the central claims.

C2.justification: V7 adds interpretations of baseline failures, reward prioritization, and training efficiency. It discusses poor solution quality on scpk4 and bppc8-02, implications of unseen constraint types, excessive reward bias, and computational bottlenecks at extreme scales. The earlier solver-integration suboptimality caveat is retained, while applicability boundaries and future optimality improvements receive substantial additional treatment.

D1.justification: V7 adds model parameter counts, explicitly lists the 15 diving and six rounding implementations, explains Transformer token construction more fully, and supplies implementation references and training details for the added baselines. The existing hardware, software versions, optimizer settings, principal training budgets, and RL-SPH training times are retained.

E1.justification: The five synthetic problem families are retained. V7 adds cross-problem IS/MVC training and transfer, 17 MIPLIB instances including mixed variable types, BA-to-ER graph distribution transfer, and SC tests at unseen sizes and densities. These substantially broaden the evaluated populations and generalization scenarios.

E2.justification: V7 adds standalone comparisons with DDIM, DiffILO, and PAS, with PAS evaluated on CA and IS, plus Gurobi comparisons in Appendix H.3. Diving and Rounding are merely renamed DHF and RHF with the same constituent families. The earlier SCIP and PAS+SCIP comparison is retained as Table 16.

E3.justification: V7 introduces first-feasible-solution timing, new E2EPH evaluation budgets of 300/300/30 seconds for SC/CA/IS, controlled joint training with MVC resized to 1,500 variables, and 100-second MIPLIB evaluations. It also changes the reported NBI objective-coefficient generator from randint[-10,1] to randint[-10,-1]. This documents a setting revision without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained architecture ablation, v7 tests whether feasibility-aware variable selection accelerates feasibility and whether trajectories satisfy the theoretical reward conditions. It adds presolving ablations, transfer and robustness tests, neighborhood-ratio and movement-magnitude sensitivities, attention and training analyses, and extends the reward-bias comparison from alpha=1,2 to alpha=1,2,5.

E5.justification: V7 replaces several asymmetric, zero-truncated spreads with symmetric reporting, such as IS primal gap 0.14 with +0.59/-0.14 becoming 0.14±0.59. It also removes v5's explicit statement identifying the spreads as NumPy standard deviations. SCIP randomization remains zero; no increase in independent repetitions is documented.

E6.justification: V7 adds extensive timing, comparator, transfer, MIPLIB, and sensitivity results while retaining the original binary benchmark means and SCIP integration results. Newly reported direct IS/MVC transfer fails at 0% feasibility, whereas joint training achieves 100%. Headline averages change from 44×/2.3× to 28.6×/2.6× for primal gap/integral under expanded comparisons, and bias-ablation values are revised; these do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core two-phase actor–critic and Transformer search remains. However, v7 revises phase-one reward gating from nonnegative to strictly positive constraint improvement, corrects bound conditions, and changes Appendix C's training pseudocode to retain the stay flag until Tstay. Appendix I.7 also introduces tested larger action-space variants; naming the architecture ILP-GT alone is not a method change.

P1.justification: The introduction and contributions are extensively rewritten, the architecture receives the ILP-GT name, and the methodology is reorganized. Background and related work move into Appendices D and E, the solver comparison moves to Appendix H, and substantial main-text and appendix discussion sections reshape the narrative around standalone feasibility.

P2.justification: V7 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws explanatory diagrams, expands Table 1 with timing and NBI rows, and adds optimization curves, trajectory plots, attention heatmaps, and training curves. Retained material is also reformatted: the architecture ablation changes table orientation, while solver results and reward illustrations are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands the former related-work section with DDIM, DiffILO, and NeuRewriter, among other additions. It positions RL-SPH relative to solver-independent feasibility methods, neural local rewriting, and LNS, and explains complementary initializer roles. This changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates or relocation.

T1.justification: Appendix A substantially replaces the central proof: v5 infers convergence to zero from monotonicity, whereas v7 introduces a claimed minimum positive increment delta and a finite bound T=ceil(-D0/delta). Appendix I.4 adds a search-complexity derivation. The minimum-increment justification remains incomplete for the generally real-valued coefficients permitted by the formulation.

improvement.justification: V7 substantially addresses v5's limited validation of standalone feasibility through direct comparisons with newer learning methods, empirical checks of reward-condition adherence, and transfer tests that expose failures as well as successes. These strengthen the evidential basis and clarify applicability beyond the original benchmarks. The feasibility claim is also better qualified. The proof's minimum-increment justification remains incomplete, and uncertainty reporting becomes less explicit, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny and disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-SPH research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v7 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, generalization experiments, MIPLIB evaluations, and sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and Appendices H and I.

before.justification: v5 reports original benchmark comparisons, SCIP integration experiments, architecture ablations, and reward-bias experiments in Section 4 and Appendix F.

results.title: RL-SPH: Learning to Achieve Feasible Solutions for Integer Linear Programs

C1.justification: The central automatic-tuning and Gaussian-bound contributions remain. The abstract and conclusion now explicitly claim demonstrated effectiveness on million-dimensional statistical and quantum field models. V2's speculative extension to Bayesian neural networks with minibatching noise is dropped.

C2.justification: V2's brief smaller-step validation advice becomes a detailed diagnostic proposal in Section 8, alongside new discussions of conditioning, tails, and bound failures. Section 6 adds explanations of rapid EEVPD estimation and its difference from acceptance-rate tuning. However, Section 8's statement that long tails do not increase bias overgeneralizes Figure 7, which shows a substantial increase for the heaviest tested Student-t case.

D1.justification: V3 supplies field-model couplings, boundary conditions, observable computations, and NVIDIA A100/AMD EPYC hardware information. Code-access information remains equivalent. Conversely, v2 Appendix D.3's explicit disclosure that NUTS supplies the common diagonal preconditioner is no longer stated clearly; the broader prerun discussion does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: V3 adds interacting scalar phi^4 and U(1) gauge-field sampling tasks, extending evaluation beyond the retained Bayesian and independent-product targets. Appendix C also adds Student-t and generalized-normal target families to examine different tail conditions.

E2.justification: Corresponding retained experiments preserve their comparator sets, including aLMC/MALT, aMCLMC, NUTS, and grid-search uLMC. The new field-theory comparisons use previously evaluated samplers; adjusted HMC, reported for U(1), already appears in v2 Figure 2.

E3.justification: New protocols include controlled physical couplings and Fourier-power errors for phi^4, beta=2 and Polyakov-loop errors for U(1), and 100-dimensional tail sweeps at EEVPD=10^-3 with 50-million-step chains. The retained Bayesian benchmarks keep their error thresholds and EEVPD targets.

E4.justification: Appendix C/Figure 7 adds a systematic investigation of how heavier and lighter tails affect the Gaussian-derived bias bound. Section 6.1 also adds EEVPD autocorrelation and convergence diagnostics. The earlier EEVPD ablation and funnel case study remain, rather than being replaced by these analyses.

E5.justification: V3 specifies that the new 1024^2-dimensional phi^4 experiment uses only two chains because of GPU capacity. The retained benchmarks still use at least 128 chains and 100 bootstrap resamples, with unchanged Table 4 uncertainties. This is new experiment-specific run information, not a reduction in repetitions of an earlier experiment.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and uncertainty tables retain their values. New phi^4 results report 1,344 gradient calls for uMCLMC, 39,240 for aMCLMC, and 133,266 for NUTS. New U(1) results report 198, 15,578, 17,699, and 127,875 for uMCLMC, aMCLMC, adjusted HMC, and NUTS respectively. Figure 7 additionally reports tail-dependent bias, including an exceedance of the Gaussian reference at Student-t nu=3.

M1.justification: The EEVPD-based step-size procedure and Algorithm 1 retain the same updates and weighting scheme, moving from Appendix D.2 to Appendix E. Momentum-length adaptation and diagonal preconditioning were already discussed in v2; their expanded description does not establish a new method component.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and conclusion are rewritten. Tuning gains subsections, experimental setup moves into the main text, limitations become a separate section, and the appendices are substantially reorganized into tuning, model details, further experiments, and reproducibility sections.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column conference main text. V3 adds Figures 5–7, adds tuning-method subheaders to benchmark tables, and relocates the conversion and covariance-result tables to the appendices. Existing tuning and ablation figures are retained as Figures 8–9 within the reorganized layout.

R1.justification: V3 adds field-theory and diagnostic references, including Albergo et al., Kanwar et al., Vierhaus, and Gelman–Rubin. Appendix F.1 newly distinguishes its sequential-chain evaluation from Hoffman–Sountsov's many-short-chains setting. The central positioning as practical automatic tuning of existing unadjusted samplers remains.

T1.justification: The Gaussian bounds, covariance-error lemmas, supporting proofs, and bias–variance derivation remain unchanged after matching renumbered content. Appendices F.2–F.3 add mathematical definitions of the field actions and gauge-invariant observables, including the Polyakov-loop relationship to static potential. No new general bias theorem is established.

improvement.justification: V2's dimensional-scaling evidence chiefly concerned independent-product targets. V3's interacting field-theory evaluations, with physically relevant observables, substantially strengthen evidence for the central practical scalability claim. Tail-sensitivity experiments and concrete bias diagnostics also make applicability easier to assess. These gains outweigh limited weaknesses: the largest phi^4 test has only two chains, and the new blanket interpretation of long-tail behavior is inconsistent with Figure 7.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EEVPD-based tuning work, despite the changed title and format. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds lattice field-theory evaluations, a distribution-tail sensitivity study, and tuning-convergence measurements.

before.justification: V2 reports original sampling experiments, including dimensionality scaling, numerical bias measurements, Bayesian benchmark results, and an EEVPD ablation.

results.title: Practical and Scalable Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Without the Metropolis Test

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add a central claim that SyMerge can merge experts trained from different initializations where tested alternatives fail. The introduction sharpens synergy into representation-level compatibility, and the conclusion adds intrinsic encoder improvement beyond task-specific tuning. The original single-layer and broad benchmark-performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v4 distinguishes structural motivation from directly optimizing cross-task performance, explains encoder improvement and limited corruption spillover, and qualifies synergy using both positive and negative transfer. Individual experts become a reference rather than an upper bound. Limitations now address biased experts and privacy/latency constraints on unlabeled inputs; the new backdoor results still show substantial residual vulnerability.

D1.justification: v4 specifies hard one-hot pseudo-labels, explains on-the-fly versus cached expert predictions, and supplies settings for new experiments. Core training details and the project link remain. However, v3's PyTorch 1.12.1 and RTX 4090/A6000 disclosure, along with direct model-source footnotes, is removed.

E1.justification: v4 retains the original datasets but expands task and scenario coverage: eight GLUE tasks are additionally evaluated as text generation, streaming inputs are tested, and a six-expert backdoor scenario introduces triggered-input evaluation. These extend task requirements and input conditions beyond v3's coverage.

E2.justification: v4 adds LOT Merging to the vision comparison in Table 1, TSV-M and ISO-Merging to the RoBERTa comparison in Table 3, and DARE and DARE+TIES to the new generative comparison. Pretrained reference rows are removed from vision and corruption tables. ISO-Merging matches the earlier ISO-CTS method rather than constituting a new vision baseline.

E3.justification: New protocols include FLAN-T5 Base adaptation with batch size 4 for 1,000 iterations; single-pass streaming adaptation with batch size 1 and immediate evaluation; and adaptation using 1–100% of unlabeled data. v4 also introduces different-initialization, random-expert, backdoor/attack-success-rate, and batch-size-16 resource-profiling settings. The retained main experiments keep their stated hyperparameters.

E4.justification: v4 adds controls testing encoder improvement independently of the adapted classifier, the contribution of confidence filtering, and the cross-task-linearity assumption. It also adds different-initialization and unreliable-expert stress tests, data-scarcity analyses, and broader initialization and learning-rate sensitivity studies. The prediction-discrepancy analysis is retained and moved, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report five-run means and standard deviations in Table 1 and retain Figure 2's correlation, p-value, and 95% confidence interval. The new filtering ablation uses the existing five-run reporting practice; no increased run count or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is established.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores, layer ablations, loss correlations, and cross-task heatmap values are unchanged, apart from removed pretrained result rows. Substantial new results include 79.1% average accuracy for differently initialized experts, an 82.5 average on generative GLUE, and 82.4% with the SyMerge encoder and original zero-shot heads. Additional robustness, filtering, sensitivity, and efficiency results are reported under new conditions.

M1.justification: The joint optimization of merging coefficients and one task-specific layer using expert supervision is retained. For the new different-initialization experiment, Section 4.3 defines task vectors relative to the experts' weight average instead of a common pretrained model, introducing a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, and the empirical-analysis narrative is reordered and reframed. Appendices are reorganized around a new related-work section, with expanded explanations throughout. The reproducibility and LLM-use statements are removed, while acknowledgements and an impact statement are added.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout, extensively resizing and relocating displays. New experimental tables are added, and initialization/learning-rate figures are reorganized and expanded. v4 also corrects the layer-index axis and the loss-correlation caption's unsupported ViT-B/16 listing.

R1.justification: The new related-work appendix substantially broadens positioning around task affinity, positive transfer, synergy embeddings, and forward/backward transfer in continual learning. It explicitly distinguishes SyMerge's post-hoc merging setting from these traditions. New references also support LOT Merging, different pretrained experts, generative evaluation, and backdoor testing; bibliographic updates to retained works are not counted as additions.

T1.justification: v3's Proposition 1 and Appendix C proof become Proposition 3.1 and Appendix D, retaining the cross-task-linearity and output-convexity assumptions and the same Jensen-inequality bounds. v4 clarifies these assumptions and tests linearity empirically, but does not materially revise the formal argument.

improvement.justification: The encoder control, filtering ablation, and empirical linearity checks substantially strengthen evidence about the source of gains and the assumptions motivating SyMerge. New stress tests and resource measurements make its practical strengths and limitations easier to assess, while expanded related work clarifies its contribution. These gains outweigh the loss of software/hardware disclosures, although that omission limits reproducibility of the new timing results. The improvement comes from stronger validation and explanation, not changed headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SyMerge research. All 25 pages of v3 and 29 pages of v4, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds generative-language evaluations, expert-corruption tests, data-scarcity experiments, and additional empirical analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original model-merging experiments on vision, NYUv2 dense prediction, and GLUE tasks, alongside pilot studies, ablations, and robustness analyses.

results.title: SyMerge: From Non-Interference to Synergistic Merging via Single-Layer Adaptation

C1.justification: The abstract removes the restriction that the outperformed conventional mitigation methods involve retraining, modestly broadening its comparison claim. The introduction's six contributions and the conclusion otherwise retain the same claims about training-free mitigation, blind operation, herringbone artifacts, and adaptive attacks.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations of inference-time and memory costs, the performance ceiling imposed by the pretrained reconstruction model, and the requirement for data fidelity when extending the defense. Appendices I–J explain how denoising or purification can disrupt the relationship between aliased inputs and the forward operator; Appendix L interprets mismatched-coil attacks as weaker threats.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-availability statement and repository link, absent from v3. It also documents complex-valued JPEG processing, TV settings, 50-sample randomized smoothing, diffusion purification and fine-tuning parameters, and inpainting training and mask construction. These materially expand reproducibility information, although the code's availability is not verified by the PDFs.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained knee and brain MRI coverage, v4 evaluates short-axis cardiac cine data for 2D and dynamic reconstruction scalability and introduces CelebA natural-image inpainting with 30% pixel sampling in Appendix M. This substantially expands both the represented data and reconstruction tasks.

E2.justification: The existing adversarial-training and SMUG comparisons are retained. Appendix I adds evaluated JPEG compression, TV denoising, and randomized-smoothing defenses in Table 15; Appendix J adds diffusion purification with and without MoDL fine-tuning in Table 16.

E3.justification: v4 adds distinct protocols: diffusion comparisons use 320×320 images and random R=4 masks; cardiac scalability compares individual phases with ten-phase inputs; inpainting uses 1,000 training images, 100 epochs, and 200 test images. Appendix L adds first-epoch model and cross-subject coil-map controls. These supplement the retained original MRI settings.

E4.justification: New analyses measure errors separately on acquired and complementary k-space locations (Appendix E), tune randomized-smoothing noise (Table 14), test suboptimal models and mismatched attack-generation coil maps (Appendix L), and examine computational scalability. The reconstruction-depth ablation already present in v3 Appendix H is retained as v4 Appendix K.

E5.justification: v4 introduces ± reporting for PSNR and SSIM in the diffusion and inpainting comparisons (Tables 16 and 19). The statistic represented by ± is not defined, and repeated-run or seed counts are not supplied. The earlier detection violin plots already reported medians and interquartile ranges.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1 and 2 retain their values, while substantial results are added. Table 15 reports PSNR 35.14 for the proposed defense versus 30.71 for randomized smoothing; the separate diffusion setting reports 30.88 versus 20.14 for fine-tuned purification. Table 19 adds inpainting PSNR 24.05 before mitigation and 30.69 afterward. Runtime, robustness, and population herringbone results are also newly reported; these are additions, not improvements to the original same-setting scores.

M1.justification: The cyclic-consistency objective, reverse-PGD updates in Algorithm 1, blind parameter search, and adaptive-attack formulation are retained. The added dynamic MRI and inpainting evaluations reuse this defense with task-specific reconstruction networks and forward operators, without introducing a new defense component.

P1.justification: The title and publication header change, several passages receive limited editing, and acknowledgements and an Impact Statement are added. The proof and empirical appendices are reordered and new subsections are introduced, but most existing prose, the contribution list, and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Figure 1 is redrawn, and v4 adds a mitigation schematic, a k-space error plot, comparison and inpainting figures, and runtime and additional-results tables. Many original displays are retained under new numbering.

R1.justification: v4 adds literature on input-transformation defenses, randomized smoothing, diffusion methods, and the added applications. Appendices I–J substantially expand positioning relative to prior defenses, particularly Alkhouri's previously cited purification work, discussing aliasing consistency, fine-tuning requirements, and adaptive-attack evaluation.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 becomes Theorem 3.1, and its proof moves from Appendix G to Appendix D with the same assumptions, lemmas, and stability-bound derivation. The added k-space error evaluation supplies empirical corroboration; the new comparator formulas document standard procedures rather than a new theoretical argument.

improvement.justification: v3 lacked direct comparisons with other training-free defenses and quantitative accounting of the defense's computational costs. v4 substantially addresses both gaps through Appendices I–J and Table 3, making its comparative advantages and substantial inference costs assessable. Added robustness tests and explicit applicability limits further strengthen the evidence. Undefined ± notation and incomplete hardware reporting remain weaknesses, but the gains in comparative evaluation and practical transparency constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same cyclic-consistency defense, with matching authors, algorithms, theory, and original MRI experiments despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds defense comparisons, computational measurements, robustness analyses, and natural-image inpainting results.

before.justification: v3 reports original MRI reconstruction experiments, including knee and brain results in Table 1, adaptive-attack results in Table 2, and additional evaluations and ablations in the appendices.

P1.justification: v4 applies targeted copyediting and results rewrites, promotes held-out prediction to Section 4.3, consolidates module interpretation and enrichment in Appendix A.11, and regroups threshold details. These changes substantially revise the visual presentation.

Existing gradient and DataComp filtering baselines remain, while Table 1 removes the reference-model comparison rows.

V3 introduces no new uncertainty-estimation procedure, confidence-interval reporting, or significance testing; its additional experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained method scores in Table 1 and the original DataComp and temperature results remain unchanged; v1 Tables 3 and 6 reappear in v3 Tables 8 and 9. M1.justification: Equation 2 and Algorithm 1 change softmax(-m/tau) to softmax(m/tau), correcting the specified weighting rule to favor higher Mimic Scores. This is a localized correction within the retained two-stage framework; the PDFs do not establish whether the implementation changed. The new Stage 2 pseudocode documents the previously described selection and aggregation procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition undergo extensive rewriting around efficiency and online/offline selection. Section headings and subsection organization change, the appendices expand and reorganize into A–G, and limitations move to the end. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: V3 shortens main-text Table 3 while preserving its full contents in Table 8, merges v1 Figures 5–6 into Figure 5, and adds a convergence panel to Figure 4. E6.justification: All 77 matched method–dataset–environment rows retain their utilization, packed-item counts and adaptation deltas. v2 nevertheless adds substantial results: MCTS reference scores, action-inclusion rates, alternative proposal-size scores and inference, training and adaptation timings. Figure 2 combines retained frequency curves with new retention plots; the dataset figure moves to the appendix, which adds diagnostic plots, timing charts and tables.

results.title: ASAP: Exploiting the Satisficing Generalization Edge in Neural Combinatorial Optimization

E6.justification: v2 replaces the principal parametric result curves under revised settings, adds four kernel-bandit comparison panels in Figure 1, and reports six new data-derived comparisons in Figure 2. M1.justification: The restart, detector, and forced-exploration loop is retained, but v2 adds a substantive kernel-bandit adaptation: exploration actions are selected through a finite covering construction, with a full-action-set fallback for finite kernel experiments (Proposition 4.2, Corollary 4.4, Appendix A.2). This extends the procedure beyond v1's parametric linear-independence construction.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, method exposition, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around DAL and practical non-stationary learning. Experiments now precede theoretical analysis, detector details move to an experimental appendix, and the theoretical appendix is reorganized. This substantially changes the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: v1's separate principal experimental figures are consolidated into v2's 16-panel Figure 1, with revised styling and shared legends. v2 adds a six-panel benchmark figure and five data visualizations, redraws the retained sensitivity plot, and relocates and expands Table 1 with kernel rows and a stationary-input regret column. The overall document template also changes.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through kernel/GP-bandit literature, newer stationary algorithms, and benchmark sources, including works by Chowdhury and Gopalan, Deng et al., Salgia et al., and Lee et al. It also explicitly identifies Huang et al.'s modular MAB work as the closest precursor and presents the main regret theorem as following from that work.

T1.justification: v2 adds RKHS and information-gain definitions, covering-set propositions and proofs, and a generalized regret theorem and corollary incorporating kernel complexity and exploration-set size. It also replaces v1's explicit finite-time regret decomposition and detailed Appendix A proof with a generalized order bound and the reference-dependent proof sketch in Appendix B.4.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for practical applicability beyond v1's exclusively synthetic parametric evaluation through kernel experiments and six diverse data-derived benchmarks. Added preprocessing, resource information, and covering analysis make the expanded scope more assessable. Tradeoffs include fewer reported runs, unmatched SCB base learners, conflicting Yahoo! preprocessing descriptions, and replacement of the detailed regret proof with a sketch. These weaknesses limit verification but do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support across application settings.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with DAB renamed DAL and its scope expanded. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison; visual inspection resolved extraction problems in v1's plots.

after.justification: Section 3 reports original synthetic and data-derived benchmark experiments, including kernel bandits and six real-world benchmarks. Section 4.3 also retains the original drift-sensitivity experiment.

It also acknowledges that exact prefetcher traces cannot be reconstructed without the original experimental stack. The existing slow-drift interpretation and separation-condition limitations remain.

These reported settings do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 retains the same random-walk drift sensitivity experiment comparing DAL+LinUCB with WeightUCB, and Figure 3 is unchanged. No additional ablation, error analysis or dedicated robustness study is reported; the added benchmark panels extend evaluation coverage.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over 15 independent runs or trials and display shaded bands without defining their statistical meaning. v4 adds no seed information, confidence levels or significance-testing procedure; the additional panels continue the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Figure 1 adds contextual regret results for three change-point frequencies and drifting conditions. Figure 2 adds R6B, clinical and prefetcher cumulative-reward results, showing DAL leading their respective comparisons. Matched legacy benchmark results and Figure 3 are retained, so the principal change is newly reported evidence, not a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes from action-only reward histories to observing contexts and maintaining detection histories for context-action pairs. The exploration-and-restart framework remains, but this contextual adaptation substantively changes its inputs and detection procedure; v4 also instantiates DAL with SquareCB.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, literature review, framework exposition and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and condensation. Benchmark narratives are reordered, and Appendix A.2 gains separate construction, implementation and experimental-choice blocks. The main section sequence remains recognizable, but the prose and organization within sections change extensively.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is transposed and expanded from 16 to 20 panels. Figure 2 is redesigned from six to nine panels grouped by evaluation metric. Three appendix dataset visualizations and a PS-CB block in Table 1 are added; several existing figures are relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion expands to non-stationary contextual methods, including work by Chen, Luo and Wu and their coauthors, alongside SquareCB and ILTCB references. New application literature accompanies a substantive repositioning of DAL as addressing insufficient real-world evaluation of order-optimal methods.

T1.justification: v2's Theorem 4.3 and Corollary 4.4 become the contextual generalizations numbered 4.4 and 4.5 in v4, introducing context-frequency-dependent separation conditions and context/policy-dependent regret terms. Appendix B.4 adds context-sampling events and concentration/union-bound reasoning, and B.5 adds a contextual derivation. Reward, regret and detectable-change definitions are also generalized.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for DAL's generality through an explicit contextual procedure, accompanying assumptions and analysis, and synthetic and logged-data comparisons against a dedicated contextual baseline. Clinical and prefetcher evaluations test additional practical settings, while expanded construction instructions make the evidence easier to assess. These are substantive gains beyond stronger performance claims. Reproducibility remains imperfect: the changed exploration schedule is not reconciled with retained curves, prefetcher-data release is prospective, and uncertainty bands remain undefined.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAL research work. Their complete main texts and Appendices A–B, including equations, figures and tables, are readable and support reliable matching across the expanded scope and relocated material.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds contextual-bandit experiments and evaluations using Yahoo! R6B, COVID-NMA and prefetcher-selection data.

after.justification: V5 retains original synthetic and real-world evaluations and additionally reports GSR detector comparisons and computational runtime results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same conformal prediction-based machine unlearning study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

Reported total compute increases from approximately 602 to 651 GPU-days. These substantially expand reproducibility information while retaining most original Llama and hardware details.

E1.justification: v3 adds dedicated mathematical chain-of-thought training using UltraInteract Math CoT and evaluation on GSM8K, MATH500, AMC23, MinervaMath, and AIME24/25 (Appendix B). It also adds MT-Bench evaluation (Appendix I). This substantially extends v2's instruction-following and summarization coverage.

E2.justification: The original eight DAAs remain in the corresponding comparisons. v3 Tables 12–13 additionally evaluate AlphaPO Pair, AlphaPO Point, fKL Pair, and fKL Point. These additions substantially broaden the compared score families and provide matched pairwise/pointwise comparisons absent from v2.

E3.justification: New settings include Mistral 7B and Qwen2.5 7B/14B experiments, math evaluation using avg@8 or avg@32 with temperature 1.0, and MT-Bench judging by Kimi K2.5. Appendix A.2.2 also excludes the 3e-7 learning rate for DPO/IPO Llama sweeps, revising v2's stated four-rate search; this reported protocol revision does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds matched-score pairwise/pointwise tests for AlphaPO and f-DPO, alignment-quality analysis against the learning-rate/beta ratio (Figure 9), and top-three configuration robustness (Table 16). These examine score-family dependence and sensitivity to selecting a single best configuration. The existing SFT-volume, toy-bias, and real-data ICC analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 introduces exact one-sided permutation tests over 70 method-group assignments (Table 15) and four-seed averaging with across-seed standard deviations for math evaluation. Table 16 adds dispersion across hyperparameter configurations, rather than independent training reruns. The toy experiment's 1,000 seeds and 95% confidence intervals were already reported in v2.

E6.justification: The original Llama Table 2 scores and TL;DR win rates are retained. Substantial new results include Mistral IPO's 24.52% AlpacaEval LC and SimPO's 22.3% ArenaHard score, Qwen2.5-14B mean Avg@K of 0.3278 for DPO versus 0.3078 for ASFT, and MT-Bench, permutation-test, and robustness results. These are newly reported evaluations, not same-setting gains over v2.

M1.justification: The two-stage ORPO/ASFT adaptation and beta-scaled losses are already present in v2. v3 Appendix B.4 additionally constructs and evaluates ASFT-style pointwise objectives using AlphaPO and f-DPO Forward-KL scores alongside their pairwise forms. These are limited loss extensions within the retained framework.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, discussion, related work, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. v3 introduces an explicit contributions list, integrates research questions into the methodology, moves related work before the conclusion, and adds an appendix contents list. These are extensive narrative and organizational changes beyond the added scientific material.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. v2's TL;DR bar chart becomes v3 Table 3, and the Pareto plot labelled Table 3 becomes Figure 4. Table 2 gains Mistral columns; new math, MT-Bench, permutation, and robustness tables and the learning-rate/beta figure substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2's brief related-work discussion becomes a structured comparison of unifying frameworks, supervision beyond binary preferences, and online versus offline optimization. v3 adds substantive positioning against Saeidi's comparative study and discusses AlphaPO, f-DPO, AlphaDPO, TriplePO, TreePO, and online preference research. Publication-year and venue updates to retained references are not counted as new works.

T1.justification: New Appendix G defines the scalar-score family and empirical prompt bias, states a non-degeneracy assumption, and develops proofs concerning bias gradients, pairwise shift invariance, and pointwise coupling. This substantially extends v2's theory. The existing BCE and ORPO/ASFT derivations are retained, with the missing logarithm in v2's ASFT-proof score definition corrected.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's limited model-family coverage and reliance on GPT-based task evaluation through Mistral replication and verifiable Qwen mathematics experiments. Permutation tests and hyperparameter robustness checks strengthen support for the ranking-type finding, while Appendix G clarifies the bias argument's mathematical scope. The full bias–capacity mechanism remains incompletely established, but the gains in validation and precision are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DAA comparison study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds Mistral evaluations, Qwen mathematical reasoning experiments, MT-Bench scores, and statistical and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original Llama alignment evaluations, SFT-data and beta sensitivity experiments, and controlled simulations and real-data prompt-bias analyses.

results.title: The Differences Between Direct Alignment Algorithms are a Blur

C1.justification: V1 claims performance approaching SAM while surpassing FastSAM and emphasizes interpretable separation of identity and location. V2 drops that disentanglement contribution and claims superior aggregate accuracy over SAM variants, over 1000-fold parameter savings for FLIP-Tiny, and approximately sixfold faster FLIP-Large inference. Energy savings and real-time applicability receive stronger emphasis in the abstract and contributions.

C2.justification: V2 removes the strict what/where separation explanation and adds substantive interpretations of sparse boundary sampling, architectural robustness, patch-size tradeoffs, and hierarchical inference's accuracy/runtime compromise. Sections 4.3–4.6 discuss these mechanisms and applicability implications. The absolute-pixel-size explanation remains, while v1's caveat about unoptimized patch-processing time disappears.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands implementation documentation, including bilinear patch extraction, spatial hashing and a Python C extension, MLP and residual-scaling details, seven sampling-distance bins, 2048 sampled pixels, and refinement defaults. It adds RTX4090 timing hardware and a project-page link. The newly stated 256-pixel ObjaScale object-size cap documents generation more precisely without establishing that the dataset changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds COCO and LVIS evaluation, substantially extending natural-image instance-segmentation coverage, including large-vocabulary annotations. Hypersim, KITTI-360, OpenImages, and ObjaScale remain. Both versions train on the Segment Anything dataset, called SA-1B in v2; that naming change does not add training coverage.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates SAM-B/L/H and FastSAM-s/x. V2 retains these and adds MobileSAM and EfficientSAM-T/S to the main comparison, introducing two relevant efficient segmentation families. Figure 7 also adds EfficientSAM-S and MobileSAM to the retained ObjaScale heatmap comparison.

E3.justification: The reported training schedule changes from approximately 1.5M updates with successive 128/512/4096-token phases to 2.7–8.5M updates, depending on model size, with tokens varied around 512. Three model configurations become four spanning 0.51–96.6M parameters. V2 also introduces architectural controls, standard versus hierarchical inference comparisons, a below-1%-area evaluation subset, and six-dataset averages.

E4.justification: V2 adds six architectural ablations addressing positional embeddings, normalization, patch-size limits, and adaptive sampling, evaluated with both inference modes in Table 2. Table 3 adds systematic small-object analysis across datasets. Scale heatmaps remain and expand, but v1's token-budget sensitivity experiment in Figure 9 is removed.

E5.justification: V1's Figure 10 reports 95% confidence bands, and Figure 9 includes a band labeled '50% quantile'; both plots disappear. Mean ± standard deviation IoU reporting remains in v2's tables. Neither version reports repeated-run counts or seeds, and the additional table rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: V2 substantially replaces and expands the results. For example, Table 1 reports ObjaScale IoU of 89.02% for FLIP-Large (96.6M parameters), versus 84.94% for v1's FLIP-L (26.5M); changed architecture and training prevent treating this as a controlled gain. FastSAM-x's Hypersim IoU also changes from 43.39% to 34.36%. New baseline, dataset, ablation, hierarchical-inference, and small-object results are added.

M1.justification: V2 replaces v1's separate perceptual/positional codes and patch decoder with pixel-query attention and sparse mask prediction. Positional embeddings now enter values as well as queries and keys, and normalization changes. The mask/position/box objective becomes adaptive sparse BCE training. Controlled patch overlap, 5-sigma inference bounds, and optional hierarchical refinement also change the procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The method narrative replaces the what/where subsection with pixel prediction and explicit inference descriptions, while the results section is reorganized around overall performance, efficiency, small objects, ablations, and generalization. This exceeds terminology or numbering changes.

P2.justification: Architecture diagrams are redrawn, a Pixel-Predictor diagram and runtime plot are added, and Figure 7 expands from three to five heatmaps. Figure 1 changes from ObjaScale-only to six-dataset averages. Table 1 expands while losing its timing breakdown, and Tables 2–3 are added. V1's sampling diagram and two curve plots disappear; the KITTI and ObjaScale example displays are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: The introduction adds discussion and citations for EfficientSAM, MobileSAM, and TinyViT, and the evaluation adds COCO/LVIS references. The Xiong et al. (2020) normalization reference is removed. The Related Work section and the central positioning against full-image encoding largely remain, making this a limited literature expansion.

T1.justification: The mathematical specification changes substantially: v1's perceptual/positional code definitions, Gaussian output-patch construction, and three-loss formulation are removed. V2 defines revised attention computations, pixel-query prediction, sparse BCE, 5-sigma inference bounds, and logarithmic refinement depth, alongside new computational-complexity arguments. These are substantive mathematical changes, although neither version presents theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked component ablations and comparisons with lightweight transformer baselines. V2's Tables 1–3 address these important validation gaps and examine the accuracy/runtime tradeoff, while expanded implementation and hardware details improve assessability. These gains substantially strengthen support for the central efficiency claim. They outweigh the removed token-budget/uncertainty plots and timing breakdown, although energy-saving claims lack direct measurements and Figure 8 ambiguously labels hierarchical results without their suffixes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FLIP and ObjaScale, despite the changed title and substantial method revision. All pages, equations, figures, tables, and references support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original results across six datasets, including architectural ablations, hierarchical inference comparisons, and small-object evaluations in Tables 1–3.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation and runtime results in Table 1, plus object-size and token-budget experiments in Figures 7, 9, and 10.

results.title: Looking Locally: Object-Centric Vision Transformers as Foundation Models for Efficient Segmentation

C1.justification: The central contributions—foveated segmentation, parameter efficiency and scale invariance—remain. v3 explicitly extends superiority claims to SAM2 and qualifies practical applicability through dependence on accurate prompts, while retaining the broader foundation-model ambition.

C2.justification: v3 explains the extra shape/orientation information in mask-derived Gaussians and limits ObjaScale's interpretation to a controlled, single-target scale diagnostic. It attributes noise failures to the prompt controlling both sampled patches and queried pixels, and adds deployment and prompt-interface limitations. These substantially qualify v2's broader performance and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Section 3.1 substantially expand sampler documentation with boundary rejection, a 10Ni attempt limit, retention of underfilled patch buffers and coordinate normalization. v3 also specifies box-to-Gaussian constants and final fine-tuning sampling settings. These disclosures improve reproducibility without establishing that the original sampler itself changed.

E1.justification: SA-1B training and evaluation on Hypersim, KITTI-360, OpenImages, COCO, LVIS and ObjaScale remain. New noisy-box tests expand input-condition coverage to localization errors. The fuller description of ObjaScale's centered target clarifies existing data rather than establishing a changed dataset.

E2.justification: v3 adds SAM2-T, SAM2-S, SAM2-B+ and SAM2-L to the overall and small-object comparisons, and STT-H to the ObjaScale heatmaps in Figure 7. The earlier SAM, EfficientSAM, MobileSAM and FastSAM comparators remain. This substantially strengthens coverage of competing segmentation and foveated methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces final fine-tuning without augmentation, fixing N=512, coverage=1.44 and overlap threshold=2.67. It adds matched box-information evaluations and a controlled noise protocol using shared instance subsets, corresponding clean controls, box-center/size perturbations and dataset-balanced averages. These are substantive additions to training and evaluation settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic prompt-robustness tests at 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% box noise, with per-dataset breakdowns in Appendix C, exposing dependence on localization accuracy. Figure 8 also illustrates sampling sensitivity to coverage, overlap and patch budget. The original architectural ablation results remain unchanged in Table 9.

E5.justification: v3 newly states that noisy evaluations are averaged over repeated perturbations, without giving repetition counts or seeds. It also clarifies that the main tables' standard deviations describe per-instance IoU variability. Existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting remains; no confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v3's fine-tuned headline means are 79.90% for FLIP-Tiny and 83.26% for FLIP-Large, versus 78.24% and 80.33% in v2. The original overall results remain unchanged in v3 Table 10, so these are different training conditions. New box-prompt, SAM2 and noise results substantially expand the evidence; Table 2 shows FLIPbb-Large dropping from 79.53% clean to 26.34% at 20% noise. The original small-object hierarchical rows are replaced.

M1.justification: v3 adds FLIPbb variants that convert boxes into Gaussian prompts, undergo prompt-specific fine-tuning and restrict mask queries to the supplied box. It also adds augmentation-free final fine-tuning for Gaussian-prompt variants. These extend the procedure while retaining the foveated encoder, pixel predictor, sparse BCE loss and hierarchical inference.

P1.justification: v3 reorganizes detailed architecture mathematics, small-object analysis, architectural ablations, cross-dataset discussion and hierarchical inference into appendices. Main-text method descriptions are condensed, sampling explanations expanded, and results and conclusion rewritten around prompt types and robustness. An impact statement is also added.

P2.justification: Figure 7 expands from five to eight heatmaps; new Figures 5 and 8 illustrate sampling behavior. v2's separate attention and predictor diagrams are combined into v3 Figure 9 with an added standard-attention panel. Performance plots and tables are expanded, noise tables added, and numerous displays relocated between main text and appendices.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around SAM2, MaskFormer/Mask2Former, DAT, recent foveated backbones and especially STT. It distinguishes STT's fixed point-centered tokenization from FLIP's object-conditioned sampling and explicitly positions FLIP as complementary to object-discovery models, refining the novelty and task relationship described in v2.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.3 newly defines the box-derived Gaussian using the box midpoint, diagonal covariance, and standard deviations of 0.188 times width and 0.34 times height. The existing attention, predictor, loss and hierarchical-refinement mathematics are retained, largely in Appendices A and F. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2's central comparisons leave unequal prompt information and sensitivity to inaccurate localization insufficiently examined. v3 addresses these deficiencies through matched box-prompt comparisons and controlled noise tests, while explaining the richer Gaussian prompts and ObjaScale's diagnostic limits. This substantially improves evidential validity and practical interpretation. Fine-tuning budgets and perturbation repetition counts remain incompletely documented, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FLIP segmentation work. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated from v2's main text into v3's Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional fine-tuned models, baseline comparisons and prompt-noise experiments in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original segmentation accuracy, runtime measurements, architectural ablations and object-scale analyses across six evaluation datasets.

results.title: Looking Locally: Object-Centric Vision Transformers as Foundation Models for Efficient Segmentation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the contribution from an exact-inversion solver for diffusion SDEs to a unified ODE/SDE solver family supporting both prediction parameterizations and arbitrarily high ODE convergence order. The claim of exact SDE inversion without storing the entire Brownian trajectory is retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability qualifications beyond v1's general stability discussion and proof-of-concept limitation. Sections 5.2 and I.3 and Appendix J connect interpolation problems to distorted latent distributions and near-zero singularities, recommend noise prediction for editing, and explain that numerical overflow can defeat algebraic reversibility in practice.

D1.justification: v2 adds noise-schedule formulas and inverses, endpoint cutoffs, final-step solver choices, and model, baseline, and metric repository references (Appendices H–I). Reported hardware changes from V100 32 GB to H100 80 GB; both retain torchsde's Brownian Interval. However, v1's explicit spherical interpolation and auxiliary-state interpolation instructions are no longer stated.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from face interpolation to unconditional face generation and COCO-caption-conditioned text-to-image generation with Stable Diffusion v1.5. CelebA-HQ and FRLL remain represented, while the conditional generation task substantially broadens the evaluated content and input requirements (Section 5 and Appendix I).

E2.justification: v1 evaluates DDIM and McCallum–Foster applied to DDIM against the proposed SDE solver. v2 newly evaluates EDICT, BDIA, and O-BELM in Tables 1–2 and uses BELM in the interpolation comparison in Figure 5. DDIM remains a generation baseline but is absent from that interpolation panel; citations and theoretical comparisons alone were not counted.

E3.justification: The interpolation experiment changes from a pretrained latent diffusion model with 20 steps to a DDPM with 50 steps. New generation protocols evaluate 10, 20, and 50 steps, use FID with 10,240 generated faces and 30,000 real references, and average CLIP Score and Image Reward over 1,000 COCO captions (Section 5 and Appendix I).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's low-step interpolation stress test, Appendix J adds analyses of data versus noise prediction, coupling sensitivity, behavior with up to 250 steps, latent-space distortion, and reconstruction failure. Appendix K.1 adds a solver-choice ablation comparing five underlying schemes using FID.

E5.justification: v1 does not disclose an experimental seed practice. v2 reports fixed seeds shared across solvers and software components (Section 5 and Appendix I). This adds seed information, without establishing increased independent repetitions; neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1 provides qualitative interpolation results; v2 adds numerical generation results in Tables 1, 2, and 4, generation examples, and inversion failures. For example, Table 1 reports 50-step FID of 19.77 for Rex Euler-Maruyama versus 21.35 for Rex RK4, while O-BELM leads at 10 and 20 steps. These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: v2 extends and revises v1's data-prediction SDE construction into the Rex family, with time-dependent coupling weights and Lawson/Runge-Kutta constructions for both ODEs and SDEs. It adds noise-prediction formulations and multistage variants, including ShARK with space-time Lévy increments (Section 3 and Appendix C). These change the solver procedures beyond renaming.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and its abstract, introduction, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. The standalone Motivation section gives way to integrated reversible-solver background and a reorganized ODE/SDE presentation. The appendices gain substantial navigation and restructuring, alongside new reproducibility and ethics statements.

P2.justification: v1's interpolation figure is replaced by a different comparison in v2 Figure 5. v2 adds computation diagrams, numerical result tables, a theoretical comparison table, generation grids, and inversion visualizations. The construction diagram is also redisplayed in Appendix E; this repetition is distinct from the new evidence.

R1.justification: The brief related-work discussion becomes an extensive positioning analysis covering reversible numerical methods, diffusion inversion, stochastic Lawson schemes, and SEEDS (Appendix A). Appendix E adds claimed relationships to DDIM, DPM-Solver variants, SEEDS-1, and gDDIM. New Lawson, stochastic Runge-Kutta, rough-path, and Brownian-simulation references substantially broaden the research context.

T1.justification: v1's exact SDE-solution derivation is substantially extended with ODE/SDE data- and noise-prediction derivations, an ODE convergence-order theorem, and a strong-order result for the underlying stochastic scheme Ψ (Theorems 4.1–4.2). Appendices A and E add formal stability and solver-equivalence analyses, while Appendix D states additional assumptions including alpha_T > 0.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's explicitly acknowledged proof-of-concept-only support through quantitative generation comparisons, solver ablations, convergence analysis, and detailed implementation information. Appendix J also exposes practical failure conditions, making applicability easier to assess. Missing uncertainty estimates and omitted interpolation instructions remain weaknesses, but the gains in empirical support, scrutiny, and practical guidance constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reversible diffusion-solver research, despite substantial expansion and retitling. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison: Appendices A–C in v1 and A–K in v2.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices J–K report original generation, interpolation, inversion, and solver-ablation results, including numerical evaluations in Tables 1, 2, and 4.

before.justification: Section 5 and Figure 1 report original face-interpolation experiments comparing three solvers using FRLL images and a pretrained CelebA-HQ latent diffusion model.

results.title: Rex: A Family of Reversible Exponential (Stochastic) Runge-Kutta Solvers

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from conditional safety adapters intended to preserve benign generation quality to training-free, model-agnostic prototype moderation claimed to rival guard models and accommodate emerging risks. The observation that models recognize harmful inputs yet produce harmful responses is retained, but the principal method and benefit claims are substantially redefined.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking instruction tuning to cross-dataset generalization, classification errors to annotation ambiguity, and shared-covariance performance to estimation difficulties. It explicitly limits applicability through dependence on backbone representations and an input-only moderation scope. v1's Transformer-overfitting discussion and its inference that safety fine-tuning necessarily degrades utility are no longer developed.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information through dataset/class counts and usage rules, ten exact assessment prompts, representation-extraction and covariance defaults, specific Llama version information, A100 40GB hardware disclosure and a code/scripts access link. v1 provides only brief classifier architectures and one assessment prompt; the obsolete classifier specifications disappear. Newly supplied counts do not establish that retained datasets were resplit.

E1.justification: v2 retains WildJailbreak and MMLU-Redux but expands coverage to eight harmfulness and seven neutral datasets (Appendix A). Additions include Aegis, HarmBench, ToxicChat and XSTest, alongside programming, mathematics and conversational prompts from Codex, GSM8k and MTBench. These broaden risk and benign-input coverage. v1's direct MMLU answer-quality evaluation is no longer reported.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's Llama-Guard comparison, v2 Table 1 evaluates LlamaGuard1/2/3, Aegis-Guard-P, Aegis-Guard-D and WildGuard. WildGuard also enters the prompted-model comparison. The original MLP/Transformer comparisons, including their safety-prompt variants, disappear. This substantially changes the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 replaces accuracy and the harmonic Balanced Score with harmfulness F1 and neutral-input true negative rate. Prompted assessment expands to ten formulations requesting bare binary responses, whereas v1 requests JSON. New protocols compare model families, sizes and alignment stages, and introduce risk categories sequentially while evaluating full WildGuardMix. The LoRA-weight interpolation protocol is removed.

E4.justification: v1's LoRA-strength, classifier-architecture and detector-prompt-conditioning studies disappear; its layer-analysis question is revisited using LPM across three models. v2 adds distance and covariance ablations, hierarchical adaptation, pretrained-versus-instruction-tuned comparisons, sample-size and prompt sensitivity, and category-specific errors with examples (Section 5; Appendices C–E). These substantially expand the questions investigated.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 1 already contains error bars without an explained estimation procedure. v2 explicitly reports minimum, mean and maximum performance across ten prompt formulations and averages over five random subsamples for the sample-size study, with shaded variability in Figure 6b. The band definition remains unspecified; this establishes limited additional variability reporting, not increased repetitions of v1's experiments.

E6.justification: The original LoRA trade-off and MLP/Transformer accuracy results are replaced by extensive LPM, prompting, adaptation and robustness outcomes. For example, v2 Table 1 reports average harmfulness F1 of 89.44 for OLMo2-7B LPM-M versus 88.93 for WildGuard. These are newly reported comparisons under different methods and metrics, rather than measured gains over v1. Some LPM-E averages conflict between v2 Tables 1 and 4.

M1.justification: v1 proposes trained MLP/Transformer safety classifiers and conditional application of a safety LoRA adapter. v2 replaces this procedure with Latent Prototype Moderator (LPM), which classifies final-token representations using class prototypes and Euclidean or Mahalanobis distance, including regularized covariance estimation and hierarchical prototypes for new risks. The representation source is retained, but the classifier and moderation procedure fundamentally change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusions are extensively rewritten. The narrative moves from a safety/helpfulness trade-off and classifier-design study to motivating safety understanding, formally introducing LPM and systematically evaluating it. Related work gains thematic subsections, and the short original appendix becomes organized Appendices A–E with a contents page.

P2.justification: v2 introduces latent-space and scaling graphics, a recognition-versus-generation illustration, prompting bars and multiple adaptation/robustness panels. The layer analysis is redrawn for multiple models, while the LoRA plot disappears. The main comparison table is rebuilt around datasets and guard models, and extensive appendix result tables, error examples and prompt displays are added.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the work as an adaptable alternative to costly, fixed-size guard models. Related-work and method discussions add Aegis, WildGuard, Constitutional Classifiers, BingoGuard, prototype classification and covariance-estimation literature. The earlier conditional-adapter emphasis and associated LoRA and linear-probing references are removed, substantially changing the research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Section 4 adds formal prototype definitions, a regularized precision-matrix estimator, Euclidean and Mahalanobis classification rules, a Gaussian-discriminant classification derivation and hierarchical probability aggregation (Equations 1–6). v1 contains no corresponding mathematical development beyond its adapter-interpolation description.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence through tests of generalization, incremental adaptation, component choices, data scarcity and failure categories that were largely absent from v1's Mistral-only study. Method specification, limitations and reproducibility information also improve. Conflicting LPM-E averages in Tables 1 and 4, such as 73.86 versus 77.17 for Llama-8B, weaken precise ablation claims, and direct generation-utility testing is lost. Nevertheless, the expanded controlled evidence provides substantially stronger support and clearer boundaries for the revised input-moderation contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs concern safety information in LLM input representations and retain the central recognition-versus-behavior observation. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable. The substantial methodological revision does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original LPM benchmark comparisons, prompting experiments, adaptation studies, robustness tests and appendix error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Mistral-7B LoRA experiments, safety-classifier comparisons and layer-probing results on WildJailbreak and MMLU-Redux.

results.title: Efficient LLM Moderation with Multi-Layer Latent Prototypes

C1.justification: The main contribution remains non-parametric responsiveness metrics. The abstract and conclusion narrow the advertised role from calibrating ratings and improving evaluation accuracy to interpreting feedback and informing alignment. The contribution list also shifts from sampling highly responsive groups toward selecting responsive raters across groups.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of reference-dependent demographic rankings, including why collective judgments may poorly represent marginalized groups. Section 6 and Appendix G add metric-pattern diagnoses, auditing recommendations, and an explicit descriptive, noncausal limitation. They recommend responsive individuals from every group. v1's separate discussion of rater distress and exposure mitigation is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly supplies a Python implementation of MPA, WRA, and their harmonic mean, including input/output specifications and handling of unused scores and absent reference classes. It also states CPU feasibility and an O(NKR) complexity estimate. This substantially expands reproducibility information beyond v1's mathematical descriptions.

E1.justification: v2 Appendix H adds evaluation on Kumar et al.'s toxicity dataset of 107,620 comments, with groups defined by religious leaning, sexuality, and age. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained prompt-image safety dataset and its gender, ethnicity, and age groups.

E2.justification: v2 adds AUROC to the guideline-reference demographic and violation-type comparisons, where v1 compares against Kendall's tau. The new crowd-reference comparison additionally evaluates Mokken H and IRT discrimination alpha (Figure 3), substantially expanding the comparator families. The four traditional simulation comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v1 resolves plurality ties toward the most unsafe score; v2 specifies random, reproducible tie-breaking. v2 adds crowd references excluding the evaluated group and micro-averaging over thresholds 1–4, plus a median-above-2 reference protocol for toxicity. The stated simulation generator also switches from rater-specific to item-specific bias. The PDFs do not establish which retained analyses were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 Section 5.2 adds an analysis of reference dependence by contrasting guideline-derived and crowd-derived judgments, which v1 leaves to future work. Appendix C.3 also repeats the scoring-pattern simulations for K=6–24 and reports stable trends. These extend the investigation of reference sensitivity and robustness to scale length.

E5.justification: v1 already reports confidence-interval bounds and group-cohesion significance. v2 newly specifies 100 bootstrap trials for reported intervals and adds permutation-test significance for demographic responsiveness findings. This extends statistical reporting without establishing an increase in independent experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds crowd-reference results placing Black trisections lowest in responsiveness and toxicity results across religious leaning, sexuality, and age. Simulation values also change: downward-shift WRA is approximately 0.65 in v1 Figure 7 and 0.74 in v2 Figure 6, under revised reported settings. The 30 top-level violation rows in v1 Table 5 remain numerically unchanged in v2 Table 3.

M1.justification: The core MPA, WRA, harmonic-mean combination, and reference constructions are retained. However, v1 Section 4.1 explicitly clips negative MPA areas to zero; this step is absent from both v2's description and its Appendix B implementation. This changes the documented computation for negative-area cases.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, model explanation, metric interpretation, and closing discussion are extensively rewritten. v2 changes the title and author list, distinguishes trained raters from the dataset's experts, moves proofs into Appendix A, places recommendations before the conclusion, and reorganizes the appendices into a substantially different narrative.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column layout with a single-column format, rearranges precision/recall panels, and vertically translates comparison curves with offsets documented in legends. It adds crowd-reference, toxicity, and diagnostic displays, merges violation-type plots, and relocates existing material. Two detailed numerical tables are removed while corresponding results remain graphed.

R1.justification: v2 adds works on RLHF, annotator demographics, community norm elicitation, and toxicity data, including Kaufmann et al., Pei and Jurgens, Davani et al., Bergman et al., and Kumar et al. Works supporting the deleted impact statement are removed. The core ordinal-measurement and calibration literature remains, with a limited shift toward feedback interpretation and alignment.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the simplified model from F'(V_i, b_j), using shared item severity and rater bias, to F'(V_i^j, c_i), using rater-perceived severity and item bias. v2 formalizes guideline and crowd severity references and adds a statistical-consistency argument. The two threshold-aggregation proofs are retained in Appendix A; the rewritten normalization constant is algebraically equivalent.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves v1's important untested crowd-reference limitation and demonstrates that demographic responsiveness depends on the reference, substantially improving interpretation. Appendix H extends validation to text toxicity, while implementation code and statistical procedures improve inspectability. Narrower descriptive claims better match the demonstrated capabilities. Removing exact-value tables and omitting MPA zero clipping weaken numerical transparency and consistency with the claimed [0,1] range, but the added validation and clearer interpretation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MPA/WRA responsiveness study despite different titles and substantial reorganization. All 16 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their appendices, support reliable comparison of the text, equations, figures, and tables.

after.justification: v2 retains original analyses and simulations and adds crowd-reference results, scale-length robustness findings, and original analyses of a text-toxicity dataset in Appendix H.

before.justification: v1 reports original demographic analyses of existing image-safety ratings and original scoring-pattern simulations, including Figures 3–7 and Appendix A.

V3 reframes the abstract around complementing 2D video generation and adds a conclusion-level claim that spatially grounded interactions ensure realistic dynamics. These refine the positioning and claimed properties without redefining the central contribution.

The discussion introduces a tradeoff between 3D spatial constraints and generative freedom. It also interprets particle penetration and disappearing-hand failures as evidence of learned spatial causality, extending v2's interpretations.

It also specifies Spring-Gaus inputs, four-frame velocity initialization, and three evaluated trajectories per object. MOVI provenance is newly disclosed, and reported H100 training time changes from approximately five to six days.

V2 covers synthetic rigid, elastic, cloth, and edited/multibody scenes. The new MOVI attribution identifies the source of the retained rigid dataset rather than establishing additional coverage.
