HO-Cap introduces 15 FPS training and three context cameras without additional target-camera supervision. The reported Cosmos conditioning changes from nine to five frames; this does not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The six original appendix ablation tables survive unchanged as v3 Tables S3-S8. New analyses examine variable-length inference, HO-Cap rollout degradation and failures, and CosmosFT editing/multibody errors. V3 Table 1 labels 18.19 PSNR as 'Without TEM', but retained Table S8 assigns that result to early merging with embeddings, leaving a distinct no-TEM experiment unestablished.

E5.justification: V2 already reports ± values and shaded curves. V3 additionally defines the HO-Cap bands as standard deviations across sequences and explains the averaging in Appendix F.3. Neither version supplies training-seed or repeated-training-run counts.

E6.justification: V3 adds Spring-Gaus, HO-Cap, variable-input, and FVD outcomes. Comparing v2 Figure 11 with v3 Table S1, rigid 4-12 latent future PSNR changes from 28.28 to 28.35, and cloth 4-8 latent from 26.98 to 26.46. V2 discussed action conditioning only as future work.

P1.justification: The abstract, inverse-renderer explanation, benchmarking, generalization, and discussion undergo substantial rewriting. V3 adds a main-text ablation section, moves simulation-speed reporting and detailed benchmark results into the supplement, and reorganizes the appendices into six thematic sections with expanded explanatory prose.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout, removes the original simulator-overview table, and replaces the small main-text results display with an expanded appendix table containing FVD. It adds an ablation summary, CosmosFT curves and comparison panels, and HO-Cap visualizations and metric plots. Existing architecture diagrams and synthetic rollouts are largely retained but relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: New Appendix D substantially expands the distinction between predictive simulation, dynamic reconstruction, and per-scene analytical simulation, discussing 4DGS, DeformableGS, PhysGaussian, PhysDreamer, and Spring-Gaus. New references also support HO-Cap, DepthAnything3, DINOv3, and other positioning updates. This exceeds bibliographic or citation-style changes.

T1.justification: The Gaussian representation, serialization, temporal encoding/merging, reconstruction objective, and appendix equations retain their mathematical substance. Equations are renumbered or split for presentation. New spatial-causality arguments are conceptual interpretations, without new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v2's synthetic-only proof of concept through an implemented action-conditioned HO-Cap adaptation, a documented 3D comparator, and tests exposing input-window and rollout limitations. These address important validation gaps. The gains outweigh the reporting problems, although unequal Spring-Gaus settings, the conflicting TEM ablation label, and stronger causal interpretations limit the conclusions supported by the expanded evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3DGSim research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V3 retains original simulation experiments and adds Spring-Gaus comparisons, variable-input evaluations, and real-world HO-Cap results.

These refine the scope already acknowledged in v2. The central finding that visually convincing generations violate physical principles remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations involving boundary conditioning, object permanence, architecture, and possible training-data effects. It interprets weak human agreement with invariance scores as motivation for physics-based evaluation and filter false negatives as evidence of conservative filtering. It also argues robustness to calibration and minor dissipation, while Appendix E retains the earlier warnings about evaluator mismatch and limited applicability.

The abstract's access link changes from the project website to the Morpheus repository. Existing generation settings and prompt tables are retained; the settings table still does not cover the added proprietary models.

E1.justification: The nine documented physical tasks, recording counts, and style-augmentation coverage remain unchanged in Appendices A–B. v3 adds evaluation under rescaled, jittered, and partially missing trajectory inputs. The additional non_holonomic category displayed in v2's results disappears, but the PDFs do not explain whether it was excluded or regrouped.

E2.justification: The main physics comparisons add Kling-2.5-Turbo, Veo3, and Veo3-fast (Figures 6–7). v2 already reported the Veo variants in its depth-consistency analysis but explicitly excluded them from the final physics comparisons. v3 also actually evaluates VideoPHY2-AUTOEVAL and Physics-IQ as alternative evaluators in Appendix D.6–D.7.

New protocols include architecture and scaling sweeps, trajectory corruption, full-trajectory scoring, real-versus-real trajectory matching, and a 65-video human-validation study. These are substantial changes to the reported evaluation design.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands metric validation through scale tests, depth-estimator comparisons, PINN architecture ablations, jitter/gap and smoothing tests, and scoring-window sensitivity analysis. It also adds human alignment, component-wise correlations, and a discard-filter confusion matrix (Appendix D.3–D.10). Earlier prompting, augmentation, and trajectory case analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 introduces 95% confidence intervals for VLM scores and pass rates, specifies standard-error calculations and a confidence-interval nonoverlap significance criterion, and reports Spearman/Kendall correlations with p-values for human alignment. These uncertainty and statistical-testing practices are absent from v2. Neither PDF establishes an increase in repeated generation runs.

E6.justification: Results are extensively revised: Figures 6–7 change WAN-2.1 keyframe's aggregate score from 0.55 to 0.66 and discard rate from 0.23 to 0.16; COSMOS-predict2 single-frame changes from 0.43 to 0.50. Appendix scores and prompting/augmentation trends also change, and numerous validation results are added. These are updated results under revised evaluation procedures, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core tracking, PINN fitting, and conservation-scoring framework remains. However, the specified PINN objective changes from a universal physics-loss weight of 1 to system-dependent weighting, including 5 for chaotic systems such as the double pendulum (v2 Appendix D.3; v3 D.5). This is a limited refinement of the evaluator.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution statement, experimental interpretation, main limitations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 5 gains thematic organization, and Appendix D is substantially reorganized around validation questions. The title and author/front matter change, the author-contribution and LLM-use statements disappear, and impact and acknowledgment sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. Figures 6–7 are redesigned with separate single-frame, multi-frame, and keyframe groups; heatmaps gain model columns; Figure 8 moves into the main text and gains an overall bar. New validation tables, scatterplots, and a confusion matrix substantially expand the displays, while several earlier illustrations are retained or relocated.

R1.justification: v3 substantially develops positioning around embodied AI and robot world models, adding discussions and citations involving Gemini Robotics, GR00T, vision-language-action models, and robot simulation. It adds foundational physics-informed learning references and distinguishes LikePhys's likelihood-based evaluation from evaluating generated physical behavior. These extend the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates to retained works.

T1.justification: The dynamical-score definition is corrected from Sdyn = min(1 − NMSE, 0) in v2 Appendix D.3 to max(1 − NMSE, 0) in v3 D.5, restoring the intended nonnegative clipping. The physical-law equations and conservation derivations otherwise remain substantively unchanged; the added scale checks are empirical rather than new proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 mainly validated its evaluator against real recordings. v3 adds human-rating and filter validation, alternative-evaluator checks, and sensitivity tests for noise, scale, architecture, and scoring windows (Appendix D.3–D.10), substantially strengthening evidence about metric reliability and failure modes. It also corrects the clipping formula and standardizes relative scoring windows. Some interpretations overreach: the nonsignificant invariance–human correlation does not establish human inability to judge invariants, and Table 3 limits broad architecture-insensitivity claims. These weaknesses qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Morpheus, with matching experimental recordings, trajectory extraction, and physics-informed scoring. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison despite the changed title and extensive revision.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations and adds evaluator comparisons, robustness experiments, and human-rating and filter-validation results in Appendix D.

before.justification: v2 reports original video-generation evaluations, discard rates, physical scores, and analyses of prompting and appearance augmentation, including appendix results.

results.title: Evaluating Newtonian Mechanics in Video Generative Models with Real Physical Systems

C1.justification: The headline empirical claim expands from superiority on GSM8K to superiority across reasoning benchmarks and hardware configurations, including gradient accumulation. The conclusion newly presents robustness across down-sampling ratios and superiority over random and reward-only selection as contributions. The abstract and introduction also focus the framing on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving inference saturation and diminishing returns when increasing rollout counts, and qualifies robustness when update subsets become very small. Its new limitations discuss mathematical-task coverage, prompt diversity as an alternative efficiency strategy, and selective sampling's incompatibility with strict on-policy guarantees. v1 lacks these substantive qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies Unsloth, TRL, AdamW, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, the open-r1 integration and reward-function source, and an experiment-code URL. It documents L40S and eight-H100 implementations and explains batching across prompts. However, v1's constant learning-rate schedule and 0.01 warmup ratio are omitted; this is lost disclosure, not evidence of changed settings.

E1.justification: v1 trains and evaluates only on GSM8K. v2 retains GSM8K and adds actual MATH training and evaluation, substantially broadening the benchmark coverage beyond the original single dataset. Hardware and fine-tuning changes are separate experimental-setting changes.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates max-variance PODS against standard GRPO and only describes random and max-reward selection. v2 newly evaluates both selection alternatives against max-variance selection in Section 4.3 and Figure 4, substantially expanding the direct comparisons supporting the selection criterion. GRPO remains the principal baseline.

E3.justification: The main GSM8K LoRA comparison changes PODS from (n,m)=(32,16) to (64,16), and evaluation changes from every 100 steps to every half-hour. v2 adds MATH settings, full-parameter training on eight H100s with sequence length 1536 and gradient-accumulation controls, parameter sweeps, and per-step runtime and completion-length measurements. The earlier (32,16) configuration also appears in the new sweep.

E4.justification: v1 contains no empirical ablations. v2 tests sensitivity to generated rollout count and update subset size in Section 4.2, compares selection rules in Section 4.3, and examines completion-length behavior across these experiments in Appendix A. These additions directly investigate configuration sensitivity and the value of reward-variance selection.

E5.justification: v1 specifies eight training runs with different seeds and five test evaluations per checkpoint. v2 omits these counts while retaining bands described as 1.96 times the standard error. This reduces statistical reporting detail; it does not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: v1's A6000 accuracy comparison is replaced by results under revised L40S settings and supplemented with MATH and eight-H100 results. Figure 2 adds runtime findings: PODS takes longer per step on one GPU but less time per global step on eight GPUs. Figure 4 reports max-variance above random and max-reward selection, and Appendix A adds completion-length results. These are not same-setting performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 changes its initial candidate from indices {1,...,m} to the first m reward-sorted indices, a limited procedural correction. The PODS objective, subset-based advantages, and max-variance selection criterion remain unchanged. The binary-reward theorem characterizes the existing criterion rather than introducing a different method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and explanatory method passages undergo extensive rewriting. The brief experimental section becomes three organized subsections, and the conclusion becomes a structured discussion with limitations, future work, and broader impact. These are substantial narrative revisions beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adds a training-pipeline schematic as Figure 1 and replaces the original single accuracy display with paired accuracy/runtime panels across Figures 2–4. Appendix A adds completion-length Figures 5–7. The visual organization, captions, legends, and panel layouts are substantially expanded; neither version contains result tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for MATH, Robust Autonomy Emerges from Self-Play, Unsloth, TRL, ZeRO, and open-r1, while dropping the Qwen2.5 and LoRA references despite retaining their use. The positioning relative to DAPO, VAPO, and prior data-selection work remains substantially the same.

T1.justification: The central extreme-reward subset lemma and its proof are retained. v2 adds an explicit correctness and prefix-sum complexity proof for Theorem 1, formalizing the O(n log n) implementation already mentioned as possible in v1. New Theorem 2 proves the equal top/bottom selection characterization for binary rewards and even m, a bounded extension of the existing theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited empirical support: the added benchmark and distributed experiments test broader applicability, while selection-rule comparisons and parameter sweeps directly examine why and when PODS helps. Appendix A, additional proofs, implementation disclosures, and specific applicability limitations strengthen the paper further. Omitting run counts and scheduler details weakens reproducibility, but the more diagnostic evidence and better-qualified conclusions provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PODS research. Text, equations, algorithms, references, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2's Appendix A and its completion-length figures were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original GSM8K and MATH experiments, distributed training comparisons, selection-rule and rollout-size ablations, and completion-length measurements in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original GSM8K experiments comparing GRPO and GRPO-PODS with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, including accuracy curves and uncertainty bands in Figure 1.

C1.justification: v4's introduction adds substantive claims of generalization from short, segmented solutions to long, unsegmented reasoning and superiority to self-consistency under matched compute, especially at larger budgets. These expand the original claims about data-efficient verification and test-time scaling.

C2.justification: v4 explains long-trace verification through implicit step extraction and interprets automatic-label results as showing independence from the labeling strategy. It removes v3's speculative suggestion to allocate verification compute by problem difficulty. Overconfidence, step-label interference, and computational-overhead limitations remain.

However, v3's explicit rule for choosing the final beam-search answer by majority is omitted.

E3.justification: v4 adds comparisons against self-consistency using estimated FLOP budgets on MATH-500 and GPQA-Physics, introducing a substantive resource-matching control. It also adds Qwen3-1.7B-thinking evaluation on all 500 MATH-500 problems (Figure 11), beyond the retained 100-problem experiments. These are added evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: New Sections 5.2–5.4 investigate long-trace generalization, whether verification improves on spending compute on additional generator samples, and training with automatic rather than manual labels. Figure 29 adds a long-trace verification case. Earlier filtering, data-scaling, and difficulty analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The parenthesized percentages in the ProcessBench tables remain invalid-output rates rather than uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 11 adds long-trace and compute-matched findings. New Table 3 reports Math-Shepherd-trained ThinkPRM-1.5B F1 scores of 75.8/76.5 on OlympiadBench/OmniMath, alongside the retained PRM800K-trained scores of 76.3/75.7. These are results under alternative training conditions, not same-setting improvements over v3. Existing benchmark plots and Table 2 retain their results.

M1.justification: The synthetic-chain filtering, supervised finetuning, score extraction, and parallel/sequential verification procedures remain unchanged. v4 tests automatic labels and longer inputs without introducing a new algorithmic component; automatic labels were already contemplated in v3.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, method explanation, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting and condensation. Contribution bullets become a findings paragraph, the analysis subsections are reorganized, and Appendix G collects ThinkPRM examples. This exceeds localized language editing.

P2.justification: v4 adds the three-panel Figure 11 and automatic-label Table 3, moves the difficulty plot into the appendix, and expands the earlier verification example in Appendix G alongside a new case. Figure 4 adopts matching frequency axes, and the beam-search plot enlarges axis labels without changing results.

R1.justification: v4 adds Singhi et al. (2025) and the Qwen3 technical report, removes Li et al. (2025) on learning from demonstrations, and more explicitly positions ThinkPRM against GenRM's short, outcome-level verification. The broader related-work coverage remains.

T1.justification: There are no added formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations. Appendix E.1 retains the same verification-score calculation; additional mathematical passages belong to verification examples.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens practical validation: Figure 11 addresses v3's missing compute-matched comparison against self-consistency and tests long, unsegmented reasoning, while Table 3 tests reliance on manual labels. These address important evidential gaps. FLOP accounting remains underdescribed, and Appendix E.5's universal 100-problem statement conflicts with the new full-set test, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Process Reward Models That Think. Their text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and expanded material.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds long-reasoning evaluation, compute-matched analyses, and results from training with automatic step labels.

before.justification: v3 reports original ProcessBench verification results, best-of-N and guided-search experiments, and training-data and filtering analyses.

results.title: Process Reward Models That Think

C1.justification: v2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion claim a fully connected low-loss space, absence of parameter redundancy at the space level, diagnostic PCA visualizations, and improved generalization. v4 replaces these contributions with a focused empirical framework for connecting independently trained modes, emphasizing architectural breadth, reproducibility, and connections between models trained with different hyperparameters.

C2.justification: v4 removes interpretations linking PCA fluctuations to input features and residual connections, SVD spans to parameter nonredundancy, and generalization gains to incomplete hyperparameter search. It adds explanations of cross-sphere connections and explicitly qualifies cross-paper loss comparability. The lack of guaranteed test generalization was already acknowledged in v2; its dedicated limitations section is largely a relocation. Specific VGG16 and Adam-trained ResNet18 failure examples disappear.

D1.justification: v4 expands layer schedules and training configurations in Tables 2–4, adds implementation sources, and reports equivalent-epoch budgets alongside updated hardware and reference times in Table 6. It states that code and further settings are in supplementary material. However, v2's detailed recipe for the retained below-0.006 experiment is removed, along with several runtime entries and ImageNet-specific settings.

E1.justification: v4 removes the ImageNet1k evaluation and its pretrained ResNet18 generalization study from v2 Section 5, eliminating the only large-scale image dataset evaluated by the work. MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 remain; all were already present in v2. Additional architectures change model configurations rather than dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v4 Table 1 expands the reported comparison beyond AutoNEB to include FGE and SPRO. FGE receives a cited worst-case loss of 0.022; SPRO receives qualitative comparison entries with loss unreported. These are literature-based comparisons across different architectures, and neither PDF establishes matched baseline reruns.

It adds training accuracy and continuity evaluation using 50 interpolation samples per segment in Figure 5. The shorter CCT7 FDF schedule is an additional experimental configuration; the earlier manual schedule and retained datasets' preprocessing remain documented.

E4.justification: v4 adds direct checks that interpolations between consecutive LLPF points maintain low loss, addressing continuity beyond the sampled points (Figure 5 and Appendix A.7). It also tests connections across weight-decay configurations. Conversely, v2's PCA layer diagnostics and SVD dimensionality analysis disappear. The 100-model variance/mean checks and below-0.006 path experiment are retained.

E5.justification: v2 specifies 200, 40, and 10 repetitions for its principal experiments; v4 uses the less specific 'at least 10' statement. Previously single-run supplementary comparisons in v2 Figure 8 receive variability bands in v4 Figure 9. Mean/standard-deviation reporting remains the convention. The PDFs do not establish that earlier run counts were reduced.

E6.justification: v4 reports additional successful architecture connections, connections across weight-decay settings, low-loss interpolants, and training-accuracy trajectories. It removes the PCA/SVD findings and the reported ImageNet accuracy improvement from 69.758% to 70.55%. The below-0.006 result already appears in v2 Figure 10; v4 Figure 6 retains its loss curve but removes distance and test-performance panels. AutoNEB's 0.016 minimum in v2 and 0.0324 worst-case loss in v4 are different statistics.

M1.justification: The two LLPF algorithms remain, but v4 adds a step_c contribution to MOVE and introduces the Follow Data Flow layer-ordering strategy, with distinct CCT7 and DLA schedules. Section 5 also specifies a connection procedure that targets a projection onto the destination variance sphere using adapted M2O, then concatenates an M2M path. These extend the procedure beyond v2's existing layer-wise framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution list, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Definitions become a standalone section preceding related work; the geometric/generalization section disappears; evaluation gains new subsections; and limitations receive a dedicated section. Terminology shifts toward modes and mode connectivity throughout.

P2.justification: v4 adds a comparison table and connection/continuity figures, expands appendix result grids and configuration tables, and adds training-accuracy axes to the main plots. LeNet panels move to the appendix, PCA figures disappear, and the stringent-loss experiment retains only its loss panel. The new layout also introduces Figure 1 caption overlap on page 6 and architecture mismatches between captions and panels in Figures 11–12.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion shifts from singular learning theory and global loss-space geometry toward empirical mode connectivity. v4 adds substantial positioning around SPRO, layer-wise connectivity, spawning, and permutation methods, including Adilova, Benton, Ainsworth, Entezari, and Frankle. It explicitly distinguishes independent training from shared-pretraining and permutation settings, while removing much of v2's singular-learning and redundancy-related literature.

T1.justification: The low-loss and variance-sphere definitions, Equations 1–6, and norm–variance derivation are retained; the proof moves from Appendix A.3 to A.8. v4 introduces training-loss tolerance as the gap between terminal-mode loss and maximum path loss. This is a limited mathematical definition addition, without a new connectivity theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially improves alignment between claims and evidence: v2 extrapolates finite path and SVD observations to global connectivity and nonredundancy, whereas v4 focuses on experimentally supported mode connections. Interpolation checks directly address the earlier gap between discrete outputs and claimed continuous paths, while broader architecture and unequal-weight-decay experiments support the revised scope. These gains outweigh reduced ImageNet coverage, loss of the detailed 0.006-loss recipe, and caption/layout defects. The cross-model comparison remains limited, but v4 now explicitly acknowledges that limitation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLPF research, despite the changed title and emphasis. Their complete main texts and appendices support reliable comparison; equations, figures, tables, and relocated material can be matched.

after.justification: v4 retains original LLPF experiments and reports additional architecture evaluations, connections across training configurations, and interpolation-based continuity checks.

before.justification: v2 reports original LLPF experiments, repeated path measurements, PCA and SVD analyses, and post-training generalization results, including appendix experiments.

results.title: Connecting Independently Trained Modes via Layer-Wise Connectivity

C1.justification: The three central contributions—broader architecture support, consistency across random seeds and connections across training hyperparameters—remain. v5's conclusion additionally claims lower worst-case training loss than existing methods, while its abstract more categorically characterizes previous independent-mode connectivity methods as unreliable.

C2.justification: v5 removes v4's prose flat-minimum prerequisite and argues that sharper minima can also be connected, although the pseudocode still specifies flat low-loss regions. Section 6 adds interpretations involving low-loss tunnels and a qualified conjecture of full SGD-basin path-connectedness. New passages explain variance-range limits, RegNet variability and LeNet's normalization-related degradation. The training/test-loss caveat remains in Section 5.

D1.justification: v5 supplies a source-code URL where v4 promised later release. Table 6 newly specifies the 140-epoch endpoint recipe for the existing Figure 6 result and alternate learning-rate/weight-decay recipes for cross-sphere experiments. Appendices C and F add the FGE code version and commands and AutoNEB configuration references. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the underlying LLPF implementation.

E1.justification: v5 Figure 10 adds evaluations labeled ImageNet10 for ResNet18 and DLA to the retained MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 coverage. This is a limited extension of image-classification coverage. Additional architectures evaluated on CIFAR100 extend model configurations within an existing dataset and task.

E2.justification: v4 principally provides a literature-based comparison in Table 1. v5 adds original FGE testing in Appendix C and AutoNEB comparisons using standard/fast configurations in Table 9 and CCT mode pairs in Appendix J. SPRO disappears from the summary table, but neither PDF reports an original SPRO experiment.

E3.justification: v5 introduces controlled default-seed versus changed-seed FGE tests, standard/fast AutoNEB protocols, additional CIFAR100 model configurations, a weight-decay sweep with a 4000-iteration M2O path, and relative-flatness/random-perturbation evaluations. These substantially extend the evaluation design. The existing main LLPF search schedules are retained in renumbered Tables 4–5.

E4.justification: New Appendix I tests the necessity of layer-wise movement, retraining and variance correction. Appendices J–L add an AutoNEB failure case, an investigation of reachable variance spheres and connections between sharper minima. Figures 7–8 also expand and revise the variance/mean validation. The earlier continuity and loss-tolerance checks remain.

E5.justification: The mean/standard-deviation convention remains, but v5 specifies three runs for ResNet18/DLA on CIFAR100 and single runs for other Figure 10 cases, refining v4's broad at-least-10 statement. It also reports four runs per AutoNEB configuration and uncertainty over 100 sharpness perturbation directions. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments had their run counts reduced.

E6.justification: v5 adds substantial benchmark, ablation, sharpness and baseline results. Table 9 reports AutoNEB saddle losses of 0.519–1.648 for standard runs and 1.240–4.200 for fast runs on ResNet20/CIFAR10; its LLPF row uses ResNet18, preventing a matched performance-gain interpretation. The headline ResNet18 loss bound below 0.006 in Figure 6 was already reported in v4.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same movement, variance correction, retraining and AngleConformal procedures. FDF layer ordering and the two-stage construction across variance spheres are also retained. The new ablations and endpoint experiments evaluate these existing procedures rather than introduce method components.

P1.justification: The introduction, baseline discussion and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting, and Section 6 changes from a limitations section to a discussion of landscape geometry. The appendix is reorganized into separate lettered sections with expanded explanations and model-selection rationale. P2.justification: v5 replaces the single-column main text with a two-column layout and relocates algorithms and figures. Figures 7–8 become multi-model displays, appendix benchmark panels are split and expanded, and Figure 2 gains phase annotations. Numerous diagnostic figures and comparison tables are added. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

It also expands discussion of landscape connectivity and sharpness through works such as Kuditipudi et al., Lubana et al. and Petzka et al. This goes beyond the numerous bibliographic metadata updates.

It adds no connectivity theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v4 demonstrated many successful paths but offered little direct testing of component necessity and endpoint restrictions. v5's ablations, sharper-minimum and variance-range investigations, baseline experiments and expanded reproducibility information substantially strengthen the empirical case for LLPF. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, although comparative claims require caution: Table 9 mixes architectures and computational budgets, and the categorical FGE criticism extends beyond the default-script and limited independent-pair evidence presented.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLPF research work. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additions in v5.

after.justification: v5 retains original connectivity results and adds baseline experiments, component ablations, dataset results, variance-range investigations and sharper-minimum tests.

before.justification: v4 reports original neural-network connectivity experiments, including path loss and accuracy, repeated-mode comparisons, continuity checks and appendix analyses.

results.title: Connecting Independently Trained Modes via Layer-Wise Connectivity

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same novelty, memory-efficiency, approximation, and downstream-performance claims. The revised technical guarantees do not redefine these headline contributions.

D1.justification: Both versions retain the same code-access statement, experimental settings, HP Omen 25L hardware disclosure, GPU/PyTorch implementation information, and pure-Python streaming implementation caveat.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same comparators: full SW and SW with random sampling where previously evaluated, and sliding-window SW for change-point detection. No evaluated baseline is added or removed.

E3.justification: The data splits, sample counts, sketch-size and projection grids, metrics, gradient-flow settings, and change-point testing procedures are retained. No protocol revision or rerun is documented alongside the changed runtime entry.

E4.justification: The sketch-size and sample-size sweeps, noncompact Gaussian tests, gradient-flow visualizations, and computational scalability analysis remain. No distinct ablation, robustness test, or supplementary analytical question is added or removed.

E5.justification: Ten-run reporting for simulations and MNIST, three-run reporting for gradient flows, error bars, and tabulated uncertainty remain unchanged. The change-point bootstrap and threshold-estimation procedures are also retained.

E6.justification: Table 7 changes SW with random sampling's runtime at n = 50,000 and k = 10,000 from 376.9238 s to 4200.1544 s. Stream-SW remains 9.4384 s for that row. Tables 1–6, all other Table 7 entries, and the plotted results are unchanged.

M1.justification: The compaction procedure, quantile sketches, streaming Wasserstein estimators, and Monte Carlo slicing are unchanged. Correcting KKL to KLL and removing an unused sketch argument from the one-sided definition do not change the method.

P1.justification: Targeted edits correct KKL to KLL, spelling, grammar, and the appendix roadmap. Proof explanations are expanded or streamlined, especially in A.1 and A.3–A.5, while the overall section sequence and main narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: All figures and tables are retained. Figure 5 is slightly resized, appendix tables and gradient-flow figures are redistributed, and some displayed definitions move inline. These are layout refinements rather than new visual evidence.

R1.justification: Goldfeld et al. (2024), Statistical inference with regularized optimal transport, is removed from the references and Appendix A.3, where reliance on its lemma is replaced by a direct argument. The broader positioning relative to quantile sketches and streaming optimal transport is unchanged.

T1.justification: Propositions 1–4 revise integrated and transport-error probability bounds with 1/epsilon prefactors, and the stated sketch-size requirements gain logarithmic dependence on epsilon. Appendix A adds a uniform-CDF grid/union-bound argument, corrects the power inequality and transport-map reasoning, and replaces Corollary 1's tail-integration proof with a direct moment argument retaining its rates. Sections 3.1/3.3 revise compaction cost from O((n/k) log(n/k)) to O(n log k) per projection by accounting for sorting. A.6 also corrects the Monte Carlo variance expression.

improvement.justification: v5 addresses important theoretical deficiencies: A.1 supplies the missing pointwise-to-uniform argument, A.3 fixes an invalid inequality, and Sections 3.1/3.3 account for sorting costs. Although the probability bounds become more conservative, A.5 provides new support for the retained Stream-SW expectation rates. These corrections substantially improve the justification of a central contribution; the empirical evidence remains essentially unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Streaming Sliced Optimal Transport by Khai Nguyen. The main text, equations, eight figures, seven tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched despite reformatting.

after.justification: v5.pdf retains these original empirical results in Section 4 and Appendix C, including approximation errors, classification accuracies, detection outcomes, and runtimes.

before.justification: v4.pdf reports original simulations, point-cloud classification and gradient-flow experiments, change-point detection, and MNIST and runtime analyses in Section 4 and Appendix C.

The formal-proof contribution disappears, while answer-format preservation and deployment without additional inference overhead remain central claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations linking attention to planning and execution, smaller gradient norms to optimization efficiency, balanced feedback to avoiding indiscriminate agreement, and model differences to receptivity and alignment data. It acknowledges that counterfactual robustness has not been investigated at scale. The limitations discussion is substantially rewritten, reducing v1's explicit dataset-generalization and critique-generation-bias caveats.

The supplied PDFs establish this disclosure, but cannot verify the archive's availability or contents.

E1.justification: The original training datasets and benchmark coverage are retained. V3 adds AIME24 in Table 3 and OpenMathInstruct2 diagnostics in Appendix C, including testing with factual versus irrelevant critiques. These extend mathematical evaluation and self-correction scenarios within the existing reasoning focus.

E2.justification: V3 introduces an RL comparison against SimpleRL-Zero in Table 3, substantially broadening the comparison beyond supervised and critique-based fine-tuning. It explicitly uses the comparator's official reported scores, rather than claiming a new replication. Table 8 also adds direct teacher-model reference results; the original SFT, Distilled SFT, and CFT comparisons remain.

E5.justification: V1 provides point estimates without seed counts or formal uncertainty reporting. V3 newly states that performance is averaged over three random seeds, adds paired t-tests in Table 9, gradient-norm standard deviations in Table 10, and 95% confidence intervals over 50 samples in Figure 9. This establishes expanded reporting, not an explicit increase in training runs.

E6.justification: The original benchmark tables retain their scores, but v3 adds extensive results: S1.1 achieves 61.8 versus CFT's 49.6 on MATH500, and the new base-model RL comparison reports averages of 11.9 versus 10.6, while CGD trails on AMC23. M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Equation 1 retain the same student-answer generation, teacher critique and refinement, and negative-log-likelihood training on the full input triplet. V3 explicitly clarifies prompt-only, single-pass deployment; the PDFs do not establish a procedural change from v1's already claimed deployment without additional inference cost.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, method explanation, results narrative, limitations, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. Section 3 becomes an overview and training-objective presentation, limitations precede the conclusion, and the supplement is organized into setup, experiments, diagnostics, examples, and code instructions. Existing Bayesian discussion and MetaMathQA results are relocated rather than deleted.

P2.justification: V3 relocates the overview and method-comparison diagrams, removes the optimization cartoon, redraws the benchmark plots, and expands the critique ablation into two student panels. Table 1 gains student blocks, Table 2 wraps beside prose, and new result tables, training curves, attention plots, and heatmaps substantially change the visual presentation. Headers, typography, captions, and appendix layouts also change.

R1.justification: Although much of the related-work section remains, v3 substantially repositions CGD as an efficient alternative to RL, adding discussion of DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1, and SimpleRL-Zero. New model and alignment-data references support its architectural interpretations. The Swamy et al. likelihood reference disappears with the formal analysis; the corrected CFT bibliography still denotes the same prior work.

T1.justification: V3 removes v1's Lemma 1, its Jensen-based proof, and the associated KL optimization derivations in Equations 2–9. The proof's concluding inequality reverses the implication of its displayed Jensen step. The Bayesian equation is retained in Appendix C.5, with an added unnormalized-scoring interpretation; it is not a replacement proof of the removed guarantee.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves scrutiny of student/teacher dependence and training robustness, supplies previously missing reproducibility details, and introduces statistical reporting. Removing v1's flawed KL proof also resolves an important theoretical defect. These gains outweigh significant qualifications: critique-conditioned diagnostics do not establish the mechanism of prompt-only deployment, some new performance summaries overstate their tables, and the abstract's 60x compute claim lacks transparent reconciliation with Section 4.2.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CGD research work despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds student/teacher comparisons, controlled ablations, and quantitative diagnostics. Its separately attributed SimpleRL-Zero scores are not the sole empirical evidence.

before.justification: V1 reports original CGD and baseline experiments across mathematical reasoning and general-capability benchmarks, with ablations and qualitative examples.

results.title: Critique-Guided Distillation for Robust Reasoning via Refinement

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adaptive motif tokenization, lightweight conditional decoding, and meaningful token representations. The headline 36% forecasting improvement, 1990% efficiency improvement, and up-to-44% decoding improvement are unchanged. New experiments primarily support existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations linking noise resistance to coarse quantization, the Weather ablation disadvantage to unusually high compression, and handling unfamiliar patterns to single-sample fallback. It also discusses non-stationary applicability and possible overfitting with higher-order decoding. Some new robustness wording overgeneralizes: Figure 17 shows that superiority over Chronos depends on dataset and noise level.

D1.justification: v2 largely refers readers to Chronos hyperparameters. v3 Table 8 explicitly lists model dimensions, layers, heads, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, dropout, batch size, and training steps. Appendix B additionally identifies A6000 profiling hardware, inclusion of tokenization in timing, CPU memory use, pipelining guidance, and expanded computational budgets. These are substantial disclosure improvements, not evidence that retained training settings changed.

E1.justification: The Chronos training corpus and five forecasting benchmarks are retained. v3 Appendix C.6 extends their test scenarios with Gaussian noise on all five benchmarks and linear/exponential trends and transients on Electricity. This expands input conditions within the existing task and domains.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands the central comparison by adding patch-based Chronos models with patch lengths 4 and 8 across five model sizes in Table 3. It also evaluates discretization-only models in Table 13. Earlier comparators are retained, including Moirai, spelled Morai in v2.

E3.justification: New protocols include non-overlapping patch baselines trained with MSE loss, a 37-bin control without motif discovery, Gaussian noise up to sigma 0.3, trend perturbations up to absolute alpha 0.5, and transients with 1% probability and amplitude 3. These substantially extend experimental controls and testing procedures; retained forecasting horizons and splits are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds an ablation separating discretization from motif representation in Appendix C.2, controlled noise/trend/transient robustness tests in C.6, and motif-hierarchy analysis in C.5. These address new questions about the source of forecasting gains, behavior under disturbances, and vocabulary structure. Earlier preprocessing, token-occurrence, training-size, and embedding analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 provides no across-seed uncertainty estimates. v3 Appendix B reports six-seed training experiments and MSE standard deviations for selected small motif-based, single-sample Chronos, and patch-based Chronos models. It also discloses seed 2024 and profiling with two warm-up and two measurement runs per batch, reporting timing standard deviations below 2%. These checks do not cover every configuration.

E6.justification: Headline results and existing comparator scores are retained, while Tables 3 and 13 and Appendix C.6 add substantial comparison, ablation, and robustness findings. For example, Table 17 reports clean/transient MSE of 0.261/0.398 for Chronos and 0.170/0.203 for the proposed method, with compression falling from 3.95 to 3.38. These are newly reported perturbation results, not performance changes between versions.

M1.justification: The quantization-plus-BPE tokenizer, T5 next-token objective, and analytic conditional decoder remain unchanged in Equations (1)–(6) and Appendix A. The added patch-based and discretization-only models are experimental comparators. Newly explaining fallback to individual samples does not introduce a new algorithmic step.

P1.justification: v3 locally restructures Section 5.2 into patch-based Chronos and broader literature comparisons, tightens the representation discussion, clarifies decoding terminology, removes the Outlook, and adds an Impact statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing prose remain, so this is a limited narrative revision.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout with extensive display repositioning. Figure 1 is redrawn, Table 3 expands substantially, and new uncertainty, ablation, robustness, hierarchy, and motif displays appear. Figure 4 loses its Weather panel, retained in Appendix Figure 10; the shortened Table 5 retains its full original contents in Appendix Table 16.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds classical time-series symbolization and pattern-discovery references, including Lin et al. and Berndt and Clifford, alongside newer foundation models. It qualifies the unexplored area as the proposed data-dependent tokenization for machine-learning-based analysis and changes the categorization of wavelet tokenization. Removing the Outlook also removes its associated references; the overall related-work framework remains.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.2 adds an explicit O(n) sequence-length complexity assertion without an accompanying proof. Existing mathematical definitions, quantization bounds, and conditional-decoding derivations are retained. Naming the first-order Markov assumption clarifies conditioning already present in v2's equations.

improvement.justification: The new same-backbone patch controls and discretization-only ablation substantially strengthen attribution that v2's confounded patch comparisons could not provide. Repeated-seed evidence and explicit training/profiling details also materially improve assessability and reproducibility. Some new noise-robustness prose overstates Figure 17, and uncertainty checks cover selected small models, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial strengthening of the empirical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds patch-based comparisons, a discretization-only ablation, repeated-seed measurements, and controlled robustness experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting and efficiency measurements, conditional-decoding experiments, and tokenizer analyses in Sections 4–5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Byte Pair Encoding for Efficient Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction raise the claimed forecasting improvement from 36% to 40%, efficiency boost from 1990% to 2314%, and conditional-decoding improvement from up to 44% to 48%. These update quantitative claims under broader evaluation; the three central contributions and conclusion remain substantively stable.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly interprets target-data conditional decoding as domain adaptation (Section 5.3), attributes matched-input gains to motif expressiveness (Appendix C.2), and discusses marginal higher-order benefits versus parameter growth (Appendix C.3). Existing robustness interpretations and limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v4 documents the Fev-bench dataset selection and filtering, specifies vocabulary-creation order for motif iteration in Algorithm 2, and reports that estimating conditional-decoding distributions generally takes under 10 seconds. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware, and access information are retained.

E1.justification: v4 retains Chronos training and the five original evaluation datasets, adding Solar photovoltaic forecasting and 37 selected Fev-bench datasets spanning cloud, economy, energy, mobility, and retail (Appendix B, Table 8). This substantially broadens evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Time-MoE base and large models and LightGTS to the existing patch-based Chronos, MOMENT, and Moirai comparison. The sample-based Chronos and non-foundation comparator sets elsewhere are retained.

New protocols cover Fev-bench sequence filtering and aggregation, higher-order decoding, and post-processing patch-model forecasts. The original training budgets and forecast horizon remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether longer inputs explain forecasting gains (Table 15), whether conditioning on additional previous samples helps (Table 17), and whether conditional decoding benefits continuous-output patch models (Table 18). The noise, non-stationarity, transient, and embedding analyses already appeared in v3.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same six-seed, five-dataset MSE standard deviations for selected small models (v3 Table 9; v4 Table 10). The stated training seed, timing warm-up and measurement counts, and timing uncertainty reporting are also unchanged.

E6.justification: The original five-dataset results are retained, while v4 adds benchmark, baseline, and controlled-analysis results. Section 5.1 changes reported average MSE reduction and acceleration from 36.1% and 19.90× to 39.8% and 23.14× under expanded coverage, not identical settings. The new Solar result is internally inconsistent: Tables 2–3 report 0.439 without conditional decoding, whereas Table 12 reports a best value of 0.493.

M1.justification: The BPE tokenizer, T5 training objective, and default first-order decoder are retained. Appendix C.3 adds second- and third-order decoding variants and a procedure that quantizes continuous patch-model forecasts before conditional decoding. These are localized procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Changes include local copyediting, more consistent sample-based terminology, expanded explanations, and updated affiliation and publication-header text. The main section structure and appendices A–C.9 remain, with limited reordering within Appendix C.2.

P2.justification: v4 expands Tables 2, 3, and 12, adds Tables 8, 15, 17, and 18, and adds panels to Figures 9 and 10. Table 3 gains comparator columns, while appendix body text increases from approximately 9 to 10 points, producing widespread reflow and relocation of retained material.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations for Fev-bench, Time-MoE, and LightGTS. Related work now discusses predefined multiple patch lengths and dominant-frequency-based patch selection, positioning motif tokenization against their limitations in capturing arbitrary-length patterns within a sequence.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 refines tokenization complexity from O(n) to O(|Ψ|·n), explicitly accounting for vocabulary size. The quantization-error bounds and analytical first-order conditional-decoding derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: The equal-input-length control in Table 15 addresses an important ambiguity in v3 about whether gains arose from longer raw contexts. Broader domain coverage, additional contemporary baselines, and the higher-order ablation substantially strengthen the empirical support and design justification. Explicitly identifying target-data decoding as domain adaptation improves interpretation. These gains outweigh the localized new Solar reporting inconsistency between Tables 2–3 and Table 12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C.9 are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and layout changes.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds benchmark evaluations, an input-length control, and further conditional-decoding experiments.

before.justification: v3 reports original forecasting accuracy and inference-time experiments, tokenizer ablations, robustness tests, and representation analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.

Nano Banana 2's Table 18 scores are new results under its variable-resolution setting.

The benchmark construction and main evaluation algorithms remain unchanged; expanded filtering descriptions document the existing pipeline.

Existing conditional-attribute analysis and evaluator-bias discussion move into appendices. The appendix organization changes extensively, and the standalone contents page and Limitations heading disappear, with several underlying caveats retained elsewhere.

Table 2 is reorganized into five model groups; new tables and Figures 7–8 appear; Figure 6 receives standardized vertical axes; and old Table 3 becomes appendix Table 20. Existing case-study images are rearranged from 4×3 to 6×2 grids.

improvement.justification: v2's training-versus-context argument relied on comparisons between heterogeneous generators. v3 adds a controlled SD-XL ablation and short-prompt transfer testing, substantially strengthening this central argument, alongside broader generator and evaluator validation. Some interpretation remains overstated: Table 3's 77-token long-trained configuration trails the 512-token short-trained configuration on background and style despite the claim of consistent superiority. This qualification limits the conclusion but does not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DetailMaster and provide readable text, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Content can be reliably matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.
