results.title: DetailMaster: Can Your Text-to-Image Model Handle Long Prompts?

C1.justification: The central method, probabilistic generalization, and superiority claims for the original 13 tasks remain. However, the conclusion changes from saying effectiveness was validated only with matched-cancer teachers to asserting that pretraining on one cancer fails to improve downstream performance on other cancers. This substantively revises the claimed applicability, although Table 18 presents a more mixed picture.

C2.justification: v4 replaces an untested cross-cancer limitation with interpretations of teacher mismatch, fine-tuning transfer, and direct out-of-domain prediction. It also adds explanations concerning supervision strength, limited-data robustness, GRN uncertainty, and pathway-specific biological meaning. Some summaries overgeneralize: Table 4 contains settings below GRACE, and Table 18 preserves lung-to-breast fine-tuning performance despite the conclusion's broad transfer-failure statement.

D1.justification: v4 documents the link-prediction decoder, sigmoid scoring, and BCE loss, plus patient averaging, g:Profiler use, and small-cluster exclusion for enrichment. It corrects GOOtools to GOATOOLS and removes the placeholder code-availability sentence. Existing preprocessing, hyperparameter, hardware, and timing details are largely retained; neither PDF establishes a usable code release.

E1.justification: The original three cancer cohorts and 13 downstream tasks remain. Appendix F.6 adds masked-edge link prediction on breast cancer GRNs, and Appendix G adds mismatched-teacher pretraining, cross-cancer fine-tuning, and direct prediction on unseen cancer types. These substantially expand task and test-scenario coverage without adding new cancer cohorts.

E2.justification: The original five baselines remain in Tables 2–3. v4 additionally evaluates GCA, AFGRL, and SimGRACE against SupGCL on breast cancer hazard and BP tasks in Table 16. Table 17 adds a GCLink-style comparator adapted to the estimated GRNs for link prediction. These are substantive evaluated additions, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Original benchmark splits, architecture, hyperparameter tables, and fine-tuning protocols are retained. New protocols include link prediction using 500 positive and 500 negative samples with an 80:20 split and masked target edges; temperature and encoder comparisons; patient/teacher subsampling; alternative GRN filtering thresholds; and quantitative clustering and enrichment evaluation. These substantially extend the experimental design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PCA and embedding-dimension analyses, v4 tests supervision temperature, Graph Transformer versus GAT within GRACE, cross-cancer transfer, patient and teacher sample sizes, and GRN filtering thresholds. Figure 3 adds quantitative clustering assessment, while Appendix I adds gene-cluster balance and GO/KEGG enrichment analyses. These address supervision, robustness, and biological interpretability questions largely untested in v3.

E5.justification: v3 reports means and standard deviations across folds or seeds without specifying formal significance tests. Appendix F.4 in v4 adds Student's t-tests with Bonferroni correction at 5%, reports four significant comparisons, and states that most comparisons are nonsignificant. The new link-prediction experiment specifies ten seeds, 0–9. Additional repetitions of the original experiments are not established.

E6.justification: The original main and supplementary score tables retain identical means and standard deviations. Substantial new results include temperature, comparator, transfer, robustness, and enrichment findings. For example, Table 17 newly reports SupGCL link-prediction accuracy of 0.763±0.028 and F1 of 0.855±0.018; Figure 3 adds SupGCL NMI/ARI values of 0.117/0.150. These are added evaluations, not improvements over v3 under matched settings.

M1.justification: The shared encoder, masking operations, joint loss, and Algorithm 1 are retained. However, Equation 6's description changes from a Frobenius inner product to cosine similarity via that product, while the pseudocode still shows inner products. The PDFs do not resolve whether the procedure's normalization changed or the wording corrects an existing implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction's motivation, and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten. Related work gains two focused subsections, the main results narrative is reorganized, and node-level discussion is consolidated in the appendix. An appendix contents page, revised subsection hierarchy, and separate appendix references substantially change navigation and document organization beyond copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 3 becomes graph-only and gains NMI/ARI annotations; node-level panels are consolidated and redrawn in Figure 4. Figures 7–8 and numerous tables add clustering, enrichment, ablation, transfer, and robustness displays. Existing plots, captions, legends, float placement, title formatting, and page headers are also revised, producing substantial visual changes.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reframed around augmentation-free GCL and representation learning from known GRNs. v4 adds discussion and citations for AFGRL, SimGRACE, CancerGATE, and additional GRN literature, while sharpening distinctions from already-cited MuSe-GNN and GCLink. SupGCL is positioned as exploiting measured within-modality perturbations, with explicit separation from multimodal learning and GRN inference.

T1.justification: The stated mathematical definition of simF around Equation 6 changes from a Frobenius inner product to cosine similarity via that product. Theorem 1, its independence assumption, Corollary 1, and the Appendix A derivation remain unchanged. The new explanation motivating independence does not introduce another formal result.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the evidence for biological usefulness and applicability, which v3 supported mainly through downstream scores and embedding plots. Relevant comparator tests, biological enrichment, Bonferroni-corrected significance tests, and transfer/robustness experiments make important benefits and boundaries assessable. The gains are tempered by overstatements: Table 4 contradicts the claimed advantage over GRACE in all settings, and Table 18 is more mixed than the conclusion suggests. Nevertheless, the added biological evidence and explicit exposure of statistical and transfer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SupGCL, with matching authors, core equations, datasets, and original benchmark results. The main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds temperature ablations, comparator evaluations, link prediction, cross-cancer experiments, robustness tests, and biological enrichment analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original downstream experiments on TCGA/LINCS-derived GRNs in Tables 2–3, with additional metrics, embedding analyses, and dimension experiments in Appendix F.

results.title: Supervised Graph Contrastive Learning for Gene Regulatory Networks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims: randomized benchmarks permit evaluation without fully disclosing true answers and enable contamination detection through a Bayes-accuracy ceiling. The conclusion additionally mentions theoretical support, without redefining the principal contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explains the estimator's precision cost, difficulties distinguishing small performance gaps, why benchmark-generated randomness suffices, and reasoning's role in instruction compliance. It newly qualifies disclosure-allowed defenses as addressing benign leakage and acknowledges stronger answer-recovery attacks. It also revises the canary-completion interpretation and softens eliminating a second private test set to potentially reducing that need.

D1.justification: V2 adds explicit reverse-engineering and prompt-variation templates (Tables 7–8), detailed canary query and temperature settings, H100 hardware information for 14B models, and MMLU-Pro access information. Existing dataset-access and model-merging implementation references are retained; these are bounded additions to reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds an adversarial answer-recovery scenario across eight benchmarks, supplying models with randomized answers and transformation rules (Table 3). It also includes MMLU-Pro and GPQA-diamond in the expanded evaluations. The recovery task substantially extends the tested requirements, while the existing QA domains and six-language coverage remain.

E2.justification: The competing contamination detector remains the BIG-bench canary-string approach, evaluated through log probabilities and GUID completion. Additional LLMs are evaluation subjects, and the new reasoning and unphished conditions are controls. The revised canary sampling procedure changes evaluation settings rather than comparator membership.

E3.justification: GUID completion changes from one temperature-zero completion per prefix to 1,000 queries at each of 11 temperatures, counting any successful completion (v1 Appendix B.2; v2 B.3). Model-progress tracking changes from full benchmark sizes to samples of at most 1,024 and expands from three Llama models to eleven models. V2 also adds 14B configurations, correlation metrics, and protocols for the new controlled analyses.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Bayes-accuracy sensitivity and cross-language experiments, v2 adds reverse-engineering attacks, reasoning versus no-reasoning analysis, nine prompt variants, training on original versus phished data, and checks for ignored randomization instructions (Table 3, Appendix B.2, and Figures 16–18). These test previously unexamined robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: V2 adds Kendall rank-correlation estimates and associated p-values for individual benchmarks and aggregate performance (Table 6). Both versions retain the stated three-seed mean/standard-deviation convention and the 5% binomial detection test; no increase in independent experimental runs is stated.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial ranking, scaling, recovery, and diagnostic results. Table 6 reports aggregate Kendall's tau of 0.96, but GPQA has tau 0.35 and p=0.16; new Table 3 reports GPQA recovery accuracy of 47.87% versus 37.82% with original prompts. GUID-completion curves are replaced under the expanded sampling protocol. The pretraining and model-merging values in Tables 1–2 are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds an explicit sample-based estimator that converts phished answer matches into an estimate of original accuracy. This is a limited scoring extension; the benchmark randomization procedure and binomial contamination detector are retained.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose are retained. V2 locally rewrites methods and results passages, presents practical strategies as bullets, and adds appendix subheadings. The private-evaluation rewrite also introduces an unfinished 'underlying xxx' placeholder.

P2.justification: The model-progress bar charts become scatterplots with model and release-date encodings. V2 adds reasoning, robustness, and control plots plus recovery, correlation, and prompt tables, and expands or rearranges model panels. The existing dataset-size table is expanded and renumbered from Table 3 to Table 5, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against memorization audits, membership inference, and dynamic evaluation. New discussions distinguish dataset-level detection from example-level membership inference and answer randomization from question regeneration, citing work such as Carlini and Panda's canary research, VarBench, DyVal, DARG, and KIEval.

T1.justification: V2 derives an unbiased original-accuracy estimator, adds Theorem 2 giving its variance and mean squared error, and supplies its proof in Appendix A.2. Theorem 1, Corollary 1, and their proofs are retained. The algebraic description of Z/KZ is also corrected from a finite field to an additive group.

improvement.justification: Theorem 2 and its proof quantify a previously unexamined precision cost, while the expanded ranking study replaces a three-Llama demonstration with broader quantitative evidence. New controlled analyses probe instruction-following and concealment failures, addressing central validation gaps in v1. Attack-resilience conclusions remain limited by the simple attacks tested, and an unfinished private-evaluation passage reduces polish, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in analytical and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PhishBencher work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on answer recovery, reasoning, prompt sensitivity, and additional model configurations.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on contamination detection, model-progress tracking, cross-language contamination, pretraining, and model merging in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: CapBencher: Give Your LLM Benchmark a Built-in Alarm for Test-Set Overfitting

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the learning-rate-controlled bias trade-off and the insufficiency of either bias alone to explain generalization. v2 qualifies increasing norm as an overall trend and presents the theoretical contribution more explicitly as particular scenarios and counterexamples.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands applicability qualifications and explanations: wide-network exceptions, different behavior at large initialization scales, parameterization-dependent dynamics, and divergence potentially hiding a U-shaped generalization curve. It also explicitly limits conclusions to full-batch GD and clarifies that loss-threshold stopping does not use validation loss.

D1.justification: v2 adds Lanczos/Hessian-vector-product details, explicit full-test-set usage, parameterization formulas, and architecture/preprocessing instructions for added experiments. The existing learning-rate grids, checkpoint rules, and hardware disclosures largely remain. A new release-upon-acceptance code statement accompanies the retained claim that code is supplied as supplementary material.

E1.justification: v2 extends the retained image-classification and toy-regression coverage to Wisconsin breast-cancer classification, California Housing regression, and synthetic sequence reversal. Appendix H.14 and Figure 17 establish evaluations involving substantially different data modalities and task requirements.

E2.justification: Gradient flow remains the reference for retained gradient-descent comparisons. The idealized norm-, sharpness-, and risk-minimizing rules already appear in v1 Appendix D and reappear in v2 Section 3. New KKT overlays supply analytical reference points without adding a competing training algorithm.

E3.justification: v2 adds systematic width/depth sweeps, a batch-normalized CNN, µP/kernel parameterizations, alternative sharpness metrics, and protocols for tabular and sequence tasks. Section 2.1 also revises the base FCN description from three dense layers to two; remaining three-layer wording in Appendix H prevents confidently inferring an actual change to retained runs.

E4.justification: Beyond the existing activation, loss, initialization, and norm checks, v2 adds width/depth and parameterization sensitivity studies, comparisons of six sharpness measures, distance-from-initialization analyses, and per-layer norms. The diagonal-network analysis also gains sharpness-constrained risk predictions and KKT-point comparisons (Appendix H).

E5.justification: v2 introduces parenthesized U-shape labels for inconclusive cases in Table 1, adding qualitative uncertainty reporting to the earlier configuration inventory. The initialization-seed checks using 43, 44, and 45 remain; no new repeated-run averaging, confidence intervals, or significance tests accompany these labels.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial result sets for network-size sweeps, parameterizations, alternative sharpness measures, and new domains, including decreasing or flattening norms for wider MNIST networks. The toy illustration gains generalization curves and revised trajectories. Appendix H.4 also changes the reported CE convergence-failure comparison from below 2/s0 to below 1/s0.

M1.justification: Both versions study the same full-batch gradient-descent update, gradient flow, and shared-weight diagonal regression model with square loss. Added architectures and parameterizations are experimental configurations; no new proposed optimization method is introduced.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: Sections 2.2–2.4 are consolidated, established implicit-bias theorems move to Appendix B, and the generalization argument becomes central to Section 3. Terminology and explanations are revised throughout, with expanded appendix navigation and new reproducibility, ethics, and usage statements.

P2.justification: Numerous plots are redrawn with revised axes, legends, reference lines, and placement. Figures 1 and 3 display alternative norms already examined in v1's appendix. Figure 4 expands from three to six panels, several analysis figures are added, and Table 1 gains a U-Shape column and additional configurations.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on SGD stability, momentum, mirror flow, parameterization, and beyond-EoS dynamics. Appendix A explicitly distinguishes its convergent trajectories from Ghosh et al.'s sustained oscillations and discusses normalization-related trade-offs. These additions refine the established positioning; the Alligood and Vershynin references are removed.

T1.justification: v1 Lemma D.1's incorrect Gaussian-risk simplification and claimed closed-form optimum are replaced by R(w) = 0.5||w||_4^4 - ||w||_2^2 + 0.5(d+1) and a new sharpness-constrained KKT analysis in v2 Lemma E.1. Theorem 3.3 is also reformulated as Theorem B.2 with explicit additional dynamical-stability assumptions.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects an important error in the Gaussian-risk calculation underlying v1's generalization argument and develops a constrained-risk analysis connected to numerical trajectories and risk curves. Added architecture, parameterization, and domain checks strengthen the empirical basis, while explicit discussion of exceptions better bounds the claims. These are substantial gains in scientific support, although some experimental descriptions remain inconsistent and statistical validation remains limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of norm and sharpness biases under gradient descent. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds network-size, parameterization, sharpness-measure, tabular-data, and sequence-reversal evaluations in Appendices H and I.

before.justification: v1 reports original learning-rate experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 with several architectures, plus numerical diagonal-network trajectories, including extensive appendix results.

results.title: Conflicting Biases at the Edge of Stability: Norm versus Sharpness Regularization

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list now explicitly claim profitability after accounting for verification costs and add a contribution on variable profit margins and preserving their average when changing pricing. v1 emphasized overcharging and incentive-compatible character pricing without this developed operational claim. The central tokenization vulnerability and hardness claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the negligible-verification-cost argument with conditional profitability reasoning. It explains variable and sometimes negative margins, language-dependent pricing effects, and incentives facing low-margin providers. New qualifications address unverifiable inference information, tokenizer substitution, verbosity under character pricing, and the restriction to individual interactions rather than market dynamics. The speculative explanation linking Gemma-3-4B's behavior to multimodality is removed.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the system prompt and documents pynvml measurement, GPU isolation, KV caching, and multilingual sampling/calibration procedures. These disclosures do not establish that the previously undocumented system prompt changed. Reproducibility remains imperfect: Appendix A describes every experiment as using an A100, whereas Figure 11 and Table 1 specify an H100.

E1.justification: v1's LMSYS evaluations use English prompts. v2 retains English overcharging experiments but adds English, Spanish, Russian, and Chinese prompts for pricing evaluations, including separate language-specific analyses in Appendix C.4. This substantially broadens the represented language populations.

E2.justification: Faithful reporting under pay-per-token remains the reference for evaluating overcharging. The new randomized splitter is demonstrated separately rather than added as a comparator against the retained heuristic. Added related-work methods, including Sun et al., are not empirically benchmarked.

E3.justification: Retained overcharging figures change from 400 to 600 prompts. New pricing experiments estimate character prices on 600 multilingual prompts and evaluate margins on different prompts. v2 also introduces utility and profit-margin metrics and energy-measurement protocols using temperature 1, no top-p filtering, and KV caching. These extend the evaluation design substantially.

E4.justification: v2 adds profitability sensitivity to provider margins, generation-versus-verification energy analysis across output lengths, multilingual margin stratification, and an alternate randomly sampled prompt-set check. It replaces v1's exhaustive two-string tokenization study with randomized-splitting diagnostics. Existing temperature/top-p analyses and tokenization examples are largely retained, although the plausibility figure drops two model rows.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independently seeded generations and symmetric 90% confidence intervals using the same t-distribution critical value, 2.015. The added energy and utility results use the existing reporting practice. The alternate prompt-set check does not establish increased per-condition seed counts or a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: For Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct at temperature 1.3, reported maximum overcharging changes from 9.5%, 1.6%, and 0.3% to 11.2%, 1.8%, and 0.28% at p = 0.99, 0.95, and 0.90. Prompt counts also change, so these are revised results rather than controlled performance gains. v2 adds energy, net-utility, and multilingual margin results, while removing v1's single-character overcharging table and exhaustive tokenization histograms.

M1.justification: The central plausibility-preserving heuristic is retained as Algorithm 2, formerly Algorithm 1. v2 adds a simple randomized splitting policy without plausibility checking. It also changes character-price calibration from r0/cpt to r0 times the mean per-output token-to-character ratio, targeting average profit margin rather than preserving revenue and user cost.

P1.justification: Sections 2–4 are substantially rewritten around reporting policies and clearer distinctions among revenue, utility, and profit margin. The abstract, contribution list, pricing-transition explanation, and limitations receive corresponding revisions. The six-section organization and Appendix A–C framework remain, but the explanatory narrative changes extensively.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the original Table 1 and Figure 1, expands Figure 2 from two to three model panels, and adds utility, margin-distribution, energy, and language-stratified displays. The retained plausibility figure is reduced from five model rows to three. Tokenization examples are retained with renumbering, while captions, optimal-iteration markers, and figure placement are revised.

R1.justification: v2 identifies Sun et al.'s COIN as the closest work and distinguishes hidden-reasoning-token injection from output retokenization. It adds supporting references on energy, tokenization alternatives, verification, and multilingual costs. The established positioning within tokenization, LLM economics, and mechanism design remains; publication updates to retained references do not constitute new research coverage.

T1.justification: v2 introduces reporting policies with explicit GPU-energy costs into the utility model, revises incentive compatibility accordingly, and rewrites Proposition 5's proof. It adds the profitability condition in Eq. 4 and Corollary 7 concerning incompatibility with positive constant per-token pricing. The NP-hardness proofs and character-additive pricing characterization remain substantially intact; the earlier heuristic complexity bound is omitted.

improvement.justification: v1's financial-benefit argument relied on assuming negligible verification costs. v2 addresses this central gap with explicit cost accounting, energy measurements in Appendix C.3, and profitability conditions and evaluations in Eq. 4 and Figures 3/7. Its revised pricing calibration and multilingual analysis also reveal operational tradeoffs, including loss-making outputs. These substantially strengthen the economic argument within the stated GPU-energy cost model. Hardware-description and figure-label inconsistencies limit reproducibility but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original overcharging experiments and adds GPU-energy measurements, utility calculations, and multilingual pricing evaluations in the main text and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on tokenization and overcharging using five LLMs and LMSYS prompts, including temperature-dependent results and examples in Appendix C.

results.title: Is Your LLM Overcharging You? Tokenization, Transparency, and Incentives

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion shift from compression and the 2-bit/8-fold communication headline to improved worker scaling, larger critical batch sizes, single-worker performance–time efficiency, and scalability to 15B. v2 also makes pseudogradient structure and its theoretical explanation central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds spectral interference and step-alignment explanations for worker scaling, while explicitly acknowledging that the evidence does not establish causality. It qualifies error-feedback usefulness by quantization regime and discusses dense-transformer/20-token-per-parameter scope, extrapolation uncertainty, incomplete 15B tuning, and assumptions behind idealized timing comparisons.

D1.justification: v1's Optax implementation description is replaced by distributed Muon and fused PyTorch implementations using TorchTitan/TorchFT. v2 adds a project code link, H100/H200 and distributed-training details, extensive per-scale hyperparameter tables, fitting procedures and evaluation-loss instructions. However, v1's explicit error-feedback beta selections are no longer provided.

E1.justification: Pretraining changes from FineWeb-EDU to high-quality Nemotron-CC. v2 also adds zero-shot evaluation on MMLU, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, ARC-E, ARC-C and OBQA (Tables 3 and 8), substantially extending v1's pretraining-loss evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: The principal optimizer comparators remain DiLoCo, data-parallel AdamW and data-parallel Muon. v2 additionally evaluates Streaming DiLoCo and distinguishes global/row-wise linear and statistical quantizer comparisons. v1's DCT Top-k and Random-k comparisons disappear (v1 Appendix C; v2 Figures 8 and 15).

E3.justification: v1's single roughly 220M model, GPT-2 tokenizer, 512-token context and 3.6B-token budget are replaced by Gemma3-style models, Llama3 tokenization, 2048-token contexts and a 150M–15B scaling study. v2 sweeps worker counts, synchronization intervals, batch sizes and additional optimizer hyperparameters, introduces new evaluation procedures, and extrapolates rather than fully tunes 15B settings (Sections 5–7; Appendices E–F).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's compression and error-feedback ablations, v2 adds controlled pseudogradient alignment, spectral interference and step-norm analyses; worker-count and synchronization sensitivity; streaming tests; critical-batch-size studies; and scaling-law sensitivity analyses. Appendices C, D and F add supporting diagnostics. The earlier DCT and Random-k analyses are removed.

E5.justification: v2 introduces a time-weighted EMA final-loss estimator (Appendix F), robust log-space Huber scaling-law estimation with 512 fitting restarts (Section 7.1), and median system timings over 500 steps. These substantially expand statistical estimation beyond v1. Fitting restarts are not repeated training runs; neither version reports training-seed confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v1's near-lossless 2-bit MuLoCo result with error feedback gives way to quantizer-dependent findings under v2's changed setup, including degradation with global linear quantization. Numerous scaling, diagnostic, timing and downstream results are added: Table 8 reports 3.1B mean accuracy of 57.65% for MuLoCo K=1 versus 56.79% for DiLoCo K=1. v2's Tables 3 and 7 disagree on 15B loss rankings, limiting precise interpretation.

M1.justification: The Muon inner optimizer, Nesterov outer optimizer and optional error-feedback rule remain. v2 adds a streaming adaptation with staggered updates across three parameter partitions and explicitly incorporates two quantizations into compressed communication (Section 6.4; Appendix C.1). These extend communication handling while retaining the core optimizer.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, method narrative and conclusion. It moves related work into the main text, reorganizes results into communication and scaling studies, and introduces explicit findings, a limitations section and an appendix contents page. This is a broad narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The two-column main paper becomes a largely single-column report with a redesigned title panel. The opening figure is replaced, algorithm presentation is split, and substantial diagnostic, scaling, batch-size and systems displays are added. Some panels are redisplayed rather than new evidence, notably across Figures 1/6 and 7/15.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around single-worker optimization, discussing Lookahead, Reptile, SNOO and GPA, and adds SparseLoCo and extensive large-batch/scaling-law literature. These new relationships and novelty claims go beyond relocating v1's communication-focused related work from Appendix D into the main text.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the formal interference-gap definition, Proposition 4.2 relating pseudogradient nuclear norm to step alignment and magnitude, Muon/AdamW corollaries, and an Appendix B proof. This adds substantial mathematical analysis beyond v1's algorithm and background, including assumptions about orthonormal updates and negligible weight decay.

improvement.justification: v1's practicality claim rested on one small-model study without wall-clock accounting. v2 substantially strengthens its support through tuned worker/batch-size studies, downstream evaluations up to 15B, measured optimizer overhead and fuller reproducibility information. These gains outweigh reporting problems, including unexplained 15B loss disagreements between Tables 3 and 7 and quantization discrepancies between Figure 7 and Table 5. Those inconsistencies still weaken precise numerical claims, and the bandwidth-dependent training times remain idealized estimates.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MuLoCo and retain the same core optimization framework. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable. Changed experimental settings and internal reporting inconsistencies limit particular performance interpretations but do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original pretraining experiments from 150M to 15B parameters, pseudogradient analyses, downstream benchmark evaluations and system measurements in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model pretraining experiments comparing MuLoCo, DiLoCo, data-parallel baselines and compression methods, including additional experiments in Appendix C.

results.title: MuLoCo: Muon is a Practical Inner Optimizer for DiLoCo

C1.justification: v1 leaves imperfect-information robustness as future work in Section 7. v2 makes guarantees for noisy totals and noisy frequency multisets main contributions in the abstract and Section 1.1. It also adds randomized-impossibility claims under adaptive adversaries and pathwise ex post guarantees, while retaining the earlier exact-advice claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantial applicability qualifications: uncertain totals yield additive EF1 versus multiplicative PROP1, and frequency guarantees concern predicted shares and error from both prediction and online matching. Appendix A specifies the strong pathwise meaning of randomized guarantees and discusses weaker alternatives. Appendix B explains Algorithm 1's failure of multiplicative EF1, although Section 4.1 phrases this limitation more broadly.

D1.justification: v2 adds implementation details and complexity statements: maintained outside maxima and O(mn) time for Algorithm 1, O(m²n) total time for Algorithm 2, and closest-unused-value matching using balanced search trees with O(log m) time per agent per arrival. Neither version provides code or data access.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks for empirical training or evaluation. The added noisy-advice settings extend mathematical models rather than evaluated data or task coverage.

E2.justification: No empirical baseline comparisons are added. The analytical comparisons retain the same methods, including Zhou et al. (2023) and its six-good PROP1 counterexample in Section 4; newly cited works are not added evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental protocols or settings. Certified advice intervals, instantiation-error assumptions and pathwise randomization guarantees are formal model specifications, assessed under T1.

E4.justification: Neither PDF contains experimental ablations, sensitivity studies or robustness tests. Sections 4.1 and 5.1 and Appendix B add mathematical bounds and a constructed counterexample, covered under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated runs, seeds, statistical uncertainty or significance tests. The new certified bounds on valuation totals are assumptions about advice, not statistical confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance, empirical rankings or experimental findings. The principal exact-information approximation guarantees are retained; new error-dependent bounds and revised counterexample values are theoretical changes.

M1.justification: v2 adds noisy-advice adaptations: scaling valuations by certified lower totals and matching arrivals to unused predicted values before applying the frequency algorithm to virtual valuations. Algorithm 1 also gains explicit termination when removals empty its active set. These are limited procedural extensions and corrections; the central allocation rules remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution narrative and related-work organization are extensively rewritten. Several existing proofs are restructured, and explanations of certificates and picking sequences are expanded. Sections 4.1 and 5.1 and Appendices A–B extend the structure beyond these substantial revisions to existing prose.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 summarizing fairness guarantees, replaces Proposition 3.1's valuation table with equations, and expands the Algorithm 1 display. Most other valuation tables, the three algorithm blocks and the basic single-column layout are retained, with ordinary reflow.

R1.justification: Section 1.2 substantially revises positioning relative to learning-augmented and partial-information research. It adds Choo et al. (2025), Amanatidis et al. (2025), Wang and Wei (2026), and repeated-allocation work; the conclusion expands connections to entitlements and richer valuations. Earlier discussions and citations including Cookson et al. (2025) and Huang et al. (2023) are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorem 4.5 on additive EF1 and multiplicative PROP1 under uncertain totals, Theorem 5.7 on noisy frequency predictions, and the lemma and counterexample in Appendices A–B. It also repairs existing arguments: Proposition 3.1 changes remaining agents' later values from 0 to 1; Theorems 4.1–4.2 replace the all-agents-inactive argument with final-certificate reasoning; Theorems 4.3 and 6.3 address missing cases, with 6.3 also correcting normalization. Section 3 supplies an explicit PROP1 corollary.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for central results: Algorithm 1 handles an emptied active set, Theorems 4.1–4.2 replace an unsupported termination argument, and Theorem 6.3 repairs normalization and missing adversarial cases. It also develops imperfect-advice guarantees left as future work in v1. Qualifications remain: the frequency bound depends on instantiation error and predicted shares, and Appendix B establishes only Algorithm 1's failure despite broader wording in Section 4.1. These limitations are outweighed by the repairs to core correctness arguments and the substantive new theory.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and provide readable text, equations, algorithms and valuation tables. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains Appendices A–B, which are included in this comparison.

after.justification: The new noisy-advice guarantees and Appendices A–B are theoretical. v2 contains no original experimental, simulation, user-study or data-analysis results.

before.justification: v1 reports mathematical theorems, proofs and constructed examples, but no original experimental, simulation, user-study or data-analysis results.

results.title: Online Fair Division with Additional Information

C1.justification: The central problem, potential-outcomes framework, optimization-aware estimators, and practical-utility contributions remain. The abstract narrows the claim that the method can identify and remove spurious correlations to identifying associated stages and guiding targeted follow-up interventions.

C2.justification: V5 substantially expands applicability guidance: Section 6 explains how stage granularity changes interpretation and distinguishes diagnostic attribution from responsible mitigation. The new analyses explain I/O-driven overhead and why fully mixed poisoning weakens batch-level discrimination, recommending data-point attribution for extreme dispersion. These extend v4's existing approximation, scalability, and logging limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly specifies checkpoint resumption, optimizer/scheduler reinitialization between stages, and scheduler advancement during skipped MNIST anomaly updates. V5 also documents gradient/state logging and LoRA parameter counts. Most existing hyperparameters remain unchanged, while v4's explicit Hessian-approximation formula and explanation disappear. The new protocol disclosure does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: V5 adds CIFAR-10 backdoor attribution under BadNets poisoning, comparing dispersed poisoned batches with poisoning mixed into every batch. This is a focused extension to adversarial training conditions. The earlier image, text, and medical datasets and tasks remain; the additional model-size experiments do not themselves expand task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 introduce the first evaluated attribution-method comparator: DVEmb adapted by aggregating example effects into batch and stage effects. V4 compared AA-Score only with retraining-derived ground truth. Adding this comparator throughout the central MNIST, CelebA, CivilComments, and X-ray evaluations substantially changes the comparative evidence.

E3.justification: New runtime protocols vary training-set size across 2K, 4K, and 8K examples, use ResNet18/34 and Pythia-70M/160M/410M with LoRA, and measure logging time, attribution time, and peak memory. Their fidelity evaluation uses a 20-update-step stage. V5 also introduces separate pure-poisoned-batch and mixed-batch testing procedures. These extend the evaluation design beyond the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Sections 5.4–5.5 and Appendices C.2/E.6 add computational scaling and associated attribution-fidelity analyses, plus robustness tests of dispersed backdoor poisoning. They examine practical cost and the loss of batch-level discrimination under mixed poisoning, questions not experimentally analyzed in v4. The earlier MNIST sensitivity and case-study analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V5 continues to report point estimates for the additional experiments.

E6.justification: The original AA-Score correlations and spurious-correlation intervention results remain unchanged. Added DVEmb results give MNIST averages of 0.9417 versus AA-Score's retained 0.9456; AA-Score exceeds DVEmb in eight of nine Table 2 entries, with X-ray Stage 1 the exception. New Tables 3–5 report runtime, memory, and scaling correlations, while Figures 6–7 add backdoor-attribution findings.

M1.justification: The stage-skipping formulation, momentum-aware propagator, summed single-step estimator, and gradient-dot-product AA-Score remain. Appendix C.1 adds an optional within-layer block approximation that discards cross-block interactions, extending v4's layer-wise and selected-layer approximations. This is a limited computational variant, without evidence of a replacement of the core algorithm.

P1.justification: The main text undergoes extensive paragraph editing and terminology refinement, including replacing stage-embedding language with stage representations. Estimator accuracy receives a dedicated subsection, interpolation detail moves into Appendix A, computational discussion moves and expands into Appendix C, and the discussion/impact organization changes. These exceed edits attributable solely to added experiments.

P2.justification: V5 replaces the single-column preprint main text with a two-column conference layout and revises title, headers, typography, and figure placement. Figures 1–2 receive revised labels, Tables 1–2 gain comparator structure, and three runtime/scaling tables plus two backdoor figures are added. The earlier detailed X-ray table survives as Table 6.

R1.justification: V5 adds references covering SGD-Influence, Data Banzhaf, group attribution, ensembling, a data-attribution survey, Pythia, BadNets, and BackdoorBench; Cook–Weisberg and Martens references disappear. The positioning relative to causal responsibility, learning dynamics, and data attribution remains, including DVEmb as the closest prior work.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 changes from a bound on final-state estimation error to a bound on performance-effect estimation error. V5 adds stability assumptions on the actual update maps and bounded first and second derivatives of the performance function. Appendix B replaces the earlier single-step/state-error argument with a substantially rewritten stage-level proof and an effective constant incorporating performance derivatives and the remaining training horizon.

improvement.justification: V4 lacked an evaluated attribution baseline and measured computational costs. V5 addresses both important gaps through Tables 1–5, demonstrates a concrete failure boundary under mixed poisoning, and better calibrates mitigation claims as diagnostic guidance. These changes substantially strengthen the empirical support and practical interpretation of the work. Losing the explicit Hessian-approximation description reduces reproducibility detail, but does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same accountability-attribution framework. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: V5 retains these original results and adds DVEmb comparisons, runtime and memory measurements, scaling experiments, and backdoor-attribution experiments.

before.justification: V4 reports original attribution experiments on MNIST, CelebA, CivilComments, and chest X-ray datasets, including counterfactual-retraining correlations and stage-removal results.

results.title: Who Gets Credit or Blame? Attributing Accountability in Modern AI Systems

C1.justification: The central claim of scalable hierarchical joint topology/feature generation for graphs and hypergraphs remains. v3 tempers the abstract's state-of-the-art claim to competitive or state-of-the-art performance, explicitly emphasizes quasi-linear complexity, and adds a claimed gradient-signal benefit to the conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 adds the explanation that stationary regions dominate the learning objective and that masking preserves useful refinement gradients (Section 4). It also extends the mesh interpretation to comparisons with naive joint generators. Limitations concerning large structures, richer attributes, and computational expense remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds an open-source code link, AdamW and its learning rate, Heun integration, dataset-specific spectral or random conditioning details, explicit loss masks, and parameter counts and training instructions for new mesh baselines. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v2.

E1.justification: v3 retains the original datasets and adds five unfeatured graph benchmarks: SBM, Tree, Planar, Protein, and household-object point clouds (Appendix E.3). These extend task and domain coverage; the ordinary SBM and Tree graphs are distinct from the retained hypergraph datasets.

E2.justification: Mesh comparisons expand from the sequential baseline alone to include WGAN, Flow Matching, and VAE (Table 7 in both versions). v3 also introduces reported graph comparisons with HSpectre and BwR. Its Table 3 adds a Flow Matching OOM entry for featured point clouds, although Appendix Table 9 omits that row.

E3.justification: v2 Appendix D specifies 25 sampling steps throughout; v3 Appendix E specifies 256 for unfeatured hypergraphs and featured point clouds, retaining 25 for meshes. v3 also introduces coverage/diversity metrics, protocols for the added graph benchmarks, and 100-epoch training for new mesh baselines. The sampling-budget revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original budget/OT ablations remain, including those moved out of the main text. v3 adds a focused comparison of random, feature-preserving, and spectrum-preserving coarsening on both mesh categories (Table 12), and extends existing mesh ablations with coverage/diversity measurements.

E5.justification: v3 Table 7 first supplies uncertainty for the existing sequential mesh baseline, which had point estimates in v2. Both appendices already define reported uncertainty as twice the standard deviation over five runs; no increase in run count is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds graph benchmark results, mesh comparator outcomes, coverage/diversity scores, and coarsening results. In appendix Table 7, sequential ChamDist changes from 0.143 to 0.082±0.074 for Airplane and from 0.117 to 0.169±0.007 for Bench. Corresponding FAHNES values remain 0.048±0.003 and 0.064±0.005; most original FAHNES results are retained.

M1.justification: The core algorithm is retained: hierarchical scale encoding renames node budgets, and explicit masked losses elaborate existing inpainting. A limited reported extension appears in v3 Section 4: optional Dirichlet feature priors and projection for simplex-valued attributes, whereas v2 specifies Gaussian feature priors.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively rewritten and terminology changes throughout. Implementation becomes a dedicated Section 4, the probabilistic derivation moves into a new Appendix A, and the remaining sections and appendices are reorganized. Impact and acknowledgment statements are also added.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column conference layout. Hypergraph summary tables are merged, graph and mesh comparison tables are added, and ablation displays and metric columns are reorganized. Figure 3 gains point-cloud coarsening sequences, while the final appendix adds graph-generation visualizations.

R1.justification: Related work adds hierarchical molecular generators, including MolGrow, MolHF, and Qiang et al., distinguishing FAHNES through domain generality and scalability. Additional references support WGAN, BwR, and graph datasets. This is a focused expansion of the retained research positioning.

T1.justification: v3 replaces the shorter-path proposition with a displacement-variance reduction proposition and proof, and adds a gradient-signal proposition and proof (Appendices B.2–B.3). It also revises total generation complexity from O(n+m+k) to O((n+m+k) log n), comparing v2 Appendix G with v3 Appendix H.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's limited comparative evidence by adding several joint mesh generators and scored comparisons on five unfeatured graph benchmarks. Coverage/diversity measurements, coarsening controls, and fuller implementation documentation make the framework easier to assess and reproduce. The unexplained sampling-budget revision and discrepancies between some summary and appendix values remain weaknesses, but the expanded evidence resolves important evaluation gaps and provides a clear overall gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FAHNES and provide readable text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Renamed components and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains original FAHNES experiments and adds unfeatured graph benchmark results and coarsening ablations in Section 5 and Appendix I.

before.justification: v2 reports original generation experiments on hypergraphs, 3D meshes, and featured graph point clouds, including component ablations in Section 4 and Appendix H.

results.title: Feature-Aware (Hyper)graph Generation via Next-Scale Prediction

C1.justification: The abstract shifts from saying TPG attains low bias and variance to describing a favorable balance relative to existing approaches. The introduction's theoretical contribution now emphasizes variance reduction at the cost of controlled mixing bias. The principal TPG, CLT, and HAC contributions remain.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds an explicit distinction between mixing's control of bias and truncation's variance reduction, with additional interpretation in Section 7. Appendix B interprets the new sensitivity results as robustness to alpha, but its new statement that larger alpha delays stopping conflicts with Algorithm 1 and Table 3's decreasing selected k.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly specifies alpha=1 as the default, explains its approximate confidence-level interpretation, and documents the sensitivity thresholds and RMSE calculation. V2 only suggested practitioner calibration, giving alpha=1.96 as an example; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. Simulator, hardware, and code-access disclosures remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same two-state MDP, hospital-arrival queueing simulation, and Manhattan ride-sharing simulation. The new diagnostics use the existing queueing case study without adding a dataset, domain, or task scenario.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain DM, untruncated PG, stationary DQ, LSTD-OPE/OPE, and bias-corrected switchback estimators. Comparator membership in Table 1 and Figures 4 and 6 is unchanged; the new tables assess TPG itself.

E3.justification: Table 2 introduces nominal 95% confidence-interval coverage evaluation across k=2–7. Appendix B adds a four-threshold sensitivity protocol using median selected k and RMSE against the queueing GATE. Existing simulation horizons and experimental designs are retained.

E4.justification: The later version adds confidence-interval calibration checks and an analysis of sensitivity to the truncation-selection threshold alpha. These extend the existing variance-validation and truncation analyses within the queueing case study.

E5.justification: Table 2 adds empirical coverage reporting for nominal 95% HAC confidence intervals, extending v2's variance and standard-error reporting. The HAC construction and existing simulation repetition counts remain unchanged; no increase in runs is documented.

E6.justification: New Table 2 reports coverage ranging from 2.0% at k=2 to 94.6% at k=5. New Table 3 reports median selected k values of 5, 4, 4, and 3, with RMSEs 0.043, 0.039, 0.040, and 0.050 across increasing alpha. Table 1 and the existing empirical plots retain their results.

M1.justification: The TPG computation in Equation 3, HAC estimator, and Algorithm 1 stopping rule are retained. Corrections to hypothetical-policy definitions and proofs change the theoretical account without changing the computed estimator.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution framing receive focused edits, and explanatory passages expand in Sections 4 and 7 and Appendix B. Lemma 2's proof moves from Appendix F to A.4, with heading and acknowledgment edits. The main section sequence and most prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 adds two tables, reformats Algorithm 1 with explicit end blocks, and removes the O(T²) and O(k²) annotations from Figure 1. Several displays move with text reflow; the existing empirical figures retain their content.

R1.justification: The reference list and related-work discussion are unchanged, including positioning relative to DQ, OPE, and switchback experiments. Adding Farias et al. (2022) to the Appendix C heading repeats an existing attribution.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 replaces the k²δ²M bias term with [(1−γ^k)/(1−γ)²]δ²M, and Proposition 2 removes the TδM term. Section 5 corrects hypothetical-policy indexing and the bias decomposition; Appendix E.3 restores missing 1/T factors. Assumption 2 now requires positive asymptotic variance, and Assumption 3 tightens Δ_T² from o(T^−1/3) to o(T^−2/3). Appendix A restricts the mixing lemma to Bernoulli policies, while Appendices D–F substantially revise perturbation, variance, and CLT arguments.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens support for the central theoretical guarantees: the revised CLT proof establishes contraction for a shifted augmented chain, the HAC assumption now matches the rate used in its proof, and variance and normalization errors are corrected. Sharper bias arguments and new calibration checks further improve the paper. The stronger assumptions narrow the guarantees, and Appendix B introduces incorrect guidance about alpha's stopping direction, but these drawbacks are outweighed by repairs to the central mathematical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TPG estimator research, with matching title and authors. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: The original simulation results remain, supplemented by confidence-interval coverage results and a truncation-selection sensitivity study.

before.justification: Section 7 and Appendix G report original simulations of a two-state nonstationary MDP, patient queues, and NYC ride-sharing, including estimator errors and variance comparisons.

results.title: Estimation of Treatment Effects Under Nonstationarity via the Truncated Policy Gradient Estimator

C1.justification: V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly emphasize linear convergence, superiority in rate over symmetric perturbation approaches, and a parameter-free construction retaining that rate. The extensive-form contribution changes from CFR+ to dilated gradient updates. The impossibility result remains but loses its former prominence as a headline contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly interprets the new sensitivity results as an accuracy-versus-convergence-speed tradeoff and explains why perturbation halving needs only finitely many stages. Behavioral-form extensions become future work rather than demonstrated applicability, and Markov games are proposed as another extension. The underlying equilibrium-invariance intuition remains.

D1.justification: V2 documents LiteEFG instead of OpenSpiel, adds game-specific learning rates and perturbation strengths in Table 4, specifies unweighted dilated regularizers, and supplies detailed stopping and initialization pseudocode for the new procedure. Hardware information remains unchanged. V1's statement that source code accompanies supplementary material is absent from v2.

E1.justification: Extensive-form coverage decreases from six games to five through removal of six-sided Liar's Dice. The other poker, dice, and Goofspiel cases and the BMP, BRPS, and M-Ne normal-form games remain; changing their strategy representation does not itself add task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated DMWU, DGDA, DOMWU, DOGDA, and SymP-DGDA comparators. SymP-CFR+ and the adaptive symmetric comparators disappear. CFR, CFR+, DCFR, and LCFR remain in Appendix A.5, while the normal-form baseline set in Figure 6 is unchanged.

E3.justification: V1 evaluates extensive-form last-iterate strategies against iterations, using mu = 0.01 for the perturbed CFR+ methods. V2 introduces separately tuned method/game settings and measures strategy-update counts. Appendix A.5 evaluates averaged CFR strategies against last-iterate perturbed strategies, substantially changing the comparison protocol.

E4.justification: V1's investigations of whether adaptive anchoring improves convergence under large perturbations, in both normal-form and extensive-form games, are removed. V2 adds convergence sensitivity curves for mu in {0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 4} on BRPS and M-Ne. The earlier BRPS trajectory sensitivity analysis remains.

E5.justification: Both versions retain 100 random initializations and standard-error shading for the normal-form comparison in Appendix A.3/Figure 6. The deleted anchoring comparison used the same reporting practice; v2 introduces no different repeated-run protocol, uncertainty estimator, or significance test.

E6.justification: The extensive-form and anchoring results are substantially replaced by AsymP-DGDA comparisons and new sensitivity curves. V2 Figure 9 reports an advantage over averaged CFR baselines on most games, with Leduc Poker as an exception. These are results under changed methods and protocols, not same-setting gains over v1; Figure 6's normal-form results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The basic AsymP-GDA update remains unchanged. However, v2 replaces the adaptive anchoring variants with a procedure using perturbation halving and gap-based stopping, and replaces AsymP-CFR+ with AsymP-DGDA using a dilated Euclidean regularizer for both perturbation and proximal updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and substantial portions of Sections 4–5 are rewritten. Symmetric-perturbation background moves into the preliminaries, its impossibility analysis moves to an appendix, and the method and proof narrative is reorganized. The NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: The extensive-form figures become five-panel displays with shared legends and linear strategy-update axes instead of the earlier six-panel iteration plots. Figures 8–9 are replaced, Table 4 is added, and Algorithm 1 is rebuilt. Figures 1 and 5 additionally highlight the equilibrium-invariance regime.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reframes its relationship to prior work through an explicit distinction from Nesterov smoothing and a linear-rate comparison with Liu et al. (2023). It adds positioning and references around dilated sequence-form methods, including Hoda, Farina, and Kroer, alongside new mathematical references supporting the revised proof.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 changes from O(1/t) to linear convergence through a new piecewise-affine/Hoffman error-bound proof. V2 adds Theorem 4.3 and its O(log(1/epsilon)) complexity analysis, removes the anchoring theorem and proofs, and revises sufficient perturbation and step-size bounds. The symmetric impossibility results are retained in relocated appendices.

improvement.justification: The new Appendix F supplies a geometric error-bound analysis supporting linear convergence of the unchanged base update, substantially strengthening the theoretical account. V2 also addresses the unknown perturbation threshold algorithmically and improves empirical comparisons through averaged CFR baselines, strategy-update accounting, and detailed hyperparameters. These gains outweigh the loss of anchoring experiments and one game variant, although the new parameter-free procedure lacks empirical validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same asymmetric-perturbation research. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 retains original normal-form simulations and reports dilated-method comparisons in extensive-form games and additional perturbation-sensitivity results.

before.justification: V1 reports original convergence simulations in normal-form and extensive-form games, including experiments on adaptive anchoring in Appendix C.

results.title: Asymmetric Perturbation in Solving Bilinear Saddle-Point Optimization

C1.justification: V1's central guarantee concerns full-history reuse and explicitly leaves finite-storage theory for future work. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion make the window-dependent partial-reuse guarantee a central contribution while retaining the best-known full-reuse rate.

C2.justification: V2 explains that a fixed reuse window retains the epsilon^-2 exponent and introduces batch-size and memory tradeoffs. It distinguishes target, cross-time, and PM biases more explicitly. Experimental interpretation now addresses uniform-weight instability and BH-PG's competitive performance with storage costs, and softens v1's claim of consistently escaping Swimmer's local optimum.

D1.justification: V2 extends hyperparameter documentation to the added baselines and specifies the revised practical coefficients. Hardware changes from a Ryzen 7800X3D with 32 GB RAM to an Apple M4 with 16 GB RAM, with eight workers specified for timing comparisons. The direct public code pointer is replaced by a statement about supplementary code and release upon acceptance.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Continuous Cart Pole, Swimmer-v4, and HalfCheetah-v4 with the same control-task requirements. The additional experiments vary configurations and comparison methods within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds MIW-PG with uniform weighting and BH-PG to the comparisons on all three environments and to the window-sensitivity study. V1 compared against GPOMDP, SVRPG, SRVRPG, STORM-PG, and DEF-PG only. The additions directly compare alternative trajectory-reuse estimators.

E3.justification: V2 adds a Cart Pole design crossing total gradient-batch sizes 32, 64, and 128 with reuse windows 2, 4, and 8, plus curve-alignment speedup and matched-data runtime protocols. Retained Cart Pole studies report zero initialization instead of standard-normal initialization. The original batch-size comparison remains in Appendix G.3; these reported setting changes do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The window-sensitivity analysis expands from RPG alone over windows 2–32 to RT-PG, MIW-PG, and BH-PG over windows 2–64, testing how weighting affects saturation and instability. V2 also adds systematic measurements of sample-efficiency benefits versus runtime costs across reuse configurations, extending v1's limited timing examples.

E5.justification: The existing practice of reporting means with 95% confidence intervals over 10 Cart Pole/Half Cheetah runs and five Swimmer runs is retained. V2 adds reported confidence intervals for fitted speedup factors, constructed using 97.5% curve bounds in Appendix G.3.1, and mean-plus-standard-deviation runtime reporting in Table 3b.

E6.justification: V2 adds MIW-PG/BH-PG curves and Table 3's speedup/runtime results, including a 2.11 sample-efficiency ratio at window 2 and total gradient-batch size 32. The reported window-sensitivity saturation shifts from around 8 to around 16 under revised settings. Half Cheetah comparisons now include competitive BH-PG performance. Timing measurements use different hardware and configurations, preventing direct across-version speed comparisons.

M1.justification: Finite-window reuse and adaptive divergence weighting already existed in v1 Appendix E. However, Algorithm 2 revises the practical PM coefficient from a confidence-dependent schedule involving iteration count k to lambda_i,k = 1/sqrt(Dhat_i N omega_k), removing delta. The theoretical prescription also changes to uniform mixing coefficients. These are limited weighting revisions within the retained estimator family.

P1.justification: The introduction and technical narrative are extensively rewritten. The combined method discussion becomes separate trajectory-reuse challenges and estimator/algorithm sections, and the appendix structure is reorganized around memory, bias proofs, and convergence analysis. RPG/PM terminology changes throughout to RT-PG/MPM.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces the two detailed dependency diagrams with a compact update graph, and redesigns experimental plots and comparator tables. It adds estimator, memory, speedup, and runtime tables. The original matched-batch Cart Pole comparison is retained in the appendix, while the main text presents new panels.

R1.justification: V2 discusses RNPG's asymptotic natural-policy-gradient guarantees and positions its own contribution as finite-time trajectory-reuse analysis. New Appendix A/Table 4 substantially extends comparisons to trajectory memory and stored policies, claiming an advantage from avoiding extra policy storage. PAGE-PG and additional bias-related prior work are also incorporated.

T1.justification: V2 extends the full-history analysis to finite-window concentration and an O-tilde(epsilon^-2 / omega) partial-reuse sample bound, retaining O-tilde(epsilon^-1) for full reuse. It adds explicit batch-size conditions ensuring valid PM coefficients, formal target/cross-time bias arguments in Appendix C, and an expected-estimation-error lemma with revised convergence proofs in Appendices D–E.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses v1's explicitly open finite-window theory problem for the deterministic-coefficient algorithm and adds direct trajectory-reuse comparisons that better test the proposed estimator. Explicit batch-size conditions, runtime tradeoffs, and acknowledgment of competitive BH-PG performance substantially improve scope and interpretation. The less direct public code-access information is a reproducibility drawback, but it does not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching title and authors. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial renaming and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on the same environments, including expanded baseline comparisons and sample-efficiency/runtime measurements in Section 7 and Appendix G.

before.justification: V1 reports original policy-gradient experiments on Continuous Cart Pole, Swimmer-v4, and HalfCheetah-v4 in Section 6 and Appendix F.

results.title: Reusing Trajectories in Policy Gradients Enables Fast Convergence

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: dense rewards learned from passive-video temporal distances, strong sparse-reward RL performance on nine of ten Meta-World tasks within 200,000 interactions, superiority over comparison rewards, and transfer from human videos. Additional evidence does not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: V1 briefly acknowledges difficulty with back-and-forth motion; v2 explains it through visually identical observations with different remaining distances and discusses history-based disambiguation. V2 also adds interpretations involving goal-conditioned representation collapse, PROGRESSOR's structural limitations, and insufficient pre-contact feedback from environment rewards. These substantially expand mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents choosing alpha as ten times the maximum dense reward over the first 100 trajectories, the closest-demonstration rule for ILfO, and use of the first 100 ManiSkill demonstrations. These are documentation additions, not established changes to earlier experiments. The hyperparameter tables retain their values. V1's project-page link is omitted, without establishing that the resource itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: Appendix A.4.9 adds PushCube-v1 from ManiSkill3, extending evaluation to another simulator's dynamics and rendering through one manipulation task. The ten Meta-World tasks and three human-video tasks remain. The additional 100-robot-plus-20-human experiment reuses existing task and domain coverage.

The original main baselines remain; GVL in the VOC comparison and BCO in the proxy-only experiment were already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols compare pretrained versus scratch ViT-B, fixed alpha values of 0.1/0.5/1 versus adaptive weighting, K=10/20/30, and 100 robot demonstrations plus 20 human videos. V2 also explicitly assigns CLIP-pretrained ViT-B to all main progress-based baselines, whereas v1 discusses VIP's ViT retraining in the appendix. Both VIP backbones were already evaluated in v1; this does not establish new runs.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation PCA across demonstrations and successful/failed rollouts, reward-weight and discretization-bin sensitivity tests, a pretraining ablation, negative sampling for PROGRESSOR, and human-video augmentation with abundant robot demonstrations. These investigate previously untested robustness and mechanism questions. The existing component ablations, VIP-backbone analysis, and proxy-only experiment are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report RL curves as mean plus or minus standard deviation over eight seeds. V2's added experiments follow the same practice; no changed run counts, confidence-interval procedures, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including PROGRESSOR's improvement from negative sampling on window-close and drawer-open but not stick-push or basketball, and performance on ManiSkill3. Figure 4 replaces Rank2Reward's noisy basketball outputs with curves separating successful and failed rollouts. Main-comparison VIP curves also change alongside the revised backbone specification, so they do not establish a same-setting gain. Figure 3's VOC values and the headline 9/10-task claim remain.

M1.justification: Section 4.1, Equation 4 replaces exponential interval sampling, proportional to exp(-lambda*Delta), with reciprocal sampling proportional to 1/Delta. The signed temporal-distance target, two-hot objective, and frozen reward model remain. V2 also introduces a feature-difference variant specifically for representation analysis; the default model still concatenates features.

P1.justification: The six main sections and much of the prose remain. V2 locally rewrites the introduction, related work, and ablation explanations, corrects wording, adds impact and acknowledgment sections, and reorganizes the appendix around the additional proof and experiments. This is a limited narrative revision alongside the substantive additions.

P2.justification: V2 converts the main text from one column to two, redraws the overview, revises the framework display, and substantially resizes and relocates existing plots. It adds eight figures, including PCA and the new experimental comparisons, and updates captions, axes, and legends. Both hyperparameter tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to temporal cycle-consistency learning, Arrow of Time, TemporalOT, ORCA, and ManiSkill3. It refines progress-based positioning around goal conditioning, signed temporal distances, and VIP's objective, replacing some emphasis on online refinement. The broader related-work categories and most cited literature remain.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 replaces v1's normalized expert-trajectory potential argument with an explicit deterministic MDP, per-step penalty, optimal-value derivation, and exact time-to-go potential at gamma=1. It adds a visual-reconstruction assumption and an aliasing counterexample. New Appendix A.3 derives unboundedness for the stated formulation of VIP's objective.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the retained claims through pretraining and parameter controls, additional OT comparisons, and a strengthened PROGRESSOR baseline. Section 4.3 makes theoretical assumptions and visual-aliasing failures explicit, while the alpha-selection disclosure improves reproducibility. The PCA uses a modified model, and the additional simulator covers only one task, limiting some interpretations. These limitations and the omitted project link do not outweigh the gains in empirical support and theoretical clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TimeRewarder and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Their retained content can be matched across the revised layout and numbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds representation analyses, controlled experiments, additional baseline comparisons, and a ManiSkill3 evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original Meta-World policy-learning results, progress-estimation evaluations, human-video transfer experiments, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

This revises application emphasis and claim scope.

It expands v1's qualitative confidence-level check into a wider numerical sweep in Tables 8–10. Existing noise, global-factor, portfolio-size, and rebalancing-frequency analyses are retained.

The notation paragraph and future-work discussion disappear, and references move before the appendices.

P2.justification: V3 adds a conceptual subspace diagram, face-result tables, sensitivity tables, and a runtime table. Existing comparison plots gain curves and revised legends, tables expand or change orientation, and heatmaps and financial graphics are relocated and resized. V3 also supplies a populated financial-metrics table where v1 displays only a caption.

R1.justification: Literature coverage is substantially rebalanced: v1's financial-network and graph-filtering discussion and associated references disappear, while v3 distinguishes variable clustering from co-clustering and adds face-subspace, EnSC/OMP, ADMM-convergence, and randomized-SVD literature. The original claim of first applying DRO to nodewise regression and subspace clustering remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1 changes from an upper bound alone to a two-sided bound, f(B)/2 <= DRO objective <= f(B), with a new lower-bound derivation in Appendix A.2. This quantifies the relaxation's approximation quality. The radius-selection theorem and assumptions are retained after relocation from v1 Section 3.3 to v3 Appendix B.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens assessability: Theorem 3.1 quantifies the previously unbounded relaxation gap, relevant additional baselines and face experiments broaden validation, and sensitivity tables with dispersion test practical dependencies. Code disclosures improve reproducibility, while expanded portfolio comparisons expose limits to superiority. Removing the finite-sample caveat and using default settings for several new baselines weaken interpretation, but do not outweigh these substantial theoretical and empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their main text and appendices support extensive comparison. However, v1 page 21 contains the caption for portfolio Table 2 without its table body, confirmed by visual rendering. This prevents complete comparison of those financial metrics with v3 Table 3.

after.justification: V3 reports original simulations, face-image clustering, financial backtests, sensitivity experiments, and runtime measurements in Sections 4–6 and Appendices C–D.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic clustering experiments and financial portfolio backtests in Sections 4–5 and Appendix B, including AMI scores and Sharpe ratios.

results.title: Variable Clustering via Distributionally Robust Nodewise Regression

C1.justification: The central claim that evolutionary search discovers superior finite-accuracy approximations remains. V2 explicitly presents the contribution as a systems demonstration combining known techniques, disclaims introducing a new search algorithm, qualifies zero-knowledge search to bounded intervals, and extends the contribution statement to additional operation sets.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive discussion of the interpretability–quality tradeoff, dependence on externally supplied range reduction, and forward versus backward stability. It explicitly rejects universal superiority across target functions and states the higher-accuracy erf failure relative to Padé. The compiler-based speedup explanation and basic compute-amortization argument are retained.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a project-code link, states that proof scripts are available, prints additional discovered programs, and reports 6,000 and 9,600 core-days for the principal searches. However, it removes v1's custom crowding and staged-selection specification, including detailed pseudocode and settings such as S = 20. Reproducibility information therefore changes substantially in both directions.
