E1.justification: V2 adds cosine and modified Bessel approximation and removes v1's float32 logarithm experiment. It also replaces the vertically shifted Airy target 1 + Ai(-7x) with Ai(-7x), introducing zero crossings into that approximation task. Exponential and error-function coverage remains.

E2.justification: The principal exponential comparator sets remain unchanged. V2 adds Frobenius and a tailored, square-root-factored Chebyshev baseline for Bessel (Section 4.4), plus random-search controls in the ablations (Section 4.8). Cosine extends evaluation of the existing Chebyshev comparator.

E3.justification: V2 uses absolute rather than relative error for Airy and erf, introduces component-removal controls, and changes the stated training sampling from 1,000 evenly spaced inputs to uniformly random inputs. The bulk-test prescription changes from 1,000 times the validation-set size to 100 times (v1 Section 4.5; v2 Appendix A.10). These reported protocol revisions do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit ablations of population selection, coefficient optimization, and mutations, reporting worse outcomes for each (Section 4.8; Figure 9). Appendix D adds cross-experiment examples of convergent program structure. Conversely, v1's search-progress analysis, code-bloat case study, and sensitivity observations about perturbing the fast exponential program disappear. Hardware-transfer testing remains.

E5.justification: V2 retains timing error bars but drops v1 Figure 3's explanation that uncertainty represents ±2SEM. It also omits the 100-repeat interleaved timing procedure described in v1 Section 4.5, while retaining general ten-repeat timing measurements. This establishes reduced statistical documentation, not that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: V2 adds cosine, Bessel, and ablation outcomes; its tailored Bessel comparison reports accuracy 7.8 with nine operations versus evolved accuracy 8.1 with eight. Airy's 20-operation, 4.7 relative-error accuracy is replaced by a 19-operation, 4.2 absolute-error accuracy under changed conditions. Logarithm results disappear, and erf now explicitly favors Padé at higher accuracies. The principal exponential curves and real-valued error-bound table remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The graph-mutation, dNSGA-II, and CMA-ES framework remains. V2 extends the available operations with square root for Bessel approximation and changes Airy and error-function coefficient optimization from relative to absolute error (Section 4.4; Appendix A.5). These are bounded adaptations of the existing method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methods explanation, results narrative, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes an early standalone section, a methods outline precedes results, detailed methods move into Appendix A, and advantages, limitations, and conclusion receive separate treatment. This substantially changes the document's organization and exposition.

P2.justification: V2 adds overview and workflow diagrams, cosine/Bessel plots, ablation plots, and several program-listing figures. It removes the search-progress and bloat displays, redistributes the real-exponential illustration, and moves the floating-point program illustration to Appendix Figure 15. Retained exponential plots receive revised styling, labels, and captions.

R1.justification: V2 adds specific comparisons with accuracy-improving program methods by Panchekha et al. and Damouche and Martel, examples of evolutionary-computation applications, and references supporting its expanded verification. It retains the main positioning relative to symbolic regression, reinforcement-learning discovery, and superoptimization.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 adds checks of individual division denominators and handles removable singularities at zero. Appendices B.3–B.4 introduce a floating-point error decomposition using Gappa and exhaustive evaluation, report a 0.654-ULP bound, and discuss stability. Appendix A.1 also corrects the range-reduction pseudocode. The earlier real-valued error bounds are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through component ablations, broader approximation tasks, and expanded domain and floating-point error arguments. Reported code/proof-script access and quantified compute costs improve auditability, while the reorganized narrative clarifies applicability. Some selection and uncertainty details are lost, and Appendix B.3 contains notation errors, including ulp(2^x) >= 1. Nevertheless, the added controls and clearer mathematical scope address important gaps in v1 and provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AutoNumerics-Zero and retain identifiable methods, programs, and exponential experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, supporting comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 retains original exponential experiments and reports additional cosine, Bessel, and component-ablation results in Sections 4.2, 4.4, and 4.8.

before.justification: V1 reports original evolutionary-search experiments, approximation errors, execution-speed measurements, and hardware-transfer results, including Figures 1–6.

results.title: AutoNumerics-Zero: Automated Discovery of State-of-the-Art Mathematical Functions

C1.justification: v2 removes the explicit claim to be the first work on multi-level non-IID federated learning and replaces claims about approximating arbitrary structures with diverse complex structures. The central contributions—additive personalization, adaptive hierarchical training, convergence analysis, and advantages over clustered and personalized FL—remain.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets clustering as sampling candidate sharing structures and discusses resource-dependent depth and parallel inference. Section 6 explicitly identifies untested alternative level-wise methods, unexplored interactions, and the limited scale and difficulty of the language evaluation. Conversely, v1 Appendix C.5's specific discussion of FedProx's superior IID results is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds substantial reproducibility information for the language experiment, including rank-4 LoRA on query/value projections, disabled thinking mode, sequence-length filtering, per-client sample counts, and a task list. It also documents new baseline configurations, including FedCAM initialization and FedEM's five models. Existing image splits, learning rate, and the code-access URL are retained.

E1.justification: v2 retains the image-classification datasets and adds a simulated language setting with 71 reported FLAN-T5/LoraHub tasks assigned to separate clients. Appendix B includes classification, question answering, generation, reasoning, editing, and translation tasks, substantially extending the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds evaluated FedEM, pFedMoE, FedCAM, and PM-MoE comparisons, while removing PFedMe and FeSEM+ columns. FedProx and FedRep, evaluated in v1 Appendix C, also disappear from the reported comparisons. Local, FedAvg, FedAvg+, Ditto, and FeSEM remain. This substantially changes the comparator set, including closer additive and mixture-model competitors.

E3.justification: The new language evaluation introduces Qwen3-4B with LoRA, 71 clients, 100 communication rounds, one local epoch, 300/50/150 training/validation/test examples per client, and ROUGE-1 evaluation. New experiments vary hierarchy depth and cluster counts. The principal image splits and 50-client setup remain, but several additional image-partition configurations reported in v1 are removed.

E4.justification: v1's component-removal ablation in Table 2 disappears. v2 adds depth sensitivity in Figure 6, cluster-count sensitivity in Table 3, an inference-storage comparison in Table 4, and language-client model-count analysis in Figure 8. Some extensive per-partition structure and convergence analyses from v1 Appendix C are removed; the representative Figure A.1 analysis is retained.

E5.justification: The main image comparisons retain mean and standard deviation over four runs. v2 explicitly displays a standard-deviation band for depth sensitivity, whereas v1's component ablation reports point differences. The new language results report four-run means without dispersion. Neither version establishes an increased run count or introduces significance testing.

E6.justification: Shared main-table FeMAM scores are retained, but many comparator and analysis results are added or removed. For Tiny ImageNet cluster-wise accuracy, FeMAM remains at 46.80%; the strongest listed comparator changes from FeSEM at 41.20% to FedCAM at 46.32%. New Table 5 reports FeMAM loss 1.040 and ROUGE-1 59.25%. The additional image results in v1 Tables C.2–C.4 are no longer fully reported.

M1.justification: The additive hierarchy, sequential training with earlier levels frozen, and validation-based pruning remain. However, v1 Algorithm 2 uses the clustered update in Eq. (B.4), including attraction toward the cluster center. v2 Algorithm 2 instead references the loss-gradient update in Eq. (6), although Eq. (C.3) retains the clustering penalty. The PDFs do not resolve whether the procedure changed or its documentation became inconsistent.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and methodology are extensively rewritten. The method is reorganized around client composition, server aggregation, assignment, sequential optimization, and pruning. Cost discussion moves into the main analysis section, experiments are divided into image and language settings, and a substantive limitations section and reorganized appendices are introduced.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column presentation. v2 replaces or redraws conceptual diagrams, introduces smartphone and residual-composition illustrations, redraws convergence and cost plots, and adds sensitivity, model-count, storage, and language-result displays. Several extensive appendix tables and figure grids are removed, while Figure A.1 is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated discussion of earlier multi-level FL approaches, including Kim et al., Guo et al., and Zhang et al., and distinguishes FeMAM through flexible additive composition rather than claiming the first multi-level formulation. It also substantially expands positioning around mixture models, boosting, and federated foundation models.

T1.justification: v1's convex-loss analysis of clustering and federated objectives is replaced by a substantially different level-wise analysis. v2 Appendix D introduces nonconvex aggregation bounds, assignment-update slack, residual-alignment assumptions, averaged-stationarity bounds, and descent across added levels. The boosting decrease also invokes a prediction-scaling step-size choice in the proof, beyond merely restating the earlier convergence argument.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness in v1 by directly comparing FeMAM with closer additive and mixture-model alternatives. Together with explicit depth/cluster sensitivity tests, language-task evaluation, and more qualified novelty positioning, this substantially strengthens assessment of the central contribution. Some broader image-partition and numerical IID evidence is lost, and the regularization ambiguity and proof-only prediction scaling limit confidence in the revised theory. The principal improvement is stronger empirical scrutiny and clearer positioning, rather than higher retained image scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FeMAM despite the changed title and presentation. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original image experiments and adds sensitivity analyses and a Qwen3-4B/LoRA evaluation on task-partitioned language data, reporting loss and ROUGE-1.

before.justification: v1 reports original Tiny ImageNet and CIFAR-100 experiments, including accuracy, Macro-F1, convergence, component ablations, and computational-cost analyses.

results.title: Personalized Additive Modeling for Multi-level Federated Learning

C1.justification: The central claim of mitigating forgetting through chained backward feature reconstruction remains. However, v2 drops the claimed novel L2-plus-cosine loss contribution, foregrounds competitive operation without saved samples and makes memory optional. The introduction and conclusion also qualify v1's claim of unchanged task training to minimal training modifications.

C2.justification: v2 adds a specific limitation concerning weaker CIFAR10 performance and possible instability in recovering fine-grained features. It develops retention/privacy tradeoffs among RFE variants and distinguishes training from inference resource costs. v1's discussion of previous-task-data dependence and GAN remedies disappears, while long-chain overhead and class-incremental confidence concerns remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project code-availability statement, gated-module dimensions, parameter accounting, implementation names for hyperparameters, ViT training details and execution-time measurements. It also documents auxiliary backbones and float32 memory accounting. Conversely, v1's eight-RTX-A5000 hardware disclosure, per-dataset selected-hyperparameter table and GAN training recipe are removed; these are substantive changes in reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The three underlying benchmarks remain CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and Tiny ImageNet. v2 Table 3 extends class-incremental evaluation to Tiny ImageNet, whereas v1 Table 2 reports that task only on CIFAR100. Longer task sequences and different backbones primarily change protocols within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The controlled comparisons become rehearsal-focused: o-EWC and LwF.mc disappear from the main task-incremental table, and ER-MKD is added. ER and AGEM also enter the CIFAR100 class-incremental comparison, where they were absent in v1. Appendix B.6 adds indirect comparisons with non-rehearsal methods using cited results under different configurations.

E3.justification: Auxiliary-network training changes from 50 epochs at 5e-4 to 40 epochs at 5e-3, and stated hyperparameter search ranges change substantially. The 5,000-sample setting disappears, while longer-sequence evaluations and a pretrained ViT protocol with 30 epochs at 1e-5 are added. v2 also resolves the standard Tiny ImageNet split description to 10 tasks, already specified in v1's appendix despite its conflicting main text.

E4.justification: v1's cosine-loss/regularization ablation and GAN-alignment comparison are removed. v2 adds gated-versus-MLP and end-to-end ablations, taskwise forgetting heatmaps, longer-chain accuracy and representation-error analyses, and timing/memory analyses. The existing PCA investigation is revised from CIFAR10 to CIFAR100 and augmented with quantitative RMSE measurements.

E5.justification: Both versions report results with plus/minus values. v2 Appendix A.4 newly specifies averaging over three runs with different random seeds. This discloses the repetition procedure but does not establish an increase in runs relative to v1; neither version clearly defines the plus/minus statistic.

E6.justification: The principal result tables change extensively. For example, CIFAR100 task-incremental accuracy with 1,000 previous-task samples changes from ILR's 78.53±0.25 in v1 Table 1 to RFE-P's 80.64±0.59 in v2 Table 2, under revised architecture and training rather than identical conditions. RFE-B, Tiny ImageNet class-incremental, ViT, timing and longer-chain results are added; GAN and 5,000-sample results are removed.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming, v2 replaces ILR's compression-and-concatenation architecture with multiplicative projections and sigmoid gates, and replaces squared-L2-plus-cosine alignment with squared L2. Training incorporates current-data feature regularization; the new RFE-B variant also updates earlier retrospectors using replay. The GAN option disappears, while Appendix B.3 introduces an end-to-end training alternative.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change throughout from ILR/rectifiers to RFE/retrospectors. Training-data explanations, contribution statements and experimental narration are substantially rewritten and reorganized. A new experimental appendix restructures the supplementary material; the existing versatility discussion moves from Appendix B to C, and the societal-impacts section disappears.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn for the gated architecture, the PCA display is replaced and augmented with RMSE, and new forgetting heatmaps and accuracy curves appear. Main tables are redesigned to distinguish training/inference parameters and expand class-incremental comparisons. Hyperparameter presentation and the overall journal layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: The existing related-work taxonomy remains, but v2 adds references including ER-MKD, HAT, winning subnetworks, HyperNet and ViT, while removing several GAN-related references. It adds positioning against frozen pretrained-model adaptation and supplementary comparisons with non-rehearsal approaches. Publication and title updates for retained references are not treated as new works.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions of feature matching and feature combination change substantively, and Appendix B.3 supplies additional projection, residual and joint-training formulations. These changes concern algorithmic definitions; neither version develops formal guarantees, theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism through longer-chain accuracy and RMSE analyses, architectural alternatives and a second backbone. Separate training/inference accounting and measured timings address v1's limited practical-cost evaluation, while three-seed reporting improves transparency. Removed loss ablations, direct regularization baselines and selected implementation disclosures are drawbacks, but the stronger validation of chaining behavior and resource tradeoffs provides a clear net improvement beyond higher reported scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continual-learning research, with ILR renamed and revised as RFE. All pages, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification results, longer-sequence experiments, architectural ablations, timing measurements and ViT evaluations in Section 4 and Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments, alignment-data comparisons, representation visualizations and loss ablations in Section 4.

results.title: Retrospective Feature Estimation for Continual Learning

C1.justification: The central contribution remains GPU harvesting through SLO-aware scheduling, layer-wise preemption, and incremental KV management. The abstract and introduction replace advertised gains over Online-Only and vLLM++ with average throughput and tail-latency gains against preemptive serving systems. This revises the principal comparative claim while retaining the overall research objective.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of DistServe-Preemptive's memory pressure and back-pressure, request-length regimes that limit harvesting benefits, and behavior under limited host memory. V1's Section 7 discussion of disaggregated-serving integration, long-context sequence parallelism, and multi-model/PEFT applicability is removed. These materially change the documented mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: Implementation documentation moves from vLLM 0.4.2 to 0.8.4 and adds 16-token KV-page granularity, a gather-and-transfer kernel, pinned-memory signaling, CUDA-graph integration, and polynomial-profiler fitting details. Hardware/software configurations and the safepoint interval change, including eight-layer to four-layer instrumentation. V1's adaptive-checkpoint threshold, customization interfaces, and Ray/multiprocessing discussion are no longer documented.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates BurstGPT alongside LongBench document summarization. V2 retains BurstGPT and explicitly evaluates DuReader benchmarking, MultiNews multi-document summarization, and VCSUM meeting summarization, separately and in mixed workloads. This broadens the reported offline task mix, although v1's unspecified LongBench subsets prevent establishing that every named dataset is newly introduced.

E2.justification: Online-Only remains, and v2's Non-Preemptive baseline corresponds to the priority-based, non-preemptive role of v1's vLLM++. V2 additionally evaluates Sarathi-Preemptive and DistServe-Preemptive, including modified co-serving schedulers and tuned prefill/decode allocation. These are substantive comparator additions, not merely newly cited systems.

E3.justification: Evaluation changes from Llama-2-7B on an A100 to Llama-3.1 8B, Qwen-2.5 14B, and Llama-3.1 70B on one or four H100s. Synthetic defaults change from 1024/128 input/output tokens and CV=1 to 4096/256 and CV=0.5; v2 adds scaled-SLO attainment and length sweeps with inversely adjusted request rates. Its throughput definition explicitly includes prefill and decode tokens, whereas v1 describes generated-token throughput. TPOT becoming TBT preserves the per-token latency definition.

E4.justification: V2 adds SLO-slack and input/output-length sensitivity studies, a utilization-versus-load analysis, and KV-transfer microbenchmarks. Its ablation separately isolates layer-wise preemption and evaluates checkpointing/prefetching together as KV management, revising v1's component progression. V1's dedicated abrupt ON/OFF load experiment in Section 6.3.1 and Figure 6 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. P99 latencies, workload CVs, and additional result averages do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: V1's Llama-2/A100 results are replaced by extensive results under revised settings, including multi-model curves and dataset-specific entries. For example, v2 Table 2 reports ConServe's mixed-workload Llama-3.1 70B results as 1.14 s P99 TTFT, 201 ms P99 TBT, and 1553 tokens/s offline throughput. Changed hardware, models, workloads, and throughput definitions prevent interpreting these as same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: V1 restricts layer-wise preemption to offline-only batches and aborts their remaining execution. V2 Section 4.3 describes removing offline requests from mixed batches while continuing online execution, substantially extending worker behavior. V2 also selects offline batch sizes using its performance model, replacing v1's stated policy of choosing the largest batch that saturates resources.

P1.justification: The title, author list, abstract, introduction, motivation, and design narrative are extensively revised. SLO-aware scheduling moves from Section 4.5 into Section 4.2, serving-system background is consolidated into related work, evaluation is reorganized, and the standalone discussion section disappears. These are substantial narrative and structural changes.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the architecture and checkpointing diagrams, adds workload and result tables, and expands plots to five systems and a three-model request-rate/SLO grid. V1's ON/OFF plot and ablation bar chart disappear, with revised ablation findings presented in prose. The original load trace is retained, while obsolete 'Concerto' plot labels are replaced with ConServe.

R1.justification: V2 substantially reframes positioning around GPU harvesting and inference/fine-tuning co-serving, adding works such as FlexLLM, ServerlessLLM, BlendServe, and SGLang. It removes v1's extended algorithm/architecture-optimization and deep-learning-scheduler surveys. Disaggregated serving receives stronger criticism through evaluated limitations, replacing much of v1's compatibility and future-integration emphasis.

T1.justification: V1 discusses attention complexity and empirical profiling without an explicit latency equation. V2 Section 4.2 adds Latency(P,C)=k1P+k2P(P+C)+k3P+k4(P+C)+k5, defining compute/context tokens and the architectural assumptions behind its terms. This adds a mathematical performance model; neither version supplies a formal SLO-guarantee theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V1's evidence relies on one small model and a priority-only co-serving comparator. V2 substantially strengthens scrutiny through preemptive and disaggregated baselines, multi-GPU 70B evaluation, an explicit latency model, and SLO/request-length analyses. These gains outweigh losing the dedicated ON/OFF test and applicability discussion. Reporting inconsistencies remain: Table 1 contradicts the MultiNews task description, and Table 2 implies about a 1.86× average TBT advantage over Sarathi-Preemptive rather than the stated 2.86×.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ConServe and provide readable text, equations, figures, and results supporting comparison. All 18 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2 were inspected; neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original multi-model serving experiments, dataset-specific results, sensitivity analyses, ablations, and implementation microbenchmarks in Sections 3–6.

before.justification: V1 reports original serving experiments, including latency and throughput measurements, burst-response tests, and component ablations in Sections 3 and 6.

results.title: ConServe: Fine-Grained GPU Harvesting for LLM Online and Offline Co-Serving

C1.justification: v2 redefines the token contribution around absolute, count-sensitive global control and adds abstract claims of exceeding 95% of target performance, constant inference time, and superiority to heuristic and omnidirectional baselines. v1 emphasized realistic topologies and CAM-based global coherence without these quantified comparative claims. Partial diffusion remains an existing contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds a counting/density explanation for ACAM and materially qualifies applicability: comparable 32-node performance requires training exposure, networks above 40 nodes are excluded, and throughput is an upper bound excluding routing and multichannel scheduling. Algorithm 2 also acknowledges possible residual disconnection, whereas v1 described correction as ensuring connectivity.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands reproducibility information with feature width, batch size, epoch limit, weight-decay scheduling, early stopping, coordinate normalization, and the 15,000-sample mixed-size retraining procedure. Appendices add detailed generation/correction pseudocode and the physical performance model. Exact simulation parameters remain unavailable and are explicitly identified as proprietary.

E1.justification: v2 extends actual evaluation from topology generation to updates under node movement, testing standard and minor reconfigurations in Section 5.2 and Tables 5–6. v1 proposed these procedures without reporting corresponding experiments. Quantitative 32-node tables expand evidence for a network size already mentioned as tested in v1.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's graph-transformer and component comparisons, v2 evaluates GraphVAE and GT-VAE in Table 1, and omnidirectional, Huang et al., and MST+greedy comparators in Table 2. It also separately compares CAM and ACAM variants. These are evaluated additions, rather than citation changes or simple baseline renaming.

E3.justification: Reported settings change from 10 to 5 transformer blocks and from learning rates of 10^-4–10^-7 to a linear 10^-3–10^-6 schedule. Supervision changes from greedy construction to quasi-exhaustive search with a greedy fallback. v2 replaces per-user throughput reporting with link and sum-rate measures, introduces mobility-testing protocols, and specifies mixed 16/32-node retraining in Appendix 9.

E4.justification: v1 already contains architectural-feature and loss ablations. v2 extends these with explicit CAM-versus-ACAM comparisons, token-count sensitivity reporting approximately 0.8% lower saturation with 16 versus 1 tokens, and capacity-related observations. Section 5.2 and Figures 3–4 add continuity/speed analyses and examples of topology reconfiguration under movement.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates only. v2 adds ± values to selected saturation and constraint results in Tables 1 and 3–5 and discloses random seed 123. It does not define those uncertainty quantities or report a repeat count, so the additions do not establish repeated-seed experiments or a specified statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Core results are revised under changed settings: v1 reports 99.13% NetDiff connectivity, whereas v2 reports 98.68% for both CAM and ACAM. New results include NetDiff throughput upper bounds of 78.92 and 322.40 Mbps for 16 and 32 nodes, mobility continuity/speed measurements, and Appendix 9's size results. Isolated-node and range-compliance entries disappear. These changes do not establish controlled cross-version performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 introduces ACAM with unnormalized cosine-similarity aggregation and pooled global FiLM modulation, extending v1's CAM mechanism with node-dependent modulation. The cosine loss gains predicted-edge weighting. Algorithm 2 also changes substantially: parity/interference filtering, throughput-based connectivity repair, and connectivity-preserving pruning replace the simpler sector pruning and distance-based reconnection.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, architecture explanation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work becomes an introduction subsection, network evolution moves before the architecture, and features/losses become a separate section. Generation and correction algorithms move into new appendices. The title, author list, and publication header also change.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, adds a network illustration and two reconfiguration figures, and redraws the CAM architecture as ACAM. The diffusion illustration is retained with a revised caption. Existing benchmark tables are restructured, additional baseline/mobility/size tables appear, and expanded algorithms are relocated to the appendices.

R1.justification: Related work expands from a largely descriptive overview to detailed positioning around node conditioning, permutation invariance, and limitations of autoregressive, spectral, flow, and reinforcement-learning approaches. New discussions include GraphRNN, SPECTRE, DIFUSCO, virtual nodes, and directional-network methods. v2 also distinguishes TopoFormer by its lack of joint topology-parity prediction.

T1.justification: v2 revises the attention and cosine-loss definitions, introduces explicit layout-distribution and perturbation assumptions in Section 2.3, and defines a parity-gated sum-rate/interference model in Appendix 8. These are limited formal-model extensions; neither version supplies theorems or proofs. Fuller joint edge/parity notation elaborates a capability already described in v1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central claims: v1's mobility proposal gains quantitative continuity and speed evaluation, while broader generative and networking baselines and CAM/ACAM comparisons better test the proposed architecture. Expanded implementation details and explicit size-generalization limits improve assessability. These gains address important validation gaps, despite undefined uncertainty values and proprietary simulation parameters that still limit reproducibility. Changed settings prevent interpreting the revision as a controlled performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NetDiff for directional ad hoc network topology and parity generation. Their text, equations, figures, and tables are readable, including v2's appendices in Sections 7–10. v1 has no appendix. Changed experimental settings limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent a reliable document comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original baseline comparisons, component ablations, mobility-reconfiguration experiments, and quantitative 32-node results, including Appendix 9.

before.justification: v1 reports original topology-generation experiments, simulated throughput, architectural and loss ablations in Tables 1–3, and execution timings.

results.title: NetDiff: Graph Diffusion with Improved Global Capabilities to Generate and Update Mobile Network Topologies

C1.justification: The principal method, comparable-reconstruction-quality claim, and training-free motion claim remain. v2 removes the explicit first-use claim for image inverse problems and adds prominent memory/accessibility claims, including up to 77% lower memory and suitability for 8 GiB GPUs. Its conclusion further asserts an order-of-magnitude memory reduction, exceeding the unchanged table's evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of prompt dependence, possible decoder effects in prior selection, and persistent errors when prompts mismatch target faces. It acknowledges motion-quality versus path-accuracy tradeoffs and the limited ImageNet FID reference size. These provide specific applicability boundaries beyond v1's general speed, performance, and future-domain limitations.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 reports public code and supplies its repository link. v2 also documents revised optimization parameters, an alternative prior source, and clean-fid features, preprocessing, and reference statistics. Hardware reporting gains an unresolved inconsistency: Section 4.1 says all experiments use RTX 3090, while Appendix E.5 retains A6000 measurements.

E1.justification: ImageNet/FFHQ super-resolution and Gaussian deblurring remain. Motion evaluation changes substantially: v1 illustrates hand-designed forward and zigzag paths, whereas v2 evaluates HumanML3D test motions with sparse conditioning at 5 of 196 frames. This introduces a distinct sparse-control scenario; the earlier motion demonstrations are no longer reported.

E2.justification: v2 adds OmniControl and Guided Motion Diffusion (GMD) as quantitative motion comparators in Table 3, providing external comparisons absent from v1's motion demonstration. The image comparison methods remain DPS, DDRM, PSLD, ReSample, and the Markov-process variant.

E3.justification: The main image evaluations expand from 100 to 1,000 images per dataset. Reported optimization settings change, including Adam to RAdam, learning rates, schedules, and the ImageNet super-resolution KL weight. v2 also introduces SSIM/FID/KID evaluation, quantitative sparse-motion protocols, and prompt/prior controls; the prior comparison uses 100 FFHQ images.

E4.justification: Appendices E.7-E.9 add tests of text conditioning, VQDiff-ITHQ versus CVQDiff-FFHQ priors, and prompt-related failure cases. Figure 2 expands the early-structure analysis through multiple conditional samples. The existing Markov-process and forgetting-coefficient analyses are retained, with revised examples.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its results. Larger evaluation sets and additional metrics do not change the uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1-2 replace the image scores: for example, G2D2 ImageNet super-resolution changes from LPIPS/PSNR 0.349/23.20 to 0.340/23.82. Changed samples and optimization settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting gain. v2 adds motion, prompt/prior, and SSIM/FID/KID results. The memory/time values in v1 Table 4 and v2 Table 5 remain identical.

M1.justification: The reported inner optimization changes from Adam to RAdam in Section 4.1 and Appendix E.2. The variational objective, Gumbel-Softmax relaxation, star-shaped sampling, and initialization strategy remain fundamentally unchanged. The star-decomposed distribution corresponds to v1's qsampling, rather than a newly introduced sampler.

P1.justification: The introduction and methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Section 3 separates star-shaped noise, the decomposed distribution, and variational inference more explicitly, with expanded explanations and revised terminology. Ethics and reproducibility statements move into appendices, and the appendix structure is reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redraws Figures 2-3, adds prompt/prior/failure figures and motion/expanded-metric tables, and removes v1's motion Figures 6 and 14. Several retained image grids are relocated and enlarged. Typography, headings, and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: The existing related-work framework is retained. v2 adds a focused distinction from Feynman-Kac steering, a paragraph on applications across domains, and references supporting the motion comparators, alternative prior, optimizer, metrics, and prompt tuning. This extends the positioning without replacing its central relationship to continuous inverse solvers and discrete guidance.

T1.justification: Appendix D corrects important reasoning: the KL proof uses the decomposed joint, and Lemma D.1 replaces v1 Lemma B.3's unjustified Kronecker-delta return argument with successive marginalization. These substantively repair support for the retained method. However, v2's new transition-normalization condition uses (K-1)beta despite Eq. 2 containing K beta contributions per non-mask column.

improvement.justification: v2 repairs an important marginal-preservation proof and substantially strengthens validation through broader image sampling, quantitative motion comparisons, and analyses exposing prompt/prior dependencies and failures. These address weaknesses in v1's theoretical support and largely illustrative motion evidence. The gains outweigh new reporting defects, including the transition-normalization inconsistency, conflicting hardware statements, and an unsupported order-of-magnitude memory claim: Table 5 shows 4.7 versus at most 20.9 GiB. The improvement rests on stronger justification and more informative evidence, rather than the changed performance scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe G2D2 and have readable text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. The expanded and reorganized material in v2 can be matched reliably to v1.

after.justification: v2 reports original image reconstruction experiments, quantitative HumanML3D motion results, prompt and prior-model ablations, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet and FFHQ reconstruction experiments, graphical-model and forgetting-coefficient analyses, resource measurements, and qualitative motion-generation results.

results.title: G2D2: Gradient-Guided Discrete Diffusion for Inverse Problem Solving

C1.justification: v1 claims a PNP/entropy theory with an exhaustive proof and an inexpensive general frontend whose combinations surpass prior methods. v2 centers its contribution on complementary task/reconstruction forces, gradient-conflict avoidance, and encoder robustness. PNP becomes explicitly intuitive motivation, and the hybrid-SOTA contribution is dropped.

C2.justification: v2 develops substantive explanations involving task-driven routing, preservation of non-dominant encoders, complementary branch roles, and reconstruction-weight tradeoffs. It explicitly bounds applicability to separate-encoder fusion pipelines. These replace much of v1's charged-particle and performance-upper-bound interpretation; the dimensionality-related computational limitation is retained and made more explicit.

D1.justification: v2 documents activation choices, SwiGLU widths, revised optimization schedules, matrix costs, and profiling conditions. Conversely, v1's explicit FakeAVCeleb split procedure, frame/audio preprocessing, training batch-size/input-shape tables, and executable-style pseudocode are omitted. v2 adds a code-provision statement but supplies no direct access link.

E1.justification: v2 adds CMU-MOSEI audio-visual-text sentiment evaluation across available-modality combinations. It removes VGGSound event classification and the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet dimensionality experiments from v1's appendices. ActivityNet retrieval and FakeAVCeleb detection remain.

E2.justification: ActivityNet comparisons add MISA, DrFuse, AADML, DI-VTR, CMKT, Coupled Mamba, DLF, and AdaMMS, among others (Tables 3). FakeAVCeleb adds ART-AVDF, MACB-DF, CAFR, and other methods, while UAVM and Joint-AV disappear from its reported comparison (v1 Table 7; v2 Table 4). These changes extend beyond the CLIP/CMMP naming difference.

E3.justification: Reported GMF/SCFAE training changes from SGD with 20 epochs to AdamW with warmup/cosine scheduling and 10 epochs on the retained datasets; default expansion changes from 4 to 2. FakeAVCeleb documents R(2+1)D-34 instead of -18. ActivityNet drops the 4096–4096 configuration and mAP@20. v2 also introduces controlled encoder probing and batch-size-1 FP32 profiling.

E4.justification: v2 adds component and reconstruction-metric ablations, expansion/boundary/loss-weight sensitivity, modality-order tests, and branch masking (Tables 7–11 and 14). Figure 4 and Table 6 directly examine gradient behavior, feature organization, and encoder degradation. Conversely, v1's CIFAR/ImageNet dimensionality-validation analyses are removed.

E5.justification: v1 specifies seed 1; its ImageNet ranges describe validation-checkpoint minima and maxima. v2 Appendix B.3 reports four additional trials with different seeds and ± summaries for FakeAVCeleb AUC and ActivityNet mAP@100. This is a limited extension: the dispersion statistic is unspecified, and uncertainty is not reported throughout the comparison tables.

E6.justification: ActivityNet 128–128 mAP@100 is 0.308 for v1 GMF and 0.321 for v2 SCFAE under revised method/training settings, so this is not a controlled same-setting gain. FakeAVCeleb's reported MDS ACC/AUC changes from 83.86/86.71 to 82.80/86.50, beyond rounding. v2 adds MOSEI and extensive analysis results while removing VGGSound, dimensionality-study, and hybrid-model results.

M1.justification: The expansion, shared/specific split, cyclic exchange, and reconstruction pipeline is retained. However, v2 adds GeLU and pre/post SwiGLU processing to v1's linear mappings and replaces MSE reconstruction with a cosine-based objective (Section 4; Appendix A). The separate GMF-MAE integration described in v1 Appendix I is no longer included.

P1.justification: The title, terminology, abstract, introduction, related work, method explanation, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten around gradient coherence. Experiments are organized by fusion challenges, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. The retained gradient/residual discussion moves from v1 Appendix A to v2 Appendix C.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text, redraws the architecture, adds a teaser and gradient/t-SNE panels, and removes the physical-cell, dimensionality-study, and GMF-MAE illustrations. Tables are extensively restructured, including moving the expanded FakeAVCeleb comparison into the main text. Entropy, gradient-flow, and residual diagrams have identifiable retained or revised counterparts.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from native/extended/general multimodal task categories to coupled versus decoupled fusion and gradient-stability positioning. The comparison framework and bibliography substantially expand to recent retrieval, missing-modality, and deepfake approaches, including Coupled Mamba, MCULoRA, DLF, and AdaMMS, alongside additional gradient-learning literature.

T1.justification: v1's constrained entropy objective survives as v2 Equation 1. However, the optimal-dimension and mapping theorems, PNP-to-reconstruction derivation, performance-bound conjecture, and their supporting derivations are removed. v2 instead gives a brief self-consistent-field formulation and qualitative gradient arguments; the residual discussion remains without v1's mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for the mechanism through component/branch ablations, gradient and encoder probes, and seed checks, addressing v1's limited direct component validation. It also recasts the claimed exhaustive PNP proof, acknowledged incomplete in v1 Appendix B, as intuition. These gains outweigh lost preprocessing, split, and pseudocode detail, although those omissions and the unclear positive-cosine reconstruction-loss convention in Equations 5–6 remain material weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multimodal fusion research, substantially revised from GMF to SCFAE. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained architectural elements and benchmarks support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original SCFAE evaluations, component ablations, gradient analyses, and additional runtime, branch-masking, and seed experiments, including Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original GMF experiments on VGGSound, ActivityNet, and FakeAVCeleb, plus CIFAR and ImageNet dimensionality studies in Appendices C–D.

results.title: Multimodal Fusion via Self-Consistent Task-Gradient Fields

C1.justification: The central novelty claim shifts from pioneering Event Cloud representation to integrating polarity into structural decisions beyond input-level inclusion. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion explicitly broaden the scalability claim to high-resolution as well as long-sequence events. Despite the classification-focused new title, all three original task families remain part of the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations of structural polarity integration, local Spatial-FA versus long-range Temporal-FA processing, and explicit versus implicit temporal features. Appendices I and J explicitly discuss accuracy–computation and input-size–inference-speed tradeoffs, while Appendix E acknowledges SECNet's own scaling costs. These substantially qualify and explain v1's more general efficiency arguments.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies random downsampling, Min-Max normalization, learnable scaling, FFT tensor reshaping, and the FPGA platform and clock. Much existing architecture and training information merely moves to appendices. Conversely, v1's explicit DHP19 subject and two-front-camera details disappear, and the abstract changes from code 'is available' to 'will be available' at a different repository.

E1.justification: All nine original datasets and three task families remain. v2 adds THU E-ACT-50, a real 1280×800, 50-class action recognition benchmark, extending evaluation to higher-resolution event data within an existing task family.

E2.justification: v2 adds EDGCN to object classification and EVSTr and EventMamba to the action accuracy comparison. THU E-ACT-50 introduces HMAX SNN, Motion SNN, and EV-ACT comparisons. The replacement hardware benchmark adds methods including C3D, ResNext-50, EventLSTM, and EventMamba while dropping several former hardware comparators. EventMamba was already cited in v1 but was not evaluated in these comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a controlled FPGA comparison at 200 MHz, joint event-count/centroid sweeps, and cross-dataset average accuracy reporting. The server hardware benchmark switches from DVS128 Gesture to UCF101-DVS. Its Table 6 specifies filename-based partitioning, whereas Appendix D retains random 20% testing; the actual UCF101 split and whether retained results were rerun are therefore unclear. The stated optimizer, learning rate, and epoch budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate D-FPS, EF-KNN, and Spatial-FA removal tests, a six-dataset comparison against the convolutional ECNet variant, computational-cost breakdowns, event/centroid sensitivity measurements, and qualitative pose comparisons. The original event-count study is retained. The old joint grouping ablation reappears as 'Input P' with identical results, rather than constituting a new experiment.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's new Average columns aggregate accuracies across datasets and do not provide uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: DailyDVS accuracy changes from 0.993 to 0.9965, while the five object-classification accuracies and DHP19 pose errors remain unchanged. New results include THU E-ACT-50 accuracy of 97.25 versus EV-ACT's 92.7, FPGA SFA latency of 1.97 ms versus MLP latencies of 31.51–125.96 ms, and extensive ablation and runtime entries. The hardware table's 229.7 FPS on DVS128 Gesture is replaced by 120 FPS on UCF101-DVS; these are different settings, not evidence of a same-setting slowdown.

M1.justification: The matched pipeline retains D-FPS, feature-based KNN, coordinate averaging, Spatial-FA, attention aggregation, Temporal-FA, residual blocks, and prediction heads. v2's stage-indexed equations restate v1's Algorithm 1. Newly specifying learnable scaling, random downsampling, and Min-Max normalization does not establish a change from v1's less explicit implementation.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively reframed around scalability, with a new title and network name, revised contribution statements, and an expanded architecture-first method description. Dataset details, implementation material, hardware discussion, and pseudocode are reorganized across the main text and appendices. Additional module explanations substantially expand the narrative beyond simple renaming.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from an accuracy–compute–throughput plot to a seven-dataset radar chart, and Figure 3 is rearranged and relabeled. New displays include the tensor-dimension diagram, computational-cost chart, pose visualizations, FPGA comparison, architecture comparison, and runtime and ablation tables. Existing tables gain average columns and revised structures, alongside a new document layout and single-column appendices.

R1.justification: v2 attributes Event Cloud representation to prior work and substantially expands positioning against EventNet and voxel methods through Appendix B and Table 11, emphasizing structural rather than input-only polarity use. References are added for high-resolution action recognition, EDGCN, EventLSTM, and other supporting work. EventMamba's preprint-to-publication update is the same cited work, not a new reference.

T1.justification: The Event Cloud definition, grouping and normalization mathematics, Fourier identities, conjugate-symmetry argument, and quadratic-versus-FFT complexity comparison are retained. Added stage indices and pipeline equations restate existing operations. The appendices supply conceptual explanations rather than new formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central efficiency contribution: the convolutional replacement study isolates Spatial-FA's accuracy–cost tradeoff, FPGA measurements test hardware benefits directly, and the high-resolution benchmark extends scalability evidence. These address important gaps in v1's support for its design. Conflicting UCF101 split descriptions, the weaker code-release statement, and overstated total-GMAC savings in Appendix I limit reproducibility and precision, but the targeted experimental and explanatory gains provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Event Cloud network, renamed from FECNet to SECNet. The architecture, equations, retained experiments, figures, and tables can be matched reliably. Both documents are readable, including v2's appendices A–L; v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains original network results and adds high-resolution action recognition, FPGA measurements, further ablations, runtime sweeps, and pose prediction examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, action recognition, human pose estimation, runtime, and component and event-count ablation results for FECNet.

results.title: Scalable Event Cloud Network for Event-based Classification

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the central performance claim from outperforming structural pruning to outperforming both pruning and MoE-construction techniques. Detailed analysis becomes an additional stated contribution. The original claims about uncovering experts without updating pretrained weights and jointly learning routing and expert configurations remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking the modest VO-routing benefit to small head dimensions and poor head-pruning performance to distorted attention features. It also discusses temperature robustness, recommends fewer than 16 experts, and qualifies comparable throughput by sufficiently large batch size. Existing interpretations of expert semantics and width allocation are retained.

D1.justification: The abstract adds a code-availability statement and repository address. New comparisons disclose training-token budgets and the matched-iteration fine-tuning setting for LLaMA-MoE. The detailed module configurations, optimizer settings, GPU allocations, and data-processing instructions already present in v1 remain substantially unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated BoolQ, SciQ, TruthfulQA, and MMLU benchmarks in Tables 5–6 and Figure 10, substantially broadening task coverage beyond the original language-modeling and five commonsense benchmarks. The original training datasets and evaluation coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Tables 4–6 add evaluated LLaMA-MoE, G-MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE comparators, including multiple configurations and fine-tuned variants. This introduces a substantial direct MoE-construction comparison group. The original structural and semi-structured pruning comparators remain represented.

E3.justification: Alongside the retained zero-shot protocols, v2 introduces 32-shot BoolQ, 5-shot WinoGrande and MMLU, 25-shot ARC-c, and 10-shot HellaSwag evaluations. It also introduces throughput measurements at batch sizes 512, 1024, and 1536. These are additional evaluation designs; the original default 10,000-iteration training setup remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained loss, dataset, and expert-count analyses, Table 13 tests local embeddings, head pruning, removal of VO routing, and temperature sensitivity. Figure 4 adds aggregate expert-utilization analysis, Figure 10 examines the MMLU accuracy–parameter trade-off, and Table 15 examines throughput scaling with batch size.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained expert-width boxplots describe variation among experts rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: Original benchmark values are retained, including LLaMA-2 rows relocated from Table 3 to Table 12. v2 adds substantial MoE, MMLU, ablation, and throughput results: Table 13 reports 56.07 for full ToMoE versus 44.99 for head pruning, and Table 15 reports 2360.38–2919.45 tokens/s across batch sizes. Section 4.3 also incorrectly redescribes the unchanged 3.14-point advantage over ModeGPT-Alpaca as '3.14 times'.

M1.justification: The core architecture, expert construction, routing, and frozen-weight training remain the same. However, Section 3.4 changes the load-balancing probability calculation from explicitly defined softmax in v1 to GSmax in v2 without explaining whether this represents a changed calculation or inconsistent notation. An actual loss modification cannot be established reliably.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, condenses the introductory background, edits method explanations and notation, updates author information, and removes the Impact Statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing method and appendix prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a two-column conference layout to a single-column journal layout with substantially different front matter and table placement. v2 adds comparison and ablation tables and new plots, moves part of Table 3 into appendix Table 12, and combines v1 Figures 5–6 into v2 Figure 6.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning against contextual sparsity through Deja Vu, CATS, and structured-sparsity work, and broadens dense-to-MoE discussion and comparisons through MoEfication, generalized MoEfication, LLaMA-MoE-v2, and CMoE. This substantially expands the prior-work context for its unified expert-construction and router-training claim.

T1.justification: New Appendix F derives the effective query–key width from overlapping binary pruning masks, showing that it reaches the allocated width K only when the masks coincide. This adds a focused mathematical justification to the qualitative concern already stated in v1 Appendix A.2.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1: a dense-to-MoE method was evaluated mainly against pruning. Direct MoE comparisons, component validation, and measured throughput materially strengthen the evidence for its contribution. These gains outweigh new reporting problems, although the broader superiority claim needs qualification: Table 6 reports 57.40 for ToMoE versus 59.61 and 59.31 for LLaMA-MoE-v2, with very different training-token budgets. Those results support an efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ToMoE. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results between v1's Appendices A–E and v2's Appendices A–F.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds MoE comparisons, additional benchmarks, component ablations, and inference-throughput measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original ToMoE perplexity and zero-shot evaluation results, loss and dataset ablations, and expert analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: ToMoE: Converting Dense Large Language Models to Mixture-of-Experts through Dynamic Structural Pruning

C1.justification: V1's abstract and Section 5 claim greedy optimality when the surrogate accurately learns the utility. V2 narrows this to approximation guarantees under sufficient conditions. It also expands the headline empirical contribution to large-scale LLM fine-tuning, while retaining the central sequential-selection and ADP interpretation.

C2.justification: V2 replaces claims of directly controlling curvature and validating quadratic decay with a qualitative substitutability-proxy interpretation. It explains that low MSE does not establish the uniform conditions required by its guarantee. New LLM qualifications disclose potential reference-label leakage and coverage saturation after only 1–5 selections, making most remaining selections depend on the similarity fallback.

D1.justification: V2 adds a public-code pointer, classical CPU and DVRL configuration disclosures, and graph-search implementation details. Appendix J.7 supplies extensive LLM data preparation, reference construction, embedding, LoRA, evaluation, hardware, and timing information, including distinguishing timed H100 runs from H200 headline runs. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds instruction-selection and LLM fine-tuning coverage through DATE-LM, using Tulu 3 instruction data and evaluating MMLU, GSM8K, and BBH. These introduce knowledge and reasoning tasks beyond the retained eight classical datasets and synthetic substitutability experiment.

E2.justification: The nine classical comparison methods remain. V2 adds evaluated Linear and MLP predictors in the surrogate comparison (Table 3), and BM25, Rep-Sim, RDS+, Grad-Sim, and LESS in the LLM comparisons (Tables 6–7). These are substantive additions to the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a budget-500 protocol reporting mean accuracy across selection sizes 1–500. Its new LLM protocol selects 10,000 of 200,000 instructions, performs two-epoch LoRA training of Llama-3.1-8B, and uses task-specific zero-, eight-, and three-shot evaluation. It also introduces shared-subset surrogate-error comparisons with fitted-intercept controls. The original small-budget dataset splits are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct analysis of surrogate prediction quality using training/test MAE and MSE (Table 3), plus seven embedding variants testing representation choice for BipCov (Table 8). Conversely, v1's six-level curvature plots are condensed to endpoint panels in v2 Figure 3, omitting the intermediate plotted evidence.

E5.justification: Classical per-dataset reporting remains mean and standard deviation over 20 runs. V2 specifies three fine-tuning seeds for its headline LLM comparison and distinguishes these results from single-seed baseline and embedding experiments. The aggregate Std Dev row from v1 Table 1 is omitted in v2 Table 9; no new significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: V2 adds budget-500 results, surrogate errors, and LLM results, including BipCov's 63.89±0.34% average versus RDS+'s 62.88±0.25% in Table 6. In the matched small-budget tables, DVRL values change, including bbc-embeddings from 0.560 to 0.653, and aggregate averages are corrected, including Bipartite from 0.041 to 0.750. Most other per-dataset entries remain unchanged; the new settings do not establish improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

M1.justification: V2 adds the BipCov adaptation: an embedding-based top-L similarity graph, greedy reference coverage, and mean-similarity filling after coverage saturates (Appendix J.7). This substantially extends v1's fitted, label-matched distance-threshold graph procedure. Threshold fitting is also reported as minimizing MSE rather than the absolute error specified in v1 Algorithm 2; the core exact-DP selection algorithm remains equivalent.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theory exposition, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. Preliminaries are reorganized around explicit assumptions, regression characterization is separated from policy equivalence, and detailed RQ1 discussion moves to Appendix M. The appendix structure is extensively reorganized, including moving the DP algorithm from Appendix B to Appendix L.

P2.justification: V1's full DP comparison curves are replaced by a compact summary table, and its six-setting curvature figures become a smaller endpoint display. V2 redraws the main selection curves with revised styling and adds tables for larger budgets, surrogate errors, regression formulations, computational costs, LLM comparisons, and embedding ablations. The retained detailed results table also changes its summary-row structure.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around semi-values, submodular optimization, optimization from samples, datamodel/DsDm surrogates, and efficient valuation methods. Appendix A adds many substantive citations and explicitly distinguishes the approach from GraphFilter. The earlier detailed ADP literature survey is also replaced.

T1.justification: V1's common efficiency-constrained regression argument is replaced by separate Shapley, Banzhaf, and Beta Shapley formulations and proofs, including centered features and parameter restrictions (v2 Appendices B–D). V1 Appendix G's exact greedy-optimality theorem is replaced by a conditional (1-epsilon)(1-1/e) approximation theorem in v2 Appendix H. Normalization assumptions and the distinction between optimal subsets and optimal sequence prefixes are also corrected or formalized.

improvement.justification: Replacing v1's exact greedy-optimality claim and common efficiency-constrained regression argument with appropriately qualified formulations and proofs substantially improves the central theoretical support. Corrected result summaries, utility diagnostics, and fuller experimental documentation further strengthen the paper. Some detailed original curves disappear, and the LLM evidence has disclosed leakage and coverage-saturation limitations, but these tradeoffs do not outweigh the substantial corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sequential data-valuation framework and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained experiments and reorganized theoretical material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains original classical experiments and adds budget-500 evaluations, surrogate-prediction experiments, and LLM fine-tuning results and embedding ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original selection experiments on eight datasets and controlled message-passing experiments examining data substitutability, including Figures 3–6 and Appendix J.

results.title: Unifying and Optimizing Data Values for Selection via Sequential Decision-Making

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from DABUF's classifier-assisted gradient attribution to a theoretically motivated denoising framework applicable to both gradient and hidden-state attribution. v2's conclusion also newly claims that gradient-based approaches consistently produce the safest retrained models, changing the paper's practical takeaway.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes noisy long responses and explains Ada3's filtering failures through indiscriminate semantic matching. v2 emphasizes high-variance nuisance dimensions, complementary denoising and selection, and gradient attribution's purported ability to capture training dynamics. Its homogeneous-injection, detection-taxonomy, and adversarial-attribution limitations remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds the safety-judging rubric, fixed GPT-4o version 2024-11-20, score-5 ASR threshold, and DRA's selected dimension count of 30. Conversely, it replaces explicit jailbreak split descriptions with a benchmark reference and omits v1's specified jailbreak filtering budget and gradient-projection details. Most LoRA training hyperparameters and hardware information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate jailbreak injection using UltraChat, ToxicChat, and XSTest-Response, and gender-bias detection and mitigation using Bias in Bios. v2's adoption of the DATE-LM setup does not introduce an additional dataset, domain, or task in the supplied evidence.

E2.justification: v2 adds RepSim to jailbreak comparisons. Its jailbreak retraining comparison retains Wildguard but removes OpenAI Moderation, Llama-Guard, and GradSafe. Gender-bias comparisons replace Ada3 with Wildguard, GradSim, and RepSim. Plain response-gradient attribution already appears in v1 Appendix B, so GradSim is not wholly new to the paper.

E3.justification: Detection evaluation drops the reported top-100 precision, recall, and F1 measures in favor of AUPRC. Gender-bias filtering increases from 100 to 500 removed samples. v2 also constructs targets by pooling unsafe or biased outputs across ten inference runs and references DATE-LM's official test splits instead of v1's explicit custom split description.

E4.justification: v1's token-level attribution and token-count analyses are removed. v2 adds raw-versus-denoised t-SNE visualizations, an empirical relationship between discriminability and AUPRC, and separate denoising and dimension-selection ablations in Appendices C–E. The target-size analysis is revised to compare GradSim with GradSim-DRA.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports ten-run inference averaging for ASR and gender-bias evaluations; this does not establish additional independently trained models. Target-size resampling increases from ten repetitions in v1 to fifty in v2, retaining mean and standard-deviation reporting. Main result tables still lack uncertainty intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Primary numerical results are extensively replaced. For example, v1 Table 2 reports Llama DABUF AUPRC of 52.0%/74.1% on ToxicChat/XSTest-Response; v2 Table 1 reports 83.2%/81.5% for GradSim-DRA and 92.6%/98.6% for RepSim-DRA. Baseline scores, retraining outcomes, and gender-bias results also change. Revised methods and settings prevent interpreting these as matched performance gains.

M1.justification: v1's DABUF uses gradient cosine similarity and classifier-screened, human-verified training examples as jailbreak attribution targets. v2's DRA instead centers and whitens representations, then selects dimensions using a leave-target-out discriminability objective. It operates on gradients or hidden states and uses unsafe model outputs as targets. These changes substantially alter representation processing, scoring, and target construction.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method exposition, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around DRA. Related work is reorganized and the appendices are restructured. The gender-data construction and much of the training-details text are retained through relocation rather than newly introduced.

P2.justification: Results tables are substantially redesigned with backbone-specific method groups and improvement columns, while precision/recall/F1 tables disappear. v2 replaces the token-count plot with representation visualizations, redraws the target-size comparison, and adds a discriminability scatterplot, component-ablation table, and boxed safety rubric.

R1.justification: v2 substantially repositions the contribution within representation-based detection and signal detection theory, adding DATE-LM, LARF, RepSim, a data-attribution survey, and theoretical references. The broader standalone attribution survey in v1 is condensed, with several simulator, valuation, and game-theoretic references removed.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's gradient-influence and token-aggregation definitions, v2 introduces a signal-detection formulation, a discriminability objective, and Lemma 3.1's optimal linear-score derivation. It develops covariance-based whitening and a target-based dimension-selection surrogate, with assumptions about rare unsafe data and alignment between target and unsafe-data means.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the treatment of noisy attribution through an explicit denoising formulation, mathematical derivation, and controlled component ablations, addressing v1's reliance on manually verified training targets for jailbreaks. Specified safety judging and repeated inference also improve evaluation transparency. These gains outweigh lost setup details and an overbroad conclusion: v2 Table 6 favors RepSim-DRA over GradSim-DRA for Llama gender-bias mitigation, contradicting the claim that gradients consistently produce the safest models. Higher cross-version scores alone do not establish improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work on detecting and filtering unsafe training data. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial methodological revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original detection and retraining experiments for DRA, supplemented by representation visualizations, target-size experiments, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak-detection, retraining-safety, and gender-bias experiments, plus token-level and target-set-size analyses.

results.title: Detecting and Filtering Unsafe Training Data via Data Attribution with Denoised Representation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add variance reduction as a central theoretical contribution and MR-BMIA as an implemented extension benefiting from additional references. Validation claims expand to text datasets. The introductory example is corrected from 37.5% TPR and a 64% improvement on CIFAR-10 to 35.75% and 54% on CIFAR-100, consistent with Table 1.

C2.justification: v2 explains the different roles of posterior sampling and independent reference datasets, including persistent variation between model centers and diminishing returns from more references. v1's abundant-resource limitation and mixture-Laplace future work become an evaluated extension. Appendix F adds substantive warnings about non-Gaussian p-value calibration, suggests unevaluated held-out calibration, and distinguishes empirical attack power from mechanism-level privacy guarantees.

D1.justification: v2 adds a BMIA implementation-code link, PyTorch and RTX 4090/L40 hardware disclosures, and detailed storage/scalability accounting. However, v1 Appendix B's epoch budgets, learning-rate decay schedules, MLP layer widths and explicit RMIA population-set assignment are omitted rather than relocated. Most Laplace implementation details survive in Appendix G. These additions and removals substantially alter the available reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 adds five text-classification datasets: Emotion, TREC-6, 20 Newsgroups, DBpedia and AG News. It also evaluates references trained on CINIC-10 against CIFAR-10 targets, a distinct distribution-mismatch scenario from the retained experiment using CINIC-10 only for non-member queries. Original image, tabular and toy-regression coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 newly compares BatchEnsemble, Packed Ensemble, Masksembles, SWAG and MC Dropout with Laplace-based BMIA. Table 4 adds Attack-R, LiRA and RMIA to an architecture-mismatch evaluation previously showing only BMIA. Conversely, QMIA's Texas-100, Purchase-100 and ImageNet comparisons disappear; its CIFAR results remain in Table 2.

E3.justification: v2 introduces 64-reference comparisons, reference-count scaling through K=128, single-reference RMIA comparisons, and text evaluation using BERT, DistilBERT and TF-IDF/MLP models. The stated image/tabular weight decay changes from 0.0001 in v1 Appendix B to 0.0005 in v2 Section 4.1; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that experiments were rerun. The original dataset split proportions remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test alternative Bayesian approximations, reference-count scaling, reference-training distribution shift, and Gaussian assumptions through score histograms, QQ-plots and t-statistic distributions. Architecture-mismatch analysis gains baseline comparisons. The original sampling-size, Hessian, prior-tuning and predictive-distribution ablations remain, with several relocated or renumbered.

E5.justification: v2 Table 9 newly reports means and standard deviations across reference models trained on distinct data subsets. For example, CIFAR-10 TPR at 1% FPR is reported as mean 9.48% and standard deviation 0.63 percentage points. v1 lacks this variability reporting; v2 still does not specify the run count or seeds.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive text, multi-reference and supplementary results. Table 1 revises BMIA's CIFAR-10 TPRs from 2.28/8.87 to 2.84/9.48 at 0.1%/1% FPR, and RMIA with two references changes from 8.39 to 12.86 at 1% FPR on CIFAR-100. Several training-time entries also change. Table 3 newly reports MR-BMIA TPRs of 12.48% and 45.57% at 1% FPR on CIFAR-10/100. Changed methods/settings prevent interpreting these revisions as controlled before-and-after performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes the test-statistic denominator from sigma/sqrt(N) to sigma*sqrt(1+1/M), explicitly accounting for target-score variability. v2 also introduces MR-BMIA: multiple reference-model posteriors, separate intra/inter-model variance estimates and a Welch-Satterthwaite degrees-of-freedom approximation (Algorithm 2; Appendix C). These change the inference procedure substantially.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and substantially rewrites its abstract, introduction, background and method exposition. The former motivation and conditional-attack theory move into appendices, while discussion material becomes structured ablation and robustness subsections. The narrative is reorganized around Bayesian sampling, variance reduction and the multi-reference extension.

P2.justification: v2 adds multiple comparison/result tables, normality diagnostics, a t-statistic plot and a log-scale ROC plot. v1's OOD table becomes Figure 2b with only two FPR thresholds, and its architecture-mismatch plot becomes Figure 2c. Existing toy and conditional-distribution illustrations move into appendices; retained Laplace-ablation plots are relaid out.

R1.justification: v2 expands recent MIA coverage, including recommender-system attacks, and substantially rewrites Bayesian-method positioning around post-hoc Laplace versus SWAG, MC Dropout and efficient ensembles. This replaces much of v1's variational-inference/MCMC overview. New discussions also connect the method to mixture Laplace approximations and hypothesis-testing privacy frameworks.

T1.justification: v2 adds the intra/inter-model variance decomposition, Proposition 3.1, power-monotonicity Theorem 3.2 and their proofs, a linear-regression comparison of posterior sampling and retraining, and multi-reference variance estimators. Existing conditional-attack propositions move to Appendix B; the conditional-TPR statement changes its quantile-term sign to agree with the retained proof. The single-reference test-variance derivation is also revised.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's multi-reference future-work limitation into a specified, evaluated method (Algorithm 2; Tables 3 and 7), accounts for target-score variance, and adds comparisons and diagnostics that directly test methodological choices and assumptions. These substantially strengthen the work's scope and evidential support. The gains outweigh omitted training schedules and an overbroad Theorem 3.2 statement: its proof requires alpha < 0.5 although the theorem claims alpha in (0,1).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BMIA research despite the changed title and substantial expansion. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved from the main text into appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds text-dataset evaluations, multi-reference experiments, alternative Bayesian-method comparisons and distribution diagnostics.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack evaluations on image and tabular datasets, a toy regression experiment, robustness tests and Laplace-approximation ablations.

results.title: How does Bayesian Sampling help Membership Inference Attacks?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion drop the efficient Nash-RS algorithm contribution and its advertised 60.55% win rate. The central probability claims expand to bounded non-uniform Luce preferences, and the contribution narrative shifts toward extending statistical bounds beyond the uniform setting.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly qualifies collapse comparisons by the vanishing-KL-regularization regime and describes impartial culture as restrictive. Section 3.4 tempers v1's algorithmic-fairness conclusion to an output-diversity interpretation.
