The reward-hacking hypothesis disappears, while the principal interpretation linking Condorcet structure to collapse remains.

D1.justification: V2 removes the Nash-RS code link, model and dataset access details, four-A800 hardware disclosure, sampling batch sizes, and Table 7's training hyperparameters. Appendix F instead documents the synthetic weight construction, parameter grid, and simulation count. Removing the code disclosure does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: The LLM alignment experiments using OpenRLHF/prompt-collection-v0.1 are removed. V2 adds synthetic Condorcet-winner evaluations under uniform and non-uniform Luce preferences, including preferential weighting of one response. The earlier three-response simplex Monte Carlo example remains.

E2.justification: V1 Tables 5–6 evaluate Nash-RS against the base model, PPO, and Online-IPO; these empirical comparisons disappear from v2. Retained theoretical comparisons between RLHF and NLHF do not replace the removed evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V1's one-epoch LLM training on 2,048 prompts, evaluation on 512 held-out prompts, and reward/win-rate metrics are removed. V2 introduces a simulation protocol estimating a designated response's winning probability: m = 3–6, n = 100–300 or 200–400 depending on m, and varying Luce weights. These are new protocols, not revised scores under the earlier settings.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix F.1 analyzes reward-function stability across preference ratios, reference-policy probabilities, and regularization strengths; this analysis is removed. V2 instead tests the predicted Condorcet-probability decay across preference bias, voter counts, and response counts in Figures 3 and 7.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix F explicitly reports 1,000,000 simulation trials per configuration, whereas v1 provides no comparable replication count. This adds statistical estimation information for new experiments, without establishing increased repetitions of existing experiments. Neither version reports corresponding confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 removes the LLM reward and win-rate results, including Table 5's mean rewards of -0.3859 for the base model and -0.1001 for Nash-RS. It adds simulated winning-probability curves for a designated response, compared with n^(-m/ceil(m/2)). These are different outcomes under new settings, not LLM performance improvements.

M1.justification: V2 removes the proposed policy-reward reformulation, Nash Rejection Sampling, implicit-reward computation, and associated PPO training procedure from v1 Section 4. These are substantive method removals. The response-set decomposition algorithm remains, renumbered from Algorithm 3 to Algorithm 1.

P1.justification: The contribution narrative is substantially rewritten around statistical theory. V1 Sections 3.6–3.7 become separate proof Sections 4–5, related-work material moves to Appendix A.2, and the appendices are reorganized around generalized proofs and simulations. This changes the paper's narrative structure beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: V1's comparison, result, and hyperparameter Tables 4–7 and reward-visualization Figure 5 are removed. V2 adds the rate-comparison and simulation displays in Figures 2, 3, and 7 and redraws Figure 1. Existing tournament diagrams are retained, renumbered, and consolidated onto one appendix page.

R1.justification: V2 newly credits Sauermann (2022) with the tight uniform-ranking result and positions its advance around non-uniform preferences. It adds substantial social-choice alignment context and removes Nash-RS's rejection-sampling novelty discussion. The DPO and game-based optimization discussion is largely relocated to Appendix A.2, not deleted.

T1.justification: V2 generalizes Theorems 3.2–3.3 from impartial culture to bounded Luce weights and adds Theorem 2.3 and Corollary 3.8 with supporting proofs. It corrects Definition 2.3's implication, revises Theorem 2.1's proof and assumptions, and handles the singleton case in Lemma B.3. V1's policy-reward theorems and their proofs are removed.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the central statistical argument by extending restrictive uniform-ranking bounds to bounded non-uniform preferences, correcting the reward-consistency definition and proof, and acknowledging the prior tight uniform result. Explicit applicability conditions and targeted simulations further support this argument. Removing Nash-RS and its LLM experiments reduces practical coverage, but the improvements to the central theory's formulation, generality, and positioning outweigh that loss.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial changes in scope.

after.justification: V2 retains the Section 2.3 Monte Carlo finding and adds original Condorcet-winner simulations in Section 3.3, Appendix F, and Figures 3 and 7.

before.justification: V1 reports original Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct fine-tuning results in Section 4.4 and Tables 5–6, plus a Monte Carlo finding about cyclic preferences in Section 2.3.

results.title: Statistical Impossibility and Possibility of Aligning LLMs with Human Preferences: From Condorcet Paradox to Nash Equilibrium

C1.justification: The central contribution changes from dual-phase semantic disambiguation and fused layout masking to a composition-aware cross-attention variant using subject presence and relational alignment. The abstract and conclusion expand the main applicability claim to compositional image generation and foreground Wan results, while no longer foregrounding trajectory control. Training-free operation and model independence remain core claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for IoU feedback, preservation of general video quality, context-dependent interpolation, and tolerance of imperfect layouts. Appendix F explains motion/size planning failures and why sparse keyframes help. Conversely, v1's explicit caveats about ambiguous prompts, precise trajectories, and frame-level temporal control disappear; the general dependence on backbone capabilities remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds architecture-specific adaptation instructions, baseline-result provenance, shared-layout information, API cost and latency, and a revised planning template. However, it removes v1's explicit sampler, denoising-step, guidance-scale, resolution, and frame-count table, as well as its project-page link. These substantially change reproducibility documentation; removal of the link does not establish that the resource became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 adds compositional image generation on T2I-CompBench and dynamic-attribute evaluation within T2V-CompBench. VBench coverage expands from two object/spatial aspects to its full 16-dimension quality and semantics suite. v1's separate trajectory-control demonstration is no longer included, although v2 still discusses customizable layouts.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces numerous comparators, including ZeroScope, Latte, and VideoRepair, with methods including Dreamina1.2, Kling-1.0, T2V-Turbo-V2, MAGI-1, and SkyReels-v2. LVD and ViCo remain; DreamRunner leaves the main benchmark comparison but remains in component comparisons. v2 additionally evaluates SEGA, ToMe, VideoGrain, and the image-generation comparators SiamLayout and HybridLayout.

E3.justification: T2V-CompBench changes from 100 to 200 prompts per category, and CogVideoX-2B is replaced by CogVideoX-5B alongside additional Wan configurations. v2 compares LVD, ViCo, and Comp-Attn on shared backbones, with shared layouts for LVD. It reports intervention during the first 20% of denoising, versus v1's 10% rule for DLFA, and changes hardware from A100 to H100. Layout planning changes from ChatGLM-4 with 13 planned keyframes to GPT-4o-mini with four keyframes and interpolation.

E4.justification: v2 revises component ablations and adds an explicit removal test for IoU guidance, a fixed-interpolation coefficient sweep, and a manual layout-error analysis covering 1,400 prompts. The interpolation sweep extends v1's direct Word Swap control rather than introducing an entirely unrelated comparison. Appendix F newly tests dense versus sparse layout planning and distinguishes motion and size errors.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. v2's layout-error frequencies are additional empirical outcomes, not uncertainty estimates for the reported generation results.

E6.justification: The benchmark and ablation results are substantially replaced and expanded. Newly reported within-v2 comparisons include Wan2.2's T2V-CompBench average increasing from 0.5742 to 0.6414 with Comp-Attn, FLUX's image-generation average from 0.5819 to 0.6131, and layout-error rates of 2.93% versus 1.14%. These are new comparisons, not matched v1-to-v2 performance gains; backbone and evaluation settings changed.

M1.justification: DLFA's union of prior and adaptive masks and restricted attention is replaced by LAM's additive attention biases, controlled by layout IoU. Adaptive layouts change from prior-size-based top-k thresholding to mean thresholding, and CogVideoX modulation targets only video-to-text attention. By contrast, SAD becoming SCI does not itself change the conditioning calculation: the saliency score complements the former confusion score, preserving the interpolation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method and results passages are rewritten around the Present-and-Align narrative. SAD/DLFA terminology becomes SCI/LAM, the standalone Applications section disappears, and the supplement is reorganized into Appendices A–G. The changes constitute extensive narrative restructuring, beyond text added for new experiments.

P2.justification: The overview and architecture diagrams are redrawn, and the similarity and mask-fusion illustrations are replaced by attention-response and distribution analyses. The main comparison table is reorganized into backbone-specific groups, with separate VBench, image-generation, latency, and diagnostic tables. Appendix galleries are regrouped by model, and the layout prompt is redesigned as a planning/interpolation diagram.

R1.justification: Related work is repositioned around complementary shortcomings of layout control and inference-time optimization, extending the discussion from video to compositional visual generation. New substantive references include SEGA, Attend-and-Excite, ConceptAttention, Wan, autoregressive diffusion methods, and recent layout-to-image approaches. This changes the methodological context and novelty argument beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: The attention formalization is substantially revised: v1's size-derived thresholds, mask unions, and supplementary block-mask equations are replaced by mean-threshold layouts and signed, IoU-weighted attention-bias definitions in v2 Equations 4–12. This changes the mathematical operator, not merely notation. The complementary confusion/saliency formulations remain equivalent, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence supporting effectiveness and applicability: shared-backbone comparisons reduce confounding, full VBench evaluation checks quality tradeoffs, and targeted ablations plus the layout audit investigate mechanisms and failures that v1 leaves weakly tested. Image-generation experiments support the broader applicability claim. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit hyperparameters and remaining overstatements, such as the broad LAM-superiority interpretation despite VideoGrain's higher Interaction score in Table 6.

A1.justification: The PDFs describe successive versions of the same compositional generation work, renamed from MagicComp to Comp-Attn. Both main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, and image-only figures, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original video and image generation evaluations, component ablations, latency measurements, and a manual audit of generated layouts. Appendix B distinguishes reproduced experiments from externally sourced baseline scores.

before.justification: v1 reports original generated-video evaluations on T2V-CompBench and VBench, component ablations, inference timings, and qualitative demonstrations.

results.title: Comp-Attn: Present-and-Align Attention for Compositional Video Generation

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes compression improvements over MiniCache and compatibility with MLA. V2 expands the central contribution to selective reconstruction, multi-turn robustness, and practical latency reduction, claiming up to 4.23× generation throughput and approximately 30% higher throughput than ShadowKV. Its conclusion also broadens comparative accuracy claims to quantization and token-eviction methods.

C2.justification: V2 replaces v1's prospective system discussion with explanations of dense reconstruction's compute bottleneck, offloading's PCIe limits, and SR's efficiency tradeoffs. It adds interpretations of multi-turn eviction failures and window-size saturation. Long generation becomes an explicit unresolved limitation, whereas v1 suggested periodically recompressing generated tokens.

D1.justification: V2 adds SR pseudocode and implementation details, baseline implementation sources, hardware information, and a custom randomized SVD kernel using 16-bit operations and shifted Cholesky QR. The code URL remains unchanged. V1's explicit MLA-specific treatment of latent and decoupled RoPE caches is omitted, and v2's prefill hardware attribution conflicts between prose and table captions.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates RULER and the LCC/RepoBench-P coding tasks. V2 adds broader LongBench coverage, including document QA, summarization, few-shot and synthetic tasks, plus five-turn NIAH evaluation. The multi-turn setting tests preservation of context across changing queries, extending the original task requirements.

E2.justification: V1 compares against MiniCache, Single SVD, and uncompressed models. V2 adds evaluated KIVI-2, PyramidKV, and SnapKV comparisons in RULER Table 1; Quest, ShadowKV, and value-compressed ShadowKV comparisons in Table 2; and StreamingLLM in LongBench Table 6.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a fixed 2K selected-token budget for its 64K RULER selection comparisons, A100 80GB efficiency tests across batch sizes at 60K/122K lengths, and prefill timing across 64K–256K contexts. Window-size and quantization experiments add controlled settings. These are new evaluation protocols; the PDFs do not establish why retained accuracy scores changed.

E4.justification: The original separate key/value ablation is retained as Figure 6. V2 adds window-size comparisons through eight layers across three variants, 3-bit/4-bit quantization compatibility tests, and CKA analyses for Llama-3.2-1B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Qwen3-4B. Multi-turn tests additionally probe robustness to changing queries.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The expanded results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial SR, multi-turn, LongBench, efficiency, and quantization results; Table 2 reports xKV-SR averaging 89.69 at 5.35× compression. Retained numerical entries also change: Llama-3.1-8B Single SVD at 64K and 8.4× compression changes from 35.3 to 45.71 average accuracy. Conflicting Qwen-7B/14B labels between v2's prose and tables prevent confident matching of some Qwen results.

M1.justification: The grouped cross-layer SVD remains, renamed Cross-Layer Factorization. V2 adds Selective Reconstruction, using query-dependent, head-specific token selection instead of reconstructing every prompt token, and introduces xK-SR with CPU-offloaded values. Section 3 and Appendix B describe a substantive extension of the inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, analysis, and methodology are extensively rewritten, with a new contribution list and revised terminology. Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 6, accuracy and efficiency receive separate sections, and the original MLA evaluation and key/value ablation move into appendices. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, replaces the opening performance chart with a strategy-comparison schematic, and redraws the inference diagram to include SR. It adds multi-turn, efficiency, and broader CKA figures, expanded tables, and algorithm boxes. The MLA chart is relocated and revised; the key/value ablation plot is retained in the appendix.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around dynamic token selection and offloading, explicitly acknowledging ShadowKV's selective reconstruction and presenting xKV as its cross-layer, fully GPU-resident extension. It adds references including Quest, MInference, SCBench, and KVzip, broadening the discussion beyond v1's low-rank and inter-layer emphasis.

T1.justification: Appendix A retains the CKA/SVD alignment derivation apart from notation. V2 adds a limited computational-cost analysis in Section 3 and Appendix D.6, deriving dense versus selective reconstruction FLOPs, factor and landmark storage, and GPU versus total-memory compression ratios.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly lacked an end-to-end system demonstration. V2 addresses that important gap with an implemented SR pipeline and measured latency/throughput comparisons in Section 5, while broader baselines and multi-turn tests strengthen practical validation. Conflicting Qwen labels and prefill figures, plus superiority claims broader than Tables 1 and 6 support, weaken reporting precision. Nevertheless, resolving the system-validation gap provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same xKV research, and their text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable. The original method, analyses, and evaluations can be matched despite extensive revision. Some internal inconsistencies in v2 limit individual numerical comparisons.

after.justification: V2 reports original accuracy, multi-turn retrieval, latency, throughput, quantization, and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original RULER accuracy results, DeepSeek coding evaluations, cross-layer similarity analyses, and key/value compression ablations.

results.title: xKV: Cross-Layer KV-Cache Compression via Aligned Singular Vector Extraction

C1.justification: The abstract and central introductory/concluding claims remain the same: combining Python world-model synthesis with hierarchical abstractions improves planning and learning efficiency. The conclusion retains the 24.5-fold API-usage reduction claim. New experiments expand support without redefining these main contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of initialization traps, overgeneralization of death-avoidance rules, and differences between object-oriented exploration and GPT-o1's repetitive behavior. It proposes maintaining alternative world models. Demonstrated transfer across visually distinct games in v1 becomes a future-work possibility in Section 4.5, although Section 4.2 still retains the Baba is AI success statement.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new WorldCoder comparison's MCTS depth, request cap, and curriculum matching, and specifies that the full-PDDL baseline is manually constructed without learning or revision. Existing API settings, the code-access link, and Appendix A's initialization and revision prompts remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Sections 4.7–4.8 add two KekeCompetition levels requiring sacrifice of controlled characters and a ten-level custom box-clustering game with lethal cherries. These introduce distinct task requirements. Baba is AI coverage remains reported in Section 4.2 despite removal of its dedicated transfer section.

E2.justification: v2 adds EMPA to the reported VGDL comparison in Table 3, a fully specified PDDL/Fast Downward baseline to the runtime comparison in Table 4, and WorldCoder to the BabyAI/Minigrid comparison in Table 7. v1 primarily compares against GPT-o1 and TheoryCoder's own ablation.

E3.justification: New evaluations introduce environment-step and learning-efficiency metrics, token accounting, a 500-environment-step budget, and a matched WorldCoder curriculum with MCTS depth 30 and 50 API calls per level. A failure case is tested through 25 calls. The original six-call benchmark allowance and 500-second planning timeout remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds gameplay heatmaps for KekeCompetition levels 11 and 13, initialization-failure observations, two challenging failure cases, and a custom-game test addressing possible training-data contamination. These substantially extend diagnosis beyond v1's planning and prompting ablations. The dedicated transfer illustration is removed, although its broad outcome remains mentioned.

E5.justification: Section 4.7 newly discloses qualitatively that repeated runs sometimes become stuck. It supplies no run count, seeds, failure frequency, or uncertainty estimates. Runtime averaging over five runs was already reported in v1 and is retained; an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: v2 adds EMPA step/success results, FD runtimes, and WorldCoder comparisons: Table 7 reports 69,402 tokens and 100% success for TheoryCoder versus 388,861 and 83% for WorldCoder. Figure 15 adds four API calls across ten custom-game levels; Section 4.7 reports two failures, one after 25 calls. Original API-call totals persist; reversed Sokoban level/runtime ordering does not establish a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes v1's model-predicted next-state assignment from the environment-execution loop before storing actual transitions. This is a limited pseudocode correction; both versions already describe collecting real environment transitions. The hierarchical planning architecture, synthesis/refinement procedure, and Appendix A prompts remain unchanged.

P1.justification: Related work gains numbered subsections, while the introduction and method exposition are shortened by removing travel and household examples and repetitive PDDL explanations. New experimental subsections are integrated, and publication and author-role text changes. Most existing prose and the main section organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with new comparison tables, an FD column in the runtime table, a learning-efficiency chart, gameplay heatmaps, failure illustrations, and custom-game screenshots/results. It also replaces the BabyAI screenshot and removes v1's transfer figure. These changes extend beyond renumbering and page reflow.

R1.justification: v2 adds references and discussion concerning Guzdial et al.'s game-engine learning, Ruoss et al.'s LMAct benchmark, Minigrid, and Sutton et al.'s temporal abstraction framework. The principal positioning within theory-based RL, program synthesis, and bilevel planning remains intact.

T1.justification: The classical-planning formulation, abstraction definitions, and Equations 1–4 retain their mathematical substance. The added learning-efficiency formula is an adopted evaluation metric credited to prior work, not a new theoretical development. No proofs or formal guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: v2 materially addresses v1's limited comparative validation through relevant WorldCoder and full-PDDL baselines, environment-step comparisons, a custom-game test, and concrete failure cases. These strengthen evidence for the contribution and clarify its limits. Sparse uncertainty reporting, conflicting transfer language, and an apparent Figure 6/Table 3 inconsistency remain: the Push Boulders efficiency bar is about 0.021, whereas the stated formula and table imply 4/236, about 0.017. Despite these weaknesses, the stronger comparisons and explicit failure evidence provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TheoryCoder under the same title and authors. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendix A are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparator evaluations, behavioral analyses, failure cases, and a custom-game experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original TheoryCoder evaluations on grid-world games, including API usage, task success, planning-time ablations, and model-transfer results.

results.title: Synthesizing world models for bilevel planning

C1.justification: The central claims of KNG-based private geodesic regression, Jacobi-field sensitivity, and general Riemannian applicability remain. V2 drops the separately advertised linear-regression contribution and benchmarking promise from the title and introduction. The additional manifold demonstrations principally support the retained central claim.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly acknowledges that the empirical residual bound used in both versions violates privacy and discusses how approximate MCMC sampling weakens pure-DP guarantees under mixing assumptions. It also explains instability under extreme budget allocations and cautions that similar-looking SPD ellipses need not be close geometrically. These materially qualify v1's more affirmative privacy and robustness interpretation.

D1.justification: V2 newly identifies the nonprivate regression implementation as Regmi (2020) and discloses a 16 GB RAM laptop, Windows 11, and Jupyter environment. It documents ADNI landmark normalization and age scaling, plus SPD data generation and noise parameters. These are useful documentation additions, without establishing a solver change or providing a complete implementation release.

E1.justification: V2 removes the Wine Quality/Euclidean regression evaluation and adds synthetic SPD(2) regression and ADNI corpus-callosum shape regression. The latter uses 100 shapes represented by 50 landmarks and ages as predictors. Sphere evaluation remains, so coverage shifts substantially toward different manifold geometries and medical shape data.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates IBM Diffprivlib and Opacus against DPGR in Table 1 and Figure 4. That entire competitive comparison disappears; v2 compares its manifold results with nonprivate regression fits. Laplace, Gaussian, exponential-mechanism, and DP-SGD alternatives are discussed in Section 5 but are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Sphere utility evaluation changes from MAE summaries to log-average MSE. V2 introduces equal-budget sweeps with total epsilon 0.2–2.0 and unequal allocations totaling 2.02, instead of the principal fixed 1+1 allocation. It also changes sample-size conditions and uses 10 footpoints with 10 vectors each per budget, replacing the earlier 200-replicate summaries.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic tests of budget imbalance and total budget, plus sphere data-spread experiments with noise levels 0.001, 0.01, and 0.1. The existing adjacent-dataset sensitivity validation expands from the sphere to SPD(2) and multiple dataset sizes. V1's separate footpoint-distance and shooting-angle diagnostics disappear.

E5.justification: V1 reports means, standard deviations, and utility error bars; v2's utility curves omit uncertainty intervals while sensitivity ratios are summarized with boxplots. The validation reports 100 adjacent-dataset pairs in v1 versus 20 pairs per size and manifold in v2. These revise replication and descriptive reporting without introducing significance testing or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: V1's Wine Quality MSE entries—0.873 nonprivate, 0.954 DPGR, 7.856 Diffprivlib, and 0.982 Opacus—are removed, alongside its sphere MAE summaries. V2 supplies new log-MSE curves, shape and ellipse predictions, and sensitivity-ratio distributions. The new curves show higher errors at restrictive or extremely unequal budgets; changed metrics and settings prevent interpreting them as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Sequential KNG sampling is retained, but its sensitivity-based noise calibration changes substantially. V1's sphere bounds use cosine and sine Jacobi factors; v2 uses 2 tau/n for both parameters on nonnegatively curved manifolds and explicit hyperbolic-function bounds for negative curvature. These changes alter the sampling distributions, beyond merely explaining the existing procedure.

P1.justification: The sensitivity exposition, experimental narrative, and discussion are substantially rewritten. Common evaluation procedures move ahead of manifold-specific subsections, and the appendices are reorganized: geometry moves from C to B, sensitivity validation from B to G, and new derivation and analysis sections are integrated. The title and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. V1's comparison table and principal histograms are removed, while v2 introduces budget curves, shape predictions, noise-dependent sphere views, ellipse predictions, and sensitivity boxplots. The curvature schematic is retained and relocated from v1 Figure 7 to v2 Figure 4, rather than newly added.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from comparison with established private-linear-regression tools to a manifold-regression setting claimed to lack existing DP alternatives. Section 5 develops substantive arguments about difficulties with output perturbation, exponential mechanisms, and DP-SGD. V2 also adds MCMC-privacy, shape-data, and SPD references while removing the Diffprivlib and Opacus references.

T1.justification: V2 replaces the upper-curvature sensitivity argument with two-sided curvature assumptions and lower-curvature comparison bounds using operator norms and parallel/perpendicular Jacobi components. It adds gradient derivations and a geodesic-reach bound in Appendices B.3 and C, and rewrites Appendix D. However, Theorem D.1's negative-curvature formula differs from the proof's Equation 44 and main-text Equation 20.

improvement.justification: V2 materially strengthens the central sensitivity argument by correcting the curvature-comparison direction and accounting for both Jacobi components. Shape/SPD experiments and budget/noise analyses provide substantially better support for manifold applicability, while explicit privacy qualifications improve transparency. These gains outweigh the lost Euclidean comparisons and utility error bars. Important issues remain: the experimental tau is nonprivate, and Theorem D.1 conflicts with Equations 20 and 44.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KNG-based private geodesic-regression work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original sphere, ADNI shape, and SPD(2) regression experiments, including budget, noise, and sensitivity-bound analyses in Section 4 and Appendices E–G.

before.justification: V1 reports original sphere simulations, Wine Quality regression comparisons, and empirical sensitivity-bound checks in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: Differentially Private Geodesic Regression

C1.justification: The central claim of learning constraints without known costs or budgets remains. However, v3 elevates approximation-gap analysis and robustness under limited data, noisy labels, human feedback, and sparser supervision into its principal contributions. These materially extend the abstract, introduction, and conclusion beyond v1's benchmark-performance and credit-assignment claims.

C2.justification: v3 interprets learned credits as supervision-aligned surrogates rather than identifiable ground-truth costs, distinguishes CV dispersion from epistemic uncertainty, and discusses the Jensen bound's looseness over long horizons. It adds explanations for sparse-feedback failures and an explicit limitations section covering unsafe training rollouts, label availability, and inconsistent or drifting supervision.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents network sizes, the two-stack GRU with hidden dimension four, optimization hyperparameters, clamping, checkpoint-label frequencies, retraining triggers, hardware, and measured computational overhead (Appendix B and Table 2). It also supplies training pseudocode and a code-access link. These substantially improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments.

E1.justification: The original 12 benchmark tasks and offline pretraining source remain. v3 expands evaluation to a distinct human-labeled HalfCheetah fall-avoidance task, corrupted-feedback scenarios with up to 20% label noise, and an alternative acceptance threshold of 50 (Appendices C.9, C.11, C.15), substantially broadening the tested supervision and constraint conditions.

E2.justification: v3 adds evaluated oracle comparators CPPO-PID, CUP, FOCOPS, and TRPO-Saute across the benchmark suites (Tables 1, 3–5). PPO-Lagrangian and RLSF remain; C-T is the renamed C&B baseline, not an additional method. Both versions omit RLSF from Bullet Safety Gym because its implementation does not support that suite.

E3.justification: The original main training budgets and 100-trajectory evaluation remain. v3 adds fixed labeling budgets, training without offline pretraining, checkpoint intervals of 40 and 100 steps, and terminal-only supervision with 5,000 labeled trajectories. Its human study disables environment-reward learning and uses 150-step rollouts, 100 training labels per seed, and blinded evaluation of 10 rollouts per seed.

E4.justification: v1's selective-versus-all-feedback ablation is replaced by CV-versus-random selection at a matched 1,000-trajectory budget (v3 Table 10). v3 also adds analyses of label-budget fairness, low data, pretraining dependence, acceptability-rate sensitivity, label noise, clamping, checkpoint sparsity, terminal-only feedback, and an alternative constraint threshold. The original credit-localization diagnostics are largely retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means and standard deviations over eight seeds. v3 adds an explicitly stated three-seed design for the human experiment and specifies the statistical meaning of shaded curve bands and boxplot elements. It does not introduce confidence intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: All shared numerical entries in v1 Tables 1–2 are retained in v3 Tables 1 and 4, including under renamed methods. Substantial new results cover the additional baselines and experimental settings; for example, Table 11 reports human-evaluated non-violation rates of 66.7% for TraCeS, 50.0% for RLSF, and 33.3% for C-T. The former all-feedback ablation comparison is removed. These additions do not demonstrate improved performance over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The recurrent summary encoder/decoder, multiplicative safety scores, cross-entropy training, augmented-state PPO-Lagrangian, and CV-based trajectory selection are retained. Negative-lognormal decoding already appears in v1 Appendix C.2. The renaming and newly documented GRU and clamping details do not establish a changed underlying method.

P1.justification: The introduction, problem formulation, method explanation, results discussion, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around observed-prefix non-violation and surrogate credit. Related work becomes a standalone section, trajectory selection moves into the main method presentation, and the appendices are reorganized into theory, implementation, experiments, pseudocode, and limitations. The title and terminology also change throughout.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text to a two-column layout, adds a pipeline diagram, redraws and separates the estimator architectures, and reformats the trajectory-attribution examples. Comparison tables gain baseline and knowledge-level columns; numerous experimental tables, a hyperparameter table, ablation curves, and human-study images are added. Existing diagnostics are also relocated and relabeled.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands research positioning to shielding and barrier functions, robust safe RL, preference learning/RLHF, and return decomposition, including RUDDER and RRD. It explicitly distinguishes learning control-relevant violation surrogates from recovering hidden costs or redistributing scalar returns. This goes well beyond bibliographic updates to v1's narrower discussion.

T1.justification: v3 adds a Jensen-gap bound, its Taylor-expansion proof, and a worst-case corollary (Theorem 4.5 and Appendix A.1), beyond v1's Jensen-based reformulation. It also revises the monotonicity/range reasoning, makes estimator-capacity and on-policy approximation conditions explicit, and supplies a derivation of conditional variance additivity for CV scoring.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited reproducibility information and weakly controlled evidence for feedback efficiency through detailed implementation documentation, matched-budget comparisons, and extensive sensitivity studies. The added theory and explicit limitations make the justification and applicability clearer. Some new robustness prose overstates the evidence—for example, Table 13 reports Hopper cost 33.9 at 5% noise against a threshold of 25—but this does not outweigh the substantial gains in reproducibility and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TraCeS research, with directly matchable methods, experiments, and results despite substantial rewriting and expansion. The complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, and equations, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains the original empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, controlled-budget experiments, robustness studies, and a human-annotation experiment in Section 5 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on 12 continuous-control tasks, credit-assignment analyses, and a trajectory-selection ablation in Section 4 and Appendix D.

results.title: TraCeS: Learning Per-Timestep Constraint-Violation Credit from Sparse Trajectory-Level Labels

C1.justification: v2 removes the prominent claim of matching TRELLIS with 4% of its training data and 17% of its parameters, retaining a broader efficiency claim. It emphasizes fully supervised prediction and annotations for five datasets. The central contribution—single-view, feed-forward, view-aligned reconstruction of visible and occluded geometry across objects and scenes—remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of design choices: it attributes shared-encoder degradation to task competition, depth-output degradation to focal-length ambiguity, and deeper-layer errors to reduced context. It also qualifies full-system efficiency relative to MoGe, explicitly discusses synthetic-to-real domain gaps, and explains why incomplete ScanNet++ geometry limits quantitative evaluation.

D1.justification: Beyond relocating existing annotation descriptions, v2 supplies camera-axis conventions, rotation-transposition requirements, per-layer head details, ground-truth sampling sources, ten-layer scene ground truth, and 1,000 rotation candidates for registration. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments. The project link and promised pipeline release remain; v1's explicit promise to release evaluation data and scripts is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds quantitative evaluation on held-out synthetic indoor scenes from 3D-FRONT, previously used only for training, and qualitative evaluation on non-training ScanNet++ images. The object and indoor-scene tasks, training sources, and GSO/SCRREAM benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: The GSO view-aligned comparison expands from SF3D, SPAR3D and TRELLIS in v1 Table 1 to also include DUSt3R, VGGT and MoGe in v2 Table 2. This adds a distinct geometric-foundation-model comparator group to a central experiment. The original object baselines and quantitative scene comparator set are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a disjoint 2,300-image 3D-FRONT test subset, filtered for at least 30% unseen pixels, and additional experimental configurations for the new ablations. Efficiency evaluation now also includes both networks together, while the separately reported fixed-sampling Ours* setting disappears. Existing training hyperparameters and GSO/SCRREAM point-sampling budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds DINOv3 pretraining, shared-versus-separate encoders, per-layer reconstruction accuracy, and point-map-versus-depth-plus-focal-length ablations, plus layer-coverage analysis in Figure 6. These address previously untested design choices and occlusion behavior. Existing layer-count and mask-strategy ablations remain; the Ours* sampling comparison is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new dataset statistics and layer-coverage plots do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Shared GSO and SCRREAM benchmark scores remain unchanged, but v2 adds substantial result sets for 3D-FRONT, new object baselines and appendix analyses. For example, LaRI's new 3D-FRONT overall results are CD 0.061 and FS@0.05 0.799. Table 6 adds combined-network measurements of 620.2M parameters and 51.5 ms; these measure a broader system than the retained point-map-only results. Ours* and some scene F-score entries disappear. Table 8's dataset attribution is unclear: its text names SCRREAM, but its separate-encoder scores match the GSO baseline.

M1.justification: Both versions use layered point maps, separate point-map and ray-stopping networks, scale-shift-aligned geometric supervision and cross-entropy stopping-index supervision. v2 explicitly describes per-layer prediction heads and tests alternative architectures and outputs, but does not establish a change to the proposed default method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial related-work and evaluation passages are rewritten. Data construction is condensed in the main text and moved into an expanded appendix, implementation explanations are reorganized, conclusions precede limitations, and an Impact Statement is added. This is substantial editorial restructuring despite the stable core method.

P2.justification: v2 adds quantitative panels to Figure 1, redesigns object and scene comparisons with multiple views, and adds coverage plots and appendix visualizations. Tables gain dataset statistics, additional comparator rows, a two-dataset scene layout, combined-network efficiency rows and new ablation displays. Conference formatting, captions, shading and placement also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 expands discussion of close work, including DRDF, MLD, Rayst3R, X-ray, Flash3D and Splatter Image, and cites VGGT and DINOv3. It more explicitly acknowledges LDI inspiration and distinguishes geometric supervision from photorealistic view synthesis. These refine positioning within the existing related-work framework; publication updates to retained references are not new works.

T1.justification: The representation, alignment loss and stopping-index mathematics are substantively unchanged. v2's head/concatenation equations and standard Chamfer-distance and F-score formulas explain existing procedures. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the evidence and transparency supporting LaRI. New design and per-layer analyses address previously untested choices, while detailed rendering and registration instructions improve reproducibility. Crucially, Table 6 reports the stopping-index network's additional cost and qualifies the efficiency advantage, correcting the incomplete accounting in v1's point-map-only comparison. Table 8's unclear dataset attribution and removal of the sampling comparison limit parts of the revision, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaRI research, with matching methods and shared experiments. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes Appendix A.1–A.6, which was included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original reconstruction experiments and adds 3D-FRONT evaluation, further comparisons and appendix ablations in Tables 2–10.

before.justification: v1 reports original GSO and SCRREAM reconstruction experiments, efficiency measurements, and layer-count, pretraining and mask-prediction ablations in Tables 1–6.

results.title: LaRI: Layered Ray Intersections for Single-view 3D Geometric Reasoning

C1.justification: v1 establishes an upper convergence bound and leaves dimensional optimality open, even suggesting linear dependence might be possible. v2 claims matching minimax optimality at d², a further dimensional penalty for non-adaptive sensing, and a new derivation of the fully observed lower bound. These substantially broaden the principal contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the dimensional penalty as unavoidable and explains adaptivity through signal capture and measurement budgets. It clarifies trailing-eigenspace noise, discusses additive measurement corruption, and replaces generic rank-k future work with specific scaling conjectures and obstacles. Sub-Gaussian extension changes from future work to an asserted extension, while tracking gains an explicit drift assumption.

D1.justification: v2 documents additional parameter grids, target errors and learning rates. Tracking now specifies the rotation rule sin²(θ)=V and initial squared alignment 0.1, improving reproducibility detail beyond v1. Neither version provides implementation code or computing-hardware information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic Gaussian principal-eigenvector estimation with stationary and drifting eigenvectors. The added dimension, eigengap and drift-speed sweeps vary parameters within these retained tasks; no new empirical dataset, domain or distribution family is evaluated.

E2.justification: v1's empirical fully sampled Oja comparator in Figure 1 is removed. v2 instead evaluates non-adaptive random measurements against adaptive sensing in Table 1, with both using two scalar measurements per iteration. This substantially changes the comparative question and comparator set.

E3.justification: The central convergence experiment changes from d=10 to d=64 and uses the revised theorem-based schedule. Added experiments introduce a 0.01/d learning rate, iterations-to-error-0.01 evaluation, dimensions 16–1024 and four eigengap settings. Tracking validation expands to five drift velocities.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct tests of the benefit of adaptivity, dimension-scaling analysis and eigengap sensitivity analysis in Section 6 and Appendix C. The existing tracking analysis gains a multi-velocity comparison of predicted and empirical steady-state errors.

E5.justification: v1 reports averaged convergence trajectories over 20 trials with 20–80 percentile bands. The revised v2 Figure 1 reports medians over 50 trials with 25–75 percentile bands. v2 also introduces least-squares scaling fits; tracking retains 20-trial, 20–80 percentile reporting.

E6.justification: New results include non-adaptive slowdowns of 4.2×, 7.1× and 14× at d=16, 32 and 64 in Table 1, a dimension-scaling exponent of 2.16, and an eigengap-fit slope of −2.42. The original fully sampled comparison is removed and convergence/tracking plots are replaced or expanded. These are changed-setting or newly reported results, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same sensing directions, projected Oja update and normalization. However, the corrected S in Theorem 4.1 changes the prescribed warmup duration and constant-then-decaying step sizes relative to v1's Theorem 2, constituting a limited schedule recalibration.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and limitations are extensively rewritten. v2 creates a separate Main Results section, recasts Methods as Proof Techniques, moves the imputation derivation into Appendix A.1, and separates tracking theory from its experimental validation.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column formatting. Both original experimental figures are redesigned, including a joint upper/lower-bound display and multi-panel tracking plots. Dimension and eigengap figures and two numerical tables are added, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against randomized and batch PCA, citing Halko, Liberty, Musco and Woodruff, and introduces minimax/Assouad references including Vu–Lei, Duchi and van der Vaart. The relationship to prior work shifts from noisy convergence analysis toward optimality and separation of observation regimes.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds Assouad-based lower bounds for fully observed, adaptive compressed and non-adaptive compressed estimation. The upper-bound proof restores the conditional-covariance contribution, changing S from λ1λ2d²/Δ² + 13λ1d/Δ to 3λ1λ2d²/Δ² + 15λ1d/Δ. Warmup algebra is revised, and Appendix A.2.11 adds an independence/zero-mean condition to the retained tracking derivation.

improvement.justification: v2 corrects an omitted variance contribution and warmup algebra, states an important tracking assumption, and supplies lower-bound arguments for v1's unresolved optimality question. Direct adaptivity and scaling experiments substantially strengthen the empirical support. These gains outweigh a remaining scope inconsistency: Theorem 4.2 omits the dimension and eigengap restrictions explicitly required in Appendix B.2.6, so its headline optimality claim still needs qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same adaptive principal-eigenvector estimation work. Their text, equations, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including v2's new Appendices B and C.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulations of convergence, adaptive versus non-adaptive sensing, dimension scaling, tracking and eigengap dependence in Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–4.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian-data simulations comparing adaptive and fully sampled Oja, plus moving-eigenvector tracking experiments in Figures 1 and 2.

C1.justification: The central dense-communication and limited-data adaptation claims remain. v2 explicitly presents learning coordination without intermediate-message labels as a contribution and relaxes the training-cost claim from less than 0.1% to less than 0.2%. The earlier similar-size-model and scaling claims remain in Appendix A.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes its implemented autoregressive network from sentence-level agent message passing and discusses learned computational roles. It adds substantive limitations concerning inference cost, model-internal access and interpretability, and cautions that observed edge patterns do not establish topology optimality. New interpretations address data scarcity, harder tasks and intermediate representations.

D1.justification: v2 replaces a future code-release promise with an availability statement and repository address. It documents the intermediate-vertex probing and output-truncation procedure, but removes most per-method E2E trainable-parameter counts previously supplied in Table 4.

E1.justification: v2 adds OpenR1-Math-220k as supplementary training data and evaluates an unseen, more challenging mathematics subset in Appendix C. This extends mathematical coverage while retaining the earlier general-capability benchmarks and MMLU, GSM8K and E2E tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds same-data SFT, Self-Refine and Self-Consistency to the general-capability comparison, and COCONUT and CODI to MMLU/GSM8K adaptation comparisons. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives. Earlier monolithic-model and PEFT comparators remain; FT becoming SFT in retained adaptation tables is a rename.

E3.justification: v2 adds 93.7k training examples to the GSM8K adaptation setting, 16-trial/iteration test-time controls, 3B/7B backbone evaluations and E2E average-rank reporting. The general-training budget changes from under 60 A100 GPU-days and at most 0.01T tokens/1e5 PFLOPs to under 100 GPU-days and 0.02T tokens/2e5 PFLOPs. These are revised reported settings; they do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds backbone-size and training-data-amount studies, expands the existing GSM8K case study with intermediate-vertex decoding, and supplies additional edge-matrix visualizations and parameter summaries. The earlier last-layer attention-map analysis is removed. E2E depth/width and PEFT-combination studies largely existed already and are redistributed rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, performance uncertainty intervals or formal significance tests. The new means and standard deviations in edge-matrix plots summarize learned parameters, rather than uncertainty in experimental performance.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for new comparators, larger backbones, augmented training and OpenR1 evaluation. Original GSM8K results remain in Table 9; Table 3's Qwen2.5-0.5B LMNet accuracy of 50.82% uses additional data, unlike the earlier 30.93%. For the retained E2E 1/2/1 configuration, MET changes from 45.7 to 46.5 and CIDEr from 2.38 to 2.48. Earlier general-capability accuracy entries remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Both versions use stripped transformer vertices, trainable attention-block edges, shared vertex parameters, summed messages and end-to-end autoregressive training. v2 expands the explanation and discusses concatenation and inner-autoregressive communication as alternatives or future work, without establishing an adopted procedural change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Method exposition is reorganized around nodes, edges and topology; complexity moves into the method section, discussion moves after experiments, and a dedicated ablation section and Appendices A-D reorganize substantial earlier material.

P2.justification: The main text changes from predominantly single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 3 is replaced with a vertex-output case-study diagram, and additional matrix plots are supplied. The original E2E table is divided across Tables 4, 6 and 11, alongside new comparison tables and relocated existing displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially reframes positioning around language model networks, supervision efficiency and distinctions from latent reasoning. It adds Compressed Chain of Thought, CODI, Self-Refine and data-efficient agentic-learning references, while removing several cognitive-science references and the earlier differentiable-RL comparison. This changes the research context beyond bibliographic editing.

T1.justification: v1 Section 3.3 supplies an explicit chain-rule derivation of vertex and edge gradients following Proposition 1. v2 retains the differentiability assertion but omits that derivation. The parameter-sharing complexity formulas remain, and no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited comparative support through same-data SFT, approximately budgeted test-time baselines and latent-reasoning comparisons. Its explicit limitations also clarify what the implemented communication actually demonstrates. These gains outweigh reduced E2E parameter-count transparency and unexplained resource/score revisions, although missing training details and uncertainty reporting still limit auditability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LMNet research despite the changed title and organization. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original LMNet results and reports additional baseline comparisons, larger-backbone experiments, training-data analyses and OpenR1-Math evaluation.

before.justification: v1 reports original LMNet experiments on general capability, MMLU/GSM8K adaptation and E2E generation, together with communication analyses.

results.title: Language Model Networks: Supervision-Efficient Learning through Dense Communication

C1.justification: V2 withdraws the PCQM4Mv2 state-of-the-art and parameter-efficiency contribution emphasized throughout v1. It instead claims graph alignment generalizes the WL test and learns a high-fidelity compression of graph structure, supported by approximately 98% reconstruction accuracy. The abstract, contributions and conclusion therefore redefine a substantial part of the paper's claimed achievement.

C2.justification: V2 adds metric-learning and denoising interpretations, a structural-bottleneck interpretation of downstream correlations, and compression/transferability interpretations of reconstruction. It explicitly discusses potentially nonoptimal planted alignments on small or highly corrupted graphs and the absence of general recovery guarantees beyond Erdős-Rényi graphs. It also attributes GPSE's ZINC advantage to cycle-count pretraining and removes the earlier edge-feature limitation.

D1.justification: V2 adds a direct repository link, extended-model hyperparameters in Table G.7, and separate pretraining/downstream runtimes in Table L.14. The multi-GPU training details for the removed leaderboard study disappear. Most existing implementation, optimizer, hardware and data-split disclosures are retained; the new link does not establish a newly released resource.

E1.justification: V2 adds adjacency-matrix reconstruction on ZINC and PCQM4Mv2, including transfer from encoders pretrained on molecular and citation graphs. This substantially extends the evaluated task requirements beyond alignment and molecular regression. The underlying dataset families are retained; ZINC already appeared in v1's regression and pretraining experiments.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds GPSE. Alignment comparisons add GraphGPS, PNA, SGC, GSN and PPGN, while reconstruction introduces a random baseline. The separate PCQM4Mv2 leaderboard comparison against Graphormer, GPS-Medium, Uni-Mol+, EGT-Large and TGT-At is removed. These changes materially alter comparator membership within the relevant experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include frozen-encoder reconstruction evaluated by edge accuracy and F1, approximately 60k/140k-parameter architecture comparisons with four/eight layers, and a two-to-seven-layer depth sweep. The larger Transformer leaderboard experiment is removed. Existing alignment splits, noise grids and retained molecular-regression settings remain unchanged; the additions do not establish reruns of those experiments.

E4.justification: V2 adds a depth/denoising ablation (Table C.3), capacity and expressivity analyses (Appendices G-H), alignment-to-downstream correlations (Appendix I), and reconstruction threshold sensitivity against a random baseline (Appendix M). The earlier noise-transfer and pretraining-source analyses remain in Appendix K rather than being newly introduced.

E5.justification: V2 introduces Pearson-correlation estimation and explicitly specifies four different random seeds for the new depth and extended-architecture studies. Existing ten-run alignment and four-run positional-encoding reporting remain unchanged. The removed leaderboard experiment's two-run averages disappear; this is not evidence of reduced replication for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Retained alignment, transfer and edge-feature tables are numerically unchanged. Added GPSE changes the best reported ZINC mean in Table 1 to 0.104 ± 0.006, versus GAPE+RWPE's retained 0.109 ± 0.005. Reconstruction adds 97.7-98.8% accuracy and 94.0-94.7% F1, alongside new depth, architecture and correlation results. V1's leaderboard GAPE MAEs of 0.0497, 0.0441 and 0.0337 are removed.

M1.justification: The central Siamese alignment and GAPE procedures remain. Algorithm 1 corrects the BFS trimming condition from <= N' to > N', and Section 6.3 adds an auxiliary frozen GAPE encoder with a trainable Transformer reconstruction decoder. These are localized procedural changes; the PDFs do not establish that the BFS implementation or original experiments changed.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, contributions and conclusion, reframes Section 6 around structural representations, and replaces its leaderboard subsection with reconstruction. It swaps the conclusion and limitations, reorganizes the appendices, removes the NeurIPS checklist, and adds impact and acknowledgement sections. These changes materially reshape the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout with running headers. V2 adds numerous analytical and experimental tables plus correlation and reconstruction-F1 figures, expands Table 1, and replaces the leaderboard Table 2 with reconstruction results. Retained diagrams, benchmark tables and noise-transfer plots are resized or relocated rather than constituting new evidence.

R1.justification: Appendix C.2 substantially expands comparison with prior combinatorial benchmarks, including counting, biconnectivity and coloring tasks. New positioning connects alignment to metric learning, denoising, BYOL and WL expressivity, with additional references supporting these discussions and GPSE/higher-order comparisons. The previous leaderboard-specific positioning and associated references are reduced.

T1.justification: Beyond the retained equivariance theorem A.1, v2 adds an automorphism-invariant-loss theorem and proof (B.2), a graph-distance derivation (C.2.2), and node-equivalence accuracy/loss bounds with a WL-hierarchy corollary (C.3). It also introduces a cited Erdős-Rényi recovery condition and formal isotropic/anisotropic definitions. This substantially expands the mathematical treatment.

improvement.justification: Broader architecture comparisons, a depth ablation, downstream correlations, and frozen-encoder reconstruction with a random control substantially strengthen evidence that alignment measures useful structural representations. Symmetry analysis, noise-validity caveats and clearer resource access also improve assessability. These gains outweigh losing the separate leaderboard study, although reconstruction protocols and uncertainty remain underdocumented, and Appendix I overstates its correlations: Figure I.1 includes -0.896 despite claiming all are below -0.90.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph-alignment benchmarking and GAPE work. Their complete text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds reconstruction experiments, architecture comparisons, depth ablations and downstream-correlation analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original graph-alignment experiments, molecular regression comparisons, noise-transfer analyses and positional-encoding experiments in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Graph Alignment for Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks and Learning Positional Encodings

C1.justification: The abstract extends its explicit empirical claim from improved semantic similarity to improved NLI entailment and hallucination-detection consistency. The central benchmark, construction-framework, and multilingual contributions, as well as the conclusion, remain substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the human audit as evidence about residual dataset noise and presents metric triangulation as addressing semantic-embedding limitations. Section 8 adds the inability to pinpoint hallucinatory text spans, replacing the earlier proposal to add NLI evaluation. Most domain, temporal, and language limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 identifies the added NLI checkpoint and HHEM-2.1 evaluator, specifies their input construction, and newly describes preliminary sampling as proportional. Section 9 adds reproducibility guidance concerning closed-source judging components. Existing code/data access, prompts, translation hyperparameters, hardware, and compute-cost disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same seven source benchmarks, domains, and six languages, with 25,905 question-path pairs and 7,095 unique questions per language. NLI, hallucination scoring, and human validation assess retained data rather than introduce new task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: The QA/KG-RAG comparisons retain Gemini 2.0 Flash, GPT-4o Mini, and Llama 3.3 70B Instruct; the preliminary judge comparison retains Gemini and GPT-4o Mini. NLI and HHEM-2.1 are added scoring tools, while human judgments provide validation labels rather than another competing method.

E3.justification: Section 3 adds multilingual NLI and English-only HHEM-2.1 evaluation, using question-plus-ground-truth as premise and generated answer as hypothesis. Human validation adds agreement/error evaluation of binarized path ratings. These substantially broaden the evaluation protocol while retaining the original generation settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds human validation of automatic path judgments in Table 4 and a quality-subset ablation in Appendix M, Table 13. The latter examines semantic scores across progressively included or excluded rating levels. These directly investigate filtering reliability beyond v1's correlations and retained error examples.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly declines formal significance testing. V2 adds Shapiro-Wilk normality tests and two-sample Cramer-von Mises tests for every model-language combination in Appendix L, plus Cohen's kappa for human–LLM agreement. Both versions still explicitly report no repeated-seed runs; existing error bars remain standard deviations across data points.

E6.justification: New Tables 5–6 report KG-RAG versus QA entailment rates of 68%/52%, 71%/45%, and 76%/40%, and English consistency rates of 87%/58%, 88%/55%, and 89%/47% for Gemini, Llama, and GPT respectively. Human-validation, significance, and quality-subset results are also added. Matched original semantic-similarity results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The entity-linking, Wikidata path-mining, two-stage path selection/scoring, translation, and prompt-based knowledge-injection procedures are retained. Corresponding SPARQL queries, property lists, and prompts are unchanged. The added evaluators change assessment, not the proposed construction or generation methods.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose revisions, corrects the reversed QA/KG-RAG parenthetical in Section 3, changes citations to author–year style, and adds reproducibility, ethics, and LLM-usage statements. The original narrative and main section sequence are largely retained.

P2.justification: The results presentation is substantially expanded with human-validation, NLI, hallucination, significance, and ablation tables. V1's main-text domain-results Table 4 moves to Appendix O as Table 15, and the document adopts a different title, heading, and table layout. Figures 1–3 themselves are unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting its evaluation choices and noise discussion, including HalluLens, HHEM-2.1, OpenFactCheck, and studies of LLM judging and NLI faithfulness. The FActScore reference is removed. The central positioning relative to multilingual QA and KG-grounded benchmarks remains unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. V2's evaluator input notation and named statistical tests do not introduce a substantive mathematical derivation, assumption, or theoretical property.

improvement.justification: V1 relies on semantic similarity despite acknowledging its factuality-evaluation weaknesses, and validates path judging mainly through correlation. V2 substantially addresses these central validation gaps through NLI/HHEM evaluation, human agreement/error measurements, and path-quality analyses, supplemented by formal significance tests. Human-annotation procedures remain underdescribed and repeated-run uncertainty remains absent, but the added evidence materially strengthens the benchmark's empirical credibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MultiHal benchmark. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds NLI and hallucination-detection scores, human validation of path judgments, and path-quality analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original QA versus KG-RAG experiments across three LLMs and six languages, plus experiments comparing path-quality judges.

results.title: MultiHal: Multilingual Dataset for Knowledge-Graph Grounded Evaluation of LLM Hallucinations

C1.justification: v2 strengthens the central empirical comparison from a smaller single SAE to an expanded SAE with matching feature count. The introduction replaces the prominently stated feature-diversity benefit with a claim of more interpretable features. These change the scope of the claimed advantages, while the bagging, boosting, and concatenation contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 newly argues that aggregate L0 is an unreliable interpretability proxy for ensembles and interprets the expanded baseline through a stability-reconstruction tradeoff. It develops guidance for single-feature versus multiple-feature concept detection and discusses negative Gemma SCR scores, TPP shortcomings, and applicability restrictions for absorption and unlearning evaluations. Earlier computational-cost and feature-redundancy limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the existing implementation recipe with Pythia-70M hyperparameters, expanded-baseline sparsity targeting, additional training times, and inference-timing hardware and procedures. It identifies default SAEBench settings and states that implementation code was submitted as supplementary material; the PDFs do not establish a public code release. Existing framework, hardware, and batch-size disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds automated feature interpretation, RAVEL attribute-value disentanglement, targeted probe perturbation, and spelling-related feature-absorption evaluations. It removes Amazon Review product-category prediction while retaining sentiment, programming-language, news-topic, document-language, and gender-debiasing tasks. These additions substantially broaden evaluated task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 introduces an expanded single-SAE comparator with the ensemble's feature count throughout the main evaluations and relevant appendix comparisons. The original smaller single SAE remains as the base SAE in Appendix D and other supplementary comparisons; it was not simply removed or renamed into the expanded baseline.

E3.justification: New controls match feature count and target boosting's aggregate L0, rather than comparing only against a smaller SAE. v2 removes relative sparsity and cosine-diversity metrics, adds AutoInterp, additional SAEBench and timing protocols, and introduces top-2 feature probing. It also evaluates retained downstream tasks with Pythia-160M and Gemma 2-2B configurations; original training-token budgets and the intrinsic test split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds first-versus-last SAE concept case studies investigating feature specificity and a top-2 feature-selection analysis. It adds expanded-SAE controls to the existing top-5 probing and SCR feature-ablation analyses. Conversely, v1's Appendix E diversity-threshold sensitivity study is removed; ensemble-size and hyperparameter sweeps remain.

E5.justification: The established reporting of means and 95% confidence intervals across five runs remains. v2 clarifies how individual runs serve as references for stability estimation and adds inference-time means and 95% intervals across ten batches in Supplementary Table 15. This does not establish an increase in training-run counts.

E6.justification: Shared ensemble scores are retained: Gemma boosting MSE remains 46.538, for example. v2 adds expanded-baseline results, including Gemma MSE 472.330, plus AutoInterp, top-2 probing, further model-specific downstream results, SAEBench scores, and timing measurements. New findings include expanded SAEs outperforming ensembles on TPP for Pythia-160M and Gemma 2-2B. Category-prediction, relative-sparsity, and diversity result entries are removed.

M1.justification: Naive bagging still averages independently initialized SAEs trained on the same data; boosting still trains sequentially on residuals and sums reconstructions. Feature concatenation and Algorithm 1 retain the same procedures. The expanded SAE is a new comparator, not a modification of the proposed methods.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much methodological exposition remain. v2 revises the abstract and experimental narrative around expanded baselines, renames Preliminaries to Formalizing SAE Ensembles, distinguishes base from expanded SAEs, and reorganizes appendices. It also adds impact and acknowledgment sections; these are targeted structural and language revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: The main text adopts a two-column conference layout, original base comparisons move into the appendix, and new qualitative, interpretability, downstream, and timing tables substantially restructure presentation. Intrinsic figures shrink from six panels to four, and diversity-threshold figures disappear. Revised Supplementary Figure 3 incorrectly labels the MSE panel as Relative Sparsity and the connectivity panel as MSE.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused distinctions from Switch SAEs, SAE Boost, and MP-SAEs, plus references supporting AutoInterp, specialized SAEs, and interpretability limitations. It removes the SAE-stitching discussion and the strong-law reference. These update neighboring-work positioning while preserving the overall relationship to classical ensembles and SAE variability.

T1.justification: The bagging proposition receives a substantive but localized revision: v1's strong-law/almost-sure argument becomes a direct 1/J variance calculation in Proposition A.2, with a changed finiteness condition and removal of the almost-sure qualifier. Remark 3.2 also corrects weight absorption from Wenc to Wdec. The feature-concatenation and boosting results otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central weakness of v1: ensembles were compared only with a much smaller SAE. The expanded comparator, with matching feature count and sparsity targeted to boosting, substantially strengthens validation. Direct interpretability assessments and broader downstream tests provide additional evidence, including exceptions to ensemble superiority. Removing category/diversity analyses and introducing mislabeled plot axes are drawbacks, but the stronger comparisons and more informative evaluation outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ensembling Sparse Autoencoders by the same authors. Their methods, experiments, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and matchable despite additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds expanded-SAE comparisons, automated interpretability assessments, further downstream evaluations, and inference-time measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAE training experiments, intrinsic evaluations, concept-detection accuracy, spurious-correlation removal results, and appendix sensitivity analyses.

results.title: Ensembling Sparse Autoencoders

C1.justification: The central claim linking backward oversmoothing to spurious near-stationarity remains. Its scope broadens substantially: v2 explicitly claims applicability to nonlinear GNNs with nonsymmetric stochastic propagation, conditional on forward oversmoothing, whereas v1's results require symmetric propagation. This extension is emphasized in the introduction and conclusion.

C2.justification: V2 identifies the unresolved nonlinear/nonsymmetric forward-smoothing case, discusses the nonzero-output assumption as a proof artifact, and interprets dataset-dependent stagnation through convergence rates. It adds substantive discussion of skip-connection stability and normalization difficulties. Conversely, v1's explicit caveat that its flat regions need not contain exact minima or saddle points is omitted.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly documents undirected/largest-component preprocessing, integer-label regression, all-node training, near-identity Gaussian initialization, Leaky ReLU and skip-connection weight scales. These disclosures substantially expand the experimental description without establishing changes to previously unspecified settings. However, v1's explicit code-access link disappears from v2.

E1.justification: V1's training illustrations concern CSBM node classification; Cora and Citeseer appear only in spectral-gap calculations. V2 evaluates regression on Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, WikiCS and synthetic graphs at two densities, converting classification labels into integer regression targets (Appendix B). This substantially broadens empirical coverage and changes the evaluated task.

E2.justification: The deep MLP comparator is retained. V2 adds explicit GNN comparisons with versus without skip connections in Figure 3, while v1's shallow GNN and shallow MLP reference curves are absent. The change concerns a limited set of comparison variants.

E3.justification: V2 explicitly uses random-walk propagation P = D−1A and MSE regression, with 100 layers except 40 for the dense synthetic graph. V1 illustrates classification with 5/40-layer models. Training plots extend from 200 to 1,000 epochs, and backward smoothing is now measured relative to the stationary distribution π. These are revised experimental settings, not comparable performance reruns.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds tests of forward smoothing when the sufficient contraction condition fails, comparing estimated decay rates with spectral quantities in Table 1. Figure 3 adds skip/no-skip comparisons and sensitivity to weight scales sL = 1, 5 and 10. V1 has no corresponding mitigation or weight-scale analysis, although it includes shallow/deep comparisons.

E5.justification: V2 first states that the oversmoothing curves in Figures 2–3 average 10 random initializations and displays shaded bands. V1 reports no repeat count or uncertainty convention. The bands' statistical meaning remains unspecified; the PDFs do not establish an increase in runs for an unchanged experiment.
