E6.justification: V2 replaces the original classification illustrations with regression trajectories and adds spectral, convergence and skip-connection results. For example, Table 1 reports WikiCS λf = 0.901, λP = 0.917 and contraction norm 9.55. Appendix B finds clearer stagnation on synthetic graphs/WikiCS than on Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed. These are new findings under changed settings, not same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Both versions analyze the same vanilla message-passing GNN, backpropagation equations and standard loss formulations; neither proposes a new training method. The generalized propagation assumptions concern theory, while skip connections are evaluated as an existing comparison variant.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, contribution discussion and explanatory passages in Sections 2–4. Section 4 moves the proof sketch before the high-loss corollary and MLP discussion and adds mitigation/numerical subsections. A dedicated experimental Appendix B is introduced, moving the technical lemmas to Appendix C. These changes materially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: V1's separate training figure and small oversmoothing inset are replaced by a combined WikiCS display in Figure 1. V2 adds Table 1 and two six-row multipanel figures with revised axes, legends and shaded bands. The WikiCS row in Figure 2 redisplays Figure 1's evidence; it is not an additional experiment.

R1.justification: The overall related-work framing remains, but v2 newly challenges Park and Kim's treatment of the smoothing limit and positions its nonsymmetric analysis against that limitation. It adds references on residual-connection theory, attention oversmoothing, WikiCS, Fixup initialization and DFA-GNN, while removing the original CSBM reference.

T1.justification: V2 generalizes symmetric bistochastic propagation to stochastic mixing with stationary distribution π, introduces Eπ and conditional forward oversmoothing, and substantially rewrites the proofs. Theorem 3 loses its probabilistic alternative. Corollary 2 becomes a deterministic centered-label/small-output-weight result with bound σ_y²/2−ε. Proposition 2 receives a new nonzero-output MLP counterexample, and Appendix A.9 adds Theorem 5 with explicit constants.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves practical relevance by extending the theory beyond v1's uncommon symmetric propagation setting, while explicitly identifying the remaining forward-smoothing condition. Appendix B tests that condition and adds informative real-graph and mitigation analyses, addressing v1's narrow empirical support. These gains outweigh the removed probabilistic alternative and code link, although reproducibility remains incomplete and the plotted uncertainty bands are undefined.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same backward-oversmoothing research. All 20 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2, including figures, equations, references and appendices, support comparison without material reading gaps.

after.justification: Figure 1 and Appendix B report original experiments on synthetic and real graphs, including convergence estimates, training trajectories and skip-connection comparisons.

before.justification: Figures 1–2 report original CSBM experiments measuring training losses, layerwise gradients and forward/backward oversmoothing. Section 2 also reports graph spectral measurements.

results.title: Backward Oversmoothing: why is it hard to train deep Graph Neural Networks?

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement and conclusion explicitly extend the empirical competitive-performance claim from Gemma to additional language and vision models. The central claims about scalable alternating optimization, Matryoshka structuring and SAE solution quality are retained.

C2.justification: v2 introduces interpretations concerning weaker SAE performance at lower embedding dimensions, saturation of visual explanations, and better isolation of individual concepts by SAE features. Appendix D.4 adds a qualified interpretation of existing curves as suggesting approximately 1.3 million samples for convergence. The discussion of benefits from partially known initialization disappears.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 documents CLS extraction, feature/image selection counts, the explanation prompt, scoring procedure and sign handling. Appendix C newly reports single-precision memory requirements, approximately 80 GB RAM and 16–32 GB GPU memory. Existing Gemma implementation details remain, while synthetic-data generation details are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-1k vision coverage through DINOv2 embeddings, image-class probing and visual autointerpretability. It removes v1's noisy synthetic task with partially known coefficient structure. The Pile-based language task remains; adding Pythia within that task is principally a model-configuration expansion.

E2.justification: The SAEBench comparator set and original KSVD timing baseline remain. The new vision comparison evaluates a modified TopK-SAE comparator: Appendix B.2 uses matching pursuit with its learned dictionary instead of its encoder. TopK-SAE itself was already represented in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds Pythia-160M and DINOv2-S/B configurations. Its new vision protocol uses 4096 dictionary elements, sparsities 16/32/64, per-class logistic probes, and GPT-4o-mini explanations scored using CLIP and Spearman correlation. Matching pursuit controls encoding across vision dictionaries. The existing Gemma training protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v1's systematic study of known initialization fractions, including Figure 3 and Appendix A.2, is removed. v2 adds sensitivity to the number of probing features per class (Table 5) and image/feature interpretation case studies (Figures 3–4). The existing coherence and training-convergence analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report the fastest of five timing trials and state that trials fall within a 10% margin. Neither provides repeated-run uncertainty estimates for dictionary-quality comparisons; the added evaluation scores introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds five-metric Pythia results and DINOv2 results while removing the synthetic initialization findings. For DINOv2-B at k=32, Table 2 reports DB-KSVD versus SAE variance explained of 0.817 versus 0.794, probing accuracy of 0.893 versus 0.932, and autointerpretability of 0.802 versus 0.797. These are new comparisons; retained Gemma results and timing values are unchanged.

M1.justification: The dictionary-learning objective, accelerated matching pursuit, inner and outer batching, dictionary updates and Matryoshka procedure remain unchanged in Sections 2 and 4. Additional complexity analysis and applications do not establish a revision to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 refines introductory and theoretical explanations, converts contribution bullets to an inline enumeration, and places benchmark and coherence results before timing results. Appendices are reorganized around visualization, experimental details, complexity and additional results. Most existing exposition is retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column formatting, with extensive resizing and relocation of retained displays. v2 adds visual feature panels, a Pythia results figure and three vision-result tables, while removing the synthetic convergence figure. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Pythia, DINOv2, ImageNet, automated neuron explanations and Prisma. Citations to weakly supervised disentanglement, Barlow Twins and VICReg disappear with the initialization study. The main related-work narrative and positioning relative to KSVD and SAEs remain stable.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 and new Appendix C extend v1's component-cost discussion into total computational and memory bounds, including Equation 8 and a cubic-scaling claim under stated parameter assumptions. This is an analytical extension; the optimization formulation, identifiability bounds and existing sample-complexity discussion remain substantially unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens applicability evidence beyond v1's single real-world embedding source by testing another language model and two vision models, revealing reconstruction–probing tradeoffs and providing inspectable feature examples. The shared matching-pursuit control and added resource documentation improve assessment of dictionary quality and feasibility. Removing the initialization study loses useful evidence, and quality-score uncertainty remains unreported, but the broader validation provides a substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DB-KSVD work. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison; retained experiments can be matched despite reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains the Gemma experiments and reports additional Pythia-160M and DINOv2 evaluations, including quantitative comparisons and visual feature examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gemma-2-2B evaluations, runtime measurements, dictionary-coherence analyses and a synthetic experiment on initialization with partially known structure.

results.title: DB-KSVD: Scalable Alternating Optimization for Disentangling High-Dimensional Embedding Spaces

C1.justification: The abstracts, introductions, and conclusions retain the central claims: nonlinear entanglement limits faithful intervention, structured COCA reasoning concentrates harmful concepts, and COCA improves jailbreak robustness while preserving benign capabilities. The formal theory changes substantially, but the headline contributions remain essentially the same.

C2.justification: v2 newly attributes residual Code Attack vulnerability to obfuscated concept identification, interprets supervision and intervention as complementary, and argues that longer reasoning alone is insufficient. It adds limitations concerning forged benign concept tags, untested 70B-plus models, teacher quality, and safety-taxonomy variation. Section 2.3 also expands the connection between the theoretical two-head abstraction and autoregressive training.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies frozen-base, trainable-adapter training and active intervention at inference, adds an explicit public-code statement and repository address, and reports annotation costs of roughly 30 A100 GPU-hours or $40 for 70K examples. Conversely, it omits v1's stated 400-example ID total and explicit pattern-matching definition of over-refusal. These are disclosure changes rather than demonstrated changes to retained experiments.

E1.justification: v2 adds gradient-based white-box GCG attacks as a distinct adversarial scenario (Appendix E, Table 9). The training datasets and existing safety, WildJailbreak, math, coding, and XsTesT coverage are retained. Additional model sizes and reasoning backbones change model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds STAIR to the main LoFiT comparison in Table 1, Prompt-Only and COCA-SFT-only controls in Tables 4–5, and SAFEPATH-style LoFiT and STAR-1 comparisons for the reasoning model in Table 10. These substantially expand the evaluated comparator set beyond v1's retained intervention and SRG baselines.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include probes trained on illegal/benign prompts and tested on jailbreak/benign prompts, reporting maximum ROC–AUC across layers; controls separating COCA supervision from active intervention; 1K/5K/10K safety-training budgets; and 3B, 14B, and reasoning-model configurations. The original training and decoding settings are largely retained, so these additions do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds quantitative separability and covariance diagnostics (Tables 3 and 12), tag-removal and STAIR-composition ablations (Figure 3b), supervision-versus-intervention controls (Table 4), data-volume sensitivity (Table 8), and GCG robustness testing (Table 9). Appendix F also adds perplexity evidence for RR's incoherent outputs. The original PCA, fixed-reasoning, and over-refusal analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added experiments do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including Prompt-Only and COCA-SFT-only OOD ASRs of 30.9% and 16.2% against the retained full-model result of 10.4% (Table 4), plus probe, GCG, scaling, and reasoning-model results. Existing results also change: v1 Table 3 to v2 Table 5 revises COCA's Cipher ASR from 2.5% to 1.5% and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct's average from 17.7% to 14.8%. These are reporting revisions, not established performance gains from rerunning the method.

M1.justification: The core structured concept-reasoning pipeline and supervised objective remain unchanged. v2 adds an implemented COCA+STAIR variant that feeds STAIR's Problem Analysis into the COCA reasoning stage, and a safety-first prefix for the reasoning-model variant. These are limited procedural extensions; the expanded adapter-training description primarily clarifies implementation.

P1.justification: The title changes, and the introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around concept-centric alignment and representation geometry. Related work moves after the method, the theoretical appendices are consolidated, and guidelines are reordered. New implementation explanations, limitations, impact discussion, and manuscript-preparation disclosure substantially alter the document's organization and exposition.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 1 with an explicit geometry illustration, and reorganizes Table 1 into side-by-side model groups with change columns. It combines the original ablation and over-refusal charts with a new component panel in Figure 3 and adds several tables. Figure 2 becomes an explicitly labeled two-panel comparison, while the original three-panel visualizations remain in the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted positioning against concept alignment, contrastive representation learning, and Intent-FT, alongside references for SAFEPATH, STAR-1, and expanded limitations. The central positioning of COCA as data-level restructuring that enables representation intervention remains. SRG's updated title and venue represent the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: v1's assertion that every nonconstant independent eraser has greater distortion than the constant mean is replaced by a conditional-mean projection lower bound and a conditional strictness statement in v2 Theorem 2.2. The linear-erasure statement is narrowed from statistical independence to linear guardedness. Appendix H.2 replaces the Taylor-based derivation with a Gaussian/Stein-identity argument and adds an approximate-isotropy error bound.

improvement.justification: The new linear probes and Prompt-Only/SFT-only/full-model controls in Tables 3–4 substantially strengthen evidence that v1 supported mainly through visualizations and combined supervision/intervention comparisons. GCG and data-volume tests add useful validation, while revised derivations expose assumptions more clearly. Some measurement details are lost, and broad impossibility wording still exceeds the revised theorem's conditional scope, but the gains in experimental support and transparency constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Despite retitling and extensive reorganization, both PDFs describe the same COCA research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains original COCA experiments and adds linear-probe measurements, controlled comparisons, data-volume ablations, white-box attack results, and additional model evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and helpfulness experiments in Tables 1–3, component ablations, representation visualizations, and additional empirical results in the appendices.

results.title: Concept Concentration for Faithful Representation Intervention

C1.justification: v2 elevates the existing sampler's superiority over DDPM into an explicit contribution and conclusion, and extends the abstract's empirical superiority claim to unconditional generation. The introduction drops v1's majority-of-tasks qualification. The central claim of combining semantic structure with discrete decoding remains.

C2.justification: v2 replaces v1's unfavorable assessment of self-conditioning's cost-benefit tradeoff with a generally favorable interpretation. It adds hypotheses about sparse-manifold solver errors and self-conditioning-related sampling mismatch, plus limitations involving embedding collapse, norm growth and distance-computation costs. The substantive fixed-length inefficiency discussion from v1 is removed.

D1.justification: v2 expands documentation with ROCStories and ParaDetox configurations, MAUVE sample counts, embedding-training details, dataset access URLs and the OpenWebText sampling recipe. Decoder-training details disappear with that ablation. The basic architecture, optimizer, hardware, checkpoint-selection description and code location remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 removes Newsela-Auto text simplification and adds ParaDetox detoxification and OpenWebText unconditional generation. Appendix F also uses Wikipedia to train GloVe embeddings for an ablation. ROCStories, XSum, Quasar-T and QQP remain; ROCStories was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated MDLM and TEncDM baselines in Tables 3–4 and GIDD in Appendix D. Within retained tasks, XSum gains GPT-2 and SeqDiffuSeq comparators, while QQP gains AR-Diffusion. DDPM and DDIM become explicit solver comparators in Table 6. TEncDM was previously cited but not included in the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: Reported settings change substantially: conditional sampling noise falls from 0.25 to 0.1, scheduler d changes from 9 to 5 or 7, and training budgets change across retained datasets. Quasar-T batch size doubles; its and QQP's documented generation steps fall from 200 to 100. v2 also allocates embedding diffusion 1.75 times more sampling steps for computational matching and introduces timing, memory and detoxification evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds DDPM/DDIM comparisons, conditional sampling-noise sweeps, embedding and scheduler ablations, training-dynamics analysis and semantic-degradation examples. Self-conditioning analysis expands beyond the single v1 Quasar-T variant, and denoising-step sensitivity is revised. The v1 contextual-decoder ablation and cross-task mean-rank analysis disappear.

E5.justification: v2 first specifies that MAUVE averages five generation batches using different seeds; v1 gives no corresponding run-count information. This establishes newly reported repeated sampling, not an increase over a known earlier count. Neither version provides confidence intervals or comparable uncertainty estimates for the main results.

E6.justification: Many reported values change under revised configurations: SMOOTHIE's XSum BERTScore changes from 68.0 to 68.8 and QQP from 83.1 to 83.9, rather than demonstrating isolated same-setting gains. v2 adds comparative ROCStories, ParaDetox, OpenWebText, efficiency and ablation results, while removing Newsela and decoder results. XSum's step-sensitivity trend changes from improvement through 500 steps to a peak at 200.

M1.justification: Self-conditioning changes from an optional Quasar-T experiment rejected for routine use in v1 to a standard training and inference component in v2 Section 4.4. Appendix D also introduces hybrid OpenWebText sampling: 40% DDPM steps followed by the existing solver. The distance representation, MSE objective and original solver itself are retained.

P1.justification: The experimental narrative is substantially reorganized: separate task-by-task discussions become a consolidated interpretation, and the mean-rank discussion disappears. The loss derivation moves to an appendix, limitations move into the main text and the appendices are extensively reorganized. Much of the introductory and background prose is retained.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column presentation. XSum and Quasar-T tables are combined, result annotations and captions change, and Figure 2 is redrawn with different axis ranges. New efficiency, solver, ablation and example tables and Figures 3–4 substantially expand the displays; mean-rank and decoder tables disappear. Figure 1 is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting masked-diffusion comparisons, DDIM, scheduler design, alternative embeddings and new datasets, and explicitly positions its solver against DDPM/DDIM. Newsela/SARI and societal-risk references are removed. Section 3's central account of continuous, discrete, simplex and smoothing approaches remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 adds a time-dependent forward covariance definition for DDPM/DDIM comparisons in Equation 11 and a computational-complexity analysis. Theorem 4.1, its proof and the simplex-special-case argument remain substantively unchanged. The variational loss derivation moves from the main text to Appendix B rather than being newly introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens experimental support: masked-diffusion baselines broaden the comparison, measured generation costs inform fairer sampling budgets, and solver, embedding, scheduler and self-conditioning analyses test previously weakly justified choices. These gains improve the credibility and interpretability of the central empirical argument. Removing Newsela loses a documented weak case, and the broader superiority wording remains insufficiently qualified by metric-level exceptions. Nevertheless, the improved controls and direct examination of design choices provide a substantial net quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SMOOTHIE and retain the same core framework. All 17 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original conditional and unconditional generation results, including OpenWebText experiments, efficiency measurements and several component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original sequence-to-sequence experiments, a ROCStories noise-sensitivity experiment, latent-space comparisons and decoder ablations.

results.title: Smoothie: Smoothing Diffusion on Token Embeddings for Text Generation

C1.justification: v3 narrows the claim of compatibility with any frozen LLM to shared or aligned token spaces and emphasizes within-family weak-to-strong transfer. It broadens headline contributions to medical/domain generalization and robustness under stochastic decoding. The abstract also removes v1's Llama-specific qualification on outperforming fine-tuning methods, changing the scope of the performance claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations linking sampling robustness to preserved backbone diversity, translation guidance to English-language reasoning, and pretrained reasoners to implicit rewards. It discusses medical accuracy/F1 tradeoffs and semantic failures. New limitations address tokenizer mismatch, conflicting module rewards and clinical applicability; the cross-tokenizer shortfall is attributed to imperfect alignment. These go beyond relocating v1's limitations.

D1.justification: v3 documents medical labels, prompts, context lengths, generation-group size and composition weights; language-prompt adaptations; and the CoS timing procedure. Appendix D supplies alignment and comparator implementation descriptions, including the Reasoning Vectors scaling factor. PhysioNet access is documented. Existing math/translation training details and the code link largely persist, but medical cohort sizes and splits remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v3 adds MIMIC-IV readmission and length-of-stay training/evaluation, transfer to mortality prediction, and MGSM problems answered in Japanese and Spanish. These substantially broaden domains, tasks and language conditions. MathVerse and Geometry3k are retained from v1 Appendix C.1, rather than newly introduced.

E2.justification: v3 evaluates Reasoning Vectors and RAST against UniR in Table 11, adding directly relevant methodological alternatives absent from v1. Table 18 also introduces a standalone distilled DeepSeek reasoner comparison. The size-ablation comparison drops GRPO Full, GRPO LoRA and the untrained 1.5B ensemble rows from v1 Table 5, although these comparisons appear elsewhere.

E3.justification: Primary evaluation changes from deterministic decoding to temperature 0.6, with greedy results retained in Appendix G. The main Qwen setting promotes the 1.5B module already evaluated in v1's appendix. New protocols include a 7B training backbone, cross-tokenizer controls, distilled-reasoner initialization, medical accuracy/F1 evaluation and latency measurement over 100 generated tokens.

E4.justification: v3 adds temperature sensitivity, reward-score separation before/after training, gradient-norm diagnostics, cross-tokenizer robustness, standalone 1.5B-module controls, pretrained-reasoner initialization and failure-case analyses. Existing size and training-dynamics analyses are retained or extended. New medical examples and semantic-error cases expand qualitative analysis, while v1's Russell example in Figure 15 is removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports deterministic benchmark point estimates and training reward-variation curves. v3 specifies ten evaluation runs with seeds 1–10 and reports means and standard deviations for Tables 1, 2 and 15. Figure 5 adds significance annotations at p < 0.001, although the test is unspecified. These additions establish evaluation uncertainty reporting, not independent training replications.

E6.justification: Many greedy results remain unchanged: Qwen with a 1.5B module averages 43.9 in both v1 Table 5 and v3 Table 16. New stochastic results report 42.7 for UniR versus 40.3 for GRPO Full, under different decoding conditions. v3 adds medical, multilingual, cross-tokenizer, efficiency and diagnostic results; the earlier greedy 0.5B comparison rows are omitted. The revised headline scores therefore do not establish same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The core GRPO-trained reasoning module, additive logit guidance and omission of UniR's KL penalty remain unchanged. v3 adds optional CoS speculative decoding and EVA alignment for guidance across different tokenizers (Appendices B.3.3 and D.2). These extend inference procedures without replacing the central method.

P1.justification: The abstract, related work, theoretical interpretation and experiment narrative are substantially rewritten. Separate main-text efficiency and training-dynamics sections move into focused appendices, while visual-math evaluation moves into the main text. Experimental settings, limitations, prompts and qualitative examples are reorganized into a substantially different appendix structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. v1's visual-math Table 4 becomes v3 Figure 4 with unchanged scores; training plots move to the appendix. The standalone-performance figure gains a third panel, and new boxplots, comparison tables, medical examples and failure displays substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially repositions UniR around modular guidance, adding TART, Reasoning Vectors and RAST and distinguishing their mechanisms. New connections cover endogenous rewards, tokenizer alignment, speculative decoding and broader RLVR applications. Earlier discussion and citations concerning Best-of-N, MCTS and RAIN are removed. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

T1.justification: v1 provides an informal soft-Q theorem and short proof. v3 adds Appendix A's reward-equivalence lemma and proof, token-decomposition corollary, and expanded optimal-policy derivation, alongside a multi-objective KL derivation in Section 4.1. The soft-Q interpretation is retained but its formal treatment expands substantially; convergence to the required optimum remains assumed.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens assessment of the central empirical claims through seeded stochastic evaluation, retained greedy controls, relevant guidance baselines and targeted robustness analyses. Tokenizer qualifications and failure cases also better delimit applicability than v1's broad universal claims. Medical reproducibility remains incomplete, and the expanded optimality argument still assumes convergence. Nevertheless, the improved uncertainty reporting and direct tests of robustness and transfer address important weaknesses in v1's evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniR research, with matching authors, method and shared experiments. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and the equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds medical prediction, multilingual evaluation, comparator experiments and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical reasoning, translation, model-transfer, visual-math and ablation results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Universal Reasoner: A Single, Composable Plug-and-Play Reasoner for Frozen LLMs

C1.justification: The original communication-efficiency claims and headline speedups remain. v2's abstract additionally claims robustness on Llama-3-8B under packet loss and dynamic networks, while the introduction adds explicit claims about heterogeneous deployment and acceleration combined with model quantization. These materially broaden the claimed applicability.

C2.justification: New discussion explicitly limits generative acceleration to prefill, clarifying an operation already described in v1. It newly explains adaptation requirements for different device counts, distinguishes bandwidth changes from retraining needs, and discusses quantization-kernel overhead. Appendix D also interprets the relationship between allocation imbalance, full-precision attention, and accuracy. Existing zero-shot generalization limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds Llama deployment hardware, a 52 GPU-hour adaptation cost, synthetic bandwidth-generation details, and explicit cache/codebook storage parameters. The existing optimizer and epoch information is relocated to Appendix D. Conversely, v1's open-source statement and repository URL are removed; this does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: v2 retains CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, Wikipedia, and Wikitext-103, and adds downstream evaluations on CoLA, SST2, AG News, and QQP. It also evaluates distinct deployment scenarios involving heterogeneous token allocations, packet loss, and dynamically varying bandwidth.

E2.justification: The original single-device, TP/Megatron-LM, SP/Voltage, and BP/DeTransformer comparisons remain. Section 4.4 adds standalone post-training-quantized ViT-Base as an evaluated alternative, comparing quantization alone against quantization combined with ASTRA. The newly discussed KV-cache compression methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Existing ViT/GPT2 training budgets are retained. New protocols include 4-/8-bit quantization tests, 8-bit Llama-3-8B evaluation on TitanX GPUs, random token allocations with FPAR-based evaluation bins, 5% packet loss without retransmission, and throughput over a synthetic 600-second bandwidth trace. Appendix F also introduces a codebook-size sweep from 256 to 2048.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of quantization compatibility, accuracy versus allocation heterogeneity, resilience to packet loss and fluctuating bandwidth, codebook-size sensitivity, and memory costs. The original noise-magnitude, distributed-class-token, and commitment-loss ablations are retained in Appendix F as Tables 12–14, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 first reports ImageNet accuracy means and standard deviations across ten seeds, 0–9, and specifies seed 42 for the main experiments. Conversely, v1's statement that latency results average 20 runs disappears. The new accuracy repetitions should not be interpreted as an increase or decrease in the earlier latency-run count.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises ImageNet accuracies for G=1/16/32 from 77.12/78.46/80.05 to 77.39/78.80/80.28; CIFAR and GPT2 entries remain unchanged. Substantial new results cover quantization, Llama, downstream tasks, heterogeneity, uncertainty, network robustness, and codebook sensitivity. These additions concern new experimental conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The core mixed-precision attention, noise augmentation, commitment loss, and distributed class tokens remain unchanged. v2 adds a heterogeneous-deployment adaptation using randomized unequal token allocations during training and larger token shares for stronger devices, extending v1's evenly partitioned procedure (Section 4.2 and Appendix D).

P1.justification: v2 renames the paper, rewrites the abstract, streamlines portions of the exposition, updates author information, and moves training details and main-text ablations into appendices. Most existing methodological prose and the principal section sequence remain recognizable; much of the expansion is new scientific content.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from predominantly single-column to two-column formatting, substantially rearranging figures and tables. Tables 2 and 4 are transposed, the framework diagram's device label is corrected, and new result tables, a dynamic-throughput figure, and an FPAR histogram are added. Existing latency plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds positioning relative to KVQuant, CacheGen, and Eigen Attention, explaining their different objectives and exclusion from the main baseline set. Citations also expand for Llama, downstream datasets, network simulation, and quantization theory. The existing distributed-inference positioning and Appendix A survey are largely retained.

T1.justification: The two central theorems and their existing arguments are retained. Appendix C adds a high-rate quantization-error bound proportional to K^(-2/d) and connects it to attention error. Appendices D and G additionally define FPAR, derive its relationship to allocation variance, and derive codebook/KV-cache memory formulas.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens deployment validation through large-model and downstream evaluations, quantization comparisons, non-ideal network tests, and accuracy uncertainty reporting. Explicit adaptation requirements and prefill limitations also improve interpretability. These gains outweigh lost repository-access and latency-run disclosures and some reporting errors: notably, Section 4.5 claims 5.13× over BP with Nb=4, whereas Table 7 supports about 2.97× at 10 Mbps; 5.13× corresponds to Nb=8.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ASTRA despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds Llama-3-8B results, downstream evaluations, network robustness tests, heterogeneous token allocations, and repeated-seed experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original ViT/GPT2 accuracy and perplexity results, distributed-inference latency measurements, and component ablations.

results.title: ASTRA: Communication-Efficient Acceleration for Multi-Device Transformer Inference

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from FuLA as a more reliable stitching objective to invariance-aware stitching across multiple objectives. V2 explicitly includes FuLA among forward-only formulations that can mislead, claims backward compatibility mitigates these failures, and foregrounds robust/non-robust discrepancies and alignment-versus-shortcut tradeoffs.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes task overfitting and FuLA's advantages; v2 explains misleading similarity through unmatched invariances and treats objective selection as an architecture-dependent tradeoff with no clear winner. It discusses relaxed-IRI semantic drift and SLM's failed ViT-Base identity check. The absence of a similarity oracle and restriction to image classification remain acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 supplies substantial new reproducibility information: IRI generation from uniform noise over 200 steps, resolution-specific parameters, SimCLR training, token-wise transformer stitching, hint selection, and augmentation/batch-statistics handling (Appendices A–D). It also adds a code-access URL. V1's cross-layer interpolation instructions disappear with that experiment.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 and LS-ImageNet-10 remain, while v2 adds high-resolution ImageNet-100 and disjoint ImageNetB-100 classification and transfer settings. It also adds cross-bias tests involving models already trained on predictive pixel cues, unlike v1's previously unseen stitching-time shortcuts. V1's ArUco and location-only shortcut settings disappear.

E2.justification: The principal stitching comparators remain after matching TLM to HLM and the trained Hint objective to DM. However, v2 excludes HLM from the robust/non-robust comparisons (Figure 5 and Appendix F.4), where v1 included TLM. Appendix G also adds an invariance-aware CKA comparator alongside standard CKA.

E3.justification: V2 replaces accuracy-based similarity with normalized agreement probability and measures shortcut exploitation against permuted-cue controls. Initialization increases from 100 to 500 samples. The reported design replaces ResNet34 and residual-free ResNet18 with VGG16 and ViT configurations, drops mixed clean/adversarial stitching, and introduces distinct augmentation and batch-normalization policies for IRI training.

E4.justification: V1's class-subset, cross-layer, hint-depth and DM implementation analyses are removed. V2 adds IRI validity checks using identical models and paired original/inverted inputs (Appendix F.1), reports an augmentation control (Appendix B.2), and expands analysis of standard versus invariance-aware CKA (Appendix G). Shortcut and robustness analyses are substantially redesigned.

E5.justification: V1 identifies separate base-model instances but does not specify repeated-run averaging. V2 reports means across three random initializations, keeping the end model fixed and varying front models (Section 3; Appendix B.2). This is newly documented replication, not an established increase from a previously stated run count; uncertainty intervals and significance tests remain unspecified.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial result sets, including near-chance cross-bias similarity for IRI-trained DM, FuLA and SLM despite high standard-stitching similarity (Figure 2), and reduced unseen-cue exploitation (Figure 4). V1's baseline-accuracy table, class-subset results and cross-layer scores disappear. Changed metrics and training conditions prevent treating the new results as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: V2 retains FuLA but introduces an invariance-aware procedure: generate identically represented inputs (IRIs), train the stitching transformation on these inputs, and evaluate on the corresponding non-inverted test data (Section 2.3.1). Applying this procedure to end-model-supervised objectives changes the method substantially beyond renaming or explaining FuLA.

P1.justification: The introduction, methods organization, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around forward–backward compatibility. Experiments are reordered, an integrated discussion is added, and appendices are reorganized from A–B into A–G. The title and TLM/HLM terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text to a two-column layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation around standard-versus-IRI agreement plots. It replaces the opening conceptual illustration, removes cross-layer heatmaps and the baseline table, and adds sanity-check and expanded CKA panels. The retained FuLA schematic is updated and moved from v1 Figure 2 to v2 Appendix Figure 6.

R1.justification: Positioning moves from a knowledge-distillation-derived alignment objective toward shared invariances and bidirectional functional similarity. Previously cited Nanda and Jones work becomes foundational, while added references such as Feather, Goel and Klabunde support metamer, error-consistency and similarity-metric discussions. This changes the relationship to prior research substantially beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: V2 introduces the forward–backward compatibility requirement, formal relaxed/exact IRI sets, and a unique-optimal-forward-alignment assumption connecting IRI training to compatibility (Section 2.3.1). It also repairs FuLA's equation to match its stated downstream, penultimate-layer objective and defines normalized agreement in Appendix C. These substantially expand the formal framework, without adding theorem proofs.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger validation of what functional similarity measures: v2 exposes cue-dependence failures of standard FuLA and tests an invariance-aware remedy with IRI/identity controls and broader architecture checks. Its qualified conclusions are better supported than v1's general preference for FuLA. Removing the baseline-accuracy table and cross-layer/class-subset analyses sacrifices useful evidence, and some identity checks still fail, but the stronger examination of the central claim provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: These are substantially revised versions of the same model-stitching study, retaining FuLA and several experimental settings. Both complete PDFs, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and results sufficient for reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original standard and invariance-aware stitching experiments, input-validity checks and CKA comparisons in Section 3 and Appendices F–G.

before.justification: V1 reports original stitching experiments involving adversarial training, shortcuts, class subsets and cross-layer alignment in Section 3 and Appendix B.

results.title: Grounding Functional Similarity by Invariance-Aware Model Stitching

C1.justification: The three principal contributions remain causal temporal mixing, cluster-aware embedding, and sequential anomaly scoring. v2 adds an explicit contribution claim about improved normal/anomalous representation separability and more precisely limits causality to temporal information flow. Boundary refinement receives greater prominence but was already described in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of mask scaling, parameter robustness, inference-time batch normalization, and causality within the input window. It discusses training contamination, correlation shifts, and computational tradeoffs, and explicitly excludes causal discovery and univariate detection. Conversely, v1's limitations concerning residual correlations from shared mixing/head layers and temporal-mixer expansion are omitted.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code repository link, a dedicated baseline/result-source table, a Gaussian-component-based recipe for restricting alpha search, and explicit training-versus-inference normalization details. These materially expand reproduction guidance. Most existing hardware, software, and training settings remain, although the explicit Windows 11 and one-causal-mixer disclosures from v1 are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate multivariate anomaly detection on SWaT, WADI, PSM, SMD, MSL, and SMAP. The added protocols and analyses use these same datasets. The correlation-shift analysis changes the training portion used for clustering, rather than introducing a new task, population, or test environment.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds TimesNet, xLSTMAD, CATCH, PatchAD, SimAD, SAT, OracleAD, PCA-Error, and CAROTS with its CAROTS+ variant, while removing GTA. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set. Online SensitiveHUE also becomes a comparator in the repeated-run and computational-cost evaluations in Tables 12–13.

E3.justification: v1 evaluates CCM-TAD on multi-entity datasets using separate models and concatenated predictions. v2 additionally evaluates pooled training and averaging entity-wise metrics, separating comparisons by protocol. It adds PR_AUC, VUS_PR, VUS_ROC, Aff_F1, R_F1, and detection-delay/false-alarm evaluation. Table 9 also replaces the general alpha search interval with restricted dataset-specific intervals for SWaT, WADI, and PSM.

E4.justification: The existing architectural and clustering-variant ablations are retained. v2 adds boundary-correction ablation, representation-separation measurements, gradient-based causality verification, sensitivity analyses for cluster count and scoring/model hyperparameters, causal-mask scaling comparisons, and clustering derived from partial versus complete training data. Sections 4.2 and Appendix J therefore test several previously unevaluated mechanisms and robustness questions.

E5.justification: v1 Appendix E reports means and sample standard deviations over three seeds. v2 Appendix I reports five-seed averages with ± quantities and adds uncertainty reporting for Online SensitiveHUE. The basic mean-plus-spread approach remains, although v2 does not explicitly identify the statistic represented by ±; additional metric rows mainly expand the results.

E6.justification: Table 2 revises CCM-TAD's WADI F1 from 0.733 to 0.761. Under the retained prediction-aggregation protocol, MSL, SMD, and SMAP entries change from 0.619/0.599/0.524 to 0.638/0.602/0.551. These are revised reported outcomes, with identical tuning not established. Numerous results are added for other protocols, metrics, analyses, and computational comparisons. The original modular and clustering-variant ablation scores remain unchanged, as do PSM correlation values despite their revised reduction-sign convention.

M1.justification: The clustering procedure, reconstruction architecture, causal mask, loss, and cumulative scoring mechanism are retained. Equation 17 changes the endpoint-search range from t_a < t <= t_b to t_a <= t <= t_b, allowing the detected segment's first point to be selected as its endpoint. This is a limited procedural correction.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, related-work discussion, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively revised. Existing material is reorganized alongside dedicated appendix sections for baseline sources, metric definitions, training behavior, causal motivation, and online applicability. The restructuring and explanatory rewriting extend beyond merely inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show the correlation-profile graph and cluster embeddings. v2 adds scoring illustrations, gradient heatmaps, distribution plots, sensitivity curves, and correlation graphs. Comparison tables are expanded and reorganized; for example, v1 Table 4 becomes the transposed v2 Table 5. The main text also changes from one-column to two-column layout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through statistical change-point and classical anomaly-detection literature, the PCA-Error critique of complex models, and newer methods including OracleAD, CAROTS, and PatchAD. It explicitly distinguishes temporal masking from Granger causality and root-cause discovery, and adds references supporting the statistical analysis and expanded evaluation metrics.

T1.justification: New Appendix A derives an approximate null distribution and expectation for the log-p-value anomaly evidence, including a negative-drift condition around alpha < 1/e. It discusses approximate uniformity of normal p-values and temporal dependence. v1 contains the algorithmic equations but lacks this substantial probabilistic derivation.

improvement.justification: Separating multi-entity evaluation protocols makes Table 2 substantially more defensible than v1's mixed-protocol comparison. Broader baselines and metrics, boundary-correction ablation, gradient checks, and sensitivity analyses provide important tests of previously under-supported claims. Comparative repeated-run results and reproduction guidance further strengthen the paper. Some earlier limitations disappear and the new ± statistic is undefined, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantial gains in evaluation credibility and explanatory support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCM-TAD research, with matching core architecture and benchmark datasets. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and reports additional protocol comparisons, ablations, sensitivity analyses, computational measurements, and repeated-run results.

before.justification: v1 reports original CCM-TAD experiments on six datasets, component and clustering ablations, and repeated-run results in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Cluster-Aware Causal Mixer for Online Anomaly Detection in Multivariate Time Series

C1.justification: The central contributions—instance-conditioned latent modeling, interacting MCMC with SA, and convergence guarantees—remain. V2 broadens the headline performance claim from RL-based methods to NCO/learning-based baselines and adds an explicit contribution concerning effectiveness under low inference budgets.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of instance conditioning, stochastic latents, training-loss differences, gradient-computation costs, and the diffusion prior's additional training requirements. It substantially expands limitations concerning scaling, longer decoding horizons, and global constraints that masking cannot enforce. The augmented CVRP150 loss to EAS remains acknowledged in Appendix F.2.2, although the main text now makes a broader all-settings superiority claim.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents encoder soft-clipping, inference updates restricted to the decoder's final layer, explicit baseline functions, budget-selection procedures, and a common PyTorch evaluation implementation. It supplies diffusion-prior training and knapsack-generation details. Existing architecture settings and the code-access link are retained. Describing R=40 as both a radius and a diameter leaves that implementation detail unresolved.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original routing coverage and adds CVRP200 evaluation in Table 11 and 0/1 Knapsack50 and Knapsack100 experiments in Table 13, extending empirical coverage beyond routing. CVRP with time windows and job shop scheduling are outlined in Appendix A.3 but are not experimentally evaluated.

E2.justification: V2 adds ELG and CNF to the corresponding TSP/CVRP comparisons, HGS to the CVRP comparison, and Adam and SGLD to the existing inference-method comparison. Table 9 additionally evaluates Active Search + IL and AGFN (greedy). These are reported comparisons absent from v1, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Reported training duration changes from 2000 epochs in v1 Appendix E.1 to 8000 in v2 Appendix F.1; v1 Figure 4 already reached 8000, so this does not demonstrate additional training. POMO computational budgets/runtimes are revised, including CVRP100 without augmentation from 10 to 40 minutes. New experiments introduce controlled latent-dimension/radius settings, a diffusion-prior training protocol, and specified knapsack sample counts and capacities.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's inference-method, particle-count, and update-frequency analyses, v2 tests cost-weighted versus POPPY training, instance-conditioned versus independent priors, COMPASS + LGS, deterministic versus stochastic latents, and encoder versus diffusion priors. Tables 6–8, 10, and 12 and Figure 7 also examine latent dimension and radius. The earlier particle-count and update-frequency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: V1 Figure 3 and v2 Figure 2 both report means over 10 inference runs, and the existing particle-count boxplots are retained. V2 does not introduce new seed reporting, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures for the expanded results.

E6.justification: The original LGS benchmark scores for TSP/CVRP100–150 remain unchanged, while POMO scores are revised alongside computational budgets. Numerous results are added: Table 7 reports CVRP100 objectives of 15.641 for the instance-independent model versus 15.524 for the conditioned model; Table 11 reports LGS's CVRP200 gap of 1.289%; Table 13 reports knapsack objectives of 20.018 and 40.512. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The reported training prescription changes materially: Equation (2) switches from +βH to −βH, while Appendix A revises the decoder entropy-gradient sign, adds entropy contributions to the encoder estimator, and changes baseline placement. V2 also introduces a separately trained diffusion-prior variant and a knapsack decoder adaptation. The core encoder-decoder and interacting MCMC/SA framework remains; these documentary changes do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The seven-section main structure and much of the existing method and theory exposition are retained. V2 rewrites portions of the introduction and related work, expands explanatory passages, adds experiment subheadings, and reorganizes appendix subsections. The supplementary contents page is removed. These narrative edits accompany the larger scientific additions.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text. The separate routing tables become a combined main comparison without augmentation, with expanded full comparisons in Appendix Tables 4–5. Existing figures are relocated, resized, or restyled; the latent visualization and inference curves exchange numbering. Tables 6–13 and the radius-sensitivity Figure 7 are new displays.

R1.justification: The new Extensive Related Work appendix positions the method against reward-guided sampling, diffusion fine-tuning, GFlowNets, and large-scale NCO approaches. Other additions connect the training objective to IWAE and best-of-many objectives and discuss newer generalization and memory-enhanced solvers. This substantially expands research positioning beyond v1's NCO and MCMC discussion.

T1.justification: V2 adds an importance-sampling derivation, Proposition A.1 and its gradient proof, an inference-gradient derivation, and a conditional proposal-symmetry argument. It makes compactness explicit in the theoretical setting and replaces the exponential Lyapunov drift arguments with whole-state minorization and V=1 in Appendices C and D. Assumptions 4 and 8 and the associated Jensen step change from squared to unsquared L2 norms.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's missing validation of central design choices through component ablations, broader baselines, and non-routing evaluation. Corrected entropy/gradient expressions and explicit applicability limits also improve technical clarity. These gains outweigh remaining defects: the main text overstates performance across all settings despite the retained EAS win in Table 5, and Appendix A.4's new importance-sampling justification does not consistently reconcile normalized ratios with the summed training weights.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LGS-Net and Latent Guided Sampling by the same authors. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 retains original routing results and reports additional component ablations, baseline comparisons, CVRP200 results, and knapsack experiments in Section 6 and Appendix F.

before.justification: V1 reports original TSP and CVRP benchmark results, inference-method comparisons, training curves, and particle-count and update-frequency analyses in Section 6 and Appendix E.

results.title: Latent Guided Sampling for Combinatorial Optimization

C1.justification: The central scientific claims remain: adaptive preconditioner dynamics can independently trigger spikes, persistent second-moment decay sustains instability, and gradient-directional curvature predicts spikes better than maximum curvature alone. The five-stage mechanism and lower-beta2 mitigation idea already appear in v1; v2 emphasizes them and supplies broader supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly introduces the frozen-time approximation and timescale-separation justification, distinguishes positive-curvature overshooting from saddle escape, and explains why increasing beta1 offers limited protection. It also adds substantive qualifications about one-dimensional theoretical guarantees, stochastic minibatch prediction noise, and computational limits beyond roughly 200M parameters.

D1.justification: v2 adds the large-Transformer hyperparameter table, ViT/ResNet and Adafactor settings, and details about power-iteration counts and Hessian-vector-product costs. It newly states that code accompanies supplementary materials, without verifiable access in these PDFs. Conversely, v1's dedicated Fig. 4 setup, including initialization distributions and separate network widths, is removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds MNIST image classification (Fig. D7) and natural-language next-token training on a 100B-token SlimPajama split (Sec. 6.2). This substantially extends coverage beyond v1's function approximation, CIFAR-10, and synthetic sequence tasks. The earlier CIFAR-10 and anchor-task experiments remain in the appendices.

E2.justification: v2 extends the controlled quadratic-optimization comparisons with evaluated AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adafactor experiments (Figs. D15–D17). These additions are confined to supplementary quadratic tests; GD and the existing maximum-eigenvalue and update-directional-curvature comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include a 187M-parameter Transformer with batch size 512 and gradient clipping, ViT/ResNet18 evaluations, and momentum-free beta2 sweeps. Fig. 3 adds a coupled case with beta1=0.6 and beta2=0.5; the earlier case survives in Fig. D21. Fig. 4's reported width changes from 1,000 to 20, but inconsistent v1 descriptions and retained curves do not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial mechanism checks: beta2 mitigation experiments in Transformers, a beta1=0 sweep isolating adaptive dynamics (Fig. D22), multiple unstable eigendirections (Fig. D18), a test of the rounding-error explanation (Fig. D20), and larger-learning-rate sensitivity (Fig. D21). Earlier epsilon/clipping interventions and spike-type case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Additional trajectories and decay fits in v2 do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results, including MNIST spike trajectories, reduced spike frequency at lower beta2 in the 187M Transformer, and contrasting AdaGrad/RMSProp/Adafactor dynamics. These are newly reported experiments, not improvements over matched v1 runs. Retained findings, such as FNN threshold crossing at epoch 179, spike onset at 184, and recovery at 206, remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Adam's update, the preconditioned Hessian in Eq. (7), the gradient-directional predictor, and its sustained version remain unchanged. However, v2 adds an Adafactor-specific preconditioned-curvature construction incorporating its scaling and clipping factors (Fig. D17), a limited adaptation of the diagnostic.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, stability explanation, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around decoupling and explicit qualifications. The former five-phase subsection becomes a standalone section, CNN discussion moves into the appendix, and the appendices are reorganized with new disclosure sections. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws Fig. 3 to display moment–gradient coupling, adds an overshooting illustration and five-stage diagrams, and reorganizes Fig. 7. Numerous new experimental figures and a hyperparameter table accompany these changes. Earlier CNN plots are relocated rather than removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds central-flow research, recent Adam convergence/ODE studies, and language-model and reasoning-task references, while clarifying its relationship to adaptive Edge of Stability. It removes Cattaneo and Shigida's lower-beta2 citation. These update the positioning without replacing the existing related-work framework.

T1.justification: v2 adds a local GD descent proposition, an exact loss-increase criterion using a path-averaged Hessian (Theorem D.1), and a decaying-learning-rate instability theorem. It also revises the momentum stability statement to require positive directional curvature and substantially reworks the existing five-stage theorem with additional assumptions, transition definitions, and finiteness arguments.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger testing of the mechanism beyond v1's predominantly toy, synthetic, and small-image-subset experiments. Natural-language training, additional architectures, and controls for momentum and alternative explanations materially strengthen empirical support. Explicit approximation and applicability limits also improve interpretation. The removed Fig. 4 setup and remaining theoretical inconsistencies, including Theorem 5.1 omitting an assumption required by Appendix D.2, temper but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Adam loss-spike mechanism and retain identifiable equations, experiments, and figures. Their text, mathematical content, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for MNIST, SlimPajama language modeling, additional architectures and optimizers, and controlled sensitivity studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original quadratic-optimization experiments and neural-network training results for function approximation, CIFAR-10, and synthetic sequence tasks, including supplementary analyses.

results.title: Adaptive Preconditioners Trigger Loss Spikes in Adam

C1.justification: The central claim of training-free, memory-bounded episodic caching with near-full-cache accuracy is retained. The abstract revises the headline accuracy advantage from up to 40% to 30% and peak-memory reduction from 3.5× to 3.7×, although v4's introduction still states 3.5×. The conclusion newly claims the first framework combining the three components and emphasizes on-device conversational AI.

C2.justification: v4 extends the earlier context-holistic explanation to argue that each episodic cache preserves dependencies across episodes, and interprets document-task results as evidence of broader applicability. It also develops conclusions about calibration-domain independence and harmful overconcentration of layer budgets. Future-work discussion expands to incremental cache updates, implicit preferences, information deletion, and persona consistency, while the earlier quantization proposal is dropped.

D1.justification: v1's detailed efficiency hardware disclosure—A100 GPUs, CPU model, and PCIe transfer configuration—is removed without an equivalent specification for v4's replacement experiment. Explicit allocation sharpness values for the retained LLaMA/Qwen2.5 experiments and the patched-prompt representative-count setting also disappear. v4 provides selected Qwen3 configurations and stage execution counts, but leaves the new episode-creation threshold unspecified and retains pseudocode that omits Stage 3b.

E1.justification: The three conversational benchmarks and BookSum calibration are retained. v4 additionally evaluates NarrativeQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and QMSum from LongBench, extending coverage beyond conversational memory to document tasks. Calibration robustness also introduces SAMSum dialogue and RepoBench-P code samples alongside BookSum.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated OracleKV and RAG-2K baselines and a Full KV with prefix caching comparator for efficiency. RAG-Episodic corresponds to v1's RAG-like alternative rather than an entirely new comparator. The original compression baselines remain represented, but v1 Figure 4c's accuracy comparisons against PyramidKV and retrieval-head allocation disappear; their KL-divergence comparison remains.

E3.justification: v4 adds Qwen3-4B/8B configurations, source-count and centroid-similarity query stratification, and calibration comparisons using one versus 100 samples. The efficiency evaluation changes from 100 queries with 100K-token histories to a single-batch, 300-turn evaluation with 90K-token histories, an 8K cache, and 90 retrieval/write-back events. It also accounts for preparation costs and prefix caching. These are substantially different evaluation designs, not directly comparable timing measurements.

E4.justification: v4 adds targeted multi-episode reasoning tests, segmentation-unit and allocation-sharpness ablations, and robustness tests for initialization, generation sampling, calibration domain, and calibration size. Encoder and episode-count analyses are revised under Qwen3 settings. Conversely, v1's block-size, segmentation-window, and medoid-count sweep plots, direct allocation-strategy accuracy comparison, and episode-switch trajectory analysis are removed. The clustering visualization and internal-state sensitivity analysis are retained.

E5.justification: v4 Figure 9 explicitly reports standard-deviation error bars over five seeds for stochasticity and calibration experiments. v1 already reported input variability and five-run averaging for efficiency, but lacked this seed-based robustness reporting. The revised efficiency experiment no longer specifies the earlier five-run averaging. This changes uncertainty reporting locally rather than throughout the main benchmark results.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial Qwen3, document-task, cross-episode, robustness, and efficiency results. Retained numerical results also change: EpiCache's LLaMA3.1-8B LoCoMo averages at 6K/8K are 49.3/52.2 in v1 Table A2 and 47.3/50.2 in v4 Table A4. The original Qwen and LongMemEval detailed tables retain their numerical entries. Some v4 Figure A4 LoCoMo points do not agree with Table A4. The new efficiency results replace measurements under different conditions and therefore do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: v1 constructs a fixed episode bank and retrieves caches for answering queries. v4 Section 3.1 adds Stage 3b: appending newly generated KV pairs, writing updated caches back, creating episodes when centroid similarity falls below a threshold, and rebuilding oversized caches. This substantially extends the procedure to ongoing conversation maintenance. Renaming medoids to centroid-closest segments does not itself change their selection.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanation, experimental narrative, and related work. Experiments are reorganized around main results, analyses, and efficiency, while appendices are restructured and original results relocated. The title and main-text terminology also change, although substantial mathematical and appendix material remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column main-text and reference layout, redraws Figure 3 to show cache updates, and introduces several new plots and tables. v1 Figure 5 moves to Figure A4 with plotted revisions, and its scalability Figure 6 becomes Figure A3. The original ablation grid and latency/episode-switch figure are removed, while efficiency is presented through a new stage-by-stage table.

R1.justification: v4 substantially expands positioning against conversational memory systems and newer cache-management approaches, including SECOM, reflective memory, TRIM-KV, Cartridges, FlowKV, ArkVale, and IceCache. It distinguishes training-free EpiCache from trained cache representations and discusses limitations of external memory banks. Earlier A2ATS and quantization discussions are removed. Publication updates for retained works such as KVzip and Ada-KV do not constitute new references.

T1.justification: The LongConvQA formulation, clustering mathematics, sensitivity definition, and budget-allocation derivation remain substantively equivalent. Removing the unused average-scoring alternative from Equation (3) and adjusting segment notation do not change the mathematical reasoning. Neither version supplies formal guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation of important assumptions that v1 supported mainly indirectly: retrieving one episode despite distributed evidence, stable calibration across domains and seeds, and efficiency after including preparation costs and prefix caching. The added comparisons and targeted analyses make the central empirical case considerably stronger. These gains outweigh the loss of some ablations and reproducibility details, although incomplete cache-update documentation and Figure A4/Table A4 inconsistencies remain meaningful weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EpiCache and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The retained method components and experiments can be matched despite substantial additions, restructuring, and renumbering.

after.justification: v4 retains original evaluations and adds Qwen3 experiments, document-task results, cross-episode analyses, robustness measurements, and a revised efficiency experiment.

before.justification: v1 reports original LongConvQA evaluations, component ablations, sensitivity analyses, and runtime measurements, including Figure 5, Figure A1, and Table A1.

results.title: EpiCache: Episodic KV Cache Management for Long-Term Conversation on Resource-Constrained Environments

C1.justification: The central contribution remains scalable latent-space transformer GANs using MNG and width-aware learning rates. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion revise the quantified headline from FID 2.96 in 40 epochs with sixfold fewer epochs to FID 2.18 in 60 epochs with fourfold fewer epochs. The main contribution is retained while its performance and efficiency claim changes.

C2.justification: v2 adds an explanation of early-layer underuse through final-output-only supervision, interprets deterioration after removing REPA as discriminator feature erosion, and discusses training-cost tradeoffs. Appendices A.8, A.10–A.11, and A.16 qualify the preliminary text-conditioning extension, simplified mathematical argument, depth/batch generalization, and limited seed coverage. These substantially expand interpretation and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, MM-GAT configuration details, alternative-tokenizer specifications, compute-accounting procedures, GPU benchmarking settings, and REPA overhead measurements. Training-resource disclosure is updated for the longer run. However, it removes v1 A.1's precise guidance recipe—strength 1.1 applied to the first 30% of blocks—and no longer clearly distinguishes guided and unguided headline results.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates class-conditional ImageNet-256 generation and latent interpolation. v2 adds ImageNet-512 generation, MS-COCO text-to-image generation, unconditional FFHQ-256 generation, and unsupervised and text-directed image editing using GANSpace and StyleCLIP. These substantially broaden the represented domains and task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds STARFlow and LightningDiT-XL/2 to the retained ImageNet comparisons. The new MS-COCO comparison in Table 8 introduces a substantial additional comparator set, including Frido, VQ-Diffusion, U-ViT variants, AttnGAN, DM-GAN, DF-GAN, XMC-GAN, and LAFITE.

E3.justification: The headline training budget increases from 40 to 60 epochs, with v2 A.1 setting the gradient-penalty coefficient to 10 for epochs 40–60 after the original 0.1 setting. Existing patch-size and ablation plots switch from FID-5K to FID-50K. v2 also introduces CLIP-FID, precision/recall, latency/memory evaluation, and a fourfold-batch-size experiment with doubled learning rate.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PCA, block-removal, and component ablations, v2 tests early-layer input/output similarity and sensitivity to latent noise, compatibility with larger batches, alternative tokenizers, and seed variation. It also adds REPA ablation at another model size, removal of REPA during continued training, and a training-compute scaling fit. These address additional mechanism and robustness questions.

E5.justification: v1 does not report a seed-replication analysis. v2 A.16 reports individual FID-5K outcomes from three differently seeded, 10-epoch GAT-S/2 runs alongside the original result. This provides limited seed-sensitivity evidence, without confidence intervals or systematic uncertainty reporting for the main comparisons.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports 40-epoch FID 3.02 without guidance and 2.96 with guidance; v2 reports 2.18 at 60 epochs under a revised training schedule, so this is not a same-setting improvement. Original 20-epoch capacity scores remain in v2 Table 5. Substantial new results include ImageNet-512 FID 4.04, MS-COCO FID 7.98, FFHQ FID 9.74, and additional diversity, resource, and robustness measurements.

M1.justification: The core GAT architecture, MNG procedure, width-aware learning-rate rule, and loss formulations remain. Appendix A.8 adds a localized MM-GAT adaptation: frozen CLIP word tokens enter through MM-DiT-style conditioning, while the sentence embedding supplies global conditioning. This changes the model's inputs and conditioning beyond merely testing it on another dataset.

P1.justification: v2 substantially edits the abstract, introductory and architectural explanations, experimental setup, and early-layer discussion. It separates early-layer diagnosis from component ablations, reorganizes the further-analysis narrative, and restructures the appendix into topical sections. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental results.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a two-column main paper with revised table and caption formatting. Figure 3 gains a training-compute panel, ablation axes are redrawn, and numerous task, metric, cost, and editing displays are added. Existing material is also relocated or condensed: v1 Tables 2–3 become v2 Tables 4–5, and v1 Figure 8 becomes v2 Figure 12; some older sample galleries are removed.

R1.justification: Literature coverage expands substantially into text-conditioned generation, latent editing, gradient normalization, and batch-size scaling, with new references including CLIP, GANSpace, StyleCLIP, and STARFlow. v2 also drops the explicit first-time claim in Section 2.2 and the connection to equalized learning rates and Karras et al. (2017). Publication updates and duplicate entries for existing works do not constitute additional research.

T1.justification: v1 states the inverse-width learning-rate rule and its rationale. v2 A.10 adds explicit independent, unit-variance channel assumptions, a definition of functional update magnitude, and a linear-layer SGD derivation relating output changes to learning rate times width. This is limited mathematical support, explicitly presented without a full proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's ImageNet-256-centered evidence. Additional generation tasks, CLIP-FID and diversity metrics, targeted mechanism and robustness tests, and resource measurements better support generality and efficiency claims. The improved headline FID uses longer training and a changed penalty, so it is not decisive by itself. Lost guidance details and the incorrect MNG labeling of the learning-rate ablation in Table 6 weaken reproducibility, but the broader, more diagnostic evidence provides a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Scalable GANs with Transformers and retain identifiable corresponding methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains original GAT experiments and adds results for higher-resolution generation, MS-COCO text-to-image generation, unconditional FFHQ generation, editing, and robustness analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet-256 generation results, model-scaling experiments, component ablations, representation analyses, and generated examples in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Scalable GANs with Transformers

C1.justification: The central fixed-budget interference–performance claim and claimed first explicit demonstration remain. V2 reframes FPE as a controlled mechanistic intervention, explicitly attributes gains to disjoint parameter allocation beyond width alone, and extends its applicability claim to jointly learned representations (Sections 2.2, 5.2, and 7).

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation and limitations: it discusses disjointness controls, feature demand growing with width, preliminary circuit evidence, small-model scope, and hardware-dependent speedups and activation overhead. Appendix A.5 also explicitly acknowledges that its independent-support analysis does not enforce FPE's disjointness constraint.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-availability link, detailed trainable-embedding and CNN specifications, baseline mask-sampling and inference procedures, and storage-cost discussion. Algorithm A3 explicitly documents pre-training, expansion, and continued training. These additions substantially expand implementation guidance; the linked resource itself was not accessed.

E1.justification: The Boolean task and four vision dataset families remain. V2 adds raw-image CIFAR-100 classification alongside frozen CLIP features and nested 40/60/80/100-class classification scenarios, expanding input conditions and task coverage within existing domains (Sections 5.2–5.3).
