E2.justification: V2 introduces two substantive comparators absent from v1: non-disjoint FPE with a fixed random mask, and DropConnect with resampled training masks and dense scaled test-time weights. Figure A6 and Tables A14–A15 explicitly evaluate these alternatives against FPE.

E3.justification: V1 lists batch size 500 and N=W=1000; v2 specifies batch size 64 with 25 pre-training and 25 fine-tuning epochs, retaining long training for the illustrative example. FashionMNIST warmup changes from 20 to 25 epochs. New experiments introduce matched mask controls and collision/clustering metrics. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds disjointness and mask-resampling controls, edge-collision measurements, clause-recovery analyses, and clustered-Gram case studies (A.8.4–A.9). The expansion-factor sensitivity panel in v1 Figure 6d is replaced by a class-count/width analysis. Depth, dynamic-mask, and 2:4 sparsity analyses were already present and are retained.

E5.justification: The main vision comparisons and Figure 6 now report ten trials where v1 generally reported five; ImageNet-1k already used ten. SEM bars and p<0.05 reporting remain. These reported-count changes do not establish additional runs, and v2's blanket ten-trial statement conflicts with retained five- and 30-trial appendix captions.

E6.justification: V2 revises vision plots and adds substantial joint-learning, class-demand, comparator, and circuit results. For example, Table A14 reports 64.8% for non-disjoint FPE versus 65.8% for FPE at width eight; at width four, the values are 51.0% versus 50.9%. These comparisons are new, while the original illustrative accuracies and several appendix tables remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The core disjoint splitting and magnitude re-pruning procedure is retained, including the previously documented deeper-network and structured-sparsity variants. V2 adds model adaptations with a trainable Boolean embedding and a jointly trained CNN feeding the classifier; expansion still operates on the classifier (Section A.7.1).

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction and conclusion, adds an explicit contribution list and scope statement, reorganizes methodology, and separates theory, symbolic results, vision results, and related work into distinct sections. The narrative shifts toward using expansion to study interference.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. The framework diagram moves to Appendix A.1, main performance figures are condensed while fuller displays remain in the appendix, and numerous accuracy tables and new control/circuit plots are added. Retained plots are distinguished from newly reported evidence.

R1.justification: The new Related Work section substantively distinguishes FPE from sparse autoencoders and DropConnect and discusses compatibility with quantization and distillation. Citations expand accordingly, including Cunningham et al., Wan et al., and GPTQ. This extends research positioning beyond relocating v1's pruning, growth, and superposition discussion.

T1.justification: The clause-coverage bound and expected collision-reduction derivation in Appendix A.5 are unchanged. V2 adds a distinct edge-level collision-rate definition—the proportion of traced edges used by at least two clauses—in A.9, a limited mathematical definition accompanying the new empirical analysis.

improvement.justification: V1 lacked controls isolating disjointness and evidence from jointly learned visual representations. V2 substantially addresses both gaps through Appendix A.8.4 and Section 5.2, while adding more direct circuit diagnostics, implementation guidance, and clearer applicability limits. These additions materially strengthen the central argument. Inconsistent trial-count summaries and preliminary mechanistic evidence remain limitations, but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental support and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FPE research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds joint representation learning, class-count sweeps, DropConnect comparisons, and circuit analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original Boolean-DNF and vision-classification experiments, including accuracy, interference measurements, and deeper-network and sparsity experiments.

results.title: Expand Neurons, Not Parameters

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims about Imitation Shock, anchor-induced suppression, and T3S gains in AR and dLLM settings. The added experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 explains recovery through changing relative gradient magnitudes and directional conflict, and interprets selector robustness as resulting from anchors emerging early and other tokens remaining suppressed late. These refine the existing suppression mechanism and its practical implications; the principal interpretation and previously stated limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 documents the concrete step-10 shortcut, the typical bottleneck window of steps 6–15, and the checkpoint choices used in its sensitivity study. Existing trace generation, filtering, and training details are retained in Appendix I, formerly Appendix E. No new hardware, runtime, or code-access information is supplied.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and task domains remain unchanged. BOBA, S1K, OpenThought3, code reasoning, and the downstream evaluation suites already appear in v1. The added 3K/100K experiments change sample counts, while the new code results concern an already represented domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated comparisons against GKD and SWITCH in Table 15 and Mix Distillation in Table 16. These substantially extend v1's comparisons with SFT, RRT, inverted T3S, and static-confidence masking. The existing main-table and dLLM comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 adds OpenThought3-3K and BOBA-100K training conditions, a Qwen3-32B teacher/Qwen3-8B student setting for tokenizer-sharing comparisons, and a selector-checkpoint sweep from steps 2 to 50. Existing main training recipes remain unchanged. Section 2.1 also changes bottleneck selection wording from validation to training accuracy, matching the existing formal definition; this does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Figure 6 examines anchor/non-anchor gradient-norm ratios and directional conflict across training. Section 4.4 and Tables 7–8 test whether precise bottleneck identification is necessary through a fixed-step variant and checkpoint sensitivity analysis. These substantially extend the existing interventions, loss-transfer analysis, static-confidence controls, and dLLM threshold analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report AIME scores averaged over 16 runs. V2 adds no new seed specification, repeated-run reporting practice, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark tables retain their scores, but v2 adds substantial results in Figure 6 and Tables 7–8 and 14–18. For example, Table 15 reports AIME24/25 scores of 80.83/70.00 for T3S, 73.33/53.33 for GKD, and 75.83/66.67 for SWITCH. Table 18 reports LiveCodeBench scores of 61.41 for T3S versus 53.29 for SFT. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements to corresponding v1 measurements.

M1.justification: Section 4.4 introduces T3S-simple, which selects tokens using checkpoint 10 instead of searching for the minimum-training-accuracy checkpoint. This is a limited procedural variant. The original AR masking objective and dLLM union-masking method remain unchanged, with the latter relocated to Appendix D.

P1.justification: The document is substantially reorganized: the method setup becomes an overview, detailed dLLM formulation and analysis move to Appendix D, and related work moves to Appendix B. Experimental discussion is regrouped, a bottleneck-robustness subsection is introduced, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. Most existing scientific prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds the gradient-dynamics figure and seven experimental tables. Table 4 changes from stacked model blocks to side-by-side model columns. Existing plots are restyled, table captions move above tables, boxed takeaways become inline text, and several figures and tables are relocated, including the dLLM efficiency and threshold tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for GKD, SWITCH, Mix Distillation, entropy-guided token dropout, and other related work. Appendix H.2 adds a positioning distinction concerning teacher-side token signals and tokenizer-sharing requirements. The existing related-work argument is largely preserved and moved to Appendix B.

T1.justification: The substantive bottleneck and token-set definitions, masked objectives, union-masking equations, and loss-transfer mathematics are retained. Moving dLLM equations to Appendix D and omitting the standard introductory AR factorization do not revise the mathematical reasoning. No new theorem, proof, or formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support by addressing v1's untested dependence on precise bottleneck selection (Tables 7–8), adding established distillation comparators (Tables 15–16), and directly measuring gradient dynamics underlying the proposed mechanism (Figure 6). Earlier results and dLLM details are preserved. The terse protocols for new Appendix H experiments limit reproducibility and some generality conclusions, but the combined gains in comparative and mechanistic evidence are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Training-Trajectory-Aware Token Selection (T3S). Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds gradient measurements, selector robustness tests, scaling results, and additional distillation comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original distillation experiments, checkpoint interventions, token analyses, and AR/dLLM evaluations, including Tables 1–12.

results.title: Training-Trajectory-Aware Token Selection

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central smoothing, accuracy, and efficiency claims. The introduction's empirical contribution now explicitly claims competitiveness with Mamba and specifies classification benchmarks. Temporal parallelization remains claimed in the surrounding prose despite removal of its separate contribution bullet.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive limitations concerning adaptive-solver dependence, bandwidth tuning, and loss of useful high-frequency information, including possible long-horizon forecasting degradation. It adds causal-window and latency qualifications, bandwidth trade-off discussion, and interpretations of head regularization, missingness robustness, smoothing-spline performance, and memory costs. These substantially expand the discussion of mechanisms and applicability.

D1.justification: v2 supplies Mamba configuration, forecasting normalization and causal refitting details, additional dataset-specific optimization settings, the head-regularization coefficient, and the smoothing-spline penalty formula. It also reports parameter counts, peak memory, and H100 profiling information. This substantially expands reproducibility documentation, although exact small-batch sizes are not supplied.

E1.justification: v2 adds ETTm1 forecasting, Speech Commands classification under missing observations, and 963-dimensional PEMS-SF classification. It also evaluates observation-drop scenarios on the three retained classification datasets. These substantially extend the tasks, domains, dimensionality, and input conditions beyond v1's coverage.

E2.justification: Mamba joins the retained three-dataset comparison in v2 Table 2, and a traditional Smoothing Spline baseline is evaluated in Table 10. The new forecasting comparison includes standard GRU, distinct from the existing GRU-D. Figure 10 also adds GRU-D and Mamba to the computational breakdown.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 replaces v1's fixed 128-unit setup with reported parameter matching for Linear and Cubic baselines. The UWave Cubic table tolerance changes from 0.001 to 0.0001. New protocols include 24-step context/horizon forecasting, observation-drop sweeps, solver-order comparisons, and memory measurement. Figure 10 is now specified as H100 profiling with small batches. These are reported setting changes, not proof that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds head-diversity regularization tests, missing-observation robustness, solver-order sensitivity, memory/scalability analysis, and a comparison testing whether traditional smoothing alone explains the gains (Tables 3–10). The earlier noise, head-count, bandwidth, and single-path analyses remain; the additions address substantial new robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five independent random seeds in Appendix B.2 and report uncertainty using ± values and error bars. No changed run-count policy, confidence-interval procedure, or formal significance testing is documented.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 becomes v2 Table 2 with replaced Linear/Cubic results under revised settings; CharacterTrajectories Cubic accuracy changes from 86.61% to 91.89%. The primary MVC GP accuracies remain unchanged, but added Mamba achieves 96.64% versus MVC GP's 95.07% on CharacterTrajectories. New results include ETTm1 MSE of 0.428 and extensive missingness, memory, regularization, solver, and scalability measurements.

M1.justification: The core smoothing, attention, convolutional feature extraction, and parallel integration procedures remain unchanged. v2 adds a forecasting adaptation using RevIN, context-only path construction, and a linear horizon predictor (Appendix B.6–B.7). It also tests an optional head-similarity penalty, without adopting it in the primary architecture.

P1.justification: Much of the existing abstract, introduction, method, results discussion, and conclusion is retained verbatim. Changes include localized explanatory edits, streamlined contribution bullets, new forecasting and limitations sections, Appendix C reorganization, and affiliation, disclosure, and acknowledgement additions. The revision is primarily scientific expansion rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds forecasting Table 1 and Tables 3–10, while expanding the retained comparison as Table 2. Figure 5 replaces attention heatmaps with head curves aligned to original signals. Figure 10 changes its displayed comparisons, scales, and legend; the Pareto plots add Mamba, and several figures move. These are substantial display changes beyond numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds localized positioning against GP adapters/GP-RNNs, interpolation and attention networks, and Mechanistic Neural Networks, alongside Mamba and additional GP/signature references. The central geometric-smoothing research gap remains unchanged. Publication updates for works such as DeNOTS and the clinical time-series benchmark do not represent new cited research.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.1, the spline estimates, Corollary 3.3, and Theorem 3.4 replace proportionality assertions with upper bounds up to constants. Appendix A explicitly carries solver-tolerance dependence through the smoothing and parallel-integration derivations. These revise existing mathematical claims; the derivative-bound argument, assumptions, and GP error comparison are otherwise retained.

improvement.justification: v2 materially addresses v1's limited validation and model-capacity confound through reported parameter matching, stronger comparators, forecasting and missingness tests, and explicit applicability limits. These changes substantially strengthen the evidence for when smoothing helps. Some conclusions remain overstated: Section 4.1 still claims consistent superiority although Table 2 places Mamba above MVC GP on CharacterTrajectories. That inconsistency limits the improvement but does not outweigh the stronger controls and broader, targeted validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attentive-smoothing Neural CDE work. All pages, including Appendices A–C, are readable, and the methods, equations, figures, and retained experiments can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains original classification experiments and adds forecasting, missing-observation, memory, solver-order, regularization, and high-dimensional evaluation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification, timing, NFE, noise-robustness, and architectural-ablation results on three datasets in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: Efficient Neural Controlled Differential Equations via Attentive Kernel Smoothing

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion replace the central claim of a tractable event-prior KL upper bound with an IVP representation or regularizer. The introduction also shifts graph claims from cross-channel influence toward temporal ordering and alignment. These narrow important theoretical and mechanistic claims, while annotation-free recovery and superior classification claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits ERGs to sensor-space timing summaries, excluding source-level causal, anatomical, or synaptic interpretations, and identifies the event-prior term as a regularizer rather than an exact path-measure KL. It also explains baseline boundary-output limitations and Cohort B variability. Its new channel-representativeness discussion requires qualification: Table 9 supports generally higher HC frequencies, but AD–MCI ordering is mixed.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access URL, explicit auxiliary-weight sweep values, and updated regularizer pseudocode. Most architectural and optimization details in Appendix F are unchanged. Conversely, v1's explicit most-recent-event definition of cross-channel lags in Section 4.6 is no longer specified as precisely.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three synthetic frequency bands and EEG cohorts A and B, with the same participant groups. The added timing, weight-sensitivity, and channel analyses concern existing data and tasks; reporting more of the already-used 19 channels does not expand dataset coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain NODE, ODE-RNN, and STRODE for synthetic comparisons and EEGNet, LCADNet, LSTM, ATCNet, ADFormer, and LEAD for EEG classification. The new runtime comparison uses the existing computational-comparison methods. Newly discussed point-process models are not evaluated.

E3.justification: V2 adds one-factor sweeps of three auxiliary weights on Cohort A while holding the remaining protocol fixed, and introduces per-window forward time as an evaluation metric. Existing subject splits, two-second windowing, normalization, aggregation, training budget, and classification metrics remain unchanged. Detailed runtime measurement conditions are not supplied.

E4.justification: Appendix E.5 adds systematic sensitivity studies for dLIF, ERG, and IVP-KL weights, extending the existing prior-removal ablation to regularization-strength robustness. Appendix E.6 additionally tests whether the four plotted frequency patterns represent all 19 channels. These substantially expand the supplementary analyses; the original prior ablation remains numerically unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions retain mean and standard deviation across five test folds and the synthetic event-rate intervals obtained through nonparametric resampling. The new runtime table also uses mean and standard deviation, without introducing a new uncertainty procedure or specifying repetition counts. No seed information or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Tables 3, 8, and 9 add substantial results on runtime, regularization sensitivity, and channel-wide frequency patterns. Examples include LERD's 9.209 ms mean forward time and ERG-weight sweep accuracies ranging from 63.73% to 75.03%. Fifteen previously unreported channels extend Figure 2; HC is highest in 18/19, with T4 an exception. All original benchmark, ablation, computational-cost, and supplementary diagnostic-metric values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The architecture and EPDE/MELP/ERG procedures remain largely unchanged, but the specified training regularizer changes. Section 4.3 and Algorithm 4 replace v1's U_epsilon upper-bound surrogate with a finite-horizon IVP integral using a normalized first-event prior. This revises one auxiliary loss; the PDFs do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: V2 makes targeted rewrites to the abstract, problem formulation, method explanations, visualizations, and conclusion. It relocates some theoretical setup, adds appendix subsections and acknowledgments, and updates author order, affiliations, and publication information. The overall main-section and appendix organization remains recognizable.

P2.justification: V2 adds runtime, sensitivity, and channel-frequency tables. Figure 4 retains the same plots but enlarges and rearranges them from two rows of three panels to three rows of two, pairing methods by frequency band. Other figures and retained tables largely preserve their displays despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds mechanistic Bayesian reasoning as context, citing additional Bayesian event/graph models, and contrasts LERD with observed-event point-process methods such as Smith and Brown and Truccolo et al. This expands the rationale for its annotation-free positioning while retaining the existing supervised-EEG and latent-dynamics literature structure.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix B replace the claimed upper bound with a normalized finite-horizon KL representation, correcting the change-of-variable integrand and integration endpoints and stating an integrability assumption. V1's Corollary A.2 becomes A.3: general sub-Gaussian, zero-centered concentration is replaced by Gaussian concentration around the expected perturbation, with explicit bias and a revised matrix bound. Appendix D supplies a substantially revised proof.

improvement.justification: V2 repairs two central mathematical deficiencies: the incorrectly constructed finite-window KL bound and the uncentered concentration claim for nonlinear graph perturbations. The replacement results and explicit limits on causal and path-KL interpretations substantially improve soundness. Sensitivity tests and full-channel reporting also improve transparency without changing classification scores. Some lag-construction detail is lost and runtime documentation remains incomplete, but these limited drawbacks do not outweigh the corrections to the paper's theoretical foundations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LERD study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds measured inference times, auxiliary-weight sensitivity results, and additional channel-frequency summaries.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic event-recovery experiments, classification on two EEG cohorts, prior ablations, and analyses of inferred frequencies and graphs.

results.title: LERD: Latent Event-Relational Dynamics for Neurodegenerative Classification
